Your town needs something fixed. The network to deliver it is here.

Towns post what they need, experts do the work, sponsors fund it, and every step is checked on one public ledger. Back a project and it becomes partly yours: you follow every dollar and every step until it is done.
Free to join · vetted once

Whoever you are, there is a way in

Five roles run the network. Residents need no account: report on Baladi Map or confirm a report. Everyone else registers once, is vetted once, and can act on any request.

  • Checked twice before any money. Government certifies the request, then an independent verifier signs it off and sets the price range.
  • Nobody doing the work holds the money. Pledges sit in escrow and leave one verified milestone at a time.
  • Your record is public. What you deliver, fund or reject is on one ledger.

Manāra connects them: one request, five separate roles, every step on a public record.

The network

Five roles, five separate jobs. The fifth exists so the other four can be checked.

How the five fit together

A fix needs five things: someone to report it, and four roles that must never share hands.

  • ResidentsReport and confirm problems.
  • GovernmentCertifies and picks the expert. Never prices, never holds money.
  • Expert organisationsBid, build, and get paid on verified proof.
  • SponsorsFund escrow, released by milestone or refunded.
  • Independent verifiersSign off and gate each release. A second line checks them.

Four roles work on the project. The fifth works on the process, which is why outsiders can believe it.

Read the lines, not the boxes. A Baladi Map report goes to government, which certifies it into a request. Experts and sponsors connect to the project, never the request. The first-line verifier only gates: it signs off the request, gates each release and closes the escrow. The second line checks the first, seeing no names. Neither builds or pays, so both can be believed.

Read the lines, not the boxes. Government certifies the report into a request. Experts and sponsors feed the project. One verifier gates all three; a second checks the first.

Checks

Independent verifiers

The fourth role, and the reason the other three can be believed. A verifier signs off the request with government before it can take a pledge. A second-line verifier reviews that sign-off pseudonymously. The first then confirms that each milestone actually happened before any money moves — and is structurally barred from being the body that certified the request, the organisation doing the work, or anyone funding it.

Who steps in, and when

Every request below passes through the same four hands in the same order — and the order is the safeguard, not a formality.

When each role is brought in — and why the timing matters

It starts with residents. Three roles work on the project; the fourth works on the process, and is brought in before the first of them can start.

1 Residents Reported

On Baladi Map, or filed here. Neighbours confirm it.

2 Government Certified

Real, lawful, in jurisdiction. Scope, never price.

3 Verifier Signed off

Milestones, evidence, cost bracket. The second line reviews.

4 Experts Bid

Ranked half on quality, half on price. Government picks.

5 Sponsors Escrowed

Held by a custodian before work starts.

6 Verifier Released

Each milestone checked. Changes need both lines.

Change the order and each safeguard stops working. Certify after the pledges and funders back an unapproved request. Open bids before the bracket and the price is a negotiation. Bring the verifier in late and the party being checked picks its own examiner.

Why Manāra exists

The problem

Lebanon has people who want things fixed and money to fix them. It has no way to connect the two that anyone can check. Here is how we found that out, who it hurts, and what the numbers say.

Residents report, then waitA report goes on the map. Then nothing: no owner, no date, no answer.
Municipalities know, and cannot actNo budget, no expert, no one whose job it is to finish.
Experts are ready, and cannot be hiredSkilled people want the work, but there is no certified market for public fixes and no open way to fund it.
Money arrives, and stopsFamily money holds the country up and rarely reaches the street outside.
Nobody checks the workNo independent person confirms the price, the steps or the proof, so nobody can trust the result.

1. Who it hurts

Five roles, five versions of the same problem.

ReportResidents

TodayA report goes up. Nobody says who will fix it, by when, or what it costs.

With ManāraThe report becomes a request with a named expert, a checker, a budget and a date. The people who confirmed it get a seat in the request’s chat.

CertifyGovernment

TodayEveryone assumes the worst of it. For fifty years it has pushed public costs onto private people.

With ManāraIt keeps the two jobs only it can do: say the request is real, and pick the expert. It never sets the price and never holds the money.

SolveExperts

TodayHundreds of good contractors with no way to reach public work, and the same hurdles on every job.

With ManāraProblems are posted. Experts bid inside a checked price range. The best bid wins on half quality, half price. Payment follows proof.

FundSponsors

TodayNo way to pay for one specific thing back home and see it happen. So the money stays with family.

With ManāraA sponsor funds a named request. Money sits in escrow and leaves one checked step at a time. If the request stalls, it all comes back.

CheckVerifiers

TodayNobody independent checks the price, the steps or the proof. So nobody outside can believe the result.

With ManāraAn independent checker approves the request before any money is taken, sets the price range, and signs each step. A second checker, who sees no names, checks the first.

2. How we found out

Six things that happened, in order.

1
A dirty plot of land

Rubbish piled up on public land near home. We cleaned it by hand, twice a week, and took photos to the municipality. Nobody knew whose job it was. We only reached the board through a friend. The meeting was an argument. No budget, no expert, no plan.

2
No way to be heard

A think-tank idea, Project Pulse, would put twenty people in a room with a minister each week. Good for listening. But listening does nothing on its own; someone still has to act.

3
One number that kept coming back

At a political event, one fact stood out: Lebanese abroad send home about $5.8 billion a year. That money keeps the country going. It goes to one family and stops. Nobody tracks what it does. The idea on the way home: let a public record, not a promise, make people trust each other.

4
One person doing too much

A recycling pioneer told us what every clean project costs him: the same paperwork and the same corruption, every time. Lebanon has hundreds of small good efforts and nothing that joins them up.

5
Baladi Map

Baladi Map is very good at finding problems and getting people onto one map. We built a demo of the “next” and showed the founder. We are now partners: a problem enters on Baladi Map, and Manāra is what happens after.

6
The pattern

Good intent, then a stalled project, every time. The cause is always the same: a hand-off nobody owns and nobody can see. Make every hand-off visible and the work gets done.

3. What the numbers say

Five findings from the white paper, and what each one changed in the design.

FindingWhat is wrongWhat we do
Money from abroad stops at the first door

About 14 million Lebanese abroad send home around $6 billion a year, among the highest shares of any economy. Since the banks failed in 2019 it moves outside the system. It is sent out of love, so it stops at one household.

Map the cities the money comes from. Let towns post exact jobs. Let senders back one job and watch it. Take the commitment first, which cuts cheating.

Public things became private

A generator instead of a grid. A private garden instead of a park. When only the rich can reach a public good, it stops being public.

Put private money into public things through a public process, and pay local experts so the money stays in the country.

Good people are not joined up

Lebanon does not need new organisations. It needs the ones it has to work together. They stay apart because nobody built the easy way to join.

The Network page: 181 organisations, five roles, one process.

Trust comes from results, not words

People remember 2019. They discount every promise until they see results they can check. Being watched stops cheating better than being punished.

Small projects, finished on a public timeline, with the figures published. The ledger, the checker register and the scoreboard do exactly this.

Listening once is not a system

One good evening of listening is a moment. It needs a record of what was heard and what was done.

The request ledger is that record, and the affected residents sit in every request’s chat.

Our values

What the mechanics on this page are actually in service of.

👁

Transparency

Every pledge, escrow state and milestone sits on one public ledger. Nothing about where the money went is held back from the people who gave it.

🛡

Non-partisanship

Certification runs on technical and regulatory review, not political or sectarian standing. No party, sect, or patron gets a faster lane.

👥

Community

A request only carries weight once residents have confirmed the need is real. The network follows the community — not the other way around.

⚖

Accountability

Sponsors, implementers and government branches all answer to the same public record. No side channel, for anyone.

Who does the verifying

The fourth role — and the reason the other three can be believed.

A verifier confirms that a milestone actually happened before any money moves, and is structurally barred from being the body that certified the request, the organisation doing the work, or anyone funding it. Independence is not a box someone ticks: five tests run against each request’s own records, and the results are shown on the request itself with their outcomes.

Where they fit — and why the timing is the whole point

A verifier is assigned at certification: before a single pledge, and long before any work. They sign off the request, a second-line verifier reviews that sign-off without seeing a name, and every release waits on the first verifier again.

1 Request certified, verifier assigned

Rotated from the pool that passes the independence tests for this request, and recorded publicly with who assigned them.

2 Request signed off

The verifier confirms the milestones and the evidence each will need, and sets the cost bracket. Government certifies scope and jurisdiction, never price.

3 Second-line review

A senior verifier reviews that sign-off seeing no names, and confirms it or sends it back. Only then does the request open for pledges.

4 Escrow confirmed, work starts

The implementer already knows who will check them — and could not choose that person. Every tranche waits on their sign-off.

Bring the verifier in after the money is committed and funders are backing a request nobody has confirmed can be checked. Bring them in after the work is done and the party being checked is picking their own examiner. That ordering is the difference between verification and a formality, which is why it sits in the workflow as its own step rather than as an implementation detail.

Optional: a contract layer on top

Where a sponsor or a municipality wants a stronger guarantee than a promise, the release rules can be written into a smart contract: funds move only on signatures from assigned verifiers, the signer list excludes the implementer, certifier and funders by construction, the tranche schedule is fixed when funding closes, and unreleased money returns automatically if a request stalls.

What it does not do: a contract cannot know whether the wall was built. Someone still has to look. It makes the process tamper-evident — who signed, when, and that nobody moved money alone — not the underlying facts true. It is an added layer for those who want it, never a replacement for the verifier.

How the money is actually verified

Six steps, each one checkable.

01 · INTAKE

A named, checkable need

Requests come from a registered municipality, a vetted NGO, or a recognised business partner — many grounded in a citizen report already confirmed by other affected residents.

02 · VETTING

Whole-partner review

Before a request goes live, the implementing partner is checked once — legal registration, past project record, references.

03 · ESCROW

Money moves, but doesn't land yet

Pledges sit in escrow held by an independent custodian — never a government account, never the implementer's — until a milestone is verified.

04 · VERIFICATION

A claim and a check are different steps

Evidence sits as "submitted" until an unaffiliated verifier confirms it. Only then does the ledger mark it verified and escrow release. The sign-off that let the request open was itself reviewed by a second-line verifier who saw no names.

05 · OPEN LEDGER

Anyone can trace any lira

Funders — named or anonymous — see the same trail everyone else does. No private reporting track.

06 · DISPUTE

A report button that goes somewhere

Flags route to an independent oversight partner, not to the implementer being flagged.

When a request doesn’t finish

The stages nobody puts on a homepage — and where the money sits at each one.

Escrow is not a holding pen. It exists so that money which has not bought anything can go back. A request can end without finishing at four different points, and each one has a defined answer for the funds — because “what happens if it fails” is the first question a serious donor asks, and the first question a regulator asks.

StageWhere the money isCan exit to
SubmittedNothing pledgedCertified & verifier assigned, or refused
CertifiedFirst- then second-line verifier review the requestSigned off twice → bids open, or sent back
Bids openNothing pledged; bracket publishedGovernment picks from the 50/50 ranking, verifier approves the cost → open for pledges, or no eligible bid → re-scoped
Open for pledgesPledged, not capturedThreshold met, or lapsed → refunded in full
Escrow fundedHeld by the custodian, not releasableWork starts — the verifier gates the first release, not the deposit
In progressHeld, released per verified milestoneNext milestone, or stalled → balance returned
Cost or timeline changeHeld — nothing extra releasedBoth verifiers approve the variance against the published specs, or refused
Milestone rejectedHeld — nothing releasedRemediation, then resubmission
ClosedFully releasedFinal report published

A rejected milestone is not a dead request. It returns to the implementer for remediation and resubmission — because if rejection meant the project died, no verifier would ever reject anything, and the check would quietly become a formality.

Open question — partly closed

But who checks the verifier?

Everything above rests on one role. The verifier is the reason a certification can be believed, a sponsor’s money is safe, and a finished wall is really finished. So it is fair to ask the obvious next question: if the verifier checks everyone else, who checks them?

Now: a second-line verifier. Every first-line sign-off — the decision that lets a request open for pledges — is reviewed by a second, more senior verifier who sees the decision and the reasoning but no names. Every later change to cost or timeline goes through the same pair. Their record sits on the register under a pseudonym. Milestone releases are checked once by the first line, and one in ten is re-checked afterwards by the second line, which also reviews every closing report. Consequences are written too: fall below a published line and you drop a tier, and the way back is a training course run with project stakeholders. The course exists for each line, and every role has a handbook.

This is not a hypothetical worry. The closest thing to Manāra that already exists at scale is the carbon credit market, where independent auditors sign off before money moves. It went wrong, and the numbers are public.

2 in 3Accredited auditors who missed the flaws in projects later found to be overstated, across 95 projects studied.
84%Of credits across 2,346 projects that did not represent real cuts — all of them signed off by someone independent.
4Verification bodies suspended in 2025 — caught by a whistleblower, not by routine monitoring.

The cause everyone landed on was simple: the auditors were paid by the people they were checking, and the people being checked got to pick them. Manāra was built to avoid exactly that — two of the three doors are already shut.

The questionWhat went wrong elsewhereHow Manāra is built
Who picks the verifier?The party being checkedRotation from the eligible pool
Who pays the verifier?The party being checkedEscrow, never the implementer
Who checks the verifier?Nobody, until a whistleblowerA second-line verifier, seeing no names
Who re-checks a release?NobodyThe second line, one release in ten, after the money moved
What happens to a verifier who gets it wrong?Nothing, usuallyDropped a tier at a published line; a course before re-entry
Who runs the course?—Project stakeholders, in the room: an L1 and an L2 course
Who accredits verifiers in the first place?A professional bodyStill a demo — no accrediting body has signed on yet

  • Spot patterns no single municipality can see alone.

What each governorate shows

For Verifiers

Check what everyone else claims. Yours is the only signature that moves money — and the only role the other three cannot fill.

  • Get accredited once for your fields and governorates, then take assignments in rotation.
  • You are never offered a request you certified, implemented, or funded — five independence tests run before it reaches you.
  • You are assigned at certification and sign off the request before it opens for pledges — so nobody being checked ever chose you, and no money is committed to a request you could not check.
  • Your rejections are published next to your approvals. A reviewer who has never rejected anything is an unexamined one.
  • Second-line verifiers are appointed from the register, not recruited — a current licence, thirty decisions, an overturn rate in the bottom half. They review your sign-offs without seeing your name, and you will not see theirs.
  • Fall below the published line — too many decisions overturned, or too slow — and you drop a tier. The way back is a training course with project stakeholders.

What an account page should be

Where each role lands after registering. Drawn from three families of product that already solve part of this — crowdfunding portals, CRMs, and social profiles — each of which answers a different question.

Starting point

Manāra already has seven of these

Reachable today from Join → “Preview the dashboard”, or . All seven share one shape: a title, four stat tiles, a table of recent rows, and a list of standing obligations. What is missing is the connection — registering does not land you on one.

Research

Three families, three different questions

These are not three styles of the same page. Each answers something different, and the four roles need different mixes.

62%Of affluent donors evaluate the impact of their giving before deciding on the next gift. A sponsor’s page is a retention mechanism, not a receipt.
80%Of day-one persuasion is done by the empty state. Every new account here has zero requests, pledges and verifications.
3Questions an impact report has to answer, in order: what changed, who benefited, how do you know.
FamilyThe question it answersWhat is worth taking
Crowdfunding portalsWhere did my money go?Custody state as a first-class part of the page, not a settings screen. Honesty about obstacles builds more trust than a clean story.
CRM dashboardsWhat needs me today?Role-specific views onto one source of truth, and bottleneck spotting — how long something has sat in a stage.
Social profilesWhy should you believe me?Credibility signals sit above the content, because they are the reason to trust what follows.

RoleFirst question on opening itDominant model

Option A

One shell, four lenses

Keep the shape the seven demos already use — stats, table, obligations — and swap only the contents per role.

Gain. Cheapest by a distance, already half built, and consistent across every role.
Cost. Forces a sponsor’s impact story into a work-queue layout, which is the wrong shape for the one role that is not doing any work.
Option B — recommended

Private queue, public twin

Two zones: what needs you (private, CRM-style) sitting on top of your public record — the page everyone else already sees of you. An account becomes an authenticated overlay on a public identity rather than a separate private space.

Gain. The pattern already exists here: the verifier register is a public profile, and organisation and municipality pages already render publicly. This generalises them rather than inventing something. It is also the only option that is on-brand — a platform whose whole argument is public track record should not have a purely private account page.
Cost. Two zones to design per role instead of one, and it commits to every account showing its own bad numbers.
Option C

Ledger first

The account page is a filtered view of the public ledger — your slice of exactly the data anyone else can read.

Gain. Maximally consistent with the transparency claim, and it would force the browsable ledger to finally get built — the site says “open ledger” repeatedly and has no page behind it.
Cost. Badly under-serves “what needs me today”, which is the thing that makes anyone come back a second time.
Option D

Progressive

Day one is an onboarding checklist that turns into a dashboard as it fills.

Gain. Directly answers the empty-state problem, which is otherwise the day-one experience for every single new account.
Cost. Not really an alternative to A, B or C — it is a layer any of them needs anyway.

What to build: B, with D layered on it

One page per role, three bands. The same skeleton everywhere, so a reader who has seen one account page can read any of them.

1
Needs you nowThe queue — milestones awaiting a decision, requests awaiting certification, tranches awaiting release. Empty on day one, so it carries the onboarding checklist instead: get vetted, then post your first request. That is where option D lives.
2
Your recordThe public twin, credibility signals first. A verifier sees approvals, rejections and overturns; a partner sees completion rate and days-to-milestone; a sponsor sees funded and verified totals. The same numbers a stranger sees, because they are the same page.
3
Where the money isOnly for the roles that touch it. Sponsors get the impact framing — what changed, who benefited, how do you know. Municipalities and experts get escrow and tranche state, held against released.

One deliberate consequence: every account page shows its own bad numbers — rejections, overturns, stalled requests. That follows from what the site already does in publishing rejection counts next to approvals, and it is what the impact-reporting research says actually builds trust.

The problem — what Manāra is solving

Draft one, to be tuned along the way. Three sources went in: the founder’s own account of how the idea formed, the problem as each Manāra stakeholder meets it, and the two versions of the white paper written after a political movement’s public session. Placement 1 is the short block for the home page; Placement 2 is the full page, with one section per source. Open questions for the founder are listed at the end.

Placement 1 — home page

The short block, between the headline and the five role cards

The problem

Lebanon does not lack people who want things fixed, or money to fix them. It lacks a way to connect the two that anyone can check.

Residents report, then wait

Baladi Map gets a problem onto a map in minutes. Then nothing: no timeline, no owner, no answer to “who fixes this, and how would I know?”

Municipalities know, and cannot act

A board meeting on a polluted plot ends in argument: no budget, no expertise, no one whose job it is to see it through. Reaching them at all took a personal contact.

Money arrives, and stops

Remittances hold the country up, household by household, and rarely reach the street outside. Public spending is a black box, so nobody funds it twice.

Good intent keeps meeting the same three walls. Manāra is the connector: one request, five roles no two of which sit in the same hands, and a public record of every step so that trust comes from results instead of promises.

Placement 2 — its own page

The full page at #/problem, “Problem” in the nav between Home and Network

Home / The problem
Why Manāra exists

The problem

Every piece of Manāra answers a specific failure someone met in person. This page keeps those failures in view: first as the story they were met in, then as each of the five roles experiences them, then as the wider argument about remittances, public goods and trust that the story sits inside. Read it as the brief the site was built against.

1. The story

A plot of public land. It started with a piece of public land near home collecting rubbish. The first answer was to clean it by hand, twice a week, with photos, and take the photos to the municipality. Cleaning by hand does not scale, and the photos went nowhere: cold calls led to confusion about who was responsible, and the only route to a board member turned out to be a personal contact. The meeting itself showed the shape of the problem. A municipal board is not built to receive constructive criticism, let alone solve it: much internal arguing, no oversight, no expertise on the subject, no funding.

A feedback loop that does not exist. In parallel came conversations about Project Pulse, an attempt to get a programme off the ground and for now a think-tank project: twenty people from different backgrounds, a different twenty each week, sitting with a minister on a set issue. The point was a regular loop between government and people, expected problems against what is actually on the ground, something Lebanon does not have. People would be heard face to face; government would learn what to communicate. The idea is a sensor. What was missing was a mechanism to act on what the sensor reports.

A political session. That led to a public session held by a young political movement. Two things stood out. The headline topics were argued with more emotion than analysis, and with no actionable next step. And a number kept coming back: remittances from the diaspora, worth about $5.8 billion in 2024 and equal to roughly a third of the economy at the height of the crisis, are the backbone of the country, flowing in and out with no oversight of how they touch public goods, into a public sector that is a black box. The remittance path is financier abroad, to a family member, to the family first and the community second, if at all. Many points of failure, no transparency, no measure of what the money achieved. The thought on the way home was simple: build a quick demo of how code, not a promise, could let these parties trust each other. Transparency and oversight reduce corruption; a visible track record earns the next contribution.

A pioneer, carrying too much. Then a conversation with one of the people who has spent years pushing recycling and circular economies in Lebanon. The knowledge and first-hand experience were remarkable. So was the weight of administrative and corruption hurdles he had to clear for every clean project. Lebanon has many independent efforts and almost nothing that aligns them at a scale where they would benefit financially, lobby together and share a network. His answer, a new cluster of recycling and sustainability organisations built for economies of scale, is right but still small. The question that stayed: how do you take the economic and political burden off people like this so they can do more of what they are good at?

Baladi Map. The polluted plot from the first step was reported on Baladi Map when it appeared on social media. It is excellent at what it does: it identifies problems, and it has pulled the population onto one platform willing to believe. What it had not done was think about what happens next. No update, no timeline, no answer to how a report becomes a fix, what trust means here, or who oversees it. Manāra was already forming, so a supply-side demo was built and shown to the founder to see whether that thinking existed. It did not. The two are now partners: Baladi Map is where a problem enters, Manāra is what happens after.

The pattern. Good intent, then a failed or stalled project, over and over. Each time the cause was a workflow more complicated than it needed to be, with no one accountable for the hand-offs. Streamlining those hand-offs, and making each one visible, is what produces both results and trust.

2. The problem, role by role

Manāra has five roles because the failure has five faces. Each card says what breaks for that role today and what changes when the request runs through the network.

Residents, through Baladi Map

The problem. Reports surface problems and stop there. A resident who already knows government is not providing enough learns nothing about who will fix it, by when, or what it costs. The finding is free; the fixing has no path.

What Manāra changes. A Baladi Map report becomes a certified request with a named expert, a verifier, a budget and a timeline, and the reporters who confirm it get a seat in the request’s chat. Finding the problem stays free; the next steps become visible.

Government

The problem. Every sector is associated with corruption and mismanagement, which is the reason Baladi Map and this site exist at all. Distrust of public infrastructure and the economy is the biggest driver pushing people out of the country. For five decades public responsibility and spending have been offloaded onto private individuals through informal remittances and aid, an endless band-aid, before counting outright theft.

What Manāra changes. Government keeps the two things only it can do, certifying that a request is real and lawful and choosing the expert from a ranking, and gives up the two that destroy trust: it never sets the price and never holds the money. Approvals and licensing for public work become a streamlined step, and sponsors’ money reduces what the state has to spend. Proposed: the certification step links to the matching procedure on Dawlati, the state’s e-services portal, so a request cites the licence or permit it needs by name.

Expert organisations

The problem. Hundreds of independent contractors and initiatives with no link to the clients who need them most, above all government at public scale. No regulated market for public work, so the capable ones fight the same administrative and corruption hurdles alone, project after project.

What Manāra changes. Problems are posted, experts bid inside a verifier-set bracket, government picks the winner on half quality and half price, and the work is funded by direct sponsorship. A regulated supply market for public goods, extra jobs on their own schedule, payment against verified evidence, and a track record that is public.

Sponsors, local and diaspora

The problem. No channel to a specific local problem with any transparency. The same distrust that empties the country of people also empties it of contributions: money sent home stays in one household because there is nowhere accountable to send it further.

What Manāra changes. A sponsor funds a named request into escrow. The verifier prices it, money leaves one verified milestone at a time, and it comes back in full if the request stalls. Named or anonymous, local or abroad, every dollar is traceable to a step on the ledger.

Verifiers, first and second line

The problem. Lack of oversight is how public money is embezzled: projects overpriced, underdelivered, the difference split between the people who signed. Nobody independent checks the price, the milestones or the evidence, so nobody outside can believe the result.

What Manāra changes. A first-line verifier signs off the request before a pledge is taken, sets the cost bracket, gates every release and closes the ledger; a second line, seeing no names, checks the first. Costs, budgets, timelines and milestones are confirmed by someone with no stake, and the record of every verifier is public.

3. What the white paper adds

Two versions of a white paper were written after that political session, one as an open letter and one as a referenced essay. Much of it is about politics and security and belongs elsewhere. Five of its arguments are the foundations this site stands on, and they are summarised here with the thinkers the paper draws on.

Remittances stop at the first household

The diaspora, often put at around 14 million people against 4 million residents, sends home about $6 billion a year: $6.7 billion in 2023 and $5.8 billion in 2024 by the World Bank’s count, equal to 32% of GDP in 2021, 28–31% in 2023 and 18% in 2024 as the economy’s dollar size recovered, one of the highest ratios in the world. Nearly half of it comes from the Gulf. Its money moves along specific, traceable corridors: a striking share of emigrants from Jabal Mohsen, for example, settled in Australia, and money likely retraces that path. Diaspora giving runs on what Yanis Varoufakis calls experiential value, love and obligation, which is exactly why it stops where it stops: no institution translates that gift into anything with a wider life in the community it lands in. Since the 2019 banking collapse, when depositors lost access to their savings while the best-connected had already moved capital abroad, remittances travel almost entirely outside the formal system, because the formal system betrayed the people who trusted it. The paper’s proposal is the one this site is: map the largest sending cities and the localities they connect to, let municipalities and local providers post specific work with a goal, partners and a timeline, and let funders commit directly, named or anonymous, with full visibility of who does the work and how it is going. Two design details come with it: Richard Thaler’s Save More Tomorrow shows people commit more readily to future flows than present sacrifices, and Dan Ariely’s honesty research shows a declaration signed up front cuts fudging far more than one requested afterwards. Manāra’s Diaspora corridors, escrow pledges and sign-off before the first pledge are those three ideas built.

Public goods have been pushed onto private individuals

Too much of the cost of public life has quietly shifted onto private people: remittance-funded survival at the national level, affluent locals privately financing their own street at the neighbourhood level. Michael Sandel’s warning applies directly: once a public good is something only the affluent can reliably reach, a private generator instead of a grid, a private garden instead of a park, it stops being a shared civic experience and becomes a marker of inequality. Lebanon also looks outward for every injection of money, aid, remittances, loans, and lets each dollar leave again on imports, debt and capital flight before it circulates locally. The site’s answer is to route private money into public goods through a public process, and to pay local experts so the money turns over at least once inside the country.

The good actors are not coordinated

Lebanon’s civic space is full of companies, NGOs and local initiatives doing real work in slightly different directions with no shared coordination: the tragedy of the commons in miniature, in which nobody owns the coordination problem enough to solve it. Matthew Syed’s work on cognitive diversity argues alignment beats consolidation: the country does not need new institutions, it needs a deliberate network connecting the ones it has. Thaler’s status quo research supplies the detail that gets it built: people default to fragmentation because nobody has designed the easier, coordinated default. So do not ask organisations to coordinate; build a shared reporting platform, a shared funding pool and a shared calendar of public works that they would have to opt out of. That is the Network page, with its 181 organisations, and it is why the conversation with the recycling pioneer mattered.

Trust comes back through delivery, not words

Decades of underperformance did not just cost administrations their credibility; they damaged belief in the idea of government functioning at all. Thaler’s anchoring research explains why a better speech cannot fix that: the public is anchored to the memory of 2019, and every promise is discounted against it until a new, vivid, repeated data point displaces it. Ariely’s dishonesty research supplies the mechanism: across dozens of experiments the single most reliable way to reduce cheating was being observed, not punished. Syed’s account of aviation shows a culture that treats error as data rebuilt public trust where industries that hid failure stayed stuck. The prescription is concrete: three small, finishable public projects delivered visibly on a public timeline, with financials published in a form any citizen can check, then a track record that compounds. Manāra’s ledger, verifier register, standing rules and scoreboard are that prescription as software. Fritz Scharpf gives the strategy its name: where trust in process has collapsed, trust earned through checkable results is the only path back.

Institutionalise the feedback loop

The political session reconnected, for one evening, the sensor between citizens and government. One evening is a moment, not a mechanism. The paper asks for a standing, published loop, open sessions and a public tracker of what was heard and what was done, and for the movement to test every position on people predisposed to disagree before it ships. Project Pulse is the sensor; the request ledger is the tracker. The same principle applies to this site: the affected residents sit in each request’s chat, and every rejection, overturn and stalled request is published rather than hidden.

The problem 2 — carrying the political lessons without the politics

Four sections of the white paper were left off the Problem page because they argue about security, campaigns and a movement’s blind spots. Each holds a general rule that Manāra already builds by. Three ways to bring the rules in, drawn as they would appear, with a comparison at the end.

Option A — recommended

A “Four rules we build by” box on the Problem page, after “What the white paper adds”

Four one-line rules, each with the feature that embodies it. No politics named. The reader never learns the rules came from watching a political argument, only that the site keeps them.

4. Four rules we build by

The story and the white paper kept producing the same lessons about how to change behaviour in a country that has stopped believing promises. They are rules of design here, not opinions, and every one is already wired into the site.

Every “stop” comes with a “do this instead”, already built.

A demand with no destination reads as defeat. Name the alternative first, then the thing it replaces.

On Manāra: A rejected bid, an overturned sign-off or a stalled request is never just a no: the refund policy returns the money, the re-bid reopens the work, the course is the road back for a dropped verifier.

Watch first, punish last.

Being observed changes behaviour more reliably than being penalised. Build the watching in; keep the penalty for what the watching finds.

On Manāra: The verifier gates each release and the ledger is public before any sanction exists. Standing rules are computed from the record, never from an accusation.

Go where you are least welcome, and listen before you pitch.

A message built in one room does not survive contact with another. Take it to the people least likely to agree, in their language and their channels.

On Manāra: Arabic and French are not translations of the pitch, they are the pitch. Residents who confirm a report get a seat in its chat. A municipality that says “not ours” gets a real answer through Jurisdictional Match.

Nothing ships until someone who disagrees has read it.

Confident rooms are wrong in expensive ways. Put the position in front of a different set of eyes and treat the first reaction as data.

On Manāra: The second line reviews every sign-off seeing no names. Every account page publishes its own bad numbers: rejections, overturns, stalls.

Reads as: product principles. Adds: about 260 words, one grid. Visibility: high, it sits on the page people are sent to read. Risk: low; nothing in it refers to a party, a faction or a policy.
Option B

One sentence folded into each existing section, no new block

The same four rules, each placed as a single sentence inside the section it belongs to. The inserted sentences are highlighted below; the surrounding text is what is already on Page 3.

Trust comes back through delivery, not words

…Ariely’s dishonesty research supplies the mechanism: across dozens of experiments the single most reliable way to reduce cheating was being observed, not punished. That order is a rule here: the ledger and the verifier’s gate come first, and a penalty exists only for what they find. Syed’s account of aviation shows a culture that treats error as data rebuilt public trust where industries that hid failure stayed stuck…

Institutionalise the feedback loop

…Project Pulse is the sensor; the request ledger is the tracker. The paper’s other lesson is where to point the sensor: at the people least likely to agree, in their own language, listening before pitching. That is why Arabic and French are the pitch here and why residents who confirm a report get a seat in its chat. The same principle applies to this site: the affected residents sit in each request’s chat, and every rejection, overturn and stalled request is published rather than hidden.

The problem, role by role — Verifiers

…A first-line verifier signs off the request before a pledge is taken, sets the cost bracket, gates every release and closes the ledger; a second line, seeing no names, checks the first. It is the site’s standing answer to a lesson from the white paper: nothing should ship until someone who disagrees has read it.

The story — the pattern

…Streamlining those hand-offs, and making each one visible, is what produces both results and trust. One more rule came from the same year: never ask anyone to stop something without the alternative already built, which is why a stalled request refunds in full and a dropped verifier has a course to come back through.

Reads as: asides. Adds: about 120 words, spread thin. Visibility: low, no reader will collect the four into a set. Risk: lowest of the three, but the lessons lose their shape.
Option C

A separate section: “What politics taught us about design”

Says openly where the rules came from, then states them generally. Most honest about provenance, and the most likely to be read as a political statement regardless of wording.

4. What politics taught us about design

The white paper was written for a political movement, and most of it argues about things this site does not touch: security, campaigns, who gets to be in the room. Watching those arguments taught four things about changing behaviour in a country that has stopped believing promises, and they apply to a civic platform as much as to a party.

  1. A demand with no destination is refused. Ask people to give something up only when the alternative is already built and visible. Here: the refund, the re-bid, the course before re-entry.
  2. Being watched beats being punished. Monitoring, public and continuous, reduces cheating more reliably than sanction. Here: the gate at every release and a ledger anyone can read.
  3. Go to the sceptics first, in their language, and listen. Here: Arabic and French as the pitch, the residents’ seat in the chat, a real answer to “not ours”.
  4. Every position gets read by someone who disagrees before it ships. Here: the second line that sees no names, and account pages that publish their own bad numbers.
Reads as: commentary on a political movement, even with nobody named. Adds: about 230 words. Visibility: high. Risk: highest; a reader who knows which session it was will read the site as aligned with it.

The problem, stakeholder by stakeholder

Dawlati — where the state’s own procedure catalogue fits the process

Exploration only; nothing on the public pages changes. In one line: Dawlati is the government’s catalogue of its own procedures, so a request on Manāra should point at the procedure it needs rather than describe it. Below: what Dawlati is, where government already touches the process, the one change that makes the link work, where it would show, what else would move, and the ideas looked at and parked.

1 · What it is

Dawlati, in four facts

  • The state’s single e-services portal, launched by the Ministry of State for Administrative Development (OMSAR) in July 2026, at portal.dawlati.gov.lb, with a “My Government” app.
  • A catalogue of more than 2,700 procedures: which body handles each one, the documents needed, the fees, the timeline and the contact point. That catalogue is the part Manāra needs.
  • Only a small set of services can be transacted online so far (twelve at launch, tied to Agriculture, Tourism, IDAL and the Council of the South). The rest are guidance for a paper process. So the link is to a procedure page, not to a button that issues a permit.
  • Users can hold an e-account with saved documents, and the portal sorts its audience into students, businesses, residents, emigrants and foreigners.
2 · Where government touches the process today

Six places, all built, none of which names the permit a request needs

  • The data. Every request carries certifyingBody and certStatus. Nothing records which licence, permit or procedure the work depends on.
  • Stage 2 of 6, “Certified”. The status timeline says “Checked against technical and regulatory standards” without saying which.
  • The project page, “Who’s involved”. The Government card shows the ministry and the municipality, nothing about the procedure.
  • The government checklist in the handbook already asks for “the standard or code the request must meet, cited”. Today that is free text; Dawlati is the citation.
  • The verifier’s sign-off confirms scope, milestones and cost bracket. It has no line for “the permit this needs exists and is named”.
  • The bids. Experts bid inside the bracket without knowing which permit the winner will have to obtain, so the bracket cannot price it.
3 · The fit, very simply

Government names the procedure when it certifies. Everyone downstream reads it.

One new field on a request, filled once, at the step government already owns: procedure (the Dawlati name and link), body (who issues it) and reference (the permit number once it exists). After that nothing else changes hands: the expert bids knowing the permit, the verifier checks the reference exists before signing off, the sponsor and the residents can click through to the state’s own page. Manāra never copies the state’s process, it points at it.

Dawlati attaches to one stage. Government names the procedure when it certifies; the verifier confirms the reference exists when it signs off; every later stage only reads it.

A missing reference does not block sign-off; it blocks the first release. That keeps the bracket and bids moving while the paperwork catches up, and it puts the delay on the ledger.

5 · What else would move

Small, and all of it downstream of the one field

  • Data. A permit object on each request: procedure name, issuing body, Dawlati link, reference, and none with a reason. In Supabase, four columns on requests. The daily Baladi import leaves it empty; it is filled at certification, never before.
  • Government handbook. The checklist line “the standard or code the request must meet, cited” becomes “the Dawlati procedure named, or no-permit declared”, and a short “Working with Dawlati” section joins “Working with Baladi Map”.
  • Expert handbook. “What you will receive” gains: the permit the work needs, before you bid.
  • Verifier course, L1. One check added to the sign-off module: the reference exists and matches the scope.
  • Attributes. Government’s Regulatory Currency can be partly measured: share of certifications with a procedure named. Nothing else in the attribute set changes.
  • Unchanged. The six stages, the home diagram, the escrow rules, the bids ranking, the Baladi partnership. English first; Arabic and French topped up after.
6 · Explored and parked

Ideas looked at, not proposed yet

  • Sign in with Dawlati. A government account on Manāra proven by a Dawlati e-account would answer “is this really the municipality”. Dawlati offers no login for third parties today, so identity stays the manual check the handbook describes.
  • Pull permit status automatically. No public API; most procedures are still paper. The reference is typed by government and checked by the verifier, which is also the more trustworthy of the two.
  • Jurisdictional Match from Dawlati’s catalogue. Each procedure names its responsible body. That list could power the “not yours to fix” hand-off. Worth doing once the procedure field exists.
  • The emigrants category. Dawlati addresses emigrants directly. A cross-link from the Diaspora page to Dawlati’s emigrant services costs nothing and belongs there.
  • Risk to design around. Dawlati is two months old; its links may move. Store the procedure name and the body, not only the URL, and let the link be repaired without touching the record.
If we go ahead: two commits. First the field and the three project-page lines (a, b, e). Then the certify form and the bids line with the handbook and course text. Do it after the Problem page is live, so the government step is explained before it grows.

One graphic for all five “who gains” tables

The Network page shows the same five-by-five idea five times, once per section. Three ways to draw all twenty-five gains at once. All three read the same data as the sections, so they stay in step.

Option A — the matrix

Five by five: who is in the room, down the side; who gains, across the top

Every cell is one gain, in its short form. Hover a cell for the full sentence. The diagonal is what a role gets from its own presence. Read a row to see what one role brings to the other four; read a column to see everything one role receives.

Reads as: a scoreboard of the network. Best for: the Trust page, or the top of the Network page above the five sections. Cost: dense on a phone; it scrolls sideways there.
Option B — the ring

Five roles on a ring, twenty arcs between them

Each role sits on a circle; each arc is one gain, coloured by the role that gives it. Click a role to keep only what it gives, and the five lines appear beside the ring. Click again to release.

Reads as: a network, which is the point of the page. Best for: the home page’s “How the five fit together” block or the Network page opener. Cost: needs the click to be legible; static it is a pretty knot.
Option C — give and get

One card per role: what it gives the other four, and what it gets from them

The same twenty-five gains regrouped by beneficiary. The left column of each card is that role’s row from the matrix; the right column is its column. Nothing to hover or click.

Reads as: five fair trades. Best for: the Join page, where each role decides whether to sign up. Cost: longest of the three; five cards of ten lines.

Borrowing from the apps people already trust

Manāra is closer to a CRM than to a campaign page: records that move through stages, several people with a stake in each, money attached, and a queue of things to do. The apps below solved those exact problems for millions of users. Each tip names the pattern, why it works, and shows it drawn in Manāra’s own components on Manāra’s own data.

Method

How to mine other apps without copying them

  1. Start from a job, not a screen. Write the sentence a user would say: “I need to see what is waiting for me”, “I need to know where my money is”. Then find the app that is famous for that job.
  2. Look at flows, not pages. Pattern libraries such as Mobbin, Page Flows and Refero record whole sequences of real apps; a single screenshot hides the part that made it work.
  3. Name the pattern in one line. “Stage board with days-in-stage” can be rebuilt; “looks like Pipedrive” cannot.
  4. Rebuild it in our components on our data. If the pattern survives being drawn with Manāra’s cards, pills and figures, it belongs. If it needs the other app’s data to look good, it does not.
  5. Keep a swipe file. One row per borrowed pattern: which screen here, which app there, what we keep, what we drop. The one below starts it.

Phase 1 · Template 1: pothole repair

The first milestone template, built from six sources, two of them Lebanese. Read it as what a verifier would hand an expert on day one and check against on day 28. Wording and numbers are for an engineer to red-pen.

Why this one first

Potholes are a third of everything Baladi Map reports

Of 128 Baladi Map reports on the siteCountShare
Public roads7155%
…of which potholes, holes, broken asphalt3930% of all reports
…with a resident’s photo attached1128% of pothole reports
Marked fixed on Baladi Map, pothole1Tabarja–Safra highway, 12 days
Step 1 · Classify

Four repair classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Surface patchOnly the top layer is goneMill, tack coat, 5 cm wearing coursem²
Shallow patchAsphalt gone, base soundRemove asphalt, prime coat, 5 cm binder, tack, 5 cm wearingm²
Deep patchBase failed, hole keeps returningExcavate, 30 cm base, prime, 5 cm binder, tack, 5 cm wearingm²
Cold-mix permanentSmall hole, no hot mix nearbyReady-mixed cold asphalt, 5 cm, compactedm²

The four classes and their contents are the Council for Development and Reconstruction’s own bill lines for road maintenance in Koura and Bcharre (2022). A verifier picks the class at milestone 0; deep patch needs an engineer’s word, the others do not.

Step 2 · The milestones

Six milestones, each with the proof it needs and the number it must pass

#MilestoneEvidence the expert uploadsPass mark the verifier checks
0Scope and class
Measure the hole, choose the repair class, mark the area square.		Photo with a tape measure in frame showing depth and width. GPS pin. Area in m². Class chosen (see table below).Depth ≥ 40 mm and width ≥ 200 mm, or the report is not a pothole. Area and class recorded.
1Permission and traffic control
Confirm the road is the town’s to fix. Cones, signs, a lookout.		Permit or council reference (Dawlati link when live). Photo of cones and signs in place.A named authority. Traffic control visible before any cutting.
2Cut and clean
Saw-cut a rectangle bigger than the hole, down to sound road. Remove all water and loose material.		Photo of the cut hole: straight vertical edges, dry, empty.Rectangular. Edges vertical. No water, no debris. Depth about 1.5× the failed layer.
3Tack, fill, compact
Brush or spray tack coat on every face. Fill with hot mix in layers, overfill by a fifth, compact with a plate compactor.		Photo of tack on all faces. Delivery note or bag labels for the asphalt. Photo of the compactor on the patch.Tack on bottom and all four sides. Compactor smaller than the patch. Hot mix, or cold mix only for the cold-mix class.
4Finish and reopen
Leave a slight crown, seal the joint, reopen the road.		Photo with a straight edge across the patch. Photo of sealed edges. Time reopened.Patch 3 to 6 mm above the road, never below. No dip. A bucket of water poured on it drains off, no pooling.
528-day check
Come back after a month of traffic and look again.		Photo from the same spot as milestone 4, dated 28 days or more after reopening.Still within 6 mm of level. No cracks at the edges. No pooling. This is the gate for the final release.

Method and numbers: the UK council specification (saw-cut square, tack at about 1 litre/m², overfill 20–25%, compactor smaller than the patch, 3–6 mm crown, seal the joint) and the UK 40 mm / 200 mm defect threshold. The photo-with-board rule and the before-and-after pair are how UK crews already record every repair.

Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Inspect within 5 working days of the report. Repair within 7 days if on a main road or dangerous, within 28 otherwise. Then the 28-day check. The one fixed Baladi pothole took 12 days, inside the window.

Money

Priced per m² by class, as both Lebanese tenders do. No Lebanese rate is published: the CDR tender leaves it for bidders. A Beirut campaign filled 201 potholes over 293 m², so budget about 1.5 m² per hole. US hot-mix patching runs $21–54 per m² as a sanity check only. Bracket to be set from the first three real bids.

Release

Nothing up front. 70% released at milestone 4 (reopened, level, drains). 30% held until milestone 5 passes at 28 days. That mirrors the defects-liability retention the ILO uses on its Lebanese road contracts.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

Five things the verifier looks for because they are the usual failures

  • Edges not cut back. Filling the hole as found, with ragged edges, is why patches pop out within weeks. Milestone 2 catches it.
  • Water left in. Asphalt over a wet hole does not bond. The dry-hole photo is not optional.
  • Cold mix passed off as permanent. Fine for the cold-mix class or a winter emergency, otherwise a temporary repair billed as a permanent one. The delivery note settles it.
  • Compactor bridging the patch. A roller wider than the hole rides on the road and never compacts the fill. The compactor photo shows the size.
  • Flat or dished finish. No crown means a puddle, and a puddle means the same pothole next winter. The bucket test at milestone 4 is a ten-second check.
Step 5 · Tested against a real case

Baladi Map report 1180, Tabarja–Safra highway

Reported 1 September, six residents confirmed, marked fixed 13 September. Against the template: the timing passes (12 days, main road). Everything else fails for one reason: there is no evidence. No photo on the report, no photo of the repair, no class, no measurement. “Fixed” on Baladi Map is a status, not a record.

That is the point of the template. It turns “fixed” into six photographs and three numbers anyone can check, and it tells the expert what to photograph before they start rather than after a verifier asks.

Two things this template cannot do. It cannot tell whether a road belongs to the municipality or the Ministry of Public Works; milestone 1 needs a person for that. And it cannot diagnose a failed base from a photo; the deep-patch class needs an engineer on site before scoping.
Sources
  1. Thurrock Council, Procedure and specification for pothole and patching repair, after the Caltrans maintenance manual. The step-by-step method and its numbers.
  2. Worcestershire County Council, Fixing and repairing potholes. The 40 mm / 200 mm threshold, response times, Type 1 repair, photo-with-board evidence rule.
  3. ILO, EIIP Lebanon bid document, Zahle–Tarchich road maintenance, April 2019. Pothole patching as a m² bill item, labour-based method, interim certificates and defects-liability retention.
  4. Council for Development and Reconstruction, Roads routine maintenance, Koura and Bcharre, bill of quantities, September 2022. The four repair classes and their contents.
  5. Makhzoumi Foundation with Beirut Municipality, Safer Roads for Beirut, October 2025. 201 potholes, 293 m².
  6. Baladi Map report 1180, on this site, and The National on how Baladi Map fixes get recorded.

Winter rain and snow tearing up asphalt, pothole surgeRecent rain and light snow worsened streets nationwide, with videos of severely damaged roads circulating (Jordan Times).Greater Amman Municipality runs paving campaigns, e.g. 20 damaged main streets covering 500,000 m2 for JD3 million.[1]
High road-crash deaths, mostly in cities543 deaths in 2024 and 510 in 2025; about 91% of 2025 crashes were inside city limits and 96% of pedestrian run-overs were urban.Public Security Directorate enforcement campaigns and awareness weeks; injury burden documented by the World Bank Global Road Safety Facility.[1]
Flash flooding on roads from stormwater overloadAmman's built-up area grew from 83 km2 (1986) to 137 km2 (2024); simulations show a 56% rise in large flood events, driven mainly by urbanisation.GAM builds box culverts ahead of winter (1 km culvert on Princess Tharwat Street) and UN-Habitat mapped flood risk for downtown with pilot drainage works.[1]
Worn road markings and unmarked speed bumpsDriving guides report widely worn-out lane markings and speed bumps that appear on highways and residential streets without signage (anecdotal, not official audit).Jordan has a Manual on Traffic Control Devices; academic studies test driver comprehension of signs, but no systematic marking programme was found.[1]
Discontinuous, unwalkable sidewalksSidewalks lack continuity between plots, vary in height, have trees planted in the middle, and get eaten by street widening (CSBE); residents call some 'unwalkable'.GAM sidewalk-upgrade programme aiming at safe, connected pedestrian routes while relocating trees.[1]
Chronic congestion in AmmanExperts describe Amman's traffic as a persistent headache, tied to car dependence and weak public transport.Bus Rapid Transit lines (Amman BRT, Amman-Zarqa BRT) and signal/junction upgrades.[1]

ProblemHow commonHow they deal with itSource
Slow degradation of the network and poor condition knowledgeCour des comptes (2022): share of surfaces needing work rose from 43% to 53% in a decade; only 40% of sampled departments had surveyed all their pavements.13 recommendations including systematic condition surveys and asset-management plans; roads still treated as a budget adjustment variable.[1]
Potholes after wet winters straining commune budgetsEstimated 15 billion euros a year spent on roads yet potholes keep multiplying; a 6,000-inhabitant commune spends 400,000 euros a year; 37 consecutive rain days in winter 2025-26 wrecked Brittany roads.Communes ration repairs against schools and shops, pool works via intercommunalities, and some use AI-based road scanning to plan works.[1]
Non-compliant speed bumpsOf roughly 450,000 speed bumps, about 4 in 10 (some estimates half) breach decree 94-447 on height (max 10 cm) or signage; Conseil d'Etat ruling March 2025.Municipalities inventory and rebuild or remove bumps; unsigned bumps expose the commune to liability.[1]
Pedestrian and vulnerable-user deaths in townsONISR 2024: 3,193 road deaths; 451 pedestrians killed, half aged 65+; vulnerable users are 45% of deaths and 66% of serious injuries.30 km/h zones, pedestrian-priority streets and national road-safety plans.[1]
Fragmented responsibility for roadsCour des comptes warns the 3DS law transfer of national roads will further fragment road competence among State, departments and communes.Recommendation to clarify roles and share technical expertise, as State engineering staff halved in 20 years.[1]
Legal liability for pothole damageSenate questions (2024) on road managers' responsibility when potholes cause damage.Communes must prove 'normal maintenance' (signage, timely repair) to avoid liability, which pushes documented inspection.[1]

ProblemHow commonHow they deal with itSource
Deferred maintenance backlog on municipal roadsDeferred maintenance is 2-3 billion euros a year nationally, about 1 billion of it municipal; Court of Audit says backlog and safety risks are growing; VNG and IPO issued alarms in 2024.Lobbying the cabinet for structural funds; Arcadis/Berenschot estimate 1.5 billion euros a year needed for replacement of local civil works.[1]
Ageing bridges and quaysOne in three municipalities struggles with deferred maintenance on traffic bridges; deferred amounts more than doubled since 2016.Load restrictions, closures and phased replacement programmes.[1]

Roads & Traffic · Top 10

The ten problems that keep coming back

Ranked by how many of the countries share them and how hard they hit Lebanon. 0 of the 10 are already documented in Lebanon. Blue chips mark Lebanon.

#ProblemSeen inIn LebanonTypical fixSources
1Potholes and surface failure after rain
Water enters cracks, weakens the base and traffic breaks the asphalt into potholes every wet season.		JordanFranceIndiaKenyaChileMediterranean winter rain on unsealed, thin municipal asphalt is exactly the Jordan pattern, and Lebanese reporting says potholes multiply faster than they are filled.Seal cracks and surface-dress before the rains, then patch with proper cut-square, tack-coat and compacted hot or cold mix rather than throw-and-go.[1][2][3]
2Chronic maintenance underfunding
Municipalities defer routine maintenance until roads need full reconstruction at several times the cost.		FranceNetherlandsKenyaChileJordanLebanese municipalities lost most of their budgets in the 2019 collapse, so preservation-first spending is the only affordable path.Condition surveys and a prioritised preservation plan (seal early, rebuild late), backed by a ring-fenced maintenance fund such as Kenya's fuel-levy RMLF.[1][2][3]
3Blocked or missing road drainage
Absent culverts, silted ditches and encroached drains send stormwater across the carriageway, flooding roads and undermining the pavement.		JordanIndiaKenyaChileSteep mountain roads and coastal flash floods make drainage the main cause of pavement washouts, and encroached roadside drains are common.Pre-winter desilting, side ditches and cross culverts sized for the catchment, and removing structures built over drains.[1][2][3]
4Dead traffic signals during power cuts
Grid outages and unmaintained controllers leave junctions unsignalled, causing gridlock and crashes.		KenyaChileLebanon's daily EDL cuts have left Beirut signals broken for months; the Traffic Safety Committee is only now reactivating them.Solar-battery backup or UPS on each controller, LED heads to cut load, and a maintenance contract with response times.[1][2][3]
5Unsafe or missing sidewalks
Broken, discontinuous or obstructed sidewalks push pedestrians into traffic, hitting the elderly hardest.		JordanChileFranceLebanese sidewalks are routinely parked on, cut by driveways or absent, mirroring Amman's discontinuity problem, and pedestrian deaths are rising.Continuous kerbed sidewalks with dropped crossings, bollards against parking, and neighbour co-funded repair schemes like Chile's Vive tu Vereda.[1][2][3]
6Faded markings and missing signage
Worn lane lines, absent stop lines and missing or unreadable signs remove the basic cues drivers rely on, especially at night.		JordanKenyaIndiaLebanon shares Jordan's worn markings and adds unlit streets from power cuts, so retro-reflective markings and signs matter more.Annual thermoplastic remarking of priority routes and a sign inventory with retro-reflectivity checks.[1][2][3]
7Uncontrolled speed bumps
Home-made or oversized bumps without signage damage vehicles, cause crashes and expose municipalities to liability.		FranceJordanLebanese villages and informal contractors install ad-hoc bumps at will, often unpainted and unsigned.Inventory every bump, rebuild to a standard profile (France caps at 10 cm) with paint and warning signs, remove the rest.[1][2]
8Poor-quality works and unrestored utility cuts
Thin or badly compacted asphalt and trenches left by water, sewer and telecom contractors fail within months.		IndiaJordanKenyaInformal contractors and uncoordinated utility digging are routine in Lebanon, so trench reinstatement rules and defect-liability periods are the leverage point.Road-cut permits with reinstatement specifications, deposits, no-dig windows in winter, and independent verification before payment.[1][2][3]
9Crash black spots and unforgiving geometry
Sharp curves, poor sight lines, absent guardrails and mixed-speed roads concentrate deaths at identifiable spots.		IndiaNetherlandsJordanChileMountain roads with hairpins and no barriers plus coastal highways where cars and mopeds mix reproduce the Dutch 50 km/h danger pattern.Map black spots from crash data, then apply low-cost fixes: guardrails, chevrons, rumble strips, sight-line clearing and 30 km/h in villages.[1][2][3]
10Fragmented responsibility for who fixes what
Repairs stall when design, approval and funding sit with different tiers of government and nobody owns the road.		ChileFranceKenyaIn Lebanon roads split between the Ministry of Public Works, CDR and municipalities, so a certified request must name the owner before a fix can be matched.A published road-ownership register, delegated emergency-repair authority to municipalities, and time limits on approvals as in Chile's 180-to-90-day reform.[1][2][3]
Roads & Traffic · Worth copying

9 ideas that worked somewhere

Gjenge Makers plastic paversKenya

Nairobi firm founded by Nzambi Matee turns ~500 kg/day of unrecyclable plastic mixed with sand into pavers for sidewalks and driveways, claimed stronger than concrete, with ~600 jobs created. [1]

Waste-plastic bitumen roads (IRC SP 98-2020)India

Dry-process shredded plastic coating aggregate, developed by Rajagopalan Vasudevan; ~40,000 km rural and ~2,900 km highway built, and MoRTH makes it the default for renewals near cities. [1]

Asphalt Recycling TrainNetherlands

Rijkswaterstaat machine reheats and relays the existing top layer on site, nearly fully circular with ~65% lower emissions, trialled in Almere and Oss in 2025. [1]

High-RAP asphalt with rejuvenatorsNetherlands

Heijmans produces mixes with very high reclaimed-asphalt content using a rejuvenating additive, enabling circular resurfacing. [1]

Epoxy long-life asphaltNetherlands

TU Delft lab results show epoxy-modified asphalt resists fatigue and wear far better than ordinary asphalt, extending resurfacing intervals. [1]

Cold-mix and stabilised local materialsKenya

State Department for Roads promotes cold bitumen emulsion mixes and stabilising on-site gravel to cut transport and cost on low-volume roads; research blends reclaimed asphalt with gravelly soil for sub-base. [1]

AI road-condition scanning for communesFrance

Loire-Atlantique communes use camera-and-AI surveys to spot potholes and sunken shoulders and plan works before failure. [1]

Participatory Pavement Programme (DS 114)Chile

Neighbour committees co-fund 5-30% of street and sidewalk repaving with municipality and Serviu, a cost-sharing model close to Manara's sponsor-plus-municipality logic. [1]

Labour-intensive road rehabilitationLebanon

World Bank-backed programme rehabilitated 530 km and maintained 1,000 km while creating local jobs, with fatalities down over 20% on upgraded routes. [1]

Waste Collection · Top 10

The ten problems that keep coming back

Ranked by how many of the countries share them and how hard they hit Lebanon. 9 of the 10 are already documented in Lebanon. Blue chips mark Lebanon.

#ProblemSeen inIn LebanonTypical fixSources
1Open and uncontrolled dumps
Waste ends in unlined, unmanaged sites that leak leachate, emit methane, catch fire and attract vermin.		JordanIndonesiaEgyptKenyaLebanonOver 1,000 unlicensed dumps are recorded, some in mountain and coastal areas, and official landfills are near capacity.Close and rehabilitate dumps, build engineered cells with gas and leachate capture, and finance them through donor loans as Jordan did.[1][2][3]
2Open burning of waste
Households and dump operators burn mixed waste, releasing dioxins and particulates.		LebanonIndonesiaEgyptKenyaJordanHRW found waste burned weekly at more than 150 dumps and called it a violation of the right to health.Restore regular collection so burning is unnecessary, then enforce bans with fines as Egypt's 2020 law does.[1][2][3]
3Uncollected waste and service gaps
Collection covers only part of the population, so waste piles in streets, valleys and rivers.		EgyptKenyaIndonesiaJordanMunicipalities outside Beirut were left to their own devices without resources or expertise, and refugee influx added load.Fund routine collection first, using CBO or contracted collectors and simple fee models before any high-tech treatment.[1][2][3]
4No sorting at source, low recycling
Mixed waste makes recovery costly and pushes everything to dumps.		JordanEgyptKenyaLebanonSwedenSouth KoreaSource separation remains elusive; sorting plants are scarce and localised despite UNDP bin distribution and training.Municipal two- or three-stream separation with household bins, backed by small sorting centres, as UNDP piloted in Hamana and Baaqline.[1][2][3]
5Weak municipal finances and cost recovery
Fees cover a fraction of costs; central transfers arrive late; contractors go unpaid.		JordanKenyaLebanonThe Independent Municipal Fund ran a $2bn+ deficit as waste expenses multiplied, and the sector costs the state ~$180m/year.Ring-fenced waste fees on utility bills and transparent transfers, plus producer fees that reimburse municipalities as in Sweden.[1][2][3]
6Landfill capacity exhaustion and siting conflict
Existing sites overflow while communities block new ones.		South KoreaIndonesiaJordanLebanonThe 2015 crisis began when Naameh closed with no replacement; today's official landfills are again near capacity.Divert organics and recyclables to extend life, plan regional sites early, and compensate host communities as Korea's Incheon dispute shows.[1][2][3]
7Coastal, river and marine dumping
Waste is dumped on shores and riverbanks and washes into the sea.		LebanonIndonesiaEgyptKenyaCosta Brava and Bourj Hammoud-Jdeideh landfills sit on the coast, and a World Bank baseline found 82% of marine litter is land-based, mostly single-use plastic.Move dumps off the coast, install river traps and beach monitoring, and pay collectors for recovered plastic as VeryNile does.[1][2][3]
8Informal sector unrecognised
Pickers do most recycling yet work without protection and are displaced by formal contracts.		EgyptIndonesiaKenyaJordanLebanonOver 90% of Lebanon's waste pickers are Syrian, feeding informal 'bourat' yards that underpin what recycling exists.Contract or buy from pickers at fixed prices with protective gear and IDs, as Jordan's landfill contracts and Kenya's buy-back firms do.[1][2][3]
9Illegal dumping, littering and weak enforcement
Fly-tipping, cartels and street litter persist where fines are rare.		South KoreaKenyaJordanSwedenLebanonIllegal dumping persists nationwide with little enforcement capacity at municipal level.Cheap deterrents: CCTV with reporting rewards (Korea), licensing of haulers (Kenya) and producer-funded clean-up fees (Sweden).[1][2][3]
10Organic and food waste unmanaged
Wet organics dominate the stream, rot in mixed bins and generate landfill methane.		South KoreaSwedenEgyptLebanonLebanese initiatives are only starting to turn organic waste into compost or economic value at municipal scale.Separate organics for composting or biogas, with weight-based fees (Korea) or mandatory collection (Sweden).[1][2][3]
Waste Collection · Worth copying

16 ideas that worked somewhere

Zabbaleen door-to-door recyclingEgypt

Community collectors recycle about 80% of what they collect through hand-sorting and micro-enterprises. [1]

Waste banks (bank sampah)Indonesia

Residents deposit sorted recyclables and accumulate savings; UNDP is digitising them to keep plastic out of the ocean. [1]

Volume-based waste fee (pay-as-you-throw)South Korea

Since 1995 households pay via official bags; Seoul cut waste generation ~40% by 2012. [1]

RFID weight-based food-waste binsSouth Korea

Smart bins charge per gram; food-waste recycling reached 96.8% in 2023. [1]

Illegal-dumping reporting bountySouth Korea

Citizens who report dumpers receive up to 80% of the fine. [1]

Deposit return system (pant)Sweden

88.4% return rate and 3bn+ containers in 2025 through reverse vending machines. [1]

Producer littering feesSweden

Municipalities report litter clean-up costs and producers of disposables pay a fee that funds them. [1]

Waste-to-energy district heatingSweden

Roughly half of household waste is incinerated for heat and power, landfill under 1%. [1]

Landfill gas to power (Al-Ghabawi)Jordan

EBRD-financed capping and gas capture expected to cut ~150,000 t CO2/year. [1]

Formalising landfill waste pickersJordan

A recovery and recycling contract at a landfill improved picker livelihoods. [1]

VeryNile fishermen buy-backEgypt

Seven-year state programme with military clean-ups and water monitoring; funding was cut in 2020-21. [1]
