Water · Top 10

The ten problems that keep coming back

Ranked by how many of the countries share them and how hard they hit Lebanon. 0 of the 10 are already documented in Lebanon. Blue chips mark Lebanon.

#ProblemSeen inIn LebanonTypical fixSources
1Network losses (non-revenue water)
Treated water lost to leaks, illegal connections and unbilled use before reaching a paying customer.		JordanKenyaMoroccoAustraliaSingaporeLebanon's NRW is put at 40% and over 50% in the national strategy, so every cubic metre pumped on scarce electricity is half wasted.District metered areas, pressure management, acoustic leak detection and targeted pipe renewal, benchmarked annually as Kenya and Australia do.[1][2][3]
2Intermittent supply and rationing
Water arrives on a rota of hours per day or days per week rather than continuously.		JordanKenyaMoroccoAustraliaLebanese supply averages 6 hours a day in summer and 9 in winter, forcing roof tanks and tanker top-ups.Published rotation schedules, storage and pressure zoning now, with NRW reduction and new bulk sources to move zones toward continuous supply.[1][2]
3Power cuts and pumping energy cost
Pumps stop when grid power fails or when electricity and diesel become unaffordable.		JordanKenyaUNICEF found electricity shortages make it impossible to pump enough water and that establishments cannot afford diesel or spare parts.Solar PV at pumping stations and wells (Jordan's five-station programme, Kenyan pump solarisation) plus pump efficiency retrofits.[1][2][3]
4Unregulated wells and aquifer depletion
Private drilling beyond licensed volumes drops water tables and dries public sources.		JordanMoroccoKenyaHouseholds, farms and firms have dug over 60,000 unregulated wells to compensate for public supply gaps.Well registration and licensing, sealing of illegal wells, abstraction metering and basin-level aquifer contracts as in Morocco.[1][2][3]
5Private tanker and vendor markets
Unregulated tankers and vendors fill the gap at several times the piped price, often from illegal wells or tapped mains.		JordanKenyaTanker trucks and vendors are an essential part of Lebanon's supply landscape with no price or quality control.Licence and test tankers, regulate filling points, and offer public prepaid dispensers at a social tariff as Nairobi does.[1][2][3]
6No metering and flat tariffs
Utilities cannot measure production, distribution or consumption, so cannot bill by volume or locate losses.		JordanKenyaSingaporeHousehold metering was 16% in Beirut-Mount Lebanon and zero elsewhere, with a flat annual fee that rewards waste and starves the establishments.Bulk and district meters first, then customer meters and a progressive volumetric tariff; Singapore pairs smart meters with tiered pricing.[1][2][3]
7Utility financial collapse
Tariffs, collection and currency losses leave utilities unable to pay for power, chemicals, parts or staff.		JordanKenyaThe four Water Establishments lost access to hard currency and could not buy spare parts or generator fuel, leaving UNICEF to keep them running.Cost-recovery tariff path with social protection, collection enforcement, and ring-fenced O&M budgets backed by performance regulation.[1][2][3]
8Coastal saltwater intrusion
Over-pumping near the coast pulls seawater into aquifers, making well water brackish.		MoroccoKenyaSouth of Beirut TDS reaches 530-5,600 mg/L and Beirut households spend over 6.5% of income coping with salty water.Cap and meter coastal abstraction, shift supply inland or to surface sources, and use managed aquifer recharge to push back the interface.[1][2][3]
9Drought without drought rules
Multi-year dry spells empty reservoirs while towns lack pre-agreed staged restrictions.		MoroccoAustraliaJordanLebanon has no staged restriction ladder; Australia's permanent water-saving rules and four-stage system and Morocco's non-essential-use closures are ready templates.Adopt trigger-based restriction stages tied to storage levels, permanent efficiency rules, and per-person consumption targets.[1][2][3]
10Drinking water quality in small systems
Small or remote systems skip testing and treatment, delivering water outside health limits.		AustraliaKenyaWith establishments unable to buy consumables and thousands of private wells untested, municipal water quality is largely unverified.Routine chlorination and sampling, public boil-water advisories, and independent audits of small-system compliance.[1][2][3]
Water · Worth copying

18 ideas that worked somewhere

Treated wastewater for golf courses and green spaceMorocco

53 MCM of treated wastewater irrigated 30 golf courses and green spaces in 16 communities in 2024; 60% of the country's 44 courses use it, with a 474 MCM/yr reuse target for 2030. [1]

National wastewater programme 2025-2034Morocco

US$5.6bn programme; treatment plants grew from 7 in 2006 to 216 in 2024 and depollution from 7% to 58%. [1]

Aquifer contractsMorocco

Negotiated agreements between basin agencies and farmers to cap abstraction in over-exploited aquifers such as Souss. [1]

As-Samra effluent for Jordan Valley farmingJordan

Roughly 110-133 MCM/yr of treated effluent flows via King Talal Dam into Jordan Valley irrigation, freeing fresh water for towns. [1]

Solar at water pumping stationsJordan

Solar plants at five treatment and pumping stations toward 20% of the water sector's electricity from renewables. [1]

PV versus diesel for well fieldsJordan

Life-cycle study of 55 wells found PV at US$0.136/kWh against US$0.239/kWh for diesel gensets. [1]

NEWater and the Four National TapsSingapore

Reclaimed water at about 1 kWh/m3 versus 3.5 kWh/m3 for desalination, planned to supply 55% of demand by 2061. [1]

Acoustic leak sensors on trunk mainsSingapore

120 sensors on about 70 km of large mains found 13 developing leaks over three years, keeping losses near 8%. [1]

Smart meters plus tiered tariff and thimblesSingapore

300,000 smart meters by end-2024, a water conservation tax since 1991, over a million free tap thimbles, and mandatory recycling for water-intensive new projects from 2024. [1]

Stormwater harvesting with managed aquifer rechargeAustralia

City of Salisbury stores treated stormwater underground and delivers 2.5 GL/yr through 150 km of purple pipe for parks, industry and toilets. [1]

Groundwater replenishment with recycled waterAustralia

Perth's Beenyup scheme recharges up to 28 GL/yr of recycled water into confined aquifers for later drinking supply. [1]

Permanent water saving rules and Target 150Australia

Melbourne's no-end-date rules since 2011 and a 150 L/person/day target sit under a four-stage restriction ladder. [1]

National utility benchmarkingAustralia

Bureau of Meteorology publishes an annual report comparing 86 utilities on 166 indicators including leakage per connection. [1]

Prepaid water ATMs in informal settlementsKenya

Nairobi Water installed 257 dispensers selling 20 L for the social tariff of Sh2, at about KSh 200,000 per unit, undercutting vendors many times over. [1]

Volunteer hand-pump repair teamsKenya

Kenyan engineers have reinstated over 2,700 broken hand pumps serving 750,000 people, a far cheaper route than new drilling. [1]

Pump solarisationKenya

Replacing diesel with solar pumping cut energy costs by up to 70% for farming communities. [1]

Regulator league tablesKenya

WASREB's annual Impact Report ranks 94 utilities publicly on NRW, coverage and cost recovery to drive competition. [1]

Solar pumping guide for Lebanese utilitiesLebanon

ReliefWeb-hosted guide on sizing and financing solar pumping for Lebanese water systems facing grid failure. [1]

The ten problems that keep coming back

Ranked by how many of the countries share them and how hard they hit Lebanon. 9 of the 10 are already documented in Lebanon. Blue chips mark Lebanon.

#ProblemSeen inIn LebanonTypical fixSources
1Plants built but idle for lack of power and fuel
Treatment plants exist but run partially or not at all because electricity is rationed and diesel is unaffordable.		LebanonIndiaOnly about 35 of roughly 100 Lebanese plants operate, many for 12 hours a day since fuel subsidies ended in 2021.Solar or biogas self-generation, energy-lean processes, and ring-fenced O&M budgets before building new capacity.[1][2]
2Plant and network built separately, never connected
Donor-funded plants sit underused because collection networks or house connections were never finished.		LebanonBangladeshIndiaEgyptBaalbek's plant stayed disconnected for years and Tripoli and Sidon opened long after completion.Fund network and connections in the same contract and audit plants by inflow, not by capacity.[1][2][3]
3Raw sewage discharged to the sea
Coastal cities send untreated or only screened sewage through outfalls or open channels to the Mediterranean.		LebanonEgyptGhadir provides only preliminary treatment through a 2.6 km outfall and 38% of monitored bathing sites were classed polluted.Secondary treatment at coastal plants and public bathing-water monitoring to sustain pressure.[1][2][3]
4River pollution from sewered towns without treatment
Networks collect sewage and pipe it straight into rivers used for irrigation.		LebanonEgyptIndiaBekaa networks were built decades before plants, so the Litani carries domestic and industrial sewage into irrigation water.Cluster treatment plants on river basins plus drain interception, as under Namami Gange.[1][2][3]
5Village septic tanks and cesspits leaking to groundwater
Unsewered villages use open-bottom pits that seep into aquifers and springs.		LebanonEgyptFranceBangladeshIndiaKarstic aquifers make Lebanese villages on cesspits especially prone to bacterial contamination of springs.Periodic inspection of tanks (French SPANC model) and small-scale decentralised treatment for clusters of houses.[1][2][3]
6Combined sewers overflowing in rain
Stormwater and sewage share pipes, so heavy rain floods streets and homes with sewage.		LebanonFranceNetherlandsEgyptBeirut's combined pipes silt up and overflow every winter, with drains further blocked by swept litter.Separate rainwater where feasible, add storage basins like Austerlitz, and clean drains before the wet season.[1][2][3]
7No money for operation and maintenance
Plants and pumps decay because tariffs do not cover chemicals, spare parts and staff.		LebanonIndiaFranceWater establishments' revenues collapsed with the currency, leaving arrears and no budget for consumables.A sanitation charge on the water bill and results-based funding tied to plant performance.[1][2]
8Blocked drains, open manholes and clogged canals
Litter, silt and encroachment block drains and manholes so sewage surfaces in streets.		LebanonBangladeshEgyptWinter flooding in Beirut and the North kills people yearly, worsened by undersized and unmaintained drains.Scheduled drain cleaning, manhole cover replacement and canal reclamation before the rainy season.[1][2]
9Ageing, leaking networks
Old pipes infiltrate groundwater or exfiltrate sewage, cutting plant capacity and polluting soil.		FranceNetherlandsBangladeshLebanon's older urban networks predate the plants they feed and are rarely inspected.Camera inspection and a fixed annual renewal rate funded by sanitation levies.[1][2]
10Sludge with nowhere to go
Working plants produce sludge that is dumped or stored because disposal was never planned.		LebanonNetherlandsBangladeshSludge handling is a neglected operating cost at Lebanese plants.Dry beds or digesters with agricultural reuse, or energy recovery on the Dutch model.[1][2]

Electricity · Top 10

The ten problems that keep coming back

Ranked by how many of the countries share them and how hard they hit Lebanon. 5 of the 10 are already documented in Lebanon. Blue chips mark Lebanon.

#ProblemSeen inIn LebanonTypical fixSources
1Grid supplies only a few hours a day
Public utility cannot meet demand so households and municipalities live on rationed hours.		LebanonPakistanKenyaEDL reported a national average of about four hours a day in July 2026 after briefly reaching seven to nine hours.Publish honest feeder schedules and protect critical municipal loads (water pumps, clinics, lighting) with solar plus storage.[1][2][3]
2Unregulated private generator market
Neighbourhood diesel operators charge flat fees, resist meters and pollute heavily.		LebanonDiesel generators produced about 44% of Lebanon's CO2-equivalent in 2022 and operators drew thousands of complaints in summer 2025.Mandatory meters with a monthly ministry-set kWh tariff, inspections and seizure of non-compliant generators.[1][2][3]
3Theft and non-payment
Illegal hooks, meter tampering and unpaid bills push losses far above technical norms.		PakistanJordanKenyaIndiaEDL's collection depends on ending illegal connections and arrears, and Pakistan shows how theft-heavy feeders end up with the longest cuts.Smart or prepaid meters, joint inspection campaigns with police and courts, and feeder-level loss tracking.[1][2][3]
4Unsafe cable webs and electrocution
Illegal hooks, internet cables on power poles and exposed wiring kill people, especially in rain.		PakistanKenyaIndiaLebanon's poles carry tangles of generator, EDL and telecom cables and the same rain-season electrocution risk.Pole-by-pole audits, removal of illegal attachments, insulated bundled cable and public safety campaigns before the wet season.[1][2][3]
5Household solar boom without standards
Rapid uptake by untrained installers with cheap imports causes fires, undersized systems and battery waste.		LebanonPakistanJordanNo licensing exists for solar companies, LCEC's qualified list held only three firms in 2022, and fires and battery explosions are reported.Enforce mandatory LIBNOR standards with IRI testing, a public list of qualified installers and inspection before connection.[1][2][3]
6Utility death spiral from grid defection
Paying customers leave for solar, fixed costs fall on fewer users and tariffs rise further.		PakistanJordanLebanonSolar rose roughly eight-fold since 2020 while EDL's paying base shrinks, mirroring Pakistan's trajectory.Move to net billing or a grid fee, reform tariffs and keep reliable service for those who stay connected.[1][2][3]
7Dark streets from broken lighting
Street lights fail through neglect, load shedding and no procurement, hurting safety.		PakistanJordanIndiaKenyaLebanese municipalities face the same dark streets since EDL cannot power lights; no Lebanon-specific audit was found.LED retrofit financed from savings, a maintenance contract with an inventory, and solar on main arteries.[1][2][3]
8Solar street lights and off-grid assets that fail or get stolen
Batteries die in heat, panels and lamps are stolen for scrap, and nobody budgets maintenance.		KenyaIndiaMoroccoMunicipal solar lights in Lebanon fail the same way; Kenya and India show theft and no-maintenance as the usual causes.Anti-theft mounting, asset tagging, a funded maintenance line and community ownership of the lights.[1][2][3]
9Public building energy bills
Energy eats a large share of municipal budgets and public buildings sit unserved.		JordanMoroccoLebanese municipalities pay generator fees for offices, schools and pumps; Jordan's fund model shows rooftop PV can cut this.Rooftop PV on municipal buildings via a dedicated fund or ESCO contract paid from savings.[1][2][3]
10Battery and solar e-waste
Lead-acid and lithium batteries from the solar boom have no collection or recycling route.		LebanonKenyaLebanon has no recycling programme or safe landfill for the batteries installed since 2021.Take-back schemes, refurbishment and second-life battery use, with a licensed recycler.[1][2]
Electricity · Worth copying

15 ideas that worked somewhere

Pay-as-you-go solar with refurbishmentKenya

M-KOPA sells solar home systems on mobile-money instalments and refurbishes nearly 90% of returned products for resale to lower-income customers. [1]

Second-life lithium batteriesKenya

Aceleron rebuilds waste solar-lantern cells into $45/kWh packs for solar home systems, about half the annual cost of lead-acid. [1]

Second-life batteries for schoolsKenya

Peer-reviewed study finds second-life batteries cut levelised electricity cost by 5.6-35.3% for primary school systems. [1]

Off-grid solar take-back schemeKenya

myclimate and Solibrium pilot take-back, reuse and recycling business models for off-grid solar batteries in Western Kenya. [1]

KOSAP solar mini-grids at uniform tariffKenya

World Bank-funded programme builds 151 mini-grids whose customers pay the same KPLC tariff, with 120 due by September 2026. [1]

Community-managed green mini-gridsKenya

Communities become producers and managers, with productive uses like cold storage stabilising revenue. [1]

Municipal rooftop PV fundJordan

JREEEF installs 20 kW systems on municipal buildings, covering 104 municipalities and 188 buildings for about JD3.4 million. [1]

LED street lighting repaid from savingsJordan

410,000 lamps replaced with half grant, half CVDB loan repaid over seven years from JD22 million annual savings. [1]

Solar on mosques and churchesJordan

JREEEF has fitted PV on 430 mosques and churches to cover their electricity needs. [1]

Solar arterial street lightingPakistan

Karachi shifted Sharae Faisal and other arteries to solar so lights stay on through load shedding. [1]

Smart-meter loss turnaroundIndia

Bihar cut AT&C losses from 20.32% to 15.51% through smart meters and digital billing. [1]

Solar for rural schools and clinicsMorocco

AMEE programmes electrified remote schools, health centres and mosques with PV and solar water heaters. [1]

Qualified solar installer listLebanon

LCEC runs a qualification and public list of recommended solar PV companies to lift installation quality. [1]

Mandatory generator meters and monthly tariffLebanon

Ministry sets a monthly kWh price for private generators and requires meters, with seizure for non-compliance. [1]

Residential solar rebateJordan

USD 11.2 million plan covers up to 30% of rooftop PV and solar thermal cost for about 9,000 homes. [1]

Tunisia · 6 problems found
ProblemHow commonHow they deal with itSource
Summer forest firesCivil Defence recorded 693 forest fires in summer 2023; about 28,500 ha burned that year, the worst season in over a decade; forests across Bizerte, Beja, Kef and the centre are hit yearly.Understaffed forest directorate (7,500 rangers vs 13,300 needed) and aging equipment, with army aircraft dropping water on large fires; prevention and community roles remain weak.[1]
Industrial coastal pollution (Gulf of Gabès)Phosphate plants at Sfax, Skhira and Gabès have discharged over 500 million tonnes of phosphogypsum into the sea since the 1970s, roughly 14,000-15,000 t/day per 2017 reports.Repeated government promises to relocate or treat discharge, with citizen protests (Oct 2025) as the main pressure; no completed clean-up.[1]
Municipal waste crisis and illegal dumpingClosure of the Agareb landfill in 2021 left about 30,000 tonnes of rubbish in Sfax streets; the country has only 11 landfill sites and no national recycling capacity.Negotiation with protesters and temporary reopening of dumps; no national waste strategy yet.[1]
Drought, water scarcity and desertificationWorst recorded drought; dam storage fell to 31% and 37% of capacity in 2023 and 2024, with dam siltation and salinity worsening.World Bank Water Security and Resilience Program (US$332.5m first phase) and irrigation efficiency loans; municipalities encouraged to take on local adaptation roles.[1]
Illegal quarries and sand extractionWeak post-2011 governance led to de facto deregulation; a draft law sought to regularise illegal marble quarries on state land (FIDH).Civil-society pushback against regularisation laws; enforcement remains weak, and Tunisia-specific data is thin.[1]
Coastal erosion and sea-level pressureSea erosion is named alongside desertification and drought as a constraint on development (AfDB drought report).Largely planned through national adaptation programmes; municipal role emerging (Carnegie).[1]

ProblemHow commonHow they deal with itSource
Forest fires and wildland-urban interfaceIn 2022, 19,711 fires burned 72,000 ha; brush-clearing (OLD) is mandatory in 48 departments covering about 7,400 communes.Legal brush-clearing obligations within 200 m of at-risk forests, enforced by prefects and mayors, plus volunteer communal fire committees that patrol and report smoke.[1]
Forest dieback from drought and pestsIGN 2024 inventory: tree mortality more than doubled in ten years, driven by successive droughts, bark beetles (scolytes) on spruce, ash dieback and chestnut disease.National forest inventory with a DEPERIS health indicator, sanitary felling and species diversification in replanting.[1]
Urban air pollution from traffic25 active low-emission zones (ZFE) in cities such as Paris, Lyon, Marseille and Toulouse restrict the dirtiest vehicles.Crit'Air sticker classes and city-set vehicle bans, though Parliament voted in May 2025 to abolish ZFEs (not yet in force).[1]

Environment · Top 10

The ten problems that keep coming back

Ranked by how many of the countries share them and how hard they hit Lebanon. 7 of the 10 are already documented in Lebanon. Blue chips mark Lebanon.

#ProblemSeen inIn LebanonTypical fixSources
1Summer forest fires with weak local capacity
Hot, dry summers ignite pine and oak forests faster than under-equipped local responders can contain them.		LebanonTunisiaFranceFires in Akkar, Dinniyeh and the south burn for days while Civil Defence and municipalities lack equipment and rely on loudspeaker appeals for volunteers.Legal brush-clearing around homes, trained volunteer communal fire committees as early-warning eyes, and rehabilitated local fire stations.[1][2][3]
2Untreated sewage into rivers, lakes and sea
Towns discharge raw wastewater into watercourses because treatment plants are missing, broken or unconnected.		LebanonIndiaCosta RicaTunisiaAbout 69 upper-basin towns send roughly 46 million m3/year of untreated sewage into the Litani, and Lake Qaraoun has had a fishing ban since 2018.Connect villages to shared treatment plants, fund municipalities to run them, and publish water-quality data.[1][2][3]
3Illegal quarries and sand mining
Unlicensed extraction scars slopes, triggers landslides, silts rivers and fragments forest.		LebanonIndiaTunisiaArmy survey in 2023 counted 1,607 quarry and crusher sites, with damage estimated at $2.4 billion and reportedly only one valid licence.Master plan of permitted zones, satellite monitoring, rehabilitation bonds, and district-level enforcement backed by courts.[1][2][3]
4Open dumps and waste burning smoke
Municipalities without landfills or budgets dump and burn waste, releasing dioxins and fine particles.		LebanonTunisiaIndiaHRW documented over 941 open dumps, 617 of them municipal, with more than 150 burned weekly, mostly in the Bekaa, south and Nabatieh.Enforce burning bans, fund municipal collection and sorting, and pair with community clean-up days.[1][2]
5Forest dieback from pests and drought
Warmer winters and repeated droughts let insects and fungi kill weakened trees.		LebanonFranceThe cedar web-spinning sawfly hit 70% of one major cedar stand in the late 1990s and now emerges yearly as forests dry out.Forest health monitoring, sanitary felling, biological control and replanting with drought-tolerant native mixes.[1][2]
6Loss of urban tree cover and green space
Concrete replaces trees, raising heat and cutting public access to green areas.		LebanonIndiaBeirut has about 0.8 m2 of green space per person against the WHO's 9 m2, and Horsh Beirut shrank from 1.25 km2 to 0.3 km2.Protect existing parks, plant street trees and pocket forests, and open closed municipal green spaces.[1][2][3]
7Unregulated pesticide use and farm runoff
Agrochemicals wash into rivers and groundwater from intensive farming.		LebanonCosta RicaThe Litani River Authority lists non-degradable pesticides and fertilisers among the four main pollution sources of the river and Lake Qaraoun.Farmer training on integrated pest management, buffer strips along streams, and residue monitoring.[1][2]
8Coastal and marine pollution
Industrial discharge, sewage outfalls and plastic degrade beaches and fisheries.		TunisiaCosta RicaIndiaLebanon's coast receives the same mix of sewage and litter; no Lebanon-specific coastal source was found in this pass.Treat or relocate industrial discharge, certify clean beaches through a Blue Flag-style programme, and organise coastal clean-ups.[1][2]
9Air pollution from traffic and biomass burning
Old vehicles, motorcycles and seasonal burning push particulate levels above safe limits.		IndiaFranceRwandaWaste-burning smoke and an aging vehicle fleet make this a health issue for Lebanese towns, though no Lebanon air-quality source was found here.Vehicle emissions testing, low-emission zones, car-free days and electric two-wheelers.[1][2][3]
10Soil erosion, drought and land degradation
Steep slopes, drought and lost vegetation strip topsoil and dry out water supplies.		RwandaTunisiaFranceLebanon's terraced hills and post-fire slopes face the same erosion and drought pressures as Tunisia's dams and Rwanda's highlands.Terracing and agroforestry on slopes, catchment restoration, and public drought-restriction maps.[1][2][3]
Environment · Worth copying

14 ideas that worked somewhere

Payment for Ecosystem Services (FONAFIFO)Costa Rica

Fuel-tax and water-fee revenue pays landowners on 5-10 year contracts to protect or replant forest; 1.16 million ha covered and cover rebuilt to about 57%. [1]

Umuganda monthly community work dayRwanda

Mandatory last-Saturday community service since 1995, with projects chosen locally; credited with clean streets and an estimated US$200m in value. [1]

Single-use plastic bag banRwanda

2008 ban with fines led to near eradication of polythene bags and better urban waste collection, per the World Bank ex-post review. [1]

Communal forest-fire committees (CCFF)France

Trained village volunteers patrol forests in summer to spot and report smoke early, acting as the 'eyes' of the fire service. [1]

Legal brush-clearing obligations (OLD)France

Owners must clear vegetation within 200 m of at-risk forests, enforced by mayors and prefects across about 7,400 communes. [1]

Ecological Blue Flag programmeCosta Rica

Low-cost certification since 1996 that rewards communities, beaches and schools for litter control, water quality and environmental education. [1]

Rwanda Green Fund (FONERWA)Rwanda

National climate fund financing 35 projects that created over 137,500 green jobs and 39,500 ha of forest and agroforestry. [1]

Car-free days and electric moto-taxi retrofitsRwanda

Kigali car-free days measurably cut pollution, and UNDP backs retrofitting petrol motorcycles to electric. [1]

Ecosystem-based erosion controlRwanda

Terracing, agroforestry and vegetation strips in hilly western catchments reduce landslides and soil loss. [1]

Community water-quality monitoringCosta Rica

Local volunteers monitor river quality to drive municipal action where treatment infrastructure lags. [1]

Public drought-restriction map (VigiEau)France

One national site shows each commune's current water-use limits, making restrictions enforceable and understood. [1]

Municipal climate adaptation rolesTunisia

Carnegie argues Tunisian municipalities can lead local adaptation despite centralised water and forest management. [1]

Miyawaki pocket forestsIndia

Dense native mini-forests planted by municipal corporations on small plots to cut urban heat; evidence mostly from practitioners. [1]

Rehabilitated Civil Defence centresLebanon

UNDP with KfW funding has rebuilt Civil Defence centres in priority areas such as Minnieh and the Beqaa since 2024. [1]

Roads & Traffic: 10 templates. Open one to read it.

1 Potholes and surface failure after rain
Why this one

Template 1: wet-season road surface repair

About a third of Lebanon's 6,500 km main road network is in fair to poor condition, and winter rain turns every open crack into a pothole by spring. Sealing before the rain costs a fraction of patching after it.

Step 1 · Classify

4 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Crack sealThe road is still sound but has open cracks, and the rains have not started.Rout or widen the crack, blow it clean and dry with compressed air, fill with hot-poured sealant, leave a thin flush overband.lm
Surface dressingThe road is grey, dry and finely cracked all over, but the base is sound.Sweep, spray bitumen emulsion binder, spread chippings, roll, sweep loose chippings after 24 hours.m2
Shallow patchAsphalt is gone in a patch but the base underneath is firm.Saw-cut a square, remove asphalt, prime coat, 5 cm binder course, tack coat, 5 cm wearing course, compact.m2
Deep patchThe hole keeps coming back, or water stands in it after digging out.Excavate to firm ground, 30 cm compacted base, prime, 5 cm binder, tack, 5 cm wearing course.m2
Step 2 · The milestones

6 milestones, each with the proof it needs and the check it must pass

#MilestoneEvidence the expert uploadsPass mark the verifier checks
0Scope and class
Walk the length with a tape and a 2 m straight edge. Measure each defect. Mark the treatment area on the road with chalk or paint. Choose one class per area.		Photo of every defect with the tape in frame showing depth and width. GPS pin for each. A one-page list of areas with class, length or area, and the date. Photo of the chalk lines.Every area has a class, a measurement and a GPS pin. Any pothole deeper than 40 mm and wider than 200 mm is a patch class, not a crack seal (threshold to confirm against a Lebanese or UK council spec). Deep patch needs a named engineer's signature before it is approved.
1Ownership, permit and traffic control
Confirm in writing who owns the road: the municipality, the Ministry of Public Works regional office, or CDR. Get the council decision or the ministry reference. Set out cones, signs and a lookout before anything is cut.		Scan of the council decision or ministry letter, with a named person and a date. Photo of cones, warning signs and the lookout in place, taken from a driver's eye view in each direction.A named authority, on paper, before work starts. Warning sign of at least 1 square metre, as CDR requires on its own maintenance lots. Traffic control visible in the photo before any cutting or spraying.
2Prepare and dry
For crack seal, rout and blow the crack clean and dry. For patches, saw-cut a rectangle down to sound material and remove all water and loose stone. For surface dressing, sweep the whole area.		Photo of each prepared area, close enough to see the edges. For patches, a photo showing straight vertical edges, no water and no loose material. Weather note: dry, and the road surface not wet.Patch edges are straight and vertical, not ragged. No standing water anywhere. Cracks are clean to the bottom. No work goes ahead on a wet surface, or within 24 hours of rain (the 24-hour wait is to confirm against the material data sheet).
3Materials on site
Photograph the delivery note and the material before it goes down. Record the mix type, the supplier and the quantity.		Photo of the delivery note or bag labels. Photo of the load or drum on site. Temperature reading of hot mix if used.Material matches the class chosen at milestone 0. Cold mix only where the scope says cold mix. Quantity delivered is within 15 per cent of the quantity the measured areas need (to confirm against the first real bids).
4Lay, compact and finish
Tack every face of a patch. Fill in layers, overfill, and compact with a plate compactor smaller than the patch. For dressing, spray, chip and roll. For crack seal, fill and strike off flush.		Photo of tack coat on all faces. Photo of the compactor sitting on the patch. Photo with a straight edge laid across each finished area. Time the road reopened.Finished surface sits between 3 mm below and 6 mm above the road around it, the as-laid tolerance used in the UK reinstatement specification. No dip. A bucket of water poured on it runs off and does not pool.
5Winter check
Come back after the first heavy rain, or 28 days after reopening, whichever is later. Photograph from the same spots as milestone 4.		Dated photos from the same positions. A short note on each area: intact, cracked, or failed. Photo of any water standing on the treated area.No area has sunk more than 10 mm below the road around it, the intervention limit the UK specification uses for a repair up to 400 mm wide. No new cracking at the edges. No pooling. This is the gate for the final payment.
Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Inspect within 5 working days of the certified request. Crack sealing and surface dressing must be finished before 15 November, because both need a dry, warm road and neither works in Lebanese winter rain. Patching can be done all year: within 7 days if the road is a main route or the hole is dangerous, within 28 days otherwise. Then the winter check, 28 days after reopening or after the first heavy rain, whichever comes later. Warranty runs 12 months from the winter check, so one full wet season is covered.

Money

Priced per linear metre for crack sealing and per square metre for dressing and patching, which is how CDR and the ILO both write their road maintenance bills of quantities. There is no public Lebanese unit rate: the CDR bill of quantities leaves the rate for bidders to fill in, in US dollars. Bracket from the first three real bids. Not included: full-depth reconstruction, kerbs, drainage, road markings, or any work outside the chalk lines agreed at milestone 0.

Release

Nothing up front. 20 per cent at milestone 1, when ownership is proved and traffic control is up, because that is real cost before any asphalt. 50 per cent at milestone 4, when the road is reopened and level. 30 per cent held until the winter check at milestone 5 passes. That retention mirrors the defects-liability holdback used on ILO labour-based road contracts in Lebanon.

Who signs off. The municipality must pass a council decision naming the road and the work. If the road is classified, the Ministry of Public Works and Transport regional office must agree in writing; CDR's own tenders say the ministry's regional offices coordinate with municipalities to pick and prioritise works. The Internal Security Forces traffic police should be told before any lane closure on a through route. A deep patch design needs an engineer registered with the Order of Engineers and Architects. If a water or power line is found in the excavation, stop and call the Water Establishment or Electricite du Liban before continuing.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Sealing a wet road. Bitumen will not stick to a damp surface, so the seal peels off in the first month and the water gets back in. Milestone 2, the dry-surface photo and the weather note.
  • Crack sealing a road that needs patching. Sealant poured into a hole hides a failed base and bills a cheap treatment for an expensive problem. Milestone 0, the depth measurement and the class rule.
  • Ragged edges on a patch. Filling the hole as found leaves weak, thin asphalt at the rim, which breaks out within weeks. Milestone 2, the straight vertical edges photo.
  • Compactor bigger than the patch. A roller wider than the hole rides on the old road and never compacts the new material. Milestone 4, the photo of the compactor sitting on the patch.
  • Work done after the rains start. Crack sealing and dressing carried out in December are money spent on a treatment that cannot bond, and nobody notices until spring. The 15 November date in the time rule, checked against the photo timestamps.
Sources
  • World Bank, Lebanon Roads and Employment Project feature, 2025 worldbank.org
  • Council for Development and Reconstruction, Roads Routine Maintenance Lots 1 to 8, request for bids, Lebanon, 2023 cdr.gov.lb
  • Council for Development and Reconstruction, Roads Routine Maintenance Lot 17, Aley and Chouf, bill of quantities, September 2023 cdr.gov.lb
  • Roadworks Scotland, Specification for the Reinstatement of Openings in Roads, 5th edition, 2023 roadworks.scot
  • Jordan Times, rain brings a curse for roads, on winter pothole damage jordantimes.com
  • L'Orient Today, road safety, a deadly summer on Lebanon's roads today.lorientlejour.com
2 Chronic maintenance underfunding
Why this one

Template 2: road condition survey and three-year preservation plan

About a third of Lebanon's 6,500 km main network is already in fair to poor condition, and municipalities lost most of their budgets after 2019. A municipality cannot spend its way out, so it has to know which roads to seal this year to avoid rebuilding them in five.

Step 1 · Classify

3 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Walking surveyThe network is under 10 km, or the roads are narrow village streets a vehicle cannot survey.Two people walk every road, record defects by type and severity on a form, photograph and GPS each one, score each section.km
Phone camera survey10 to 50 km of road, drivable, and the municipality wants a repeatable record.A phone on the windscreen films every road at a steady speed with GPS logging, then an engineer scores sections from the video and spot-checks on foot.km
Survey plus costed planThe municipality has money to spend and must decide where, not just know the condition.Any survey class above, plus a three-year plan that lists each section, the treatment, the year and the cost, and a proposed ring-fenced maintenance line in the budget.km
Step 2 · The milestones

6 milestones, each with the proof it needs and the check it must pass

#MilestoneEvidence the expert uploadsPass mark the verifier checks
0Scope and network list
List every road the municipality believes it owns. Give each one a section number, a start point and an end point. Measure the length and the average width.		A table of sections with numbers, names, start and end GPS points, length in metres and width in metres. A printed or screen map with the sections drawn on it.Every section has a number, two GPS points and a length. The total length matches the survey class being billed, within 5 per cent (tolerance to confirm). Any road the municipality is not sure it owns is flagged, not quietly included.
1Survey method agreed
Write down the scoring method before going out: which defects are counted, how severity is judged, and how a section score is calculated. Use a published method, not a private one.		A two-page method note naming the standard used, for example ASTM D6433 pavement condition index. A blank copy of the field form. Names and qualifications of the surveyors.The method is a published standard with a written reference, not the expert's own invention. The form has a place for defect type, severity, extent, photo number and GPS. At least one surveyor is an engineer registered with the Order of Engineers and Architects.
2Field survey
Survey every section listed at milestone 0. Photograph every defect that will drive a treatment decision. Record GPS with each photo.		Photo set with GPS, at least one photo per 100 m of road and one per recorded defect. The completed field forms. A daily log of which sections were done on which day.100 per cent of the listed sections covered, not a sample. Photo count is at least ten per kilometre. Every photo carries a GPS position and a date. The verifier picks three sections at random and walks them to check the recorded defects are really there.
3Scores and condition map
Turn the field data into one score per section and draw a map coloured by condition.		A spreadsheet with one row per section: score, main defect, and the treatment it points to. A colour map. A short note on how many kilometres fall in each condition band.Every section in the milestone 0 list has a score. The condition bands and their cut-off numbers are stated and come from the named standard (band cut-offs to confirm against the published ASTM D6433 tables). The map and the spreadsheet agree.
4Three-year plan and budget line
Rank the work by what stops a cheap problem becoming an expensive one. Put a treatment, a year and a cost against each section. Propose a fixed yearly maintenance line in the municipal budget.		A plan table: section, treatment, year, quantity, unit, estimated cost. A one-page summary the council can read. A draft budget line with a figure and a source of funds.Preservation treatments on sound roads come before reconstruction of failed ones, and the plan says in words why. Every cost is a quantity times a unit rate, with the rate source named. The yearly line is a number, not a promise.
5Council adoption and handover
Present the plan to the municipal council. Hand over the raw data, the photos and the map in a form the municipality can reopen next year without the expert.		Minutes or a decision of the council recording the plan was presented and what was decided. A copy of the data files and photos handed over, with a signed receipt. A one-page guide to repeating the survey.A dated council decision exists, whether or not it approves the money. Data is handed over in open formats the municipality can open, not locked inside a contractor's software. The photos are all there: the count matches milestone 2.
Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Start within 10 working days of the certified request. A walking survey should take about one working day per 2 km of road, a phone camera survey about one day per 10 km. Scores and the map within 15 working days of the last field day. The plan and the council presentation within 30 working days after that. The whole job should be finished in one season, and it must finish before the budget is set, or the plan has no effect for a year. Warranty is not a physical warranty here: the expert must correct any scoring or data error found within 90 days of handover at no cost.

Money

Priced per kilometre surveyed, with the plan and council presentation as a separate lump sum. There is no public Lebanese rate for condition surveys; bracket from the first three real bids. The cost of the survey should be small next to the works it directs, so the verifier should query any survey that costs more than a tenth of the works it plans (ratio to confirm). Not included: laboratory testing, core sampling, traffic counts, drainage design, or the works themselves.

Release

Nothing up front. 30 per cent at milestone 2, when the field survey is complete and the photos are uploaded. 40 per cent at milestone 4, when the plan and costs are delivered. 30 per cent at milestone 5, after the council has seen it and the data has been handed over and checked. Holding a third to the handover is what stops a survey ending as a PDF nobody can reuse.

Who signs off. A municipal council decision is enough to commission the survey. No ministry permit is needed to look at a road. But the Ministry of Public Works and Transport regional office should be sent the section list, because its regional offices already coordinate with municipalities to identify and prioritise works, and roads it owns should be marked as such rather than surveyed as municipal. If the survey covers a road inside a CDR maintenance lot, tell CDR so the same kilometre is not paid for twice. The Order of Engineers and Architects registration of the lead surveyor should be on file.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Sampling instead of surveying. A survey of the easy roads produces a plan that quietly leaves out the worst ones. Milestone 2, coverage checked against the milestone 0 section list and three random walked sections.
  • A private scoring method. If the method is not published, next year's survey cannot be compared with this one and the trend is lost. Milestone 1, the named standard.
  • Worst-first spending. Rebuilding the worst road uses the whole budget and lets ten sound roads slide into the same state. Milestone 4, the ranking must put preservation before reconstruction and say why.
  • Data locked in the contractor's system. The municipality cannot repeat or update the survey, so it pays again from zero in three years. Milestone 5, open-format handover with a signed receipt.
  • A plan with no budget line. A list of works with no yearly money behind it is a wish list, and the deferred maintenance keeps compounding. Milestone 4, the draft budget line must carry a figure and a source of funds.
Sources

  • Eastleigh Voice, Kenyan counties and the Roads Maintenance Levy Fund, on ring-fenced maintenance money and work plans eastleighvoice.co.ke
  • Cour des comptes, France, maintenance of national and departmental roads ccomptes.fr
  • France 3 Pays de la Loire, camera and AI road condition surveys for small communes france3-regions.franceinfo.fr
  • VNG, Dutch association of municipalities, on the local road maintenance backlog vng.nl
3 Blocked or missing road drainage
Why this one

Template 3: pre-winter road drainage clearing and culverts

On Lebanon's steep mountain roads and flat coastal strips, water that cannot leave the road takes the road with it. The ILO's labour-based programme has already built 4.3 km of storm water drainage in Mazboud and Aley for this reason, and CDR's own maintenance bills start with clearing roadway limits and drainage structures.

Step 1 · Classify

4 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Ditch and channel desiltingA side ditch or lined channel exists but is full of silt, rubbish or plant growth.Clear the channel to its original invert, remove and cart away the spoil, cut back vegetation, repair broken lining.lm
Gully and catch basin cleaningRoad gullies and their gratings are blocked, so water sheets down the carriageway.Lift the grating, empty the pot, rod the connection to the outfall, refit or replace a broken grating.each
Cross culvert, new or replacedWater crosses the road on the surface, or an existing pipe is crushed, undersized or silted solid.Excavate, lay pipe or box culvert to a fall, build headwalls and inlet and outlet aprons, backfill and compact, reinstate the road over it.lm
Removing an encroachmentA wall, ramp, shop front or fill has been built over a drain or ditch.Survey and record the encroachment, serve notice, demolish and cart away, rebuild the channel through the gap.each
Step 2 · The milestones

6 milestones, each with the proof it needs and the check it must pass

#MilestoneEvidence the expert uploadsPass mark the verifier checks
0Scope and class
Walk the road in the direction water flows. Mark every ditch length, gully, culvert and encroachment. Measure silt depth against the channel depth. Note where water crosses the road.		Photo of each item with a measuring staff or tape in frame showing silt depth and channel depth. GPS pin per item. A simple flow sketch with arrows showing where water enters and leaves. Class and quantity per item.Every item has a class, a quantity and a GPS pin. Silt depth is measured, not estimated. A channel is only a desilting item if silt fills more than a quarter of its depth (threshold to confirm). Anywhere water crosses the carriageway is a culvert item, not a desilting item.
1Ownership, permits and traffic control
Confirm who owns the road and the drain, and where the outfall goes. Get written permission for the discharge point if it is not public land. Set out traffic control before opening any excavation.		Council decision or ministry reference naming the road. A note naming the outfall owner and the permission. Photo of cones, warning signs and barriers in place in both directions.A named authority on paper. The outfall is named and legal. Nothing discharges onto a neighbour's land or into a watercourse without written consent. Warning signs and barriers visible before any digging, as CDR requires on its own maintenance lots.
2Clear, excavate and cart away
Desilt the channels, empty the gullies, excavate the culvert trench. Load the spoil and take it to an agreed tip, not the next field.		Before and after photo of every item from the same spot. Weighbridge tickets or numbered truck tickets for the spoil, with the tip named. Photo of the empty gully pot.Channel invert visible along the whole cleared length. Gully pot empty to the bottom. Spoil accounted for by ticket: the number of loads matches the volume removed, within 20 per cent (tolerance to confirm). No spoil tipped on a roadside or in a valley.
3Build and set the falls
Lay the pipe or box culvert to a steady fall. Build headwalls and aprons at inlet and outlet. Repair broken channel lining. Bed and surround the pipe as specified.		Photo of the pipe bedded in the trench before backfill, with a level or a string line in frame. Photo of the finished headwall and apron at each end. Delivery note for the pipe showing diameter and class.Pipe falls continuously from inlet to outlet, with no dip: a level or string line must show it. Diameter matches the design and the delivery note. Headwall and apron at both ends. Minimum gradient and design storm return period to confirm against a Lebanese or regional drainage standard before scoping.
4Backfill, reinstate and flow test
Backfill in compacted layers and reinstate the road surface over the trench. Then pour water in at the inlet and watch the outlet.		Photo of each compacted backfill layer before the next one goes on. Photo of the reinstated road with a straight edge across it. Video of water poured in at the inlet and running out at the outlet.Water reaches the outlet and runs clear, in the video, in one take. Reinstated surface sits between 3 mm below and 6 mm above the road around it, the as-laid tolerance in the UK reinstatement specification. No loose backfill visible.
5First storm check
Return after the first heavy rain of the season, or 60 days after completion, whichever comes first. Photograph the same points and record where water stands.		Dated photos from the same positions as milestone 0. Photo of any standing water on the carriageway, with a ruler in it. A short note per item: flowing, partly blocked, or failed.No standing water deeper than 25 mm on the carriageway at any treated point (depth to confirm). Every cleared channel still carries water along its whole length. No trench line has sunk more than 10 mm, the UK intervention limit for a repair up to 400 mm wide. This is the gate for the final payment.
Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Inspect within 5 working days of the certified request. Desilting and gully cleaning must be complete before 15 November, because after that the first storm arrives and the work is being done in a flood. Culverts take longer and should start no later than 1 September. Where a road already floods and a house or a school is at risk, treat it as an emergency: inspect within 48 hours and clear within 7 days. The first storm check follows, and the warranty runs 12 months from that check so one full wet season is covered.

Money

Desilting is priced per linear metre, gullies per unit, culverts per linear metre of pipe laid, encroachment removals per unit. CDR and the ILO both bill drainage clearing this way in Lebanon. No public Lebanese unit rate is available: CDR's bill of quantities leaves the rate to the bidder, in US dollars. Bracket from the first three real bids. Not included: a full catchment study, a new storm sewer network, pumping stations, land purchase, or compensation to the owner of an encroachment.

Release

Nothing up front. 20 per cent at milestone 2, when the channels are cleared and the spoil tickets are in, because clearing and carting is where the real labour cost sits. 50 per cent at milestone 4, when the flow test passes. 30 per cent held until the first storm check at milestone 5. Holding almost a third until it has actually rained is the only honest test of a drain.

Who signs off. The municipality passes a council decision. If the road is classified, the Ministry of Public Works and Transport regional office must agree in writing. If the outfall runs to a watercourse or the sea, the Ministry of Environment and the relevant Water Establishment should be informed before work, and their reference recorded at milestone 1. Removing an encroachment needs a formal municipal notice to the owner and, in practice, the qaimaqam's backing; do not start demolition without the paper. Spoil must go to a tip the municipality names. If the excavation exposes a water main or an Electricite du Liban cable, stop and call the Water Establishment or EDL.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Silt moved, not removed. Spoil pushed onto the verge washes straight back into the channel with the first rain, and the municipality pays twice. Milestone 2, the truck tickets and the named tip.
  • A culvert laid flat or backfalling. A pipe with no fall silts up within a season and behaves like no pipe at all. Milestone 3, the level or string line photo, and the milestone 4 flow test.
  • No outlet, or an outlet onto someone's land. Water taken off the road has to go somewhere; if nobody agreed where, the work creates a new flood and a dispute. Milestone 1, the named and consented outfall.
  • Work signed off in August. A dry channel always looks clean. Without a wet-weather check nobody knows whether it drains. Milestone 5, the first storm check, which is why 30 per cent is held.
  • Trench over the culvert left soft. Badly compacted backfill sinks into a trough across the road and becomes the next pothole complaint. Milestone 4 layer photos and the milestone 5 sunken-trench check.
Sources

  • Roadworks Scotland, Specification for the Reinstatement of Openings in Roads, 5th edition, 2023 roadworks.scot
  • Petra news agency, Greater Amman Municipality one kilometre stormwater culvert before winter, 2026 petra.gov.jo
  • Kenyans.co.ke, Ombudsman seven-day notice to KURA on drainage and potholes, December 2024 kenyans.co.ke
  • Observer Research Foundation, the monsoon verdict on India's road infrastructure orfonline.org
4 Dead traffic signals during power cuts
Why this one

Template 4: keeping one junction signalled through a power cut

Lebanon's daily Electricite du Liban cuts leave junctions unsignalled for hours, and reactivating the broken traffic lights and cameras of Greater Beirut is one of the few concrete items the Traffic Safety Committee named when it met again in 2025 after years of inactivity. A signal that dies with the grid is not a signal.

Step 1 · Classify

4 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Battery back-up onlyThe junction has a working controller and mains that comes back within a few hours.Uninterruptible power supply, battery bank in a ventilated cabinet, automatic transfer, flash-mode fallback, labels and a test log.each junction
Solar and batteryMains is off for most of the day, or there is no reliable supply at all.Solar panels, charge controller, larger battery bank, LED heads to cut the load, mounting and anti-theft fixings.each junction
LED conversion plus back-upThe junction still runs filament lamps, so any battery would be drained in minutes.Replace every signal head with LED, then fit the back-up sized to the new, lower load.each junction
Maintenance contractHardware exists and works, but nobody repairs it when it fails.Named responder, response time, spares held, monthly test and battery check, a public fault number.each junction per year
Step 2 · The milestones

6 milestones, each with the proof it needs and the check it must pass

#MilestoneEvidence the expert uploadsPass mark the verifier checks
0Scope, load and outage profile
Measure what the junction actually draws, count the heads and their type, and record the real power-cut pattern over at least seven days.		Photo of every signal head and the controller cabinet, inside and out. A table of heads by type and wattage. A seven-day log of when mains was on and off, with times. Photo of the meter or clamp meter reading.Total load in watts is measured, not assumed. The outage log covers at least seven consecutive days and shows the longest single cut. The chosen class matches: if the longest cut is longer than the battery can cover, it is a solar class, not a battery-only class.
1Permission and design
Get the municipality and the traffic authority to agree the junction, the design and who will hold the keys. Have an engineer size the battery and, if used, the solar array against the measured load and the longest cut.		Council decision naming the junction. Written agreement from the Internal Security Forces traffic branch or the body running the signals. A one-page sizing calculation signed by an engineer registered with the Order of Engineers and Architects. Equipment specification sheets.The sizing calculation shows load in watts times hours against battery capacity, with the numbers visible. It covers the longest cut in the milestone 0 log, not an average. A named person holds the cabinet key. The specification requires at least two hours of full running as an absolute floor, the minimum in the New York State DOT traffic signal battery back-up item; Lebanon needs far more, so the design hours come from the outage log.
2Install
Fit the back-up, the batteries and any solar array. Label every cable. Fix the cabinet so it cannot be opened or the batteries stolen.		Photo of the open cabinet showing the installed unit and the labelled wiring. Photo of the battery bank with model and capacity readable. Photo of the solar array and its fixings. Serial numbers of every item, photographed.Serial numbers recorded and match the delivery notes. Battery capacity on the label matches the milestone 1 calculation. Cabinet locked, vented, and fixed so the batteries cannot be lifted out in a minute. No cable left unlabelled.
3Live cut test
Switch the mains off at the junction and let it run on back-up while somebody times it. Then let it fall to flash mode and time that too.		Video showing the mains switched off and the signals still running, with a clock in frame. Timed photos at the start, at each hour, and at the moment the signals drop to flash. The recorded run time in hours and minutes.Full signal running lasts at least as long as the design hours from milestone 1, and never less than two hours. The change from mains to battery does not blank or reset the signals. Flash mode starts automatically when the batteries run low and does not leave the junction dark.
4Handover, training and fault number
Hand over to the municipality: keys, manuals, spares list, and a written fault procedure with a phone number residents can ring.		Signed handover sheet listing keys, manuals and spares. Photo of the training session with the names of who attended. The fault number, printed on the cabinet, photographed. A blank monthly test log.At least two named municipal staff have been trained, and both sign. The fault number is fixed to the cabinet and rings a real person when the verifier tries it. Spares held on site include at least one spare LED head and one set of fuses.
5Ninety-day check
Come back after three months of real Lebanese power cuts. Repeat the cut test and read the test log.		Video of a repeat cut test with a clock in frame. Photo of the completed monthly test log. Photo of the battery voltage reading. A note of every fault in the ninety days and how long each took to fix.Run time is still at least 80 per cent of the run time recorded at milestone 3 (retention figure to confirm against the battery manufacturer's data). The test log has an entry for each month. Every fault in the period was fixed within the agreed response time. This is the gate for the final payment.
Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Inspect within 5 working days of the certified request; within 48 hours if the junction is already dark and a school or hospital is on it. Measure the outage profile over at least 7 days. Install within 30 days of the design being signed. Live cut test on the day of completion, not later. Handover within 5 working days after that. Then the ninety-day check. Warranty 24 months on the electronics and 12 months on the batteries, and the maintenance class runs for one year with a named response time, which should be 24 hours for a dark junction and 72 hours for anything else.

Money

Priced per junction for the hardware classes and per junction per year for the maintenance class, so a municipality can buy one junction at a time. There is no published Lebanese rate: bracket from the first three real bids. As a warning of what the wrong shape of contract buys, Nairobi's traffic lights were reported installed at about KSh 1.4 billion and still not working. Not included: the controller itself if it is dead, signal poles, new cabling across the junction, road markings, or the electricity bill.

Release

Nothing up front. 40 per cent at milestone 2, when the equipment is installed and serial numbers are recorded, because the hardware is bought and paid for by then. 30 per cent at milestone 3, when the live cut test passes. 30 per cent at the ninety-day check. Paying nothing until a cut test has actually been run is the point: a back-up that has never been tested is a box in a cabinet.

Who signs off. The municipality passes a council decision. The body that operates the signals must agree in writing, which in Greater Beirut means going through the Internal Security Forces traffic branch and the Traffic Management Centre. Electricite du Liban must be told before anything is connected on the supply side, and its reference recorded. If the junction sits on a classified road, the Ministry of Public Works and Transport regional office must be informed. The design must be signed by an engineer registered with the Order of Engineers and Architects. Solar panels on a pole or a building may need the municipality's building permit branch to sign as well.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Battery sized from a guess. A unit rated for two hours in a country with twelve-hour cuts is dark for ten hours a day and looks like a working installation. Milestone 0 outage log against the milestone 1 sizing calculation.
  • No cut test. Nothing proves a back-up works except turning the mains off and watching. Paperwork does not. Milestone 3, the timed video.
  • Filament heads left in place. Old lamps draw several times what LEDs draw, so the batteries empty before the cut ends. Milestone 0, the head-by-head wattage table.
  • Batteries stolen. An unsecured cabinet with new batteries in it is a target, and the junction is dark again within weeks. Milestone 2 fixings photo and the milestone 5 ninety-day check.
  • Nobody owns the fault. Without a named responder and a number that rings, the first failure ends the project quietly. Milestone 4, the verifier rings the number, and milestone 5, the fault log.

5 Unsafe or missing sidewalks
Why this one

Template 5: one continuous walkable block

The World Health Organization has been reported as estimating pedestrians are close to 40 per cent of Lebanon's road deaths (to confirm), and Lebanese sidewalks are routinely parked on, cut by driveways or simply absent. The ILO has already built 7 km of sidewalk in Tripoli and 3 km in Jbeil, so the work is known and local crews can do it.

Step 1 · Classify

4 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Unblock and repairA sidewalk exists and is the right width, but is broken, or blocked by parked cars, poles, bins or shop displays.Relay or replace broken tiles and kerbstones, move or protect obstructions, fit bollards against parking, repaint the kerb line.lm
Rebuild to widthThe sidewalk is there but too narrow, or steps and level changes break it up.Demolish and rebuild the footway to a continuous clear width and a steady level, new kerbs, new surface.lm
New sidewalkThere is no sidewalk and people walk in the traffic lane.Kerbs, base, surface, drainage falls, and dropped crossings at each end.lm
Crossing pointA walkable stretch exists but stops at a road people must cross.Dropped kerbs both sides, tactile warning surface, markings, warning signs, and sight-line clearing.each
Step 2 · The milestones

6 milestones, each with the proof it needs and the check it must pass

#MilestoneEvidence the expert uploadsPass mark the verifier checks
0Scope and class
Walk the block end to end pushing a pram or a wheelchair. Measure the narrowest clear width every 10 m. Record every level change, every obstruction and every place the sidewalk stops.		Photo at each measuring point with a tape across the clear width. Photo of every obstruction and every step, with a ruler against it. GPS pins. A table of chainage, clear width, and defect. A video of the whole walk, filmed at walking pace.Clear width is measured between real obstructions, not kerb to wall. Every level change over 6 mm is recorded. The block has a start and an end that both connect to somewhere people actually go: a school, a shop, a bus stop, a clinic. A block that starts and ends nowhere is rejected here.
1Permission, utilities and traffic control
Get the council decision. Check with the Water Establishment, Electricite du Liban and Ogero for anything buried in the footway. Agree what happens to the parking the bollards will stop. Set out traffic control.		Council decision naming the block. Written replies or dated records of contact from each utility. A note of the parking spaces lost and what the council decided about them. Photo of barriers and signs in place.All three utilities contacted, with dates, before any breaking out. The parking question is answered in writing by the council, not left to the crew on the day. Pedestrians have a marked, protected route past the works, not a walk in the traffic lane.
2Build the route
Lay kerbs to a line and a level. Build the base and the surface. Keep the walking surface at a steady cross fall so water runs off but the surface is not tilted.		Photo of the kerb line with a string line in frame. Photo of the base before surfacing. Delivery notes for kerbstones and tiles. Photo of a spirit level or digital level on the finished cross fall, reading visible.Continuous clear width of at least 1,220 mm along the whole block, the minimum in the US Public Right-of-Way Accessibility Guidelines. Cross slope no more than 2.1 per cent. Length-ways slope no more than 5 per cent except where the street itself is steeper. Where the clear width is under 1,525 mm, a passing space of 1,525 mm by 1,525 mm at least every 61 m.
3Crossings and dropped kerbs
Build a dropped kerb and a tactile warning surface at each end of the block and at every side road crossed. Paint the crossing and put up the signs.		Photo of each dropped kerb with a level or a digital inclinometer on the ramp, reading visible. Photo of the tactile surface with a tape showing its depth. Photo of the painted crossing and the signs.Ramp running slope no more than 8.3 per cent. Tactile warning surface at least 610 mm deep in the direction of travel. The ramp lands flush with the road: any lip over 6 mm fails. Every side road crossed has a dropped kerb on both sides, not one.
4Obstruction removal and bollards
Move or protect every obstruction recorded at milestone 0. Fit bollards or kerb protection where cars park on the footway.		Before and after photo of every obstruction from the same spot. Photo of the bollards in place, with a tape showing the gap between them and the clear width they leave. A list of anything that could not be moved, and why.Every milestone 0 obstruction is moved, protected or explained in writing. Bollards leave at least 1,220 mm clear between them and any wall or pole. Nothing new has been planted in the walking route: a bin, a pole or a tree pit inside the clear width fails.
5Walk test and handover
Walk the whole block again, pushing a wheelchair or a pram, with a municipal representative and at least one resident who uses it daily. Film it in one take.		One continuous video from one end of the block to the other, with the wheelchair or pram visible and no cuts. Signed note from the municipal representative and the resident. Photo set matching the milestone 0 positions.The wheelchair or pram goes the full length without leaving the footway, lifting over anything, or stopping. One take, no edits. Both signatures present. Any point where the pusher had to step into the road fails the whole block.
Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Inspect within 10 working days of the certified request. Build within 60 days for one block, and do it in sections so the block is never fully closed to walkers. Crossings and dropped kerbs are finished in the same visit as the footway either side of them, never left for a later contract. Warranty 24 months on kerbs and paving, 12 months on bollards and painted crossings. A follow-up walk test at 12 months, with the same resident if possible.

Money

Priced per linear metre of footway by class, and per unit for crossings. CDR already bills sidewalk repair including tiles and kerbstones as a maintenance item, and the ILO builds sidewalk by the kilometre in Lebanon, so the unit is familiar to Lebanese contractors. There is no published Lebanese unit rate; bracket from the first three real bids. Chile's participatory pavement programme is worth copying on funding: neighbours form a committee, save a share, and the state pays the rest, on projects between 100 and 1,000 m. Not included: street lighting, tree planting, drainage beyond the footway falls, land purchase, or compensation for lost parking.

Release

Nothing up front. 20 per cent at milestone 1, when permissions and utility checks are done, because that is the part contractors skip. 50 per cent at milestone 3, when the footway and its crossings are built and measured. 30 per cent at milestone 5, after the walk test passes with a resident present. The walk test holds the last third because a sidewalk that measures right and still cannot be walked is the normal failure here.

Who signs off. A municipal council decision naming the block. The Water Establishment, Electricite du Liban and Ogero must each be asked about buried services before breaking out, and their answers kept. If the street is a classified road, the Ministry of Public Works and Transport regional office must agree. Removing or relocating a pole needs EDL or Ogero in writing. Cutting a tree needs the municipality's agreement and, for protected species, the Ministry of Agriculture. Shopfront encroachments need a formal municipal notice served on the owner before anything is removed. The design should be signed by an engineer registered with the Order of Engineers and Architects.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • A sidewalk that stops. A beautiful 80 m of footway that ends at a driveway with no dropped kerb forces the same walk in the traffic lane. Milestone 5, the one-take wheelchair video.
  • Width measured kerb to wall. The usable width is between the pole, the bin and the parked car, and it is always less than the drawing says. Milestone 0 and milestone 2, clear width measured between real obstructions.
  • Poles and bins put back in the middle. A rebuilt footway with a pole planted in the walking line is no better than the broken one. Milestone 4, the clear-width check after the obstruction work.
  • A ramp with a lip. A 30 mm step at the bottom of a dropped kerb stops a wheelchair completely, and it is invisible in a photo taken from standing height. Milestone 3, the flush check, and the milestone 5 walk test.
  • Cars parked on it the next week. Without bollards or enforcement the new footway becomes the new car park and the money is gone. Milestone 4 bollard spacing and the 12-month follow-up walk.

6 Faded markings and missing signage
Why this one

Template 6: remark and re-sign one route

Lebanese streets lose their lane lines to wear and their light to power cuts at the same time, so at night a driver has no cues at all. CDR already carries road marking, catseyes, warning signs and delineators as ordinary maintenance items, which means the work is buyable today.

Step 1 · Classify

4 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Paint remarkingA short route, low traffic, or money only stretches to one season of life.Sweep, pre-mark, apply road marking paint with glass beads, keep traffic off until dry.lm
Thermoplastic remarkingA main route, a junction approach, or anywhere the marking has to survive a year of traffic.Sweep, pre-mark, apply hot thermoplastic with beads, including stop lines, arrows and crossings.lm for lines, m2 for blocks
Sign inventory and replacementSigns are missing, turned, faded, or hidden behind growth.Photograph and GPS every sign on the route, score each one, replace or clean or re-aim, cut back the vegetation in front of it.each
Catseyes and delineatorsThe route is unlit, has bends, or a drop at the edge.Reflective road studs along the line, and roadside delineator posts on bends and embankments.each

A retroreflectivity reading on existing markings, if a meter is available.Both videos exist, cover the whole route, and the night one is filmed on dipped headlights. Every item in the table has a chainage and a GPS pin. Where a meter was used, the reading and the instrument are named; where none was, the entry says so rather than guessing.

Every proposed sign matches the Lebanese traffic code in force; a sign that is not in the code is removed from the scope here, not put up and argued about later. Any change to priority, to a crossing position or to a speed limit is approved in writing by the traffic authority, not by the contractor.
2Prepare the surface
Sweep and clean the line. Remove old loose marking. Pre-mark the new line with chalk or a string line and have it checked before laying anything permanent.		Photo of the swept surface. Photo of the pre-marked line along a straight and through a bend. Weather note: surface dry, temperature recorded.Surface dry and clean, no dust line visible under the pre-mark. The pre-marked line is straight where the road is straight; a wandering pre-mark means a wandering marking. Work stops if the road surface is wet or the air temperature is below the material's stated minimum.
3Apply markings
Lay the lines, stop lines, crossings and arrows. Apply glass beads as the material goes down, not afterwards.		Photo of the material's delivery note and batch label. Photo of a wet-film or thickness gauge on a fresh line, reading visible. Photos of each line type. Photo of the bead dispenser working.Material matches the class bought. Line width matches the agreed plan within 10 mm (tolerance to confirm against the adopted marking specification). Beads are applied during laying, visible in the photo. 4Signs and studs
Fit or replace the signs at the agreed positions and heights, aimed at the driver. Fit the studs and delineators. Cut back anything growing in front of a sign.		Photo of each sign from a driver's eye view in the approach lane, plus a photo of its post foundation before backfill. Photo of each stud or delineator run at night with headlights on. GPS pin per sign.Every sign in the milestone 1 plan is up, and no sign that is not in the plan has appeared. Each sign is readable in the driver's-eye photo from the approach. No branch or pole blocks it. Studs are in line and all of them light up in the night photo.
5Night acceptance and twelve-month check
Drive the route again after dark on dipped headlights, in one take. Then repeat the drive twelve months later.		One continuous night video of the whole route, same as the milestone 0 night drive. Retroreflectivity readings at ten points if a meter is available, with the instrument named. The same again at twelve months.Every line, stop line and sign is visible on dipped headlights in the video, with no dark stretch longer than 50 m (the 50 m figure is a working rule, to confirm). Where a meter is used, white longitudinal markings read at least 100 mcd per square metre per lux, the higher of the two minimum maintained values in the US federal standard; that is a deliberately strict target for an unlit Lebanese road. Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Inspect within 10 working days of the certified request. Mark and sign within 45 days. Do not apply marking on a wet road or below the material's minimum temperature, which in the Lebanese mountains rules out much of the winter. Night acceptance on the night of completion. Then the twelve-month night check. Warranty: markings 24 months on a main route and 12 months on a village street, signs 60 months against fading, both from the night acceptance date. The UK reinstatement specification uses a two-year guarantee for road markings, which is the floor used here.

Money

Lines are priced per linear metre and blocks such as crossings and arrows per square metre; signs, studs and delineators per unit. That is how CDR's own bill of quantities lists road marking, catseyes, warning signs and delineators. No published Lebanese unit rate exists; bracket from the first three real bids. Not included: street lighting, traffic signals, guardrail, resurfacing, or any change to the speed limit or priority, which is a legal decision and not a marking job.

Release

Nothing up front. 20 per cent at milestone 1, when the layout is approved, because agreeing the layout is the work that prevents the expensive mistakes. 50 per cent at milestone 4, when markings, signs and studs are all in place. 30 per cent at the night acceptance and held through it. If the twelve-month night check fails, the expert remarks the failing sections at their own cost under the warranty.

Who signs off. A municipal council decision for a municipal street. For a classified road, the Ministry of Public Works and Transport regional office must approve the layout. Any change to a speed limit, a priority, a one-way or a pedestrian crossing position needs the traffic authority and, in practice, the Internal Security Forces traffic branch in writing. Signs must follow the Lebanese traffic code. Lane closures should be notified to the traffic police. Traffic control during the work must use at least the temporary warning signs, barriers and cones CDR specifies for its own maintenance lots, including a warning sign of at least one square metre.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Beads thrown on afterwards. Beads scattered on a set line sit on top and sweep away in a month, so the marking looks fine by day and vanishes at night. Milestone 3, the photo of the dispenser working during laying.
  • Marking a dirty or damp road. Paint and thermoplastic do not bond to dust or water, and the line lifts off in sheets by spring. Milestone 2, the swept-surface photo and the weather note.
  • Signs nobody can see. A sign behind a tree, turned away from the driver, or set too low is money spent on a sign that does not exist. Milestone 4, the driver's-eye photo from the approach lane.
  • Inventing signs and lines. A crossing or a priority marking put in without approval creates a legal trap and municipal liability after a crash. Milestone 1, the approved plan, and the milestone 4 rule that nothing outside the plan may appear.
  • Day-only acceptance. Markings are for the dark. A daytime inspection cannot tell a reflective line from a painted one. Milestone 5, the one-take night video on dipped headlights.
