7 Uncontrolled speed bumps
Why this one

Template 7: speed bump audit, rebuild and removal

Lebanese villages and informal contractors build bumps at will, often unpainted, unsigned and far too tall. France has about 450,000 bumps and roughly four in ten are reported to be illegal, which is what happens when nobody audits them; a Lebanese municipality that audits first is ahead of that.

Step 1 · Classify

4 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Audit onlyThe municipality does not know how many bumps it has or who built them.Find, measure, photograph and GPS every bump in the area, score each one against the standard profile, and produce a keep, rebuild or remove list.each
Mark and sign an existing bumpThe bump measures within the standard profile but is invisible, unpainted or unsigned.Clean, paint the warning markings, fit the warning sign on each approach, add delineation if unlit.each
Rebuild to profileThe bump is in a sensible place but the wrong shape or height.Cut out the old bump, rebuild to the standard profile with a proper leading edge and surface, then mark and sign it.each
Remove and reinstateThe bump is in a banned place, too close to a junction or bend, on a bus or ambulance route, or duplicates another.Break out the bump, reinstate the road surface level, make good the drainage line.each
Step 2 · The milestones

6 milestones, each with the proof it needs and the check it must pass

#MilestoneEvidence the expert uploadsPass mark the verifier checks
0Find and measure every bump
Drive and walk the area. For every bump, measure height at the crown, length along the road, and width across the road. Note the road type, the speed limit and what is within 50 m either side.		For each bump: a photo with a straight edge across the road and a ruler standing on it showing the height, a photo along the road showing the length, a GPS pin, and a photo of each approach from a driver's eye view. A table of the measurements.Height measured with a straight edge spanning the bump, not a ruler on the slope. Every bump in the area is in the table, including the ones residents built. Each row records the road type, the posted speed limit and the distance to the nearest junction, bend or bus stop.
1Score against the standard
Compare each bump with the standard profile and decide: keep, mark and sign, rebuild, or remove.		A scored table with one line per bump and the decision. A one-page note of the standard used, with its reference. Photos of the worst three and the best three as examples for the council.The standard is named and written down, not remembered. Using the French NF P 98-300 profile as the reference: a round-top bump 10 cm high plus or minus 1 cm and 4 m long plus or minus 20 cm; a flat-top bump 10 cm high plus or minus 1 cm with a plateau of 2.5 to 4 m and ramps sloping 7 to 10 per cent; and on both, a leading edge under 5 mm with no tolerance. Any bump over 11 cm is a rebuild or a remove, never a keep. Lebanon has no published bump standard, so the municipality must adopt one by decision (Lebanese reference to confirm).
2Council decision and notice
Take the list to the council. Get one decision that adopts the standard and approves the keep, rebuild and remove list. Tell residents before removing anything.		The council decision, dated, listing the bumps by number. Photo of the public notice posted on or near each bump to be removed, with a date. A record of objections received.One dated decision covering the standard and the list. Every bump to be removed carried a notice for at least 14 days before removal (notice period to confirm against Lebanese municipal practice). Objections are recorded, whether or not they changed the decision.
3Rebuild and remove
Break out the bumps on the remove list and reinstate the road level. Cut out and rebuild the bumps on the rebuild list to the standard profile, set square across the road and across its full width.		Before and after photo of each bump from the same spot. Photo of a straight edge and ruler on each rebuilt bump showing the finished height. Photo of a straight edge across each removed bump's position showing the road is level. Delivery notes for materials.Every rebuilt bump measures within the profile chosen at milestone 1, checked with the straight edge in the photo. It runs square across the road and across the full carriageway width, with no gap at the kerb for a motorbike to slip through. Every removed bump leaves a surface within 6 mm of the road either side, the as-laid tolerance in the UK reinstatement specification. Water still runs along the channel and does not pond against a bump.
4Mark, sign and light
Paint the warning markings on every bump that stays. Put a warning sign on each approach. Where the street is unlit, add reflective studs or a reflective strip.		Photo of each bump from a driver's eye view on each approach, by day and after dark on dipped headlights. Photo of each sign with its post. GPS pin per sign.Every retained bump is visible in the night photo from a normal approach. A warning sign on every approach, readable from the driving lane. No bump left unmarked: an unmarked bump after this milestone fails the whole batch, because it is the one that breaks a car and creates a claim.
5Register handover and twelve-month check
Hand the municipality a register of every bump with its photos, measurements, decision and date. Repeat the night drive twelve months later.		The register, in a file the municipality can open and edit, with a signed receipt. A night drive video at twelve months covering the same bumps. A note of any new bump that has appeared.The register lists every bump found at milestone 0 with its outcome, and the count matches. At twelve months every retained bump still measures within the profile and still shows its markings. Any new unapproved bump is recorded, which tells the municipality whether the audit changed anything or not.
Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Inspect and audit within 20 working days of the certified request: a municipality of a few thousand people has tens of bumps, not hundreds. The council decision should follow within 30 days. Rebuilds and removals within 60 days of the decision. Marking and signing on the same day the bump is finished, never later, because an unmarked new bump is more dangerous than the old one. Then the twelve-month night check. Warranty 24 months on the rebuilt profile and the reinstated surface, 12 months on the markings.

Money

Priced per bump for each class, which lets a council do ten this year and ten next. CDR's Lebanese maintenance bills already carry speed calming measures as an item, so contractors know the work. There is no published Lebanese unit rate; bracket from the first three real bids. For scale only, French installation costs have been reported from about 5,000 euros for a simple cushion to about 100,000 euros for a full raised plateau with signage, which is a useful reminder that a plateau is a junction project, not a bump. Not included: raised junctions, new crossings, speed limit changes, or enforcement.

Release

Nothing up front. 30 per cent at milestone 1, when the audit and the scored list are delivered, because the audit has value on its own even if no bump is touched. 40 per cent at milestone 3, when rebuilds and removals are measured and pass. 30 per cent at milestone 4, after the night photos prove every retained bump is visible, held through to the register handover at milestone 5.

Who signs off. A municipal council decision is the core document: it adopts the standard and approves the list, and it is what protects the municipality if a driver later claims for damage. If the road is classified, the Ministry of Public Works and Transport regional office must approve any bump on it; a municipality cannot put a bump on a ministry road. The Internal Security Forces traffic branch should be told about removals and new signs. Ambulance, fire and bus operators using the route should be consulted before a bump is retained on their line. The profile and the layout should be signed by an engineer registered with the Order of Engineers and Architects.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Height measured off the slope. A ruler stood on the ramp reads less than the true height, so a 15 cm bump passes as a 10 cm one. Milestone 0, the straight edge spanning the bump with the ruler standing on it.
  • Bumps built without a standard. Without an adopted profile every dispute is an opinion, and the municipality carries the liability. Milestone 1, the named standard, and milestone 2, the council decision that adopts it.
  • A gap at the kerb. A bump that stops short of the kerb invites motorbikes to swerve round it at speed, straight through where pedestrians walk. Milestone 3, the full carriageway width check.
  • Water ponding against the bump. A bump laid across the drainage line dams the gutter and creates a puddle that freezes or hides a pothole. Milestone 3, the drainage check, and the wet-weather view at milestone 5.
  • Unmarked and unsigned. An invisible bump breaks suspensions and puts riders over the handlebars, and it is the municipality that gets sued. Milestone 4, the night driver's-eye photo on every approach.

8 Poor-quality works and unrestored utility cuts
Why this one

Template 8: road cut permit and trench reinstatement

Water, sewer, power and telecom crews dig up Lebanese streets and leave the trench behind, and CDR's own maintenance bills include milling and overlaying failed pavement over utility trenches, which is the municipality paying to fix somebody else's hole. The leverage is a permit with a deposit and a guarantee, not a complaint afterwards.

Step 1 · Classify

4 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Permit and register onlyThe municipality has no record of who digs what, and wants to start controlling it.A permit form, a deposit scale, a public register of open cuts, and a standard reinstatement specification adopted by council decision.each municipality

Permanent reinstatementA trench has been left as temporary fill, or a past cut has sunk.Saw-cut back to sound road, remove the fill, replace and compact in layers, bound base and surface courses, seal the joints, remark any lines crossed.m2 or lm for trenches under 1 m wide

6 milestones, each with the proof it needs and the check it must pass

#MilestoneEvidence the expert uploadsPass mark the verifier checks
0Scope, class and the register entry

Photo into the open trench showing the service inside it, if visible. GPS pin. A register entry: street, position, utility, permit number if any, dates.Every cut has a width, a length and a GPS pin. Each one names a utility, or says clearly that the utility is unknown. Cuts under 1 m wide are measured per linear metre, which is how CDR's own bill of quantities separates narrow trenches. 2Cut back and excavate
Saw-cut the edges back into sound, unbroken road, past any cracking around the old trench. Remove the temporary fill completely. Keep the sides vertical and supported.		Photo of the saw-cut rectangle with straight vertical edges, dry and empty. Photo showing the cut line is outside the cracked zone. Photo of any trench support. Lay the bound base and the surface course to the same thickness as the road around it. Tack every face. Seal the joint all round. Reinstate any road marking crossed.		Photo of tack coat on all faces. Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Inspect an open or reported cut within 3 working days, and within 24 hours if it is unguarded or in a walking route. A utility must complete permanent reinstatement within 6 months of the interim fill, and sooner on a main road. No new cut should be permitted in a street resurfaced in the last 3 years except for an emergency, and a no-dig window through the rainy season, roughly 15 November to 15 March, keeps crews from opening roads they cannot properly close. Guarantee 24 months as a minimum and 6 years as the target, with inspections at 6 and 24 months.

Money

Permanent reinstatement is priced per square metre, or per linear metre for trenches under 1 m wide, which matches the way CDR's Lot 17 bill of quantities separates narrow trenches. The permit and register class is a lump sum per municipality; the backlog survey is per cut. There is no published Lebanese unit rate; bracket from the first three real bids. The permit deposit should be set at the full estimated cost of the municipality doing the reinstatement itself, so that walking away is never the cheap option; the deposit scale is a council decision and should be reviewed each year against real rates. Not included: the utility's own pipe or cable work, service connections, or road resurfacing beyond the cut.

Release

Nothing up front. 30 per cent at milestone 2, when the cut is squared and excavated, because that is the part a contractor is tempted to skip. 40 per cent at milestone 4, when the surface is laid, level and sealed and the road is open. 20 per cent at the 6-month inspection. 10 per cent at the 24-month inspection. A long tail is the whole point here: trenches fail late, and the money has to still be there when they do.

Who signs off. The municipality issues the road cut permit and holds the deposit. The permit must name the utility, the dates, the length and width, and the reinstatement specification. The Water Establishment, Electricite du Liban and Ogero each dig in municipal streets and each must hold a permit, not a phone call. On a classified road the Ministry of Public Works and Transport regional office issues or co-signs the permit and the municipality is only informed. The Internal Security Forces traffic branch should be told of any lane closure. Emergency repairs to a burst main or a live cable may start first, but the permit must follow within 24 hours. The reinstatement specification the municipality adopts should be signed off by an engineer registered with the Order of Engineers and Architects.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Spoil put back as backfill. The material that came out is loose, wet and wrong, and the trench settles into a trough within one winter. Milestone 3, the delivery notes and the layer photos.
  • No layer photos. Compaction is the one thing that cannot be checked after the fact. If it was not photographed layer by layer, it was not done. Milestone 3, layer count times thickness against trench depth.
  • Edges broken out, not saw-cut. A ragged edge on cracked road gives the new work nothing to bond to, and the trench line reopens as two parallel cracks. Milestone 2, the straight vertical saw-cut photo.
  • Temporary fill left for years. Cold fill in a trench is a pothole with a start date, and without a recorded interim date nobody can prove how long it has been there. Milestone 1, the recorded interim date and the six-month deadline.
  • Deposit released too early. Trenches look perfect on the day they are finished. They fail in the second winter, after the money has gone. Milestone 5, deposit released only after the 24-month inspection.

Where records are missing, the note says so instead of filling the gap with a guess.
1Site inspection, day and night
Walk and drive the site in daylight and after dark. Measure sight distance from a driver's eye height. Record speeds if a meter is available. Note what the crash pattern has in common.		Video of each approach by day and by night on dipped headlights. Photos of the sight line from driver's eye height, with the obstruction visible. Measured sight distance in metres. Speed readings with the instrument named, or a note that none was taken. A one-page diagnosis: what kind of crash keeps happening and why.The diagnosis names one or two mechanisms and matches the crash pattern in the milestone 0 table. Sight distance is measured, not estimated. Night video exists: many Lebanese black spots are dark, not badly shaped. Where no speed meter was used, the report says so.
2Treatment chosen and approved
Pick the low-cost treatments that address the diagnosis. Get the road owner and the traffic authority to approve them in writing. Do not design a new road.		A treatment plan with a drawing or an annotated aerial image, listing each item and its position. Written approval from the road owner. Sign-off from an engineer registered with the Order of Engineers and Architects. An expected effect for each item, with the source of the figure.Every treatment traces back to the diagnosis at milestone 1. Each claimed effect names its source; for example the iRAP road safety toolkit puts the potential casualty reduction from properly designed and maintained roadside barriers at 40 to 60 per cent, with a treatment life of 10 to 20 years. Crash reduction figures for rumble strips and chevrons to confirm before they are used in a business case. Any change to a speed limit is approved by the traffic authority, in writing, before work starts.
3Clear and install
Cut back the growth and remove the obstructions first, because that is often the cheapest fix. Then install barriers, chevrons, signs, studs and markings.		Before and after photos of the sight line from driver's eye height, from the same spot. Photo of each barrier run including both end treatments, with a tape showing the length. Photo of the post foundations before backfill. Delivery notes for the barrier and the signs. GPS pins.Sight distance after clearing is measured again and is longer than at milestone 1, by a stated amount. Barrier runs have proper end treatments at both ends: a barrier that simply stops is a spear, and it fails here. Barrier length and offset from the traffic lane match the approved plan. Where iRAP's guidance on leaving room in front of a continuous barrier cannot be met, the report says so and explains.
4Night acceptance
Drive every approach after dark on dipped headlights, in one take per approach. Check that every new sign, chevron and stud does its job.		One continuous night video per approach. Photos of each chevron board and sign from the driving lane at night. A short note of anything not visible.Every chevron, sign and stud is visible on dipped headlights from the point where a driver still has time to react. No dark stretch longer than 50 m inside the site (the 50 m figure is a working rule, to confirm). Anything not visible is fixed before this milestone passes, not listed as a snag.
5Twelve-month crash review
Twelve months later, collect the crash records for the site again from the same sources, and compare.		The updated record table with the same sources and the same format. A short comparison note: crashes before and after, by severity. Photos from the milestone 3 positions showing the treatments still in place and undamaged.The comparison uses the same sources and the same site boundary as milestone 0, or it proves nothing. Every treatment is still standing and still reflective. Damaged barrier is repaired before this milestone passes. The comparison is reported honestly even when the numbers did not move: one year at one site is a small sample, and the register matters more than the headline.
Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Inspect within 10 working days of the certified request, and within 48 hours where a death has just happened at the site. Mapping within 30 days. Clearing sight lines within 30 days of approval, because it is cheap and fast. Barriers, signs and markings within 90 days. Night acceptance on the night of completion. Then the twelve-month crash review. Warranty 24 months on barriers and posts, 24 months on markings, 60 months on signs against fading. Barriers damaged in a crash must be repaired within 14 days of the municipality reporting them, for the whole warranty period.

Money

Barriers are priced per linear metre, signs and chevrons and studs per unit, mapping and village speed management as a lump sum per site. CDR already bills concrete safety barriers, delineators and warning signs as maintenance items in Lebanon. There is no published Lebanese unit rate; bracket from the first three real bids. Sight line clearing is usually the cheapest item on the list and should be priced and done first. Not included: realigning the road, widening, new street lighting, land purchase, or enforcement.

Release

Nothing up front. 20 per cent at milestone 2, when the diagnosis and the approved plan are delivered, because a wrong diagnosis wastes everything after it. 50 per cent at milestone 4, after the night acceptance. 30 per cent at the twelve-month review, released on the treatments still being in place and the review being done honestly, not on the crash count falling. Paying for a fall in crashes would pay for a small sample and reward hiding data.

Who signs off. Most Lebanese black spots are on classified roads, so the Ministry of Public Works and Transport regional office is usually the owner and must approve the treatment plan; the municipality alone cannot install a barrier on a ministry road. Where the road is a CDR maintenance lot, CDR must be told. Any speed limit change needs the traffic authority and the Internal Security Forces traffic branch in writing. Crash data has to be requested formally from the security forces, and the request and the reply should be kept as evidence. Cutting vegetation on private land needs the owner's written consent or a municipal notice. The plan must be signed by an engineer registered with the Order of Engineers and Architects.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • A site picked from one bad crash. One terrible crash is not a pattern, and treating it spends the budget where the next crash is least likely. Milestone 0, three years of records from two sources and a real cluster.
  • Treatment that does not match the diagnosis. A guardrail on a site where the crashes are pedestrians at night fixes nothing and looks like action. Milestone 2, every item traced to the milestone 1 diagnosis.
  • Barrier with no end treatment. A barrier that starts or ends square to the traffic is a solid object aimed at drivers, and it can kill people the barrier was meant to protect. Milestone 3, the photo of both ends with the tape.
  • Daytime-only acceptance. Most of these sites are dark. Chevrons and studs that look fine at noon can be invisible at 9 at night. Milestone 4, the one-take night video on each approach.
  • No before and after comparison. Without the same sources and the same boundary, the twelve-month numbers can be made to say anything. Milestone 5, same sources, same boundary, same format.
Sources
  • LBCI, Lebanon's road accident casualties near an annual record in seven months, 2025 lbcgroup.tv
  • World Bank, Lebanon Roads and Employment Project feature, 2025, crash fatalities down more than 20 per cent on upgraded routes worldbank.org
  • iRAP Road Safety Toolkit, roadside safety barriers toolkit.irap.org
  • European Transport Safety Council, on Dutch data for 50 km/h roads where cyclists and cars mix etsc.eu
  • Global Road Safety Facility, burden of road traffic injuries in Jordan globalroadsafetyfacility.org
  • Council for Development and Reconstruction, Roads Routine Maintenance Lot 17, Aley and Chouf, bill of quantities, September 2023, safety barriers and delineators cdr.gov.lb
10 Fragmented responsibility for who fixes what
Why this one

Template 10: road ownership register for one municipality

Lebanese roads split between the Ministry of Public Works and Transport, CDR and the municipality, and CDR's own tender papers say the ministry's regional offices coordinate with municipalities to pick the works. Until a request can name the owner of the road, no fix can be matched, funded or verified.

Step 1 · Classify

3 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Desk registerThe municipality has maps and decrees but nothing pulled together.Collect the classification decrees, CDR lot boundaries and municipal decisions, and build one table of every road with its owner and the document that proves it.each municipality
Desk plus field registerThe paperwork is incomplete or contradicts what is on the ground.The desk work, plus walking or driving every road to check the limits, record the surface type and photograph the boundary points where ownership changes.km
Register plus escalation mapThe municipality wants to act, not just know.The register, plus a one-page route for each owner: who to write to, at which office, with what reference, and how long they have to reply before the municipality escalates.each municipality
Step 2 · The milestones

6 milestones, each with the proof it needs and the check it must pass

#MilestoneEvidence the expert uploadsPass mark the verifier checks
0Scope and road list
List every road inside the municipal boundary. Give each one a number, a name, a start point and an end point. Measure its length.		A table of roads with numbers, names, start and end GPS points and lengths. A map with every listed road drawn. The municipal boundary shown, with the source of the boundary named.Every road inside the boundary is listed, including unnamed lanes and agricultural tracks. Lengths add up to a total the municipality accepts. The boundary comes from a named official source, not from memory.
1Collect the proof
Gather the documents that decide ownership: classification decrees for ministry roads, CDR maintenance lot boundaries, municipal council decisions, and any handover records.		A scanned file per document, named and dated. A log of every request made to the ministry regional office, to CDR and to the muhafaza, with the date sent and the date answered. Copies of replies.Every request is logged with a date, including the ones nobody answered, because an unanswered request is itself a finding. Documents are scanned and readable. No road is assigned an owner on a phone call alone; a verbal answer is recorded as verbal and flagged.
2Field check the limits
Drive or walk the roads and find the points where ownership actually changes: the end of the ministry road, the edge of a CDR lot, the start of the municipal street. Photograph and pin each one.		Photo of each boundary point in both directions, with a GPS pin. Photo of any sign, marker or change in construction that shows the limit. A note of every place the ground contradicts the paperwork.Every ownership change point on the network has a GPS pin and two photos. Contradictions between paper and ground are written down, not smoothed over. The verifier picks three boundary points at random and finds them where the register says they are.
3Build the register
Turn it all into one table: road number, name, length, owner, the document that proves it, the confidence level, and the date last checked.		The register, in an open file format the municipality can edit. A short note on how confidence was judged. A list of the roads where ownership is still disputed or unknown.Every road from milestone 0 appears, and the count matches. Each row names the proving document, or says the ownership is unknown. Confidence is marked on every row. A register with no unknowns is suspect and should be questioned: in Lebanon there are always some.
4Escalation routes
For each owner, write one page: the office, the named post to write to, the reference to quote, the reply time to expect, and what the municipality does if nobody replies.		One page per owner: Ministry of Public Works and Transport regional office, CDR, the muhafaza or qaimaqamiya, the Water Establishment, Electricite du Liban, Ogero. A template letter for each. The reply deadline the municipality adopts.Each page names a real office and a real post, not just an institution. Each carries a reply deadline the council has adopted by decision. Chile's recent reform, reported as cutting the approval window from 180 days to 90, is a useful model for what a deadline is for; the Lebanese deadline is the council's choice and must be written down.
5Council adoption, publication and handover
Take the register to the council for adoption. Publish it so residents and experts can see who owns which road. Hand over the files and show a municipal staff member how to update a row.		The dated council decision adopting the register. A screenshot or photo of the published register, on the municipal noticeboard or a website. A signed handover receipt for the files. Names of the staff trained.A dated council decision exists. The register is publicly visible in at least one place a resident can reach. At least one named municipal employee can open the file and change a row while the verifier watches. The unknown and disputed list is published too, not hidden.
Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Start within 10 working days of the certified request. Desk collection within 30 days, allowing for slow replies; the log of unanswered requests is part of the product, so slow replies do not stop the clock. Field checking at about one working day per 10 km. Register and escalation pages within 20 working days of the last field day. Council adoption at the next ordinary session. The register must be reviewed and re-dated every 12 months, and the expert should hand over a one-page method for doing that without them.

Money

Priced as a lump sum per municipality for the desk and escalation classes, and per kilometre for the field check. There is no published Lebanese rate for this work; bracket from the first three real bids. It should be one of the cheapest projects on the platform and one of the first, because every other road request depends on it. Not included: legal action over a disputed road, land survey or cadastral work, road condition assessment, or any repair.

Release

Nothing up front. 30 per cent at milestone 2, when the field check is complete and the boundary points are pinned. 40 per cent at milestone 3, when the register is delivered with its proving documents. 30 per cent at milestone 5, after the council adopts it, it is published, and a municipal employee has shown they can update it. The last third is tied to publication and training because a register nobody can see or edit stops being true within a year.

Who signs off. No permit is needed to build a register, but the work depends on formal requests. Write to the Ministry of Public Works and Transport regional office for classification decrees and its list of roads. Write to CDR for its maintenance lot boundaries, since CDR runs road maintenance lots across cazas and those boundaries decide who pays. Write to the muhafaza or qaimaqamiya for the municipal boundary. The Water Establishment, Electricite du Liban and Ogero should each be asked for their own contact point, because they appear on every road cut. The council decision adopting the register is the document that gives it force inside the municipality.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Ownership recorded from a phone call. A verbal answer cannot be shown to the ministry a year later, and the road quietly becomes nobody's. Milestone 1, the proving document per row, and the verbal flag.
  • Unanswered requests dropped. The silence is the finding. Deleting it makes the register look complete and hides the real blockage. Milestone 1, the request log including the ones with no reply.
  • A register with no unknowns. A tidy table with an owner for every road is usually guesswork, and guesswork is what stalls repairs. Milestone 3, the unknown and disputed list.
  • Paper limits never checked on the ground. Decrees describe roads that were widened, rerouted or renamed decades ago, so the paper boundary is often not where the road changes. Milestone 2, the boundary point photos and the three random checks.
  • Never published. A register kept in a drawer does not help a resident, an expert or a verifier decide who to write to, which was the whole point. Milestone 5, publication and the staff member updating a row on camera.
Sources
  • Council for Development and Reconstruction, Roads Routine Maintenance Lot 17, Aley and Chouf, bill of quantities, September 2023, ministry regional offices coordinating with municipalities cdr.gov.lb
  • Council for Development and Reconstruction, Roads Routine Maintenance Lots 1 to 8 over 13 cazas, request for bids, Lebanon, 2023 cdr.gov.lb
  • World Bank, Lebanon Roads and Employment Project feature, 2025, the 6,500 km main road network worldbank.org
  • Government of Chile, new law to speed up emergency repair of holes in streets and pavements gob.cl
  • El Pinguino, bill to make it easier for municipalities to repair streets elpinguino.com
  • Banque des Territoires, the French audit court fears a fragmentation of road maintenance responsibility banquedesterritoires.fr

Waste Collection: 10 templates. Open one to read it.

1 Open and uncontrolled dumps
Why this one

Template 1: closing and rehabilitating one open dump

Lebanon has over 1,000 unlicensed dumps on record, and one national survey mapped 617 of them. They leak, they catch fire and they are usually the nearest waste site to a village, so closing one is the single job that changes most for the people next to it.

Step 1 · Classify

4 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Class A: clean-up onlySmall site, mostly rubble and construction waste, under about 500 cubic metres, no burning, no leachate, no smell.Sort what is there, haul it to a licensed site, level the ground, fence it, put up a sign.m3 of material removed
Class B: consolidate and cap in placeMixed household waste of roughly 500 to 5,000 cubic metres, no spring, well or river within 100 m, ground not steep.Push the waste into one body, shape the slopes, cover with compacted low-permeability soil then growing soil, seed it, fit passive gas vents, fence it.m2 of capped surface
Class C: cap with gas and leachate controlOver about 5,000 cubic metres, or the site burns, smells or leaks a dark liquid.Everything in class B plus a cut-off drain around the site, a leachate collection sump, more gas vents, a surface water ditch, and twelve months of monitoring.m2 of capped surface
Class D: excavate and relocateThe dump sits in a river bed, on a steep slope, in a sinkhole or over a spring, so it cannot be left where it is.Dig out all the waste, haul it to a licensed site, restore the channel or the slope, replant.tonne removed
Step 2 · The milestones

7 milestones, each with the proof it needs and the check it must pass

#MilestoneEvidence the expert uploadsPass mark the verifier checks
0Scope and class
Walk the whole site. Measure it. Dig one test pit to find how deep the waste goes. Measure how far it is to the nearest house, school, well, spring and river. Choose the class.		GPS pin at each corner of the waste. Photos from four sides and, if possible, from a drone or a long pole. Photo of a tape measure standing in the test pit. Area in m2 and a volume estimate in m3. Photo of the nearest house, water point and school with the distance written on the note.Area, depth and volume are recorded. Distance to the nearest house, water point and school is recorded. A class is chosen. A site with a spring, well or river within 100 m cannot be class B (to confirm).
1Permission, ownership and destination
Find out who owns the land and who is allowed to close the site. Get the council decision. Inform the Ministry of Environment. Agree in writing where every load of waste will go.		Council decision number and date. Copy of the letter to the Ministry of Environment. Land title or a map extract. Written acceptance from the licensed site that will receive the waste.There is a named authority for the closure. There is a named legal destination for every tonne that leaves. No machine moves before both are on file.
2Stop the inflow
Close the site to new waste before anything else. A gate, a ditch or a line of blocks, one controlled way in, a sign in Arabic, and a named keyholder with a phone number.		Photos of the closed access, the sign and the ditch, all with GPS. Name and phone number of the keyholder. A dated photo of the tipping face on day 0 and again on day 7.Only one controlled way in. The sign is readable from the road. The day 7 photo shows no fresh waste on top of the day 0 heap.
3Fires out, hazards removed, waste shaped
Put out any smouldering fire, including fire under the surface. Pull out gas cylinders, batteries, health-care waste and anything that looks like asbestos and hand them to a licensed handler. Push the rest into one body with even slopes.		Photos before and after shaping from the same spots. Receipts or handover notes for every hazardous item. A temperature reading taken by hand in the heap, photographed with the reading visible.No smoke and no flame anywhere on the site. The heap has a flat top and side slopes no steeper than 1 in 3 (to confirm). The hazardous handover notes match the items in the photographs.
4Cap, vent and drain
Lay the cover in layers and compact each layer. Build the gas vents. Cut the surface water ditch so rain runs away from the cap, not into it. For class C, build the cut-off drain and the leachate sump.		Delivery notes for the soil. Photo of a ruler standing in a test hole in the finished cap showing each layer. Photo of every vent with its GPS pin. Photo of the ditch running downhill. For class C, photo of the sump with a dipstick.At least 45 cm of compacted low-permeability soil plus 15 cm of growing soil on top (to confirm). Top slope between 3 and 5 per cent so water runs off and does not pond (to confirm). At least one passive gas vent for every 2,500 m2 of cap (to confirm). The ditch carries water away from the cap.
5Restore, fence and hand over
Seed or plant the cap. Finish the fence. Put up the permanent sign. Hand the keys and a one-page site routine to the municipality.		Photos of the planting and the whole fence line. List of what was planted. Signed handover note from the municipality naming the keyholder.The fence has no gaps a person or a pickup can use. A bucket of water poured on the cap runs off and does not pond. Planting is in the ground and the handover note is signed.
6Six-month check
Come back after six months of weather and traffic and look at the same things again.		Photos from the same spots as milestone 5, dated at least 180 days after handover. Photo with a tape measure of any crack, hole or slip. Photo of the ditch. For class C, photo of the leachate sump and the vents.No new waste anywhere on the site. Ground cover growing over at least 70 per cent of the cap (to confirm). No crack in the cap wider than 25 mm (to confirm). No gullies cut into the slopes. No dark liquid leaving the site. This is the gate for the final release.
Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Inspect within 10 working days of the request. Finish class A within 30 days, class B within 60 days, class C and class D within 120 days. Then the six-month check, and for class C one more check at twelve months. One part must not wait for the rest: stopping the inflow at milestone 2 is cheap and it stops the dump growing while the money and the permits are being arranged, so it is due within 14 days of the council decision whatever the class.

Money

Priced per m2 of finished cap for classes B and C, per m3 removed for class A, and per tonne removed for class D. Haulage is a separate line priced per tonne-kilometre, because the distance to a licensed site changes the price more than the work does. No public Lebanese rate; bracket from first real bids. As a sanity check only, Lebanon's solid waste disposal has been costed at about 154.50 US dollars per tonne against 22.80 in Jordan, and one Lebanese operator has quoted 62 dollars per tonne. Not included: hazardous waste treatment, land purchase, compensation to the landowner, and any monitoring after twelve months.

Release

Nothing up front. 20 per cent at milestone 2, once the site is shut to new waste and the day 7 photo proves it. 50 per cent at milestone 5, capped, fenced, planted and handed over. 30 per cent held until the six-month check at milestone 6 passes. For class C, half of that last share is held further to the twelve-month check.

Who signs off. The municipal council decides first. The Ministry of Environment must be informed, and for class C and class D must approve. The Ministry of Interior and Municipalities covers the council decision. The regional water establishment must be told if the site is near a well, spring or river, and the Litani River Authority inside that basin. The Order of Engineers and Architects stamps the design for class C and class D. The Ministry of Public Health is informed if health-care waste is found. The receiving landfill operator must accept the waste in writing before it leaves. On state land or near the shore the relevant ministry, and on the coast the army, must be informed.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Cap spread too thin. A thin cover looks the same in a photograph taken from above, but rain goes straight through it and the leachate keeps running. The ruler standing in a test hole at milestone 4.
  • Waste capped where it should have been moved. A dump in a river bed or on a steep slope that is capped in place will wash out in the first heavy winter, and then it is in the water instead of on the ground. The distance and slope measurements at milestone 0, which rule out class B.
  • No gas vents. Buried waste makes methane. With no way out it kills the planting, lifts the cap and can set the site alight from inside. The vent count and GPS pins at milestone 4.
  • Fresh waste back within a month. If nothing stops the trucks, the dump restarts on top of the new cap and the whole job is wasted. The day 7 photo at milestone 2 and the six-month check at milestone 6.
  • Hazardous items buried with the rest. Gas cylinders explode, batteries poison the ground, and health-care waste injures the people doing the work. The handover receipts at milestone 3, checked against the photographs.
Sources
  • Enmaeya, Lebanon's waste crisis returns amid limited solutions and funding, 2025. Over 1,000 unlicensed dumps, waste 65 per cent organic and 25 per cent recyclable, three sorting plants working. enmaeya.com
  • Human Rights Watch, Lebanon: waste crisis posing health risks, December 2017. 617 uncontrolled dumps mapped, 77 per cent of waste openly dumped or landfilled. hrw.org
  • Human Rights Watch, Lebanon: huge cost of inaction on trash crisis, June 2020. 154.50 dollars per tonne in Lebanon against 22.80 in Jordan, 420 million dollars a year, 85 per cent to dumps or landfill. hrw.org
  • EcoMENA, Solid waste management in Jordan. Al Ghabawi at about 3,000 tonnes a day, 21 working landfills and 7 closed sites, gas collection by cell. ecomena.org
  • World Bank, Indonesia: improvement of solid waste management, environmental and social assessment, 2019. Dump closure and engineered cell practice. documents1.worldbank.org
  • World Bank, Lebanon marine litter baseline survey, 2021. 73 possible new disposal sites near perennial rivers since 2017. blogs.worldbank.org
2 Open burning of waste
Why this one

Template 2: stopping open burning at a named site

Human Rights Watch mapped 617 open dumps in Lebanon and found more than 150 of them burning at least weekly, with open burning in Mount Lebanon up 330 per cent after the 2015 collapse. Three of the burning sites they visited were beside schools.

Step 1 · Classify

3 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Class A: household burning in a neighbourhoodThere is no single site. People burn bags in yards, on street corners and on empty plots. Almost always a collection gap.House-to-house survey, restored collection round, bins, notices, follow-up visits.household
Class B: burning at one dumpOne site, one set of users, burnt either by the site operator to make room or by scavengers.Put the fire out, close the access, name a keyholder, set a watch roster, post notices, ninety days of monitoring.each site
Class C: burning of one streamTyres, cable, farm plastic or health-care waste burnt for the metal inside or to clear land.Trace where the stream comes from, open a drop-off or buy-back point for it, set a posted price, issue enforcement notices.tonne of the stream taken in
Step 2 · The milestones

6 milestones, each with the proof it needs and the check it must pass

#MilestoneEvidence the expert uploadsPass mark the verifier checks
0Scope and class
Find the fires, not the complaints. Walk the area and pin every burn scar. Measure each one. Start a simple watch log.		GPS pin on each burn scar. Photo of a tape measure laid across each scar. Photo of the ash and of what did not burn, which shows what is being burnt. Distance to the nearest home, school and clinic. Seven days of a log with date, time and whether smoke was seen, signed by a named watcher.At least seven dated log entries. Every scar pinned and its size in m2 recorded. Nearest school, clinic and home distances recorded. A class chosen. Any scar within 100 m of a school or clinic is treated first (to confirm).
1Find the reason
Ask people why they burn, on one short form, and pull the municipality's collection records for the last thirty days.		At least 20 completed forms, each asking: do you have a bin, when was the last collection, who burns, what do they burn. Copy of the collection records or the contractor's trip sheets for 30 days.At least 20 forms on file. The reason is written in one sentence and matches the class chosen. If more than half the forms say there was no collection in the last 7 days, this is class A whatever the site looks like.
2Remove the reason
Restore collection, or open the drop-off point, before any fine is mentioned. People with nowhere to put waste will keep burning it.		Route map with collection days. Photos of new or repaired bins with GPS pins. Weighbridge tickets or a counted load tally for the first two weeks. For class C, photo of the drop-off point with its posted price list.Every household on the route map is within 150 m of a bin or on a door-to-door round (to confirm). At least two collections happened in the first seven days. Tonnage or load count recorded for both weeks.
3Notice and warning period
Post the ban where people will see it and tell them out loud, before anybody is fined.		Dated photos of the notice in Arabic at the site and on the street. The council decision number quoted on the notice. Photos of the leaflet, or a note of the mosque and church announcement. List of people spoken to.Notices readable from 5 m away. A council decision number on the notice. A dated record of a warning period of at least 14 days before any fine is written (to confirm).
4Ninety-day watch
Watch the site for three months and record what happens, whether or not anything happens.		A weekly dated photo taken from the same fixed spot, marked on the ground at milestone 0. A log of every fire with time, scar size and what was burnt. Photo with a tape measure of any new scar.At least 12 weekly photos with no gap longer than 10 days. Total new burnt area at least 80 per cent smaller than the area measured at milestone 0 (to confirm). No fire at all within 100 m of a school or clinic.
5Handover and standing routine
Hand the site, the log and a one-page routine to the municipality, with a named person and a phone number for reports.		Signed handover note naming the keyholder, the watcher and the reporting phone number. The complete log. A before-and-after photo pair taken from the same fixed spot.A named person with a working phone number. The log is complete. The final photo shows no fresh ash and no smoke. This is the gate for the final release.
Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Inspect within 5 working days of the report, and within 2 days if the burning is next to a school, clinic or home. Put out the fires and close the access within 14 days. Have collection or the drop-off running within 30 days. Then 90 days of watching. The warranty is that 90-day record: if burning starts again inside it, the expert returns at their own cost and the clock restarts.

Money

Class A is priced per household served for the first three months. Class B is priced per site as a flat sum, with the 90 days of watching listed as its own line so the municipality can see what that part costs. Class C is priced per tonne of the stream taken in, plus the buy-back price if there is one. No public Lebanese rate; bracket from first real bids. Not included: fines and court costs, treatment of hazardous waste found in the ash, health screening of residents, and any medical claim.

Release

Nothing up front. 30 per cent at milestone 2, once collection or the drop-off is running and two weeks of tonnage is on file. 30 per cent at milestone 3, once the notices and the council decision are in place. 40 per cent held until the 90-day watch at milestone 4 and the handover at milestone 5 both pass. If a fire is recorded in the last 30 days of the watch, the watch restarts and the last share is not released.

Who signs off. The municipal council decides the ban and any fine. The Ministry of Environment is informed; open burning already breaks Lebanese environmental law, so this is enforcement, not new law. The Ministry of Interior and Municipalities covers enforcement by the municipal police. The Internal Security Forces are brought in if the burning is organised or if staff are threatened. Civil Defence puts out a deep fire in buried waste. The Ministry of Public Health is informed if a school or clinic sits inside the smoke. The Ministry of Agriculture is informed where farm plastic or land clearing is the source.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Fines before collection. Fining people who have nowhere to put their rubbish does not stop the burning, it moves it to the middle of the night. Milestone 1 forces the reason to be written down, and milestone 2 must pass before milestone 3.
  • Fire out on the surface only. Waste fires burn under the surface for weeks and come back up somewhere else on the site. The temperature reading at milestone 3 of template 1 and the weekly photos here.
  • Photos from different spots each week. Two pictures taken from different angles prove nothing, and the site can look better without being better. The fixed spot marked on the ground at milestone 0 and used at milestones 4 and 5.
  • Counting complaints instead of burnt ground. Complaints fall when people give up complaining. Burnt area in m2 cannot be talked away. The scar measurements at milestone 0 compared with milestone 4.
  • Tyres and cable missed. These are burnt for the metal inside and make the worst smoke of anything on the site, so they need a buy-back, not a notice. The photo of what did not burn at milestone 0. Wire in the ash means class C, not class B.
Sources

  • Egypt Today, Egypt punishes open burning of waste, 2020. A ban backed by a penalty, for comparison. egypttoday.com
  • Lloyd's Register Foundation, Open burning of waste: a critical issue in Indonesia, global report. Why open burning follows collection gaps. lrfoundation.org.uk
  • Enmaeya, Lebanon's waste crisis returns amid limited solutions and funding, 2025. Over 1,000 unlicensed dumps. enmaeya.com
3 Uncollected waste and service gaps
Why this one

Template 3: restoring a collection round

Human Rights Watch found 77 per cent of Lebanon's waste openly dumped or landfilled, and municipalities outside Beirut were left to arrange collection with no money and no staff. Everything else in waste management depends on the truck turning up.

Step 1 · Classify

4 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Class A: bring binsStreets are wide enough for a truck and households will walk up to 150 m. The cheapest option.Shared bins on stands, a fixed route and timetable, washing the bins, repairing them.household served
Class B: door-to-doorNarrow streets, a camp or an old town centre, or the municipality wants sorting later. Costs more per household but the waste is cleaner.Bags or house bins, a small vehicle or a cart, a named collector per street, a fixed day and hour.household served
Class C: transfer pointThe nearest licensed site is more than about 30 km away, so small vehicles should not drive there.A hard surface with a wall and a drain, a skip or compactor, a supervisor, a record of every load in and out.tonne through the point
Class D: emergency clearanceWaste has already piled up for weeks and must be cleared before any routine can start.One-off clearance to a licensed site, disinfection of the spot, then straight into class A or B.tonne removed
Step 2 · The milestones

6 milestones, each with the proof it needs and the check it must pass

#MilestoneEvidence the expert uploadsPass mark the verifier checks
0Scope and class

A class chosen per street, not per town.

Signed contract or council decision naming the operator. Photo of each crew member's gloves, boots, high-visibility jacket and mask. Vehicle registration and a photo of the tipper or compactor.Every household on the map is on a named route with a named day. Every crew member has gloves, boots and a high-visibility jacket in the photo. The vehicle is licensed and its capacity is recorded.

Photo of the leaflet or a note of the announcement. A list of the streets covered.A notice on every street on the route map. The notice gives the day, the hour and a phone number for missed collections.
3First month running
Run the route for thirty days and record every trip, every weight and every miss.		Trip sheets or weighbridge tickets for every trip. A missed-collection log with street, date and reason. Photos of five fixed spots taken weekly, the same spots each week.At least 90 per cent of scheduled trips completed (to confirm). Tonnage recorded for every trip. Missed streets logged with a reason, not left blank.
4Coverage and capture check
Go back to the ground and check how much waste is really being caught, not how much the trucks say they carried.		A repeat walk of the same streets with photos from the five fixed spots. Tonnage collected is at least 80 per cent of the tonnage predicted at milestone 0 (to confirm). No pile larger than 1 m3 at any of the five fixed spots.

Complete trip sheets and the missed-collection log. Before-and-after photo pairs from all five fixed spots. A one-page routine covering route, hours, kit and what to do when the truck breaks down.The handover note is signed by the municipality. The logs are complete with no gap longer than 3 days. The after photos show no pile at any fixed spot. This is the gate for the final release.
Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Inspect within 10 working days. Class D emergency clearance starts within 5 days of the council decision, because waste sitting in the street is a health matter. Class A and B start collecting within 30 days of contract signature. Class C takes up to 90 days because it needs a surface and a drain. The month at milestone 3 and the check at milestone 4 sit inside the first 60 days of service. Warranty is the first three months of running to the timetable.

Money

Priced per household served per month for classes A and B, and per tonne through the point for class C. Class D is priced per tonne removed plus haulage per tonne-kilometre. No public Lebanese rate for a municipal round; bracket from first real bids. As a sanity check only, the old Beirut contracts ran at 152 to 157 dollars a tonne all-in, one Lebanese alternative operator quoted 62 dollars a tonne, and Lebanon's national figure has been put at about 154.50 dollars a tonne against 22.80 in Jordan. Not included: disposal or landfill gate fees, buying the vehicle, and fuel if fuel is bought by the municipality.

Release

Nothing up front, except that a vehicle mobilisation sum may be released against the registration document at milestone 1 if the council has agreed it in writing. 40 per cent at milestone 3, after a full month of trip sheets. 30 per cent at milestone 4, once coverage and capture are checked on the ground. 30 per cent at milestone 5 after handover, held for 30 days of running to the timetable.

Who signs off. The municipal council decision covers the service and the route. The Ministry of Interior and Municipalities covers the contract and any union of municipalities arrangement. The Ministry of Environment is informed and must approve a transfer point. The receiving landfill or sorting plant must accept the waste in writing. The Ministry of Public Health is involved for any camp or informal settlement on the route. The Ministry of Labour matters for the crew's papers, and every worker's right to the protective kit stands whatever their nationality. Traffic and parking changes on a main road need the Ministry of Public Works and Transport.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Trip sheets with no weights. A trip sheet proves a truck moved. It does not prove waste left the street. Without weights nobody can tell a full load from an empty one. The weighbridge tickets at milestone 3 and the comparison at milestone 4.
  • Bins put where the truck likes, not where people live. A bin 400 m uphill is a bin nobody uses, and the waste ends up burnt or in the valley. The 150 m walking rule checked against the GPS bin points at milestone 4.
  • Timetable never told to anybody. If households do not know the day, waste sits out for a week and dogs open the bags. The dated notice photos at milestone 2.
  • Crew with no gloves or boots. Cuts and needle-stick injuries are the normal injury in this work, and an unprotected crew is a claim waiting to happen. The kit photos at milestone 1, repeated without warning at milestone 4.
  • Collection restored, disposal not arranged. A round with no legal destination just moves the pile from the street to a new roadside dump. The written acceptance from the receiving site, required at milestone 1 before any collection.

4 No sorting at source, low recycling
Why this one

Template 4: household sorting at source

About 65 per cent of Lebanon's waste is organic and 25 per cent is recyclable, yet fewer than 5 per cent of households sort, the recyclable share in the bin fell from 45 per cent in 2017 to 25 per cent in 2021, and the real recycling rate was under 8 per cent in 2024. Everything that is not sorted at the door has to be sorted later, by hand, for more money.

Step 1 · Classify

4 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Class A: two streamsStarting from nothing. Dry recyclables in one bag, everything else in the other. The easiest rule to teach and the easiest to check.Two house bins or two coloured bags per household, a leaflet, a separate collection day for the dry stream, a place to store and bale it.household
Class B: three streamsThe municipality already has a composting site or a partner who takes organics, and class A has been running for at least six months.Class A plus a kitchen caddy for organics, more frequent organics collection, and a named destination for the organics.household
Class C: sorting point for a neighbourhoodFlats, camps or narrow streets where per-household bins will not work.A supervised drop-off with a roof, labelled containers, opening hours, a keeper and a weight record per stream.each point
Class D: small sorting centreThere are collected dry recyclables but nowhere to sort and bale them, so they lose value or go to the dump.A shed with a sorting table or belt, a baler, scales, protective kit, and a record of what goes in and what is sold.tonne through the centre

Find out what is actually in the bin before changing anything. Open and weigh a sample of bags and write down the shares. Photos of the proposed sorting or storage space.Shares recorded by weight for organics, paper, plastic, glass, metal and the rest. Total sample at least 200 kg (to confirm). Household count on file. A class chosen. A destination named for each stream before any bin is handed out.

Find who will take each stream and at what price, in writing, before asking a single household to sort. Sorted waste with no buyer becomes mixed waste again.		Signed letter or contract from each buyer with the price per tonne and the quality they will accept. For organics, the composting or biogas site's written acceptance. Photo of the storage space with its size in m2.Every stream in the class has a named buyer or destination in writing. A price per tonne on paper for at least the main dry stream. Storage big enough for four weeks of the expected dry tonnage (to confirm).
2Bins, leaflet and teaching
Hand out the bins or bags door to door, and explain the rule at the door rather than posting it. Keep the rule to one sentence per stream.		Signed distribution list with one line per household. Photo of the bin set and the leaflet. Photos of at least 10 door visits. The collection day for each stream is printed on the bin or the bag.

Collect the streams on separate days or in separate compartments, and weigh each stream every week. Never mix them in the same truck body.		Weekly weight per stream, with photos of the scale or weighbridge ticket. Photos showing the streams kept apart in the vehicle. A log of any week a stream was mixed and why.Eight weekly weights per stream on file. No week where the dry stream went to the same truck body as the rest. Dry stream tonnage rising or steady, not falling, from week 4 to week 8.
4Contamination and participation check

At least 30 bags opened and weighed, photos of the scale and of the wrong items. A count over at least 50 houses of who put the dry bag out on the dry day. Photos of the storage area and the bales.Wrong material in the dry stream no more than 10 per cent by weight (to confirm). At least 50 per cent of sampled households putting out the right bag on the right day (to confirm). Bales stored dry and off the ground.

A one-page account: tonnes diverted, money in, cost of collection, and the landfill fee avoided.Tonnes sold match tonnes collected minus what is still in store, within 10 per cent (to confirm). Invoices show a price per tonne. The account shows tonnes kept out of the landfill.
6Six-month handover
Hand over the round, the buyer contacts, the weights and the account, and check the shares again against the baseline.		A repeat sorting study on at least 200 kg, compared with milestone 0. Complete weight records. Signed handover note from the municipality. Before-and-after photos of the storage area.Dry stream captured at least 40 per cent of the recyclable material found in the baseline (to confirm). Records complete with no gap longer than two weeks. Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Inspect within 10 working days. Baseline study within 21 days. Buyer contracts within 45 days, and this is the step worth waiting for. Bins out within 60 days. Then eight weeks of separate collection, the contamination check in week 9 or 10, and the handover at six months. Warranty is the six-month record: if the dry stream collapses inside it, the expert comes back and repeats the door visits at their own cost.

Money

Priced per household for classes A and B, per point for class C, and per tonne through the centre for class D. Bins, caddies and leaflets are priced as one kit per household and listed separately from the service. No public Lebanese rate; bracket from first real bids. Sanity check only: Lebanese wholesale prices have been reported at about 200 dollars a tonne for plastic, down from 450, 80 dollars for paper, down from 110, and 200 for steel, down from 350, so sale income is real but small and swings hard. Not included: the baler and the shed for class D if the municipality has no building, transport to the buyer if the buyer does not collect, and the landfill fee for what is still left over.

Release

Nothing up front. 20 per cent at milestone 1, once every stream has a named buyer or destination on paper. 30 per cent at milestone 2 once the bins are signed for. 25 per cent at milestone 4 once contamination and participation are measured on the ground. 25 per cent held to the six-month handover at milestone 6. Bins delivered but not signed for do not release anything.

Who signs off. The municipal council decides the service and any sorting rule. Lebanon already has a decree that requires sorting at source, so this is enforcement of an existing duty. The Ministry of Environment approves a sorting centre and is informed of the scheme. The Ministry of Interior and Municipalities covers the contract. The Ministry of Industry matters if the centre counts as a workshop. The Ministry of Public Health is informed of any medical waste found in the sample. Export of baled recyclables goes through Lebanese Customs and needs the Ministry of Environment's papers.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Bins handed out before a buyer exists. Households sort for a month, watch the two bags go into one truck, and never sort again. Trust is spent once. Milestone 1 must pass before milestone 2, and milestone 3 checks the truck body.
  • Counting bins distributed as success. A bin in a yard is not a kilo diverted. The only real measure is weight per stream over time. The weekly weights at milestone 3 and the sale invoices at milestone 5.
  • Dry stream too dirty to sell. One wet nappy in a bag of cardboard ruins the bale, and the buyer rejects the load or cuts the price. The bag-opening check at milestone 4, with the 10 per cent limit.
  • Three streams from day one. Organics are heavy, smelly and need collecting twice a week. Asking for three streams before two work is how schemes die in month two. Class B is only available where class A has run six months, checked at milestone 0.
  • No account kept. Without tonnes, prices and avoided landfill fees on one page, the council cannot defend the budget line and drops it at the next crisis. The one-page account at milestone 5.

5 Weak municipal finances and cost recovery
Why this one

Template 5: waste cost audit and a ring-fenced waste account

The Independent Municipal Fund has run a deficit of more than 2 billion dollars as waste costs multiplied, about 70 per cent of Lebanese municipalities depend on that fund for 90 per cent of their income, and some waste contracts cost up to four times a municipality's yearly allocation. This is a governance job, so the smallest thing worth commissioning is an audit and a separate account, not a machine.

Step 1 · Classify

4 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Class A: cost audit onlyThe council does not know what waste actually costs it per tonne or per household. Almost always the starting point.Twelve months of invoices, deductions and fuel opened up, tonnes counted, cost per tonne and per household worked out, one page of findings.each audit
Class B: audit plus ring-fenced accountThe audit is done and the council wants waste money kept separate from everything else.Class A plus a separate budget line and bank account, a written rule on what may be paid from it, and monthly public reporting.each account
Class C: fee design and pilotThe council wants households or businesses to pay part of the cost and needs a fee people will actually pay.Ability-to-pay survey, fee options costed, a pilot on one neighbourhood, collection rate measured, exemptions written down.household in the pilot
Class D: contract reviewThere is a live collection or disposal contract and the council suspects it is paying for work that is not done.Contract read against delivered service, tonnage checked against weighbridge, penalty clauses listed, a renegotiation note.each contract

Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Inspect within 10 working days. Class A audit finished within 45 days of document access, and the clock only starts when the documents are handed over, not when the contract is signed. Class B account open within 30 days of the audit. Class C pilot runs three months before the final check. Class D contract review within 30 days. Warranty is a repeat of the cost table after twelve months, priced as a separate small job.

Money

Priced as a flat sum per audit for classes A, B and D, and per household in the pilot for class C. Price the audit on the number of months of documents, not on the size of the budget, so the expert is never paid more for finding a bigger number. No public Lebanese rate; bracket from first real bids. Not included: legal action against a contractor, debt restructuring, external financial auditing under Lebanese audit law, and anything that requires a licensed auditor's signature.

Release

Nothing up front. 30 per cent at milestone 2, once the cost table is tied to documents. 30 per cent at milestone 3, once the gap is stated as a number. 40 per cent held to milestone 5, publication and handover. Under no circumstances is any part of the fee a share of savings found, because that pays the expert to exaggerate.

Who signs off. The municipal council decides access to its own documents. The Ministry of Interior and Municipalities oversees municipal budgets and any new fee, and a new local fee normally needs its approval. The Court of Accounts has its own role over municipal spending and is not replaced by this audit. The Ministry of Finance matters for deductions taken at source from the Independent Municipal Fund. A licensed Lebanese auditor must sign anything presented as a statutory audit; this template is a management review and must say so on its cover.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Deductions at source left out. Much of the waste bill is taken straight out of the municipal fund before the money ever reaches the town, so a cost table built only from invoices can miss most of the spend. Milestone 2 requires deduction notices as well as invoices.
  • Contractor tonnage taken on trust. Payment per tonne with no weighbridge is payment per claim. The difference is often the whole margin. Milestone 1 states the gap between claimed and weighed tonnes as a number.
  • A fee designed with no survey. A fee nobody can pay collects nothing and costs political capital, and the council then refuses to try again. The 100-household survey and the three-month collection rate at milestones 4 and 5.
  • Findings never published. An audit in a drawer changes nothing. The public page is what makes the next council keep the account separate. The dated notice-board photo at milestone 5.
  • Paying the expert a share of what they find. It rewards a big headline number rather than a true one, and the numbers stop being usable. The release rule forbids it, and the verifier checks the contract at milestone 0.

A one-page table with a line per measure: organics, dry recyclables, construction rubble, better compaction and cover. Each with tonnes a year, cost a year and months of extra life. A note of what is assumed.Every line has tonnes, cost and months. The organics line matches the town's own organic share, which nationally is about 65 per cent. The total months of extra life is stated. Nothing is counted twice.
5Council decision and public statement
Take the numbers to the council, get a decision, and publish the months of life left. For class D, hold the open meetings and record every objection with an answer.		Council decision number and date. Photo of the published page on the notice board, dated. For class D, attendance lists, photos of the meetings, and a table of objections with a written answer to each.A council decision quoting the months of life left. The figure is published. For class D, at least two open meetings held, every objection recorded, and no objection left without a written answer.
6Twelve-month re-survey
Survey the same site again from the same markers and see whether the plan changed anything.		Repeat survey from the same fixed markers, same method. New remaining volume in m3. Twelve months of tonnage. Photos from the same fixed spots as milestone 3.Measured months of life left at least as good as the plan predicted, or the difference explained line by line. Diverted tonnage backed by weighbridge or sale records, not estimates. This is the gate for the final release.
Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Inspect within 10 working days. Survey within 30 days of permission. The four weeks of intake runs alongside it. Plan and costings within 60 days. Council decision within 90 days. Then the twelve-month re-survey. If the first survey shows under six months of life left, the plan is due within 30 days instead of 60, because at that point the town is already where Beirut was in 2015.

Money

Priced as a flat sum per site for class A, per site plus a per-tonne rate for the diverted streams in class B, per m3 of airspace saved for class C, and a flat sum for the class D study. No public Lebanese rate; bracket from first real bids. Sanity check only: Lebanon's disposal has been costed at about 154.50 dollars a tonne and the country spends about 420 million dollars a year on solid waste, so a month of extra landfill life is worth roughly a month of that town's disposal bill. Not included: buying land, building a new cell, environmental impact assessment for a new site, and compensation payments to a host community.

Release

Nothing up front. 30 per cent at milestone 2, once the space and the intake are both measured. 30 per cent at milestone 4, once the plan carries tonnes, cost and months on every line. 25 per cent at milestone 5 after the council decision and publication. 15 per cent held to the twelve-month re-survey at milestone 6. For class D, nothing is released at milestone 5 until every recorded objection has a written answer.

Who signs off. The municipal council or the union of municipalities that owns the site decides. The site operator must give written permission for any survey on the ground. The Ministry of Environment approves landfill operation, expansion and any new site, and an environmental impact assessment is required for a new site. The Council for Development and Reconstruction is involved where it built or funded the site. The army must be informed before any drone flight. The Order of Engineers and Architects stamps the survey and the drawings. The regional water establishment is consulted where groundwater is close, and the Litani River Authority inside that basin.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Capacity guessed from the gate log. Tonnes in do not tell you volume left, because compaction and cover change it by a large factor. Only a survey of the surface does. Milestone 1 requires a survey with a named method and a permanent marker.
  • No fixed marker for the next survey. Without a marker that can be found again, the second survey measures a different thing and the comparison means nothing. Milestone 1 requires at least one findable ground marker, used again at milestone 6.
  • Diversion counted twice. Cardboard counted in the recyclables line and again in the general reduction line makes the plan look twice as good as it is. The no-double-counting check on the table at milestone 4.
  • Vertical expansion treated as a solution. Piling higher on a full site bought Bourj Hammoud about three months and cost the goodwill of everyone living below it. Milestone 4 makes every measure state how many months it buys, so three months looks like three months.
  • Host community told after the decision. A site announced and then explained is a site that gets blocked at the road, which is how the 2015 crisis played out. Class D milestone 5, which needs two open meetings and a written answer to every objection before any release.

Why this one

Template 7: river trap and beach litter monitoring

A World Bank baseline found 7.9 litter items per square metre on Lebanese beaches in April 2021 and 10.4 by October, a 37 per cent rise, with 76 per cent of it plastic and more than 82 per cent coming from land. Lebanon leaks about 3.1 kg of plastic per person per year, and 73 possible new dumping sites have appeared near perennial rivers since 2017.
