Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Inspect within 10 working days. Baseline survey within 21 days. Nothing goes into a watercourse between about November and March without a flood check, because a trap that dams a Lebanese river in winter is more dangerous than the litter. Trap installed within 60 days, outside the flood season. Then three months of emptying and the repeat survey. Warranty is one full winter: the trap must still be in place and undamaged after the first rainy season.

Money

Class A priced per 100 m transect cleared and surveyed. Class B priced per trap, with emptying priced separately per month so the council sees the running cost, which is the cost that actually decides whether a trap survives. Class C priced as template 1. Class D priced per kilo landed, at a posted price. No public Lebanese rate; bracket from first real bids. Sanity check only: the Nile buy-back scheme in Egypt pays fishermen per kilo and brings in 10 to 12 tonnes a month, and Lebanese wholesale plastic has been reported at about 200 dollars a tonne, so a buy-back price will not be covered by resale alone and needs a budget line. Not included: dredging, works inside the river channel bed, sea-going boat costs, and anything requiring a marine works permit.

Release

Nothing up front. 25 per cent at milestone 2 once permissions and, for class B, the stamped flood design are on file. 35 per cent at milestone 3 on installation or clearance with the disposal receipts. 20 per cent at milestone 4 after three months of weight logs. 20 per cent held to the repeat survey at milestone 5. A trap installed without the flood design releases nothing, whatever it looks like in the photograph.

Who signs off. The municipal council decides. The Ministry of Environment is informed and approves works affecting a watercourse or the shore. The Ministry of Energy and Water and the regional water establishment control rivers and channels, and the Litani River Authority inside that basin. The army must be informed for anything on the coast and before any drone flight. The Ministry of Public Works and Transport and the Directorate General of Land and Maritime Transport are involved on the maritime public domain, which covers most Lebanese beaches. The Ministry of Agriculture's fisheries department matters for class D and for anything involving fishing boats. The Order of Engineers and Architects stamps the trap design.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Weighing without counting. One wet carpet weighs more than a thousand bottles. Only a count by item type tells you what the source is, and without the source the trap is emptied for ever. The count sheet by type at milestones 0 and 5.
  • A trap that dams the river. A blocked channel in a Lebanese winter floods the houses upstream, and the municipality will cut the trap out and never allow another. The stamped flood design at milestone 2 and the 48-hour rule after heavy rain at milestone 4.
  • Clean-up day with no repeat survey. A photogenic clean-up with no second count cannot show whether anything changed, and the beach looks the same within a month. The same-transect repeat at milestone 5.
  • Collected litter dumped up the road. Material taken off the beach and tipped somewhere unlicensed is back in the sea by winter, and this happens more than anyone admits. The receipt from the licensed receiving site for every kilo at milestone 3.
  • Nobody funded to empty it. A trap is a running cost pretending to be a capital item. Unemptied, it fails in the first storm and becomes litter itself. The named person, the frequency and the separate monthly price at milestone 5.

8 Informal sector unrecognised
Why this one

Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Inspect within 10 working days. The count at milestone 0 takes a full week and cannot be shortened. Legal note and rules within 30 days. Register and kit within 45 days, and the kit does not wait for the contract, because the injury risk is there on day one. Prices posted within 60 days. Then three months of records and the review. Warranty is those three months plus one repeat spot check at six months on kit and prices.

Money

Class A priced per person registered and kitted, as a one-off, with the kit listed separately so it can be replaced later. Class B priced as a running cost per month for the point, plus the money paid out for material, which is a pass-through and must never be marked up. Class C priced per household in the zone, like a collection contract. Class D priced per site. No public Lebanese rate for a buy-back; bracket from first real bids. Sanity check only: reported Lebanese wholesale prices are about 200 dollars a tonne for plastic, down from 450, 80 for paper, down from 110, and 200 for steel, down from 350, and granules resell at about 325, so a buy-back price set above the street price needs its own budget line and cannot come out of resale alone. Not included: legal fees, work permits, health insurance, and any payment to a middleman.

Release

Nothing up front. 20 per cent at milestone 2 on the register with consent lines. 30 per cent at milestone 3 on signed kit receipts and the dated police instruction. 25 per cent at milestone 4 on posted prices and a scale that passes the check weight. 25 per cent held to milestone 6 after three months of records and the review meeting. If a person under 18 is found on the register or at the point, nothing further is released until it is resolved and reported.

Who signs off. The municipal council decides the register, the rules and any contract. The Ministry of Interior and Municipalities covers the municipal police instruction. The Ministry of Labour governs who may lawfully work and on what terms, and the legal note at milestone 1 must reflect its position rather than guess it; this template does not create a right to work and must not be used as if it does. The Ministry of Environment approves any sorting or storage point. The Ministry of Public Health is informed where health-care waste is being handled. The Ministry of Social Affairs and the child protection referral route are used for any child found working. General Security matters for residency questions, which are outside the municipality's power and must not be handled by the expert.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Kit handed out once and never replaced. Cut gloves last weeks, not years. A photo of new kit at month one says nothing about month six. The six-month spot check in the warranty, and the injury log at milestone 5.
  • Price cut at the scale. A posted price that is quietly reduced when the material is on the scale destroys the whole scheme in a fortnight, and the pickers go back to the old buyers. The dated price list, the 7-day notice rule and the check weight at milestone 4.
  • Children in the yard. Two children were killed by refuse trucks in Lebanon in 2022. This is the failure that cannot be traded off against tonnage. The under-18 rule at milestones 0, 2 and 5, with a referral, and the release stops.
  • Register used against the people on it. A list of names collected for a buy-back and then used for enforcement or handed to a contractor will not be signed a second time by anyone. The consent line and the written storage rule at milestone 2, and municipal custody of the register.
  • Formal contract that pushes pickers out. A new exclusive collection contract over the same streets removes the income of the people who were doing the recycling, which is how it has gone elsewhere in the region. Class C, which contracts the existing crew for the zone rather than replacing it, checked against the milestone 0 count.

Inspect within 10 working days. Clear within 30 days of the council decision, and within 7 days if the pile is burning, in a watercourse or beside a school. The barrier goes in on the same day as the clearance, never later, because an empty clean spot with an open access is an invitation. Then 30, 60 and 90 day visits. Warranty is the 90-day record, plus a single free return visit if new tipping is found in the first 30 days after handover.

Money

Class A priced per m3 cleared plus haulage per tonne-kilometre, with the barrier priced as its own line so it cannot be quietly dropped. Class B priced per 100 m of street. Class C priced per hauler registered plus a monthly sum for spot checks. Class D priced per tonne received. No public Lebanese rate; bracket from first real bids. Sanity check only: Lebanon's disposal has been costed at about 154.50 dollars a tonne, so haulage and gate fees usually cost more than the clearing labour. Not included: fines and their collection, rewards paid to people who report tipping, court costs, and land the municipality does not own.

Release

Nothing up front. 40 per cent at milestone 2 on disposal receipts from a licensed site. 20 per cent at milestone 3 on the barrier and the sign. 40 per cent held to the 90-day recurrence check at milestone 4 and the handover at milestone 5. Clearing without a barrier releases the 40 per cent only, and the job stays open.

Who signs off. The municipal council decides the clearance, the barrier and any fine, and the fine needs a council decision to be enforceable. The Ministry of Interior and Municipalities covers enforcement by the municipal police. The Ministry of Public Works and Transport must agree any barrier on or beside a classified road, and the road may not be the municipality's to block. The Ministry of Environment is informed, and approves a class D rubble reception point. The regional water establishment and, in that basin, the Litani River Authority are informed where the site drains to a river. The Internal Security Forces handle organised tipping. The landowner's written permission is needed for a barrier on private land.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Cleared with no barrier. A clean, empty, easy-to-reach spot is more attractive to a tipper than a full one. Without the barrier the pile is back within weeks, and it usually comes back bigger. Milestone 3 must be done the same day as milestone 2, and milestone 4 measures the result.
  • No starting volume. With no m3 at milestone 0 there is no way to tell whether 90 days later is better, worse or the same, and everyone argues from photographs. The tape measure and the volume calculation at milestone 0.
  • Enforcement with nowhere legal to tip. Fining builders who have no rubble site simply moves the tipping to the next valley, which is why class D exists. Milestone 1 names the source, and class D requires a reception point before enforcement.
  • Waste moved to another unlicensed spot. The cheapest way to clear a hotspot is to tip it somewhere quieter, and it happens often enough that receipts must be per load. The licensed-site receipt for every load at milestone 2, checked against the weighbridge total.
  • Camera with nobody watching it. A camera that records to nothing deters no one after the first week and gives the council a false sense that the spot is covered. Milestone 3 requires a named person and a written rule on who may see the footage.
Sources
  • Human Rights Watch, Lebanon: waste crisis posing health risks, December 2017. 617 uncontrolled dumps mapped, 77 per cent of waste openly dumped or landfilled. hrw.org
  • World Bank, Lebanon marine litter baseline survey, 2021. 73 possible new disposal sites near perennial rivers since 2017, over 82 per cent of marine litter land-based. blogs.worldbank.org
  • Wikipedia, recycling in South Korea. Citizens reporting illegal dumping can receive up to 80 per cent of the fine. en.wikipedia.org
  • Nation Africa, underground economy: garbage overhaul as cartels resist reforms, Nairobi. Hauler licensing against organised dumping. nation.africa
  • Swedish Environmental Protection Agency, littering fees for some producers. Municipalities report clean-up costs and producers of disposables pay them. naturvardsverket.se
  • Human Rights Watch, Lebanon: huge cost of inaction on trash crisis, June 2020. About 154.50 dollars a tonne for disposal. hrw.org
10 Organic and food waste unmanaged
Why this one

Template 10: separating organics and composting them locally

About 65 per cent of Lebanon's waste is organic and compostable, and one Lebanese operator puts it at roughly 70 kg in every 100 kg of household rubbish. That wet fraction is what makes mixed waste smell, leak and produce methane, and it is the cheapest thing to take out of the bin because it never needs to travel far.

Step 1 · Classify

4 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Class A: home compostingVillage or low-density housing with gardens. The cheapest option because there is no collection and no site.A bin or a built heap per household, a browns supply such as dry leaves or shredded card, a short training session, and follow-up visits.household
Class B: municipal windrow compostingThere is a separated organic stream and a piece of ground with a hard surface, a drain and no house within a set distance.Reception, mixing with browns, turned windrows, temperature records, screening, curing, a place to store and sell the compost.tonne received
Class C: institution or market organicsOne market, restaurant strip, school, barracks or hospital kitchen makes a large, clean, predictable organic stream.Caddies and a daily round from a small number of points, an in-vessel unit or a small windrow, and a weight record per point.tonne received
Class D: anaerobic digestion or feed-in to an existing plantThere is an existing digester or a farm unit nearby that will take the organics, so no new treatment site is needed.Separation, transport, a written acceptance and quality specification from the receiving plant, and a weight record.tonne delivered
Step 2 · The milestones

7 milestones, each with the proof it needs and the check it must pass

#MilestoneEvidence the expert uploadsPass mark the verifier checks
0Scope, class and the organic share
Weigh what is actually in the bin before designing anything, and find out where the finished compost will go. Compost with no user is just a pile in a different place.		A sorting study on at least 200 kg of waste, weighed by stream, with photos of the scale. The organic share as a percentage. Household or point count. Photos of the proposed site with its distance to the nearest house, well and watercourse. A written note naming who will use or buy the compost.Organic share measured by weight, not assumed, and compared with the national figure of about 65 per cent. A site with a hard surface and a drain for class B, or the class is not B. A named compost user or buyer in writing. Sample at least 200 kg (to confirm).
1Separate collection of organics
Set up the caddy or the bin and collect organics on their own, at least twice a week in summer. Organics collected once a week in a Lebanese August will be maggots by day four.		Signed distribution list for caddies or bins. Route map and timetable. Weekly weight of the organic stream with photos of the scale or weighbridge ticket. Photos showing organics kept apart from other waste in the vehicle.At least two organic collections a week between June and September (to confirm). Four weeks of weights on file. No week where organics shared a truck body with mixed waste.
2Site, mix and build the windrows
Prepare the pad, then mix the wet organics with dry browns before piling. Food waste on its own goes sour and smells; it needs carbon and air.		Photos of the pad, the drain and the leachate collection. Delivery notes for the browns. Photo of a windrow with a measured pole in frame for height and width. A mix record: tonnes of organics, tonnes of browns, per batch, each batch numbered.Windrow height about 1.5 to 2 m and no wider than about 3 to 4 m, so air can reach the middle (to confirm). Carbon to nitrogen ratio in the mix around 25 to 30 to 1 (to confirm). Moisture around 50 to 60 per cent, checked by the squeeze test with a photo (to confirm). Every batch numbered and traceable to a delivery week.
3Turn, measure the heat and record it
Turn each windrow on a schedule and take its temperature every day with a long-stemmed thermometer, in the middle of the pile. Heat is what kills the weed seeds and the germs.		A temperature log per batch, one reading a day at a stated depth, with a photo of the thermometer reading at least once a week. A turning log with dates. Photos of the turning. Note of any batch that went cold or wet.Every batch holds at least 55 degrees Celsius for at least three days running, measured daily in the core (to confirm). At least five turnings during the hot phase (to confirm). No gap longer than 2 days in the temperature log. A batch that fails the temperature is re-mixed and restarted, and that is recorded.
4Cure, screen and test
Let the compost finish slowly, then screen it and check it is ready. Immature compost burns plants and ruins the reputation of the whole scheme in one season.		Curing dates per batch. Photo of the screen and the screened product. A maturity test: a simple germination test on seeds in the compost, photographed at day 7 against a control. A visual impurity check with photos of glass, plastic and metal picked out of a weighed sample. Laboratory test where the buyer requires one.At least 30 days of active composting followed by about 2 months of curing before sale, as Lebanese practice describes it. Germination in the compost at least 80 per cent of the control (to confirm). Visible plastic, glass and metal not more than 0.5 per cent by weight of a screened sample (to confirm). Batch number on every bag or pile.
5Use, sell and account
Move the compost to the user, and write down what it was worth so the council can see the whole picture.		Delivery notes or sale invoices with batch numbers and weights. Photos of the compost in use. A one-page account: tonnes of organics received, tonnes of compost out, landfill fee avoided, income, running cost.Tonnes out are consistent with tonnes in, allowing for the weight lost as water and gas, which is large; roughly 70 kg of organics making about 30 kg of product matches Lebanese practice. Every delivery has a batch number. Nothing is stored more than 6 months without a user (to confirm).
6Six-month handover
Hand over the site, the logs, the routine and the buyer list, and repeat the sorting study to see what left the bin.		Repeat sorting study on at least 200 kg compared with milestone 0. Complete temperature, turning and batch records. Signed handover note. Photos of the site tidy, with the drain clear and no ponding leachate. A written routine for turning, temperature and what to do when a batch fails.Organic share in the residual bin down measurably against milestone 0, with both studies on file. Records complete with no gap longer than a week. No standing leachate on the pad. No complaint of smell or flies recorded in the last month, or each one recorded with what was done. This is the gate for the final release.
Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Inspect within 10 working days. Sorting study within 21 days. Caddies out and separate collection running within 60 days. The site pad ready before the first delivery, never after. Then the process itself sets the clock: about 30 days of active composting and about two more months of curing before anything is sold, so the first sellable batch is roughly three months after the first delivery. Handover at six months. Warranty is one full summer, because smell and flies are a summer problem and a site that passes in February proves nothing.

Money

Class A priced per household including the bin and two follow-up visits. Class B priced per tonne received, with the browns supply listed as its own line because it is the cost people forget. Class C priced per collection point per month. Class D priced per tonne delivered plus the receiving plant's gate fee. No public Lebanese rate; bracket from first real bids. Sanity check only: Lebanon's disposal has been costed at about 154.50 dollars a tonne, so every tonne composted locally avoids roughly that much in disposal and haulage, which is usually the largest number on the page. Not included: buying land, a shed or a roof over the pad, mechanical turners, laboratory testing beyond the first batch, and registration of the compost as a fertiliser for sale.

Release

Nothing up front. 20 per cent at milestone 1 after four weeks of separate organic collection with weights. 25 per cent at milestone 2 once the pad, the drain and the first mixed batches are in place. 25 per cent at milestone 3 once at least three batches have passed the temperature test. 30 per cent held to the six-month handover at milestone 6. A batch that never reached temperature does not count towards the milestone 3 release, whatever it looks like.

Who signs off. The municipal council decides the site and the service. The Ministry of Environment approves a composting site and sets its conditions, and a larger site may need an environmental assessment. The Ministry of Agriculture governs compost sold or given away as a soil improver or fertiliser, and LIBNOR holds the Lebanese standards a product would be tested against. The Ministry of Public Health is involved for flies, smell and any nuisance complaint. The regional water establishment is consulted where the pad drains near a well or spring, and the Litani River Authority inside that basin. The Order of Engineers and Architects stamps the pad and drainage design. Neighbours within the set distance must be told before the site opens, not after.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • No browns. Food waste alone is wet, packs down, goes without air and turns sour. It smells, it breeds flies and it never reaches temperature. The mix record and the carbon to nitrogen check at milestone 2, and the temperature log at milestone 3.
  • Temperature never measured. Without heat records nobody can say the compost is safe, weed seeds survive, and the first farmer who uses it will not use it again. The daily temperature log and the 55 degree rule at milestone 3.
  • Sold before it is mature. Immature compost keeps working in the soil, takes nitrogen from the plants and burns roots. One bad season ends demand in the whole village. The curing dates and the germination test at milestone 4.
  • Leachate running off the pad. Compost liquid is strong stuff. Running off an unpaved pad near a well or a spring it is a public health problem, not a smell problem. The pad, drain and collection photos at milestone 2 and the no-ponding check at milestone 6.
  • Organics collected once a week in summer. By day four in a Lebanese August the caddy is full of maggots and the household stops separating, permanently. The twice-weekly summer rule and the four weeks of weights at milestone 1.
Sources
  • Enmaeya, Lebanon's waste crisis returns amid limited solutions and funding, 2025. 65 per cent of Lebanon's waste organic and compostable, 25 per cent recyclable. enmaeya.com
  • Beirut Today, trash for profit: turning organic waste into economic opportunities, May 2022. About 70 kg of organics in every 100 kg of rubbish, 70 kg of organics making about 30 kg of product, compost in about 30 days plus two months of curing; Cedar Environmental and Compost Baladi. beirut-today.com
  • Korea Herald, on food waste recycling. Weight-based smart bins and a food waste recycling rate reported at 96.8 per cent in 2023. koreaherald.com
  • EcoMENA, solid waste management in Jordan. Organics up to 60 per cent of the stream; the Rusaifeh biomethanation plant at 60 tonnes a day and 1 MW. ecomena.org
  • IEA Bioenergy Task 36, food waste and textile waste targets for the Swedish waste management system. Mandatory separate collection of food waste. task36.ieabioenergy.com
  • Human Rights Watch, Lebanon: huge cost of inaction on trash crisis, June 2020. About 154.50 dollars a tonne, and 74 million dollars a year in possible savings from better recycling and composting. hrw.org

Water: 10 templates. Open one to read it.

1 Network losses (non-revenue water)
Why this one

Template 1: district metered area and leak reduction

Lebanon's non-revenue water was put at about 48% in 2010 and UNICEF still describes roughly 40% of water as unaccounted for. Every cubic metre pumped on scarce, expensive electricity is close to half wasted, so a leak is an electricity bill as well as a water loss.

Step 1 · Classify

4 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
DMA surveyThe network has never been split into measurable zones.Draw a zone boundary, list and close boundary valves, fit or verify the inlet bulk meter, log night flow for 14 nights, build a simple water balance.per zone (district metered area)
Leak detection sweepA sealed zone exists and its night flow is high.Step testing by valve, acoustic listening on every valve, hydrant and stop tap, correlator on trunk sections, a numbered leak list with GPS pins.per km of main surveyed
Repair and renewalLeaks have been located and pinned.Excavate, fit a repair clamp or cut in new pipe, pressure test, backfill and reinstate the surface, then re-log night flow.each repair, or metre of main replaced
Pressure managementNight pressure in the zone is far above what the tallest building needs.Fit a pressure reducing valve with a time or flow modulated profile, set it, log pressure before and after, label the setting.each pressure reducing valve
Step 2 · The milestones

7 milestones, each with the proof it needs and the check it must pass

#MilestoneEvidence the expert uploadsPass mark the verifier checks
0Scope and class
Walk the zone. Draw its boundary. List every valve that must close to seal it. Count the connections inside from the Water Establishment's subscriber register. Choose the class.		Zone map with the boundary drawn. A GPS pin and a photo for every boundary valve. The connection count as an extract from the register. Photos of the inlet chamber.Every boundary valve is listed, pinned and photographed. The connection count is written down. A named officer of the Regional Water Establishment has signed the zone map. Zone size 500 to 3,000 connections (to confirm against Lebanese practice).
1Zero-pressure test
Close every boundary valve and the inlet. Open a hydrant or tap inside the zone. Watch the pressure inside fall. If it does not reach zero, a boundary valve is passing and the zone is not sealed.		Photo of the pressure gauge reading zero, time-stamped. A time-stamped photo at each boundary valve as it is closed. The operator's log sheet, signed.Pressure inside the zone reaches 0 bar within 30 minutes of the inlet closing. If it does not, the failing valve is named and repaired or replaced before milestone 2 starts. No exceptions: every later number depends on this one.
2Bulk meter and 14 nights of logging
Fit or verify the inlet meter, fit a data logger, and record flow every 15 minutes for at least 14 nights. Record the supply hours each day alongside the flow.		Photo of the meter showing its serial number and the flow arrow. The manufacturer's accuracy certificate. The raw logger file as CSV. The daily operator log of pump and rota hours.At least 14 consecutive nights logged at 15 minute intervals. Minimum night flow between 01:00 and 04:00 reported in cubic metres per hour and in litres per connection per hour. Meter accuracy class stated. Supply hours recorded for every one of the 14 days.
3Find the leaks
Step test by shutting sub-branches one at a time and watching the inlet flow drop. Then listen acoustically at every valve, hydrant and stop tap. Use a correlator on long sections. Pin and number every find.		A numbered leak list. For each find: a GPS pin, a photo of the listening point, and the correlator screen or printout. A map with all pins on it.Every suspected leak has a GPS pin. Singapore's acoustic sensors locate to within 3 metres along the pipe, so a pin more than 5 metres from the eventual dig is re-surveyed, not excavated twice. Each find is labelled leak or illegal connection, never mixed. The list totals an estimated loss in cubic metres per day.
4Repair and reinstate
Dig, repair, pressure test the repair, backfill in layers, reinstate the road or footway to the same standard as a pothole patch.		For every excavation: a before photo with the pipe visible, an after photo of the finished repair before backfill, and a reinstatement photo. Delivery notes for clamps, pipe and fittings. The pressure test reading.Every leak on the numbered list is either closed or carries a written reason why not. Each repair holds test pressure with no drop for 15 minutes (to confirm the hold time your Water Establishment requires). Road reinstatement is level within 6 millimetres and drains, as in the pothole template.
5Re-measure night flow
Wait at least seven days after the last repair, then log the inlet for another 14 nights on the same settings as milestone 2.		The second CSV. A single chart with both 14-night periods side by side. A short note explaining anything unusual, such as a burst during the period.Minimum night flow has fallen by at least 30% against milestone 2, or the shortfall is explained in writing and a second sweep is scheduled. Zone non-revenue water recalculated and reported; under 25% is the target (to confirm against the national water strategy). This is the gate for the final release.
6Handover
Hand the Water Establishment the zone file: the map, the valve list, the leak list, both logger files, the repair records and a one-page reading routine.		Signed handover sheet with the recipient's name and role. The zone file as a PDF and a spreadsheet. A photo of the first meter reading taken by their own staff.A named Water Establishment officer has signed. The first monthly meter reading after handover was taken by their staff, not by the expert, and is in the log.
Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Survey and scoping within 10 working days of award. The zero-pressure test and the first 14 nights of logging finish inside 30 days. The leak sweep follows within 14 days. Repairs within 14 days of the leak list being issued, and sooner for any leak running into a road or a building. The second 14-night log starts no earlier than seven days after the last repair, so the network settles. End to end about 90 days. Warranty 12 months on every repair and on the pressure reducing valve setting.

Money

Priced per zone for the survey and pressure management classes, per kilometre of main surveyed for the leak sweep, and per repair or per metre of pipe for the renewal class. No public Lebanese unit rate exists for district metered area work; bracket from the first three real bids. Not included: pipe renewal beyond the metres agreed at scoping, road reinstatement outside the trench line, customer meters, electricity, and the cost of cutting illegal connections.

Release

Nothing up front. 20% at milestone 2, once the zone is proved sealed and 14 nights are logged. 50% at milestone 4, once every leak is repaired and reinstated. 30% at milestone 5, only if the second 14-night log shows the fall in night flow. If night flow does not fall, the final 30% pays for a second sweep instead.

Who signs off. The Regional Water Establishment owns the network. It must sign the zone map and approve every valve operation, and no valve is touched without its operator present or its written instruction. The municipality signs for road opening and traffic control. A classified road needs the Ministry of Public Works. The Ministry of Energy and Water is informed. The engineer who designs and supervises must be registered with the Order of Engineers and Architects. Cutting an illegal connection needs the Water Establishment's written order, never the expert's judgement.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Zone not sealed. One boundary valve that passes water makes every night-flow number meaningless, and the whole job is then measuring nothing. Milestone 1, the zero-pressure test.
  • Two nights of logging. Weather, rota hours and a single tanker filling swing night flow far more than a leak does. Two nights prove nothing. Milestone 2's 14 consecutive nights.
  • Rota supply read as continuous. In a zone with six hours of water a day, minimum night flow can read zero simply because the pump is off. The zone then looks perfect. Milestone 2 records supply hours next to flow; a night with no supply is excluded from the calculation.
  • Leaks counted, not fixed. A leak list is a document, not a saving. Zones are often surveyed twice and repaired never. Milestone 4 requires every numbered leak closed or explained, and milestone 5 measures the result.
  • Illegal connections billed as leaks. Cutting a connection is a legal act with a person at the other end of it. Treating it as a repair puts the expert in the middle of a dispute. Milestone 3 labels every find leak or illegal connection, and the Water Establishment decides what happens next.
Sources
  • Wikipedia, Water supply and sanitation in Lebanon, drawing on World Bank and ministry figures en.wikipedia.org
  • UNICEF, Water supply systems on the verge of collapse in Lebanon, 2021 unicef.org
  • Smart Water Magazine, PUB Singapore adopts smart tools to detect and pre-empt pipe leaks, on acoustic accuracy and leak rates smartwatermagazine.com
  • IFC, agreement to cut water loss and enhance water sustainability in Jordan, 2024 ifc.org
  • WASREB Kenya, Impact Report, annual utility benchmarking including non-revenue water wasreb.go.ke
2 Intermittent supply and rationing
Why this one

Template 2: published rotation schedule and zone balancing

Lebanese supply averaged 6 hours a day in summer and 9 in winter, and average weekly supply fell from 49 hours in 2019 to 22 hours in 2023. Residents plan their whole week around a rota that nobody writes down, so the first fix is to write it down and keep to it.

Step 1 · Classify

3 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Rota audit and publicationA rota exists only in the pump operator's head.Log the real valve and pump operations for 28 days, turn them into a written street-by-street rota, publish it in Arabic with a complaints number.per zone
Zone re-balancingThe far end of the zone never gets water while the near end does.Pressure log at the tail ends, a valve throttling plan, a revised rota, then re-log to prove the tail gained without the head losing.per zone
Public filling pointA neighbourhood is below the 35 litres per person per day minimum and piping to it is months away.A metered, chlorinated public filling point or a communal tank with a float valve, a hard standing, a sign and a logbook.each filling point
Step 2 · The milestones

6 milestones, each with the proof it needs and the check it must pass

#MilestoneEvidence the expert uploadsPass mark the verifier checks
0Scope and class
Count households and people in the zone from the municipality's current register. Walk to the three highest, furthest or lowest-pressure points. Photograph the pump and valve chambers. Choose the class.		Zone map. Household and population count as a register extract with a date. GPS pins and photos at three tail-end monitoring points. Photos of the pump house and every zone valve chamber.Population is from a count dated within the last 12 months, not an old census. At least three tail-end points chosen and pinned. Class agreed in writing with the Water Establishment.
1Baseline logging, 28 days
Fit pressure loggers at the zone inlet and at each tail point. Log for 28 consecutive days. Have the pump operator keep a daily sheet of hours run and valves turned, including any tanker filling.		Logger CSV files. A photo of each logger installed with its serial visible. The operator's daily sheet, signed each week.28 consecutive days at every point. Hours of supply per day reported for each point. Litres per person per day estimated for the zone. UNICEF's minimum acceptable quantity is 35 litres per person per day, and nearly 1.7 million people in Lebanon were down to that level, from a pre-2020 average of 165 litres.
2Draw the real rota
Turn 28 days of logs into a table: which street, which days, which hours. Read it back to the pump operator and have him sign it as what he actually does.		The rota table. Photos of the operator's own notebook or wall chart. A signed statement from the named operator.Every street in the zone appears in the rota, including any street currently getting nothing, which is recorded as zero hours. The written rota matches the logged supply hours within one hour a day on at least 24 of the 28 days.
3Publish it
Post the rota where residents actually look: the municipality door, main streets, the mosque or church noticeboard, and the municipality's page or WhatsApp broadcast.		Photographs of the notice at the municipality and at least three street locations, each with a GPS pin. Screenshot of the online post or broadcast. The Arabic text file.The rota is in Arabic, carries a date, and shows a phone number for changes. At least five public postings photographed and pinned. The Water Establishment has a copy in writing.
4Fix the worst tail
Throttle the over-served branches, re-time the rota, or build the filling point. Write the new valve setting on a tag fixed to the valve.		Photos of each valve with its setting written on a tag. Before and after pressure logs at the tail point. For a filling point: photos of the meter, the chlorination point, the sign and the logbook's first page.The worst tail point gains supply hours against milestone 1, and no other point loses more than one hour a day. Every valve touched carries a tag. A filling point reads on its meter and its sign shows the price, or the words free of charge, in Arabic.
5Re-measure and hand over
Log for another 14 days. Compare against the published rota. Hand the rota, the logs and the valve settings to the municipality and the Water Establishment.		Second CSV. A comparison table of published hours against logged hours. Signed handover with named recipients.At least 90% of logged supply hours match the published rota. No household in the zone is below 35 litres per person per day, or the shortfall is named, counted and costed for the next project. A named person at the municipality will answer the complaints number.
Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Baseline logging runs a full 28 days, so seasonal weeks and weekends are all covered. The rota is drawn and published within 10 days of the baseline ending. The balancing work is done inside 21 days. The re-measure runs 14 days. About 90 days end to end. Because a summer rota does not describe February, the published rota must be reviewed and re-issued twice a year, at the start of summer and the start of winter, for two years. That review is part of the job, not an extra.

Money

Priced per zone for the audit and re-balancing classes, and each for a filling point. Pressure loggers can be hired rather than bought and should be priced as hire. No public Lebanese rate exists for rota auditing; bracket from the first three real bids. Not included: new pipework, new pumps, electricity or generator fuel, tanker water, and any new source.

Release

Nothing up front. 30% at milestone 3, when the rota is published and photographed in five places. 40% at milestone 4, when the tail point gains hours without another point losing them. 30% at milestone 5, after the 14-day re-measure shows a 90% match.

Who signs off. The Regional Water Establishment must approve any valve or pump change and should provide the operator who turns them. The municipality publishes the rota and owns the noticeboards. A public filling point needs the Ministry of Public Health for water quality and the Water Establishment for the connection. The Ministry of Energy and Water is informed. Nothing in this template changes a tariff, which is not a municipal decision.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Rota published but not followed. A schedule nobody keeps is worse than none, because residents stop trusting the municipality as well as the water. Milestone 5's 90% match between published and logged hours.
  • Logged in one season only. Supply hours in Lebanon roughly halve between winter and summer. A February rota published in July is a lie. The twice-yearly review built into the time section.
  • Tail end fixed by starving the head. Throttling is a zero-sum game unless losses fall. Moving the complaint to another street is not a fix. Milestone 4's rule that no point may lose more than one hour a day.
  • Tanker filling inside the zone, unlogged. A tanker drawing from a hydrant during the supply window changes every pressure and flow number in the baseline. Milestone 1 requires the operator's daily sheet to name every tanker fill.
  • Population from an old register. Displacement and return move Lebanese household numbers fast, and litres per person is only as good as the head count. Milestone 0 requires a count dated within 12 months.
Sources
  • Wikipedia, Water supply and sanitation in Lebanon, supply hours by governorate en.wikipedia.org
  • UNICEF, Lebanon's water infrastructure struggles and remains on the brink, on the 35 litre minimum unicef.org
  • UNICEF, Water supply systems on the verge of collapse in Lebanon, on 35 versus 165 litres per person per day unicef.org
  • Noria Research, Scarcity by design: the political economy of water in Jordan noria-research.com
3 Power cuts and pumping energy cost
Why this one

Template 3: solar power for a pumping station or well

UNICEF found electricity shortages make it impossible to pump enough water and that the establishments cannot afford diesel or spare parts, and has needed US$40 to 75 million a year simply to keep Lebanese systems running. A pump with no power delivers nothing, however good the pipes are.

Step 1 · Classify

4 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Energy audit onlyNobody can say what a cubic metre of water costs to pump.Fit a kilowatt-hour meter and a flow meter, log both for 28 days, collect fuel receipts, and report kilowatt-hours per cubic metre and cost per cubic metre in US dollars.per station
Pump efficiency retrofitThe pump is old, worn or far bigger than the duty it serves.Measure flow and head, trim or replace the impeller or the pump, or fit a variable speed drive, then re-test against the same duty point.per pump
Solar with grid or generator backupThe station can pump in daylight and fill a tank, with the grid or a generator as backup.Photovoltaic array, inverter, controls, protection and metering. No batteries. The existing generator or grid connection stays as backup.per kilowatt-peak installed

Step 2 · The milestones

Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Audit and design within 21 days of award. Installation within 45 days of design sign-off, which is realistic only if panels and inverter are already in the country; if they are being imported, the clock starts at customs clearance and the delay is the sponsor's risk, not the expert's. Commissioning in the same week as the install, on a clear day. The 90-day check is fixed and cannot be brought forward. Warranty: two years on workmanship and on the inverter, the manufacturer's performance warranty on the panels, and 12 months on the pump.

Money

Priced per kilowatt-peak installed for both solar classes, per station for the audit, and per pump for the efficiency retrofit. No public Lebanese rate per kilowatt-peak for water-sector solar exists; bracket from the first three real bids. Jordan's five-station programme cost EUR 30 million for 25 to 30 megawatts a year of capacity, which is a scale check only and not a unit rate. Not included: batteries, the borehole itself, grid connection fees, security fencing, and import duties.

Release

Nothing up front. Up to 40% against delivery notes and the recorded serial numbers at milestone 3, and that portion pays for materials only. 40% at milestone 4, once the station has pumped on solar alone with the generator isolated for four hours. 20% at milestone 6, after the 90-day check and the panel count.

Who signs off. The Regional Water Establishment owns the pumping station and must approve the works in writing. EDL covers any grid connection or net metering. LCEC guidance applies to sizing and to any subsidised finance. The municipality signs for a ground-mounted array on public land, and the landowner for private land. The design carries an Order of Engineers and Architects stamp. The Ministry of Energy and Water is informed. A generator that stays as backup keeps its own fuel storage approvals.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Array sized to the pump, not the water. A pump rated at 30 kilowatts may only need to move 200 cubic metres a day. Sizing to the nameplate doubles the cost for no extra water. Milestone 1, which sizes on cubic metres per day in the worst month.
  • No shading study. One parapet wall, one tree or one neighbouring building can take a third of the year's output, and it is invisible in a midday site visit. Milestone 1's photographs at 09:00, 12:00 and 15:00 from the array position.
  • Panels not serialised. Solar theft is common and panels are untraceable without serials. There is also no warranty claim without them. Milestone 3 records every serial and milestone 6 spot-checks 10%.
  • Commissioned with the generator quietly running. A plant that has never actually run on solar alone will fail the first cloudy week, and by then the expert has been paid. Milestone 4 requires a photo of the generator isolator open and four hours of solar-only pumping.
  • Nobody trained, nobody cleans. Dust on a Lebanese summer array cuts output badly, and an untrained operator calls the contractor for a reset fault. Milestone 5 films two named operators and fixes a cleaning schedule to the wall.

4 Unregulated wells and aquifer depletion
Why this one

Template 4: municipal well register and aquifer level monitoring

Households, farms and firms have dug over 60,000 unregulated wells in Lebanon to make up for the gaps in public supply. Nobody knows how much is being taken out of any Lebanese aquifer, so the smallest useful project is to count the wells and measure the water table.

Step 1 · Classify

4 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Register onlyThe town has no list of the wells inside its boundary.Door-to-door and street survey. For each well a GPS pin, a wellhead photo, the owner, the use, the stated depth, the pump rating and whether a licence is claimed.per well recorded
Register plus level monitoringThe register exists but the trend in the water table is unknown.Choose five to ten observation wells across the town, fix and photograph a datum at each, dip monthly for at least a year, plot the trend.per observation well per year
Abstraction metering pilotA group of large users can be metered, by agreement or by order.Fit and seal a meter at each selected well, record the opening reading, read monthly, publish the zone total without naming owners.per meter
Sealing an illegal wellThe Ministry of Energy and Water has ordered a well closed.Witnessed decommissioning: pump removed, casing cut back, bore grouted full depth, the works photographed and certified.each well sealed
Step 2 · The milestones

6 milestones, each with the proof it needs and the check it must pass

#MilestoneEvidence the expert uploadsPass mark the verifier checks
0Scope and class
Agree the survey boundary with the municipality. Ask the Water Establishment and the Ministry of Energy and Water for any existing licence list, in writing. Set a target well count.		Boundary map. The written request and the reply, or a note that no reply came. Any existing list received. The class chosen and signed.Boundary drawn and agreed. A written request for the licence list is on file whether or not it was answered. A target well count is stated, with the method used to estimate it.
1Field survey

A master spreadsheet.At least 90% of the target count actually visited, with the missing ones listed and the reason given. Every record has a GPS pin accurate to within 10 metres and a wellhead photograph. No record without a surveyor name and a date. Depths given by owners are written as stated, never as measured.
2Match to licences
Check every surveyed well against the ministry's licence list. Give each one a status. Do not decide any disputed case.		The matched table with a status column reading licensed, applied, unlicensed or unknown. Scans of any licence document the owner showed. A list of disputed cases.Every well has a status. The number and the share of wells with no licence record is stated as a plain number. Disputed cases are flagged for the ministry, not ruled on by the expert.
3Measure levels and volumes

A photo of the dipper tape at the reading for each well. A level log sheet. Meter photos showing serial and reading with date and time. A photo of the datum mark on each wellhead.Each observation well dipped on the same day of the month for at least six consecutive months. Every reading is in metres below a photographed datum. Any month missed is recorded as missed, not interpolated.
4Publish and hand over
Turn the survey into a register the municipality can keep and a map the public can see. Strip owners' names from anything published.		The register as a spreadsheet and the map as a PDF. A signed handover with named recipients at the municipality and the Water Establishment. A screenshot or photo of where the register will be stored.Handed to named people at both the municipality and the Regional Water Establishment. Repeat the level readings and plot the trend. For a sealing job, complete the decommissioning with a witness present.		A second set of dipper photos. The trend chart, one line per well. For a sealing: photos of the pump removed, the casing cut, the grout going in, the depth log, and the Water Establishment witness's signature.At least six monthly readings per observation well plotted. Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Survey within 45 days for a town with under 500 wells, and pro rata beyond that. Licence matching within 21 days of the survey ending. Level monitoring monthly for at least six months, and it is worth far more if the municipality keeps it going for years. A sealing is done within 14 days of a written ministry order. No warranty attaches to a register, but the expert answers questions on it for 90 days. A sealing carries a 12-month warranty against the bore re-opening.

Money

Priced per well recorded, per observation well per year, per meter fitted, or each for a sealing. No public Lebanese rate exists for well survey work; bracket from the first three real bids. Not included: drilling, licence fees, any legal action against owners, compensation, and the cost of an alternative supply for a sealed well.

Release

Nothing up front. 40% at milestone 1, once the survey is complete and the verifier's random re-visit of 5% of records matches. 30% at milestone 4, when the register is handed over to named recipients. 30% at milestone 5, after the six-month re-dip and the trend chart.

Who signs off. Well licensing sits with the Ministry of Energy and Water, and only the ministry can declare a well illegal or order it sealed. The Regional Water Establishment holds the local records and should witness a sealing. The municipality authorises the survey and publishes the map. A hydrogeologist or an engineer registered with the Order of Engineers and Architects signs the interpretation of the levels. Personal data collected in the survey is handled under Lebanese law and is handed over, not published.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Survey done from a car window. Wells inside courtyards, behind walls and under buildings get missed, and a count that misses a third of the wells is worse than no count because it is believed. The verifier re-visits 5% of records at random and compares them with the file.
  • Stated depth recorded as measured. Owners round, guess and understate. A register of guessed depths cannot be used for any aquifer calculation. Milestone 1 requires depths to be labelled stated or measured.
  • No fixed datum. A level measured from the ground is meaningless on a slope, and it is meaningless next month if a slab has been poured. Milestone 3 requires a marked and photographed datum on each wellhead.
  • Register published with owner names. That turns a public health survey into a list of targets and ends all cooperation for the next survey. Milestone 4 publishes the map without names and hands the full register only to named officials.
  • Expert declares a well illegal. It is the ministry's decision, and an expert who rules on it loses standing and may create a legal problem for the municipality. Milestone 2 flags and lists; it does not rule.

5 Private tanker and vendor markets
Why this one

Template 5: licensed tanker filling point and a published price list

Tanker trucks are an essential part of Lebanon's supply and have no price or quality control. Trucked water reached 145,000 Lebanese pounds per 1,000 litres in April 2022, a near sixfold rise on 2019 prices, and nobody tests what is in the tank.

3 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Tanker and price surveyThe municipality does not know who is selling water, from where, or at what price.Register the trucks: plate, tank volume, owner, contact, claimed source. Record observed street prices with dates. Take a water sample from each truck.per tanker recorded

Public prepaid dispenserPoorer households are paying vendor prices for drinking water.A card or token dispenser at a social tariff, a maintenance contract, a meter and a monthly public reading. Nairobi Water installed 257 such dispensers selling 20 litres at the social tariff.each dispenser

6 milestones, each with the proof it needs and the check it must pass

#MilestoneEvidence the expert uploadsPass mark the verifier checks
0Scope and class

Per truck: a photo of the plate, a photo of the tank with its capacity plate or a tape measure in frame, and the signed form. A photo of the sample being drawn at the outlet with the plate visible. The chain-of-custody form. The laboratory report. Any failure is reported to the Ministry of Public Health and the municipality within the same week, in writing.
3Build or fix the filling point

Photos of the meter with its serial, the air gap or backflow device, the dosing point, the chlorine stock with its date and strength, the sign, and the logbook's first page. Photos of the notice at the municipality and at least three street locations, each pinned and dated. A screenshot of the online post or WhatsApp broadcast. The Arabic text file.Price per 1,000 litres published in Arabic, carrying a date, with the licensed plate numbers listed and a complaints number. At least four public postings photographed. 530-day check and handover
Read the meter, check the logbook against it, re-sample three trucks at random, and spot-check the street price.		A photo of the meter reading at 30 days. Photos of the logbook pages. Three new laboratory reports. A price spot-check record from three trucks with dates and streets.Logbook entries account for at least 80% of the metered volume; a big gap means trucks are filling unlogged. All three re-samples still pass the E. coli and chlorine checks. Street prices on the spot check sit within 20% of the published list (to confirm the tolerance the municipality wants to set). Signed handover to a named municipal officer.
Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Survey and registration within 30 days. The filling point is built within 60 days of the class being agreed. The first laboratory test happens before any truck fills at the new point, never after. Re-testing is monthly for the first six months, then quarterly. The price list is reissued monthly. Warranty 12 months on the meter, the dosing unit and the backflow device, and the backflow device is retested every year for as long as the point operates.

Money

Priced per tanker registered for the survey class, and each for a filling point or a dispenser. Laboratory fees are priced per sample and per parameter set, separately, because they dominate the running cost. No public Lebanese rate for a tanker filling point exists; bracket from the first three real bids. Nairobi's prepaid units cost around 200,000 Kenyan shillings each, which is a scale check only. Not included: the water itself, chlorine beyond the first three months, enforcement, truck repairs and any subsidy on the social tariff.

Release

Nothing up front. 30% at milestone 2, when the baseline laboratory reports are in and the failures have been reported. 40% at milestone 3, when the filling point passes its backflow and chlorine checks. 30% at milestone 5, after 30 days of logbook, the meter reconciliation and three passing re-samples.

Who signs off. The Regional Water Establishment must approve any connection to the main and any hydrant use, and it owns the water being sold. The Ministry of Public Health covers drinking water quality, advisories and laboratory accreditation. LIBNOR holds the Lebanese drinking water standard against which the laboratory reports. The municipality licenses the trucks, sets and publishes the price, and needs a local by-law backed by the Ministry of Interior and Municipalities to enforce it. Nothing here gives the expert power to stop a truck; that is the municipality's and the security forces' job.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Sample taken at the filling point, not the truck. The tank is usually where the contamination is, and a clean filling point can still deliver dirty water. Milestone 2 requires the plate in the frame while the sample is drawn from the outlet.
  • Hose pushed down into the tank. A submerged hose can siphon tank water back into the town main when pressure drops, which is how one dirty truck contaminates a street. Milestone 3's air gap or backflow preventer photograph, with no exceptions.
  • Price published once and never updated. A price in Lebanese pounds ages in weeks, and an out-of-date official price makes every honest trader look like a profiteer. Milestone 4 requires a date on the notice and a monthly reissue.
  • Licensed trucks selling unlicensed water. A truck can hold a licence, skip the filling point and load from an untested well, which is the worst of both worlds because the licence now vouches for it. Milestone 5 compares logbook volume against metered volume.
  • Only the willing get registered. A register of cooperative operators makes the market look small and well behaved when the problem is the operators who refused. Milestone 1 records refusals with plate numbers.

Why this one

Metered household connections stood at about 16% in Beirut and Mount Lebanon in 2010 and lower or zero elsewhere, with a flat annual fee of roughly US$108 to US$159 a year. Without a meter nobody can tell a leak from a customer, so every other water project is guessing.

Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Procurement and verification within 45 days of award, and longer if the meters are imported. Installation within 60 days for up to 1,000 connections. The first reading round at 30 days after the last install, the second at 60 days. Reconciliation within 14 days of the second round. Warranty 12 months on the installation work, plus the manufacturer's warranty on the meter itself. The whole pilot runs about six months.

Money

Priced per meter installed, including the box, the stop tap, the non-return valve and the reinstatement. Bulk meters are priced each, because each one needs different pipework. No public Lebanese rate per metered connection exists; bracket from the first three real bids. Not included: renewing the service pipe from the main to the box, billing software, tariff design, customer debt, and the cost of disconnecting anyone.

Release

Nothing up front. Up to 40% against delivery notes and the recorded serial numbers at milestone 1, for materials only. 40% at milestone 3, once 95% of meters have been read and every zero explained. 20% at milestone 4, when the reconciliation against the bulk meter is signed. The shadow bill test at milestone 5 is a condition of the last payment but carries no separate money, so nobody has an incentive to shape the result.

Who signs off. The Regional Water Establishment owns the connection, owns the meter once fitted and must approve the meter type. The municipality signs for footway opening and reinstatement. LIBNOR sets the meter standard. An engineer registered with the Order of Engineers and Architects signs the sizing. Any change to the tariff is a Ministry of Energy and Water and Council of Ministers decision and is outside this template. Subscriber data handed over must not be published.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Meter fitted backwards. It reads zero or counts down, and nobody notices for years because the bill was flat anyway. Milestone 2's flow-arrow photograph, which is a two-second check per connection.
  • One meter size for every house. An oversized meter under-reads small flows, and small flows are exactly where a dripping tank float wastes water all night. Milestone 0 sizes on measured or estimated flow and shows the calculation.
  • No opening reading. Without it the first bill is a guess and the customer is right to refuse it, which kills the pilot politically. Milestone 2 records an opening reading for every meter.
  • Meters installed and never read. A metering project that ends at installation has bought hardware, not information, and the meters silt up within a year. Milestone 6 makes Water Establishment staff take the second round themselves.
  • The shadow bill sent as a real bill. A pilot that suddenly charges people destroys the trust the next project needs, and it is not lawful without a tariff decision. Milestone 5 strips names, charges nothing and states whose decision a tariff change is.

7 Utility financial collapse
Why this one

Template 7: cost-to-operate audit for one water scheme

The four Water Establishments lost access to hard currency and could not buy spare parts or generator fuel, and UNICEF has had to spend US$40 to 75 million a year keeping the systems alive. A municipality cannot fix a national balance sheet, but it can prove exactly what one scheme costs to run and what it collects.

Step 1 · Classify

3 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Cost-to-operate auditNobody can say what a cubic metre from this scheme costs.Twelve months of energy, fuel, chemicals, spare parts and labour, converted at dated exchange rates, divided by twelve months of production.per scheme
Collection and subscriber auditThe subscriber register and the payment record have never been compared.Count registered subscribers, count paying subscribers, reconcile against the register, report a collection rate and a revenue per cubic metre.per zone
Ring-fenced operations account pilotThe municipality is already paying part of the scheme's costs out of its own budget.A separate municipal account for the scheme, a monthly statement, and a published one-page operations report each quarter.per scheme per year
Step 2 · The milestones

6 milestones, each with the proof it needs and the check it must pass

#MilestoneEvidence the expert uploadsPass mark the verifier checks
0Scope and class
Draw the scheme's boundary. List every well, pump, tank, chlorination point and zone inlet in it. Agree the connection count with the Water Establishment.		An asset list with a photo and a GPS pin for every asset. The boundary map. The connection count as a dated register extract. The class agreed in writing.Every pump, well, tank and chlorination point is listed with a photograph and a pin. Assets shared with a neighbouring scheme are named and the share is stated. Connection count agreed by a named officer.
1Twelve months of cost
Collect every invoice, fuel receipt, chemical delivery note and payroll share for twelve consecutive months. Enter them with the currency and the exchange rate used in that month.		Scans of every invoice and receipt, numbered. A spreadsheet with date, supplier, item, currency, amount, exchange rate and rate source. A note listing anything that could not be obtained.Twelve consecutive months, with no month missing. Every line traceable to a scanned document, and the verifier checks ten lines at random against the scans. Both Lebanese pounds and US dollars shown, with the exchange rate and its named source for each month.
2Twelve months of production
Get the volume the scheme produced for the same twelve months, from bulk meters if they exist and from pump-hour counters and measured flow if they do not.		Bulk meter readings with photographs, or hour-counter photographs plus a measured flow test at the duty point. A monthly production table.Production in cubic metres stated for each of the twelve months. The method is stated for each month. Where pump hours were used, the flow was measured on site, not taken from the nameplate, and the figure is labelled an estimate.
3Cost per cubic metre
Divide cost by production and split the answer into energy, fuel, chemicals, parts, labour and other. Write a one-page summary in Arabic.		The calculation sheet. The one-page Arabic summary. A bar chart of the cost split.Cost per cubic metre stated in US dollars, with the energy and fuel share given as a percentage. Cost per connection per year also stated, so it can be compared with the flat tariff of roughly US$108 to US$159. Any excluded cost, such as depreciation or head office overhead, is named as excluded.
4The revenue side
Count registered subscribers and paying subscribers for the same twelve months. Get the collection officer to sign the figures.		A subscriber register extract. Payment records or collection summaries. A signed statement from the named Water Establishment collection officer. The reconciliation working.Collection rate stated as paying subscribers divided by registered subscribers, with both counts given. Revenue per cubic metre compared with cost per cubic metre. The annual gap stated in US dollars. Jordan's ministry has said its water tariff covers only about 75% of operating costs, which is the kind of number this milestone produces.
5Report, council and handover
Publish a one-page public report, present it to the municipal council, and hand over the full workbook in an editable form.		The published one-pager, photographed where it is posted. The council minutes recording receipt. The signed handover. The workbook as a spreadsheet, plus the scanned invoice folder.The municipal council minutes record receipt of the report, with a date and a decision number. The workbook is editable so next year's audit can be compared line by line. No subscriber names are published. The expert answers questions for 90 days after handover.
Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Data collection 60 days, and it will be the slow part because the invoices sit in several offices. Analysis 21 days. The report is delivered within 90 days of award. The audit is repeated every year, and its value is almost entirely in the comparison between years, so the first one should be scoped knowing it will be repeated. There is no warranty on a report, but the expert must answer questions on the method for 90 days after handover.

Money

Priced as a lump sum per scheme, with a day rate for extra sites found during scoping. No public Lebanese rate for a utility cost audit exists; bracket from the first three real bids. Not included: a formal audit opinion under auditing standards, which this is not, legal opinions, tariff design, debt recovery and any software.

Release

Nothing up front. 40% at milestone 2, once twelve months of cost and production data are complete and scanned. 40% at milestone 4, once the revenue side is signed by the collection officer. 20% at milestone 5, after the council minutes record receipt of the report. Holding the last payment to the council minute is deliberate: a report that never reaches the council changes nothing.

Who signs off. The Regional Water Establishment must agree in writing to release invoices, the subscriber register and the collection data, and that agreement is obtained before any work starts, because without it the audit cannot be finished. The municipality commissions the work and publishes the one-pager. Municipal money is overseen by the Ministry of Interior and Municipalities and the Court of Accounts, so a ring-fenced account needs their route followed. Subscriber personal data is handed over, never published.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Costs in Lebanese pounds only. With a moving exchange rate, a year of pound totals adds up to a number that means nothing and cannot be compared with next year. Milestone 1 requires the exchange rate and its named source for every month.
  • Production taken from the pump nameplate. A worn pump running at 60% of rated flow makes cost per cubic metre look a third better than it is, which is the one number the whole report rests on. Milestone 2 requires a measured flow test and labels estimates as estimates.
  • Labour left out. Seconded, unpaid or municipality-paid staff are still a real cost, and leaving them out makes the scheme look nearly viable. Milestone 1 must include a labour share or state plainly that labour is excluded.
  • Collection rate from memory. Everyone has an opinion on how many people pay. Without the register and the payment record side by side it is a rumour. Milestone 4 requires both counts and the collection officer's signature.
  • Report delivered to nobody. An audit that sits in an inbox is an expense, not a project, and the same questions get asked again next year. Milestone 5 requires the council minutes before the final release.
Sources

8 Coastal saltwater intrusion
Why this one

Template 8: coastal well salinity monitoring and abstraction cap

South of Beirut, total dissolved solids in well water have been measured between 530 and 5,600 milligrams per litre, and Beirut households spend over 6.5% of their income coping with salty water. Once seawater reaches a well the well is finished, and no repair brings it back.

Step 1 · Classify

4 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Salinity baseline surveyCoastal wells have never been tested together on the same day.Field electrical conductivity, temperature and water level at each well, plus an accredited laboratory sample for total dissolved solids and chloride.per well sampled
Monitoring networkA baseline exists but the trend does not.A transect of wells running inland from the shore, a fixed datum at each, monthly field readings and quarterly laboratory samples for a full year.per well per year
Abstraction cap pilotA handful of large abstractors are driving the drawdown.A meter on each large well, a written seasonal cap in cubic metres per month, monthly meter reading and a published zone total.per abstractor
Alternative supply switchA well is past saving and an inland source or the public main can reach the users.Connect the users to the alternative supply, fit a meter, and cap the brackish well with a witnessed record.per connection switched
Step 2 · The milestones

7 milestones, each with the proof it needs and the check it must pass

#MilestoneEvidence the expert uploadsPass mark the verifier checks
0Scope, transect and datum
Choose the wells. Set at least one line of four wells running inland from the shore. Fix and photograph a permanent datum mark on every wellhead.		A map with the shoreline and every well pinned. Distance to shore in metres for each well. A photo of each wellhead and of its datum mark. Well depth and screen depth where known.At least one transect of four wells running inland. Distance to shore recorded for every well. A marked, photographed datum on every wellhead, because a level measured from the ground is not a level. Well depth labelled measured or stated.
1Baseline sampling
On one day, at the end of the dry season, take a field reading and a laboratory sample at every well. Sample at the wellhead, before any softener or filter. Dip the water level at the same visit.		A photo of the field meter reading with the well in frame at each site. Chain-of-custody forms. The accredited laboratory reports. A photo of the dipper tape reading at each well. The field meter's calibration record for that day.Electrical conductivity, total dissolved solids, chloride, pH and water level recorded at every well on the same day. Field conductivity agrees with the laboratory total dissolved solids within 10% after conversion, or the meter is recalibrated and the round repeated (to confirm the conversion factor your laboratory uses). Every sample drawn at the wellhead, not after treatment.
2Plot the interface
Chart chloride and conductivity against distance from shore and against well depth. Name the wells that are already failing.		The chart. The data table. A one-page note in Arabic for the municipality.Every sampled well appears on the chart. Wells above 250 milligrams per litre of chloride are named, that being the WHO taste threshold for chloride. Wells above 1,000 milligrams per litre of total dissolved solids are flagged as not fit for drinking without treatment, following WHO guidance on acceptability.
3Find what is driving it
At each flagged well, record pump depth, pump rating, hours run and abstraction volume. Take the figure from a meter if there is one, from an hour counter if not, and from the owner only as a last resort.		Photos of the pump plate, the hour counter and any meter with its reading. A signed statement of pumping hours from each owner. The abstraction table.Abstraction in cubic metres per day stated for every flagged well, with the source of the figure named as meter, hour counter or owner statement. Pump intake depth recorded, because a pump set too deep pulls the salt wedge up into the well.
4Agree the cap, or make the switch
Get a written, signed agreement from each large abstractor setting a monthly cap in cubic metres for the dry season. Fit and seal the meter before the cap starts. For a switch, connect the users and cap the old well.		A signed agreement per abstractor naming the monthly cap, the season and a named person. Meter installation photos with serial and opening reading. For a switch: photos of the new connection, the new meter and the capped well.Every agreement names a cap in cubic metres per month and a person, not a company alone. A meter is fitted and its opening reading photographed before the cap period begins, because a cap with no meter is a wish. The Ministry of Energy and Water is a party to each agreement.
5Twelve months of monitoring
Read conductivity and water level monthly at every well in the network. Send a laboratory sample quarterly. Read the abstraction meters monthly.		Monthly photos of the field meter and the dipper tape at each well. Four quarterly laboratory reports. Monthly meter reading photos. The running data file.At least twelve monthly rounds, with any missed month recorded as missed. A chloride trend plotted per well. Any well whose chloride rises by more than 20% over the year is reported in writing to the Water Establishment and the ministry (to confirm the threshold Lebanese practice uses). Every capped abstractor's twelve-month total compared against the agreed cap.
6Report and handover
Hand the whole monitoring file, the map and the trend charts to the municipality and the Water Establishment, and make sure a named person will take next month's reading.		Signed handover with named recipients. The data file as a spreadsheet. The map and charts as a PDF. A photo of the named person taking a reading.Named recipients at both bodies have signed. One named municipal or Water Establishment person takes the thirteenth monthly reading, watched once by the expert. The file is editable so the series can continue.
Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

The baseline is taken in one week at the end of the dry season, ideally September, when the water table is lowest and the intrusion is at its worst. The interface chart follows within 21 days. Caps are agreed within 60 days. Monitoring runs monthly for at least twelve months and is worth far more if it never stops. There is no warranty on data. Meters and any new connection carry 12 months.

Money

Priced per well sampled, per well per year monitored, per abstractor metered, or per connection switched. Laboratory fees are priced separately per sample and per parameter set. No public Lebanese rate exists for coastal salinity monitoring; bracket from the first three real bids. Not included: desalination of any kind, treatment plants, new boreholes, legal enforcement and any compensation for capped abstraction.

Release

Nothing up front. 30% at milestone 1, when the baseline laboratory reports are in and the field meter cross-check passes. 30% at milestone 4, when the agreements are signed and every meter is fitted with an opening reading. 40% spread across the twelve monitoring rounds, paid quarterly against the rounds actually delivered, with the last quarter held until the handover at milestone 6.

Who signs off. The Ministry of Energy and Water licenses abstraction and must be a party to any cap, because a municipality cannot cap a licensed well on its own. The Regional Water Establishment holds the records and controls any alternative supply. The municipality convenes the abstractors and hosts the agreement. The laboratory must be accredited, and the Ministry of Public Health covers drinking water quality. A hydrogeologist or an engineer registered with the Order of Engineers and Architects signs the interpretation, because reading a salt wedge from a chart is a specialist judgement.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Sampling in the wet season. Spring recharge pushes the interface back and hides the problem, so a March baseline makes a dying well look healthy. Milestone 1 fixes the baseline at the end of the dry season.
  • Field meter not calibrated. A conductivity meter drifts, and a drifted meter either raises a false alarm that costs an abstractor money or hides a real intrusion for a year. Milestone 1 cross-checks field readings against the laboratory within 10%.
  • One well, one reading, one conclusion. Intrusion is a trend across a transect, not a point measurement, and a single high reading can be a bad sample. Milestone 5's twelve monthly rounds across the transect.
  • A cap with no meter. An agreement to pump less that nobody can measure is a press release. Everyone signs and nothing changes. Milestone 4 fits and seals the meter before the cap period starts.
  • Sample taken after the softener. Household treatment removes exactly what the survey is looking for, so the aquifer looks fine while the well is ruined. Milestone 1 requires the sample at the wellhead, photographed.
