9 Drought without drought rules
Why this one

Template 9: a staged water restriction ladder for the town

Lebanon has no staged restriction ladder, so a dry year arrives as a surprise and is met with rota cuts nobody agreed to and nobody can predict. Melbourne has run permanent water saving rules with no end date since 2011, under a four-stage ladder and a target of 150 litres per person per day.

Step 1 · Classify

3 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Trigger and stage designThe town has no written plan for a dry year.Find the town's measurable storage and source indicators, set a trigger number for each stage, and write four stages in plain Arabic.per town
Permanent rules and enforcement planThe town wants rules that apply in every year, not just bad ones.The always-on rules, who enforces them, what a breach costs, and the by-law route through the municipal council.per town
Campaign and household efficiencyDemand is the lever the town can actually pull.Tap aerators or thimbles, leaflets, school sessions and a measured before and after. Singapore has given out over a million free tap thimbles alongside its tariff.per household reached
Step 2 · The milestones

6 milestones, each with the proof it needs and the check it must pass

#MilestoneEvidence the expert uploadsPass mark the verifier checks
0Scope and baseline
List every source the town has and what it holds. Photograph the tanks and reservoirs with a level marker. Pull twelve months of production figures and a current population count.		Source list with capacity in cubic metres. Photos of each reservoir and tank with its level marker visible. Twelve months of production data. A dated population count.Litres per person per day computed from real production and a population count dated within the last 12 months. Town storage stated in cubic metres and also in days of supply at current use, which is the number the council will remember.
1Set the triggers
For each of the four stages, pick one number that can be read off a gauge, a marker or a dipper. Name the measuring point and name the person who reads it and how often.		The trigger table. A photo of each measuring point with its datum or level marker. A named reader and a reading frequency for each point.Every stage has one measurable trigger: reservoir level in metres, spring flow in litres per second, or well level in metres below a photographed datum. Every trigger has a named measuring point and a named reader. No stage turns on by judgement alone.
2Write the four stages
Write out what each stage bans, what it still allows, at what hours, and for whom. Say what happens to the supply rota at each stage. Put the permanent rules on top, applying in every stage.		The stage table in Arabic. The permanent rules sheet. A note on which uses were deliberately left alone and why.Each stage bans specific, checkable uses following the Melbourne pattern: garden watering hours, hosing hard surfaces, car washing with potable water, filling pools, and public fountains that do not recirculate. Each stage says what happens to the rota. Each ban states who it applies to, households, businesses, farms or the municipality itself. Permanent rules apply at every stage, including stage zero.
3Adopt
Take the trigger table and the stages to the municipal council for a decision, and inform the Water Establishment in writing.		The council decision with its number and date. The signed trigger table and stage table as annexes to the decision. The minutes. The letter to the Water Establishment and its acknowledgement.A dated, numbered council decision that names the trigger table and the stages as annexes, so there is no argument later about which version was adopted. The Regional Water Establishment has acknowledged receipt in writing.
4Publish and rehearse
Post it where residents look, put it online, and run one drill: move the town to stage one on paper and see who gets told and how fast.		Photos of the notice in at least five public places, each pinned and dated. The online post or broadcast screenshot. A written drill record: the date, the reading that triggered it, who was contacted, how long it took.Published in Arabic with the trigger numbers visible, not hidden in an annex. At least five public postings photographed. One drill recorded end to end, with the contact list tested and the gaps written down.
5Season review
After one dry season, compare production and consumption against the baseline, list which stages were called and when, and either confirm or revise the triggers in writing.		Season production figures. A table of stages called, with dates and the readings that triggered them. The review note. The municipality's signature on the confirmed or revised trigger table.Litres per person per day for the season compared against milestone 0. At least one stage tested against a real reading, even if only on paper. The trigger table is confirmed or revised by a further council decision, so the ladder stays alive rather than becoming a document from one summer.
Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Baseline 30 days. Triggers and stages 30 days. Council adoption within one meeting cycle, typically 30 days, and the expert should plan the work around the council's calendar rather than hope. Publication within seven days of adoption. The drill within 30 days of publication. The review at the end of the first dry season and every year afterwards. There is no warranty on a policy; the annual review is what keeps it true.

Money

Priced as a lump sum per town for the design and the by-law classes, and per household reached for the efficiency campaign, with the fittings priced separately per item. No public Lebanese rate exists for drought planning work; bracket from the first three real bids. Not included: enforcement staff, the administration of fines, new storage, new sources, and the cost of the rota changes themselves.

Release

Nothing up front. 40% at milestone 3, when the council adopts the ladder by a numbered decision. 30% at milestone 4, when it is published in five places and one drill is recorded. 30% at milestone 5, after the first dry-season review and the council's confirmation or revision.

Who signs off. The municipal council adopts local rules and is the only body that can. The Regional Water Establishment controls the supply and must agree anything that touches the rota. The Ministry of Energy and Water is informed. Fines and enforcement need a by-law and the Ministry of Interior and Municipalities route. Restrictions that touch irrigation involve the Ministry of Agriculture, and that is the hardest conversation, so it starts at milestone 0 rather than at milestone 3.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Stages with no trigger. When it gets bad is not a stage. Without a number, the decision falls to whoever shouts loudest in August. Milestone 1 demands one measurable number and one measuring point per stage.
  • A trigger nobody reads. A reservoir level marker with no named reader and no reading day is decoration, and the ladder never gets climbed. Milestone 1 names the person and the frequency, and milestone 4's drill tests it.
  • Restrictions that only bite households. If the largest user is exempt, residents stop complying within a fortnight and the municipality loses the argument permanently. Milestone 2 requires each ban to state who it applies to, including the municipality's own watering.
  • Adopted and never published. A rule that residents have not seen cannot be followed and cannot be enforced. Milestone 4's five photographed postings and the online copy.
  • No permanent rules. A town that only saves water in a crisis loses the habit between crises, and every dry year starts from zero. Milestone 2 puts the permanent rules on top of all four stages, applying in every year.

Why this one

Template 10: chlorination and sampling for a small water system

With the establishments unable to buy chlorine and thousands of private wells never tested, the quality of most Lebanese municipal water is simply unknown. UNICEF has had to supply 143 tons of chlorine and 50 tons of ferric chloride to keep systems treating about 260,000 cubic metres a day.

Step 1 · Classify

4 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit

Advisory procedureThere is no plan for what happens when a test fails.A written boil-water advisory procedure, a named contact list, a trial notice and one logged test call.per system

0Scope, diagram and sampling points

The line diagram. Photos and GPS pins for the source, the pump, the tank and each of the three taps. The tank volume in cubic metres. The population served, dated.The diagram names the source type and the tank volume. A photo of each sample being taken, with the tap and the bottle in frame. The chain-of-custody forms. The accredited laboratory reports. Seal the wellhead so it stands above ground and sheds water away. Fit a lockable tank hatch, screen the vent and the overflow, then clean and disinfect the tank.		Photos of the wellhead seal, the closed and lockable hatch, the screened vent, the screened overflow, the inside of the cleaned tank, and where the washings were discharged. The log of the test call with a name and a time.The procedure names who declares and who lifts, and lifting requires two consecutive clear samples (to confirm what the Ministry of Public Health requires). A photo of the municipal operator taking a reading.At least twelve monthly field rounds and four laboratory rounds, with any missed round recorded as missed. Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Baseline sampling within 14 days of award, because nothing else should be designed before the water is tested. The advisory procedure is written before chlorination starts. Barriers and chlorination within 45 days. Residual checks within seven days of dosing beginning. Then monthly field tests and quarterly laboratory tests for twelve months. Warranty 12 months on the dosing equipment and on the tank and wellhead sealing work.

Money

Priced per system for the baseline, the chlorination install and the advisory procedure, and per sample for the routine programme, split between field tests and laboratory tests because the laboratory dominates the cost. No public Lebanese rate exists for small-system chlorination; bracket from the first three real bids. Not included: chlorine beyond the first three months, network replacement, any treatment beyond chlorination such as filtration or removal of nitrate, and household filters.

Release

Nothing up front. 20% at milestone 1, when the baseline laboratory report is in. 40% at milestone 3, when dosing passes the 0.5 milligrams per litre check after 30 minutes of real contact time. 20% at milestone 4, when the residual reaches the furthest tap at 0.2 milligrams per litre. 20% at milestone 6, after twelve months of results and the handover.

Who signs off. The Ministry of Public Health covers drinking water quality and is the body that issues or endorses a boil-water advisory. The Regional Water Establishment owns the system and the chlorination equipment on a public scheme. The municipality operates many small schemes and posts the advisories. LIBNOR holds the Lebanese drinking water standard and the laboratory must be accredited against it. Chlorine gas would bring in the fire service and Civil Defence, which is one good reason a small system should use sodium hypochlorite or calcium hypochlorite instead. An engineer registered with the Order of Engineers and Architects signs the dosing design.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Sampling the tap that always passes. The kitchen tap at the pump house is twenty metres from the chlorine and proves nothing about the street at the end of the line. Milestone 0 fixes three taps by address, including the genuinely furthest one.
  • Chlorine but no contact time. Dosing straight into a pipe heading for the street gives seconds of contact, not 30 minutes, so the residual reads fine and the bacteria survive. Milestone 3 calculates contact time from tank volume and flow and checks the residual after it.
  • Old hypochlorite. Sodium hypochlorite loses strength fast on a hot roof, so a full tank of weak chlorine looks like a dosed system and does almost nothing. Milestone 3's photograph of dated stock with its strength, and the residual check that follows.
  • Turbidity ignored. Chlorine cannot disinfect through cloudy water, because the particles shield the bacteria, so a good chlorine reading in turbid water is false comfort. Milestone 3 pairs the chlorine number with a turbidity below 1 NTU.
  • A failure with nobody to call. A positive E. coli result on a Friday afternoon with no named contact and no procedure is the real danger in a small system, not the bacteria themselves. Milestone 5, which is completed before dosing starts and is tested with a logged call.
Sources
  • npj Clean Water, drinking water quality and risk in small and remote systems nature.com
  • Queensland Audit Office, Managing Queensland's regional water quality, on auditing small-system compliance qao.qld.gov.au
  • iClear Kenya, tap and borehole water quality testing iclear.co.ke
  • WHO, Guidelines for drinking-water quality, fourth edition with addenda, on E. coli, chlorine residual and turbidity who.int
  • UNICEF, Lebanon's water infrastructure struggles and remains on the brink, on chlorine and ferric chloride supplied unicef.org

Sewage: 10 templates. Open one to read it.

1 Plants built but idle for lack of power and fuel
Why this one

Template 1: getting an idle treatment plant running on its own power

Lebanon has roughly 100 wastewater treatment plants and only about 35 of them run, several only part of the day, because grid power is rationed and diesel is no longer subsidised. Blowers for biological treatment eat most of a plant's electricity, so a plant with no power is a concrete box with sewage flowing past it.

Step 1 · Classify

4 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Energy audit and metering onlyNobody knows what the plant uses or when it runs. Always do this first if there is no meter log.Fit or read a kWh meter and a flow meter, log run hours for at least 14 days, list every motor with its rating, work out kWh per cubic metre treated, write a short report with the three cheapest fixes.per plant
Solar for the daytime loadThe plant has roof or fenced land, and the biggest loads can run in daylight.Sizing from the audit, stamped electrical design, panels, inverters, mounting, protection, grid or generator interface, monitoring, commissioning test.kWp installed
Aeration efficiency retrofitBlowers and diffusers are the biggest single load and are old or oversized.Replace or resize blowers, replace diffusers, fit a dissolved oxygen probe and automatic control so the blowers stop when the tank has enough oxygen.per plant
Biogas to powerThe plant already has anaerobic digesters that are sealed and working.Gas collection, cleaning, a gas engine or boiler, safety flare, electrical tie-in, gas and power metering.kWe installed
Step 2 · The milestones

7 milestones, each with the proof it needs and the check it must pass

#MilestoneEvidence the expert uploadsPass mark the verifier checks
0Scope and class
Visit the plant with the operator. Count the motors, read the nameplates, check whether a kWh meter and a flow meter exist and work. Choose the class. Agree the design flow and the flow that actually arrives.		Photos of every motor nameplate and of the meter faces. GPS pin of the plant. A one-page list of loads in kW. A note of who owns the plant and who pays the power bill.Every motor above 1 kW is on the list with a nameplate photo. Class chosen. The verifier can see a meter, or a line in the plan saying a meter will be fitted at milestone 1.
1Baseline for 14 days
Log kWh and treated flow every day for at least 14 days, and the hours the plant actually ran each day. Do not change anything during this period.		A dated table of daily kWh, daily cubic metres, daily run hours. Photo of the meter reading on the first and last day. Diesel receipts for the same period.At least 14 days with no gaps. The expert states kWh per cubic metre treated to two decimal places. Run hours per day stated. This is the number every later milestone is measured against.
2Design and approvals
Produce a stamped design for the chosen class. Get the owner of the plant, the water establishment, to approve it in writing. Apply for any grid or net-metering approval.		Design drawings and calculations stamped by an engineer registered with the Order of Engineers. Written approval from the water establishment. Copy of the EDL or net-metering application for the solar class.The stamp and registration number are readable. The design flow matches milestone 1. The predicted saving is stated in kWh per year and in kWh per cubic metre. For solar, the array size follows the audit and is not larger than the daytime load plus 20 per cent.
3Supply and install
Deliver and install the equipment. Keep the plant running while you do it, or agree a shutdown window with the water establishment in writing.		Delivery notes and serial numbers for panels, inverters, blowers, probes or engines. Photos of the equipment installed and of the serial plates. Photos of earthing and protection. Waste and packaging removed.Serial numbers on the delivery notes match the serial numbers in the photos. Nothing on site is a model different from the approved design without a written variation.
4Commission and prove
Run the new equipment and measure. For solar, record generation for seven clear days. For aeration, record dissolved oxygen and blower hours. For biogas, record gas flow and kWh generated.		Seven days of readings with dates. Photo of the monitoring screen. Signed commissioning sheet from the installer and the plant operator. Test certificates for electrical safety.Measured output is within 10 per cent of the design prediction (to confirm with the designer's own guarantee wording). For aeration, dissolved oxygen in the tank stays inside the range written in the approved design and the blowers switch off when it is met. The plant did not stop treating sewage during the works, or stopped only inside the agreed window.
5Ninety-day performance
Leave the plant alone for 90 days and keep the same daily log as milestone 1. Then compare.		Ninety days of daily kWh, cubic metres and run hours, in the same format as milestone 1. Diesel receipts for the period. Photos from the same spots as milestone 3.kWh per cubic metre treated has fallen, or run hours per day have risen, by at least the amount written in the approved design. No motor is out of service. This is the gate for the final release.
6Handover and an O and M line
Hand over manuals, spares list, the monitoring login and a one-page maintenance calendar. Get the water establishment to confirm in writing that the running cost is in a named budget line for the next year.		Signed handover note. Manuals in Arabic or with an Arabic summary. Spares list with prices. A copy of the budget line or a signed letter naming it.The handover note is signed by a named person at the water establishment and by the municipality. There is a named budget line, not a promise. Two plant staff have signed a training sheet.
Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Inspect the plant within 10 working days of the request. Finish the audit and the 14-day baseline within 30 days. Design and approvals within 60 days, because the water establishment and EDL both have to answer. Install within 90 to 180 days depending on class, with solar at the short end and biogas at the long end. Then the 90-day performance window, which is what the last payment waits for. Warranty: 24 months on solar panels, inverters and blowers, 12 months on electrical works, and the manufacturer's own longer warranty passed on to the water establishment in writing.

Money

Priced per kWp for solar, per kWe for biogas, and as a lump sum per plant for the audit and the aeration retrofit. There is no public Lebanese unit rate for any of these on a wastewater plant, and the sources below do not publish one: bracket it from the first three real bids and publish the bracket afterwards. Not included: grid reinforcement by EDL, civil works to strengthen a roof, replacing pumps that were already broken, and the diesel the plant burns while the works go on. The audit must be a separate priced line so that a municipality can buy only the audit if the money runs out.

Release

Nothing up front. 15 per cent when the 14-day baseline is accepted at milestone 1. 15 per cent when the stamped design is approved at milestone 2. 40 per cent at commissioning, milestone 4. 30 per cent after the 90-day performance check at milestone 5. If measured output is below the design prediction at milestone 5, the 30 per cent is held until the expert brings it up or the shortfall is priced off.

Who signs off. The plant belongs to one of the four Regional Water Establishments created by Law 221/2000 and amended by Laws 241/2000 and 337/2001, so their written approval is the one that matters, not the municipality's alone. Tell the municipality and get it in the council minutes. If the plant was built by the Council for Development and Reconstruction with donor money, CDR must confirm the asset transfer before anyone bolts anything to it. The electrical design needs an engineer registered with the Order of Engineers. Any grid connection or net metering needs EDL. The Ministry of Energy and Water is the policy owner and should be copied. The Lebanese Centre for Energy Conservation is the reference for solar sizing practice.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • No baseline. Without 14 days of before readings, nobody can prove any saving, and the last payment becomes an argument. This is the single most common way these projects end badly. Milestone 1. The verifier refuses to move on without a dated table.
  • Solar sized to the plant nameplate, not to the real load. The plant treats far less than its design flow, so an array sized on paper is twice what is needed and the money would have been better spent on the network. Milestone 2. The array must follow the audit, not the nameplate.
  • Blowers left on manual. A dissolved oxygen probe with no automatic control saves nothing. The operator leaves the blowers running flat out because that is safe. Milestone 4. The verifier watches the blowers switch off.
  • Power fixed, chemicals and spares still unfunded. The plant runs for six months on new solar power and then stops for want of a 200 dollar part, and the project is recorded as a failure. Milestone 6. A named budget line, in writing.
  • Equipment swapped for a cheaper model. Inverters and blowers are where a contractor saves money quietly, and the difference only shows up in year three. Milestone 3. Serial numbers on the delivery note must match the photos and the approved design.
Sources
  • Libnanews, Wastewater: history of an unfinished Lebanese system, 2025. About 100 plants, about 35 operating, some partially; blowers as the main energy load. en.libnanews.com
  • Lebanese Center for Policy Studies, Lebanon's wastewater sector: a path to development and sustainability. About half of total treatment capacity reactivated by 2025. lcps-lebanon.org
  • Water supply and sanitation in Lebanon, overview article. Law 221/2000 and the four Regional Water Establishments; no wastewater tariff and zero cost recovery. en.wikipedia.org
  • UNDP Lebanon, Energy from wastewater sewage sludge in Lebanon. Listed as the Lebanese reference for energy recovery; the page could not be fetched for this template. undp.org
2 Plant and network built separately, never connected
Why this one

Template 2: connecting houses to a plant that is already built

Lebanon keeps building plants before pipes. Baalbek's plant was finished in 2001 with a capacity of 13,000 cubic metres a day and was still not working in 2006 because the sewers never reached it. In the Litani basin only 18 km of a planned 441 km of network had been built by March 2020, and 1.8 per cent of the households meant to be connected actually were.

Step 1 · Classify

4 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Connection survey and registerNobody can say how many buildings in the town are connected. Do this before any digging.Walk every street, find every building's outlet, record whether it goes to the sewer, to a cesspit or to a channel, put it on a map with GPS, produce a numbered register.per building surveyed
Missing link between collector and plantThe network exists and the plant exists but the two do not meet.Survey the gap, design, excavate, lay the pipe, build manholes, test, reinstate the road surface.metre of pipe
House connections in one blockThe street sewer is there but buildings still discharge to a pit.Per building: a connection chamber, the lateral pipe to the street sewer, sealing and decommissioning of the old cesspit, reinstatement.per building connected
Inflow metering at the plantThe plant has no flow meter, so no one can prove the connections did anything.Fit a flow meter on the inlet with a data logger, calibrate it, train the operator to log it daily.per plant
Step 2 · The milestones

7 milestones, each with the proof it needs and the check it must pass

#MilestoneEvidence the expert uploadsPass mark the verifier checks
0Scope and class
Get the plant's design flow and the as-built network drawings from the water establishment and the Council for Development and Reconstruction. Define the block or the gap that this contract covers on a map.		Copy of the plant's design capacity in cubic metres per day. A map with the contract boundary drawn on it. GPS pins for the plant and the two ends of any missing link. Photos of the existing collector end.The boundary is a closed shape on a map, not a description. Design capacity is a number. The verifier can see, in one line, how many buildings are inside the boundary.
1Building-by-building survey
Visit every building inside the boundary. Find where its wastewater goes. Number it, photograph the outlet or the pit cover, take a GPS point, note the number of flats.		One row per building in a spreadsheet: number, GPS, flats, current outlet type, photo file name. One photo per building. A map with every building coloured by outlet type.The number of rows equals the number of buildings inside the boundary, with any refusals listed by number and reason. Every row has a GPS point and a photo. No building is marked unknown without a note saying who was asked.
2Design and permission to dig
Design the connections or the missing link. Get the water establishment to approve. Get the municipality's road-opening permission and, if the route touches a classified road, the Ministry of Public Works.		Stamped drawings with pipe sizes, gradients, manhole positions and invert levels. Written approval from the water establishment. Road-opening permit with a reference number. Traffic management plan.Every length of gravity pipe has a stated gradient on the drawing. The stamp and registration number are readable. A named authority gave permission, with a reference the verifier can quote.
3Lay, bed and test
Excavate, bed the pipe on granular material, lay to the designed gradient, build the manholes, backfill in compacted layers.		Photos of the open trench showing the bedding and the pipe before backfill, with a level staff or laser in frame. Photos of every manhole open. Delivery notes for pipe and bedding material. A water or air tightness test sheet per length.Every length has a before-backfill photo. No length is backfilled without one. Tightness test passed on every length, with the pass criterion printed on the sheet. Manhole inverts are smooth channels, not flat slabs.
4Connect and switch over
Connect each building, seal and fill the old cesspit, and make sure nothing still runs to the old outlet.		Per building: photo of the new chamber open, photo of the old cesspit being filled, a signed note from the owner or caretaker. A dye or water test video showing flow arriving in the street manhole.Every building in the register is marked connected, refused or not present, with nothing blank. Every connected building has a dye or water test showing flow reaching the sewer. Old pits are filled, not just covered.
5Inflow proof at the plant
Read the plant inlet meter for 14 days before switch-over and 14 days after. Compare.		Two dated tables of daily cubic metres, before and after, from the same meter. Photo of the meter. The operator's signature on both tables.Measured inflow rose after switch-over by an amount consistent with the number of buildings connected and the design figure used at milestone 2 (the design figure per person per day must be stated and sourced, or marked to confirm). If inflow did not move, the connections did not work and the verifier holds the release.
6Handover and road reinstatement
Reinstate every road and pavement opened. Hand over the as-built drawings, the register and the manhole schedule to the water establishment and the municipality.		Before and after photos of every road opening from the same spot. Signed handover note listing the drawings, the register and the meter readings. Photo of each manhole cover flush with the road.No trench is left with a temporary surface. Every cover sits flush, within 5 mm of the surrounding surface (to confirm against the municipality's own road specification). The register handed over is the same register used at milestone 1, filled in.
Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Inspect within 10 working days. The survey at milestone 1 should take 1 to 3 weeks for a block of a few hundred buildings. Design and permission 30 to 45 days, because two authorities have to answer. Laying and connecting, 60 to 120 days depending on how much road is opened. Then 14 days before and 14 days after at the plant meter. Do not open roads between mid-November and mid-March if the town floods; the works become the flood. Warranty: 24 months on pipework and manholes, and the road reinstatement is guaranteed for 24 months against settlement.

Money

The survey is priced per building surveyed. The missing link is priced per metre of pipe by diameter and depth, as trunk sewer bills of quantities normally are. House connections are priced per building connected, with a separate rate for filling the old cesspit. Metering is a lump sum. No public Lebanese unit rate exists for any of these: bracket from the first three real bids and publish the bracket. Not included: pumping stations, private plumbing inside the building, and any deep rock excavation, which should be a separate measured rate agreed before it is met.

Release

Nothing up front. 10 per cent when the survey register is accepted at milestone 1. 20 per cent when the design and permits are in at milestone 2. 40 per cent at milestone 4 when every building is connected and dye-tested. 30 per cent after the plant meter shows the inflow at milestone 5, which is the whole point of the contract.

Who signs off. The water establishment owns the sewer and the plant under Law 221/2000, so its written approval is the key one. The municipality gives road-opening permission and operates local sewers. The Ministry of Public Works has to agree if the route crosses a classified road. The Council for Development and Reconstruction holds the as-built drawings for donor-funded networks and plants, and should be asked first before anyone surveys from scratch. Designs must be stamped by an engineer registered with the Order of Engineers. If refugee or informal settlements are inside the boundary, tell the relevant UN agency so that the survey is not read as an eviction exercise.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Counting capacity instead of inflow. A plant is reported as working because it exists. The only honest measure is how many cubic metres a day arrive at the inlet. Milestone 5. The meter, not the nameplate.
  • Buildings left on the pit next to a live sewer. The street sewer passes the door and the owner keeps using the cesspit because the connection costs money. The plant stays half empty. Milestone 4. Every building in the register is marked, and the old pit must be photographed being filled.
  • Pipe laid to the wrong gradient. A gravity sewer with no fall blocks within a year and the town blames the plant. Milestone 3. Gradient on the drawing, and the before-backfill photo with a level in frame.
  • Backfilled before anyone looked. Once the trench is closed, the bedding and the joints can never be checked, and any defect becomes the municipality's problem. Milestone 3. No photo, no payment for that length.
  • Rainwater connected into the foul sewer. Roof and yard drains connected to the new sewer swamp the plant in the first storm and push raw sewage out of manholes. Milestone 4. The dye test shows what is connected, and the surveyor records roof drains at milestone 1.
Sources
  • Water supply and sanitation in Lebanon, overview article. Baalbek plant completed 2001 at 13,000 cubic metres a day and inoperative in 2006; Tripoli 2009 and Sidon 2010 opened late; 58 per cent sewer connection in 2002. en.wikipedia.org
  • Litani River Authority, pollution challenges page. Only 18 km of a planned 441 km of network built by March 2020, and 1.8 per cent of targeted households connected. litani.gov.lb
  • The Financial Express, Bangladesh: 41 per cent of capacity underused three years after completion. The same pattern of plants without networks. thefinancialexpress.com.bd
  • Comptroller and Auditor General of India, Namami Gange performance audit, Report No. 2 of 2025. Audit approach of judging plants by inflow rather than capacity. cag.gov.in
3 Raw sewage discharged to the sea
Why this one

Template 3: coastal outfall survey, screening and bathing-water watch

Al-Ghadir, which takes sewage from Beirut and much of Mount Lebanon, gives only preliminary treatment and then pushes it through a 2.6 km marine outfall. In 2023 the National Council for Scientific Research classed 38 per cent of monitored coastal bathing sites as polluted. A town cannot build a secondary plant this year, but it can find out exactly what is going into its own sea and prove it month by month.

Step 1 · Classify

4 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Outfall and discharge inventoryNobody has a list of what discharges to the sea along the town's coast.Walk and boat the whole coastline in the town's boundary, find every pipe and channel, GPS each one, photograph it flowing, note pipe size and what it smells and looks like, trace it back upstream to its catchment.per kilometre of coastline
Bathing-water sampling programmeThe town has beaches or swimming spots and no data.Fixed sampling points, monthly samples in the bathing season, an accredited laboratory, E. coli and intestinal enterococci, results published in plain language within 14 days.per sample
Screening and grit upgradeAn existing preliminary plant or pumping station has no working screen, so plastic and grit go straight to sea.Mechanical or manual bar screen, screenings handling and disposal, grit removal, a covered skip, odour control, operator training.per station
Secondary treatment feasibility and designThe town wants to stop discharging and needs a costed, stamped answer before it asks anyone for money.Load survey, site options, process comparison, land and power needs, capital and running cost, a stamped preliminary design and a phasing plan.per study
Step 2 · The milestones

6 milestones, each with the proof it needs and the check it must pass

#MilestoneEvidence the expert uploadsPass mark the verifier checks
0Scope and class
Draw the stretch of coast on a map. Say whether it includes a beach people swim from. Choose the class and name the laboratory you will use.		Map with the stretch drawn and its length in kilometres. Photos of the shoreline from both ends. Name and accreditation certificate of the laboratory.The stretch is a measured length, not a place name. The laboratory is named and its accreditation is current. If the class is sampling, the sampling points are marked on the map before any sample is taken.
1Find every discharge
Walk the whole stretch at low tide and again from a boat. Find every pipe, channel and seep. Photograph each one flowing. Measure or estimate the pipe diameter.		One row per discharge: GPS, diameter, material, flowing or dry, photo, short description. Photos taken with a scale object in frame. A map with every discharge numbered.The coastline was covered end to end, with a GPS track to prove it. Every discharge has a photo and a GPS point. Any pipe the expert could not reach is listed with the reason.
2Trace and name the owners
For each discharge, follow it inland far enough to say what it carries and who owns it: the water establishment's collector, a municipal storm drain, a hotel, a factory, a cluster of houses.		Per discharge: a note of the upstream manhole or channel, a photo, and the name of the owner or the sentence no owner identified. Copies of any correspondence sent asking.Every discharge is either traced to a named owner or has a written record of who was asked and when. Storm drains carrying foul sewage are flagged separately, because that is an illegal connection upstream, not a sea problem.
3Sample and test
Take samples at the fixed points, in clean sterile bottles, cool them, and get them to the laboratory the same day. Repeat monthly through the bathing season.		Chain-of-custody form per sample: point, date, time, who took it, temperature on arrival. Laboratory report with E. coli and intestinal enterococci per 100 millilitres. Photo of the sampling point on the day.Time between taking and testing is inside the laboratory's stated holding time. No gaps in the monthly series. Results are reported per 100 millilitres with the method named. The verifier compares each point to the reference the municipality adopted at milestone 0; if none exists in Lebanese law, the adopted reference and its numbers are stated and marked to confirm.
4Fix what can be fixed now
Do the class work: install or repair the screen, clear the grit, cut off any illegal foul connection found at milestone 2, or deliver the feasibility study.		Photos before and after at the same spot. Delivery notes and serial numbers for any screen. Weight or volume of screenings removed in the first week. For the study class, the stamped report.Screenings are being removed to a covered skip and taken to a legal disposal point, with a disposal note, not left on the bank. For the study class, the report is stamped by an engineer registered with the Order of Engineers and gives capital and annual running cost in dollars.
5Publish and repeat
Publish the inventory and every result in Arabic on the municipality's board and website, in plain language, and set the next season's sampling dates.		Photo of the published notice. Link or file of the published results. A signed note from the municipality naming who will take the next samples and from which budget line.Results are public within 14 days of the laboratory report. The published sheet says clearly, for each point, whether people should swim. A named person and a named budget line exist for next season. This is the gate for the final release.
Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Inspect within 10 working days. The coastal walk and inventory should finish within 30 days, and must be done in dry weather so that storm flows are not mistaken for sewage. Sampling runs monthly through the bathing season, which in Lebanon is roughly May to October, so the sampling class is a six-month contract. Screening works within 60 days, and never in the two weeks before a public holiday weekend when the beach is busiest. A feasibility study within 90 days. Warranty: 24 months on any installed screen, 12 months on electrical work.

Money

The inventory is priced per kilometre of coastline. Sampling is priced per sample, including the laboratory fee, which should be shown separately so the municipality can see the true recurring cost. The screening upgrade is a lump sum per station. The feasibility study is a lump sum. No public Lebanese unit rate exists for coastal survey or for accredited bathing-water sampling: bracket from the first three real bids and publish the bracket. Not included: boat hire in rough weather, any dredging, and the cost of the secondary treatment works the study will recommend.

Release

Nothing up front. 25 per cent when the inventory at milestone 1 and the tracing at milestone 2 are accepted. 45 per cent at milestone 4 when the physical work is done or the study is delivered. 30 per cent after milestone 5, when the results are published and next season's sampling has a named owner and a budget line. For the sampling class, pay per completed monthly round, with the last round held until publication.

Who signs off. The water establishment owns the collectors and the plant. The municipality owns storm drains and the shoreline access. The Ministry of Environment is the authority on discharge limits; the standard the country has is the Ministry of Environment's own decision on minimum levels for treated domestic wastewater, and there is no Lebanese standard for wastewater reuse. The Ministry of Public Works and Transport oversees the maritime public domain, so any work on the shore or on an outfall needs its agreement. The Ministry of Public Health has an interest in bathing water. The National Council for Scientific Research runs the existing national coastal monitoring and should be told what the town is sampling so the numbers can sit beside theirs.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Sampling only where the water looks clean. Points chosen after the fact make the town look good and tell residents nothing. Points must be fixed and mapped before the first sample. Milestone 0. Points on the map first, then sampling.
  • Samples that sit in a car boot. Bacteria counts change fast in a warm bottle, so a late sample is a wrong number, usually a flattering one. Milestone 3. The chain-of-custody form records time and arrival temperature.
  • Outfall survey done after rain. In a storm every drain runs, so the survey records rainwater as sewage and the inventory is useless. Milestone 1. The verifier checks the dates against the weather.
  • Screenings tipped beside the plant. Plastic and rags pulled out of the flow and dumped on the bank are back in the sea with the next wave, and the screen has achieved nothing. Milestone 4. Disposal notes and the covered skip photo.
  • Results collected and never published. Data held by a consultant does not change behaviour. The pressure that gets a plant funded comes from residents knowing which beach is dirty. Milestone 5. Published within 14 days, in Arabic, or no final payment.

  • Lebanese Center for Policy Studies, Lebanon's wastewater sector. 38 per cent of monitored coastal bathing sites classed polluted, 2023 CNRS data; 60 per cent of ten major rivers above permissible E. coli, 2024. lcps-lebanon.org
  • World Health Organization Regional Office for the Eastern Mediterranean, A compendium of standards for wastewater reuse in the Eastern Mediterranean Region. Lebanon has Ministry of Environment Decree 52/1 of 1996 on minimum levels for treated domestic wastewater and no reuse standard; WHO and Jordanian and Tunisian limits for comparison. applications.emro.who.int

4 River pollution from sewered towns without treatment
Why this one

Template 4: intercepting a town's sewage before it reaches the river

About 46 million cubic metres of sewage a year reach the Litani, with 47 million cubic metres coming off 69 towns in the upper basin alone, and around 4 million cubic metres of untreated industrial wastewater from 185 surveyed factories. That water is then used to irrigate food. In 2024, 60 per cent of samples from ten major Lebanese rivers were above permissible E. coli levels and 40 per cent exceeded the FAO criterion for faecal coliforms in irrigation water.

Cluster treatment for a village with no plantNo plant is within reach and the village has a few hundred to a few thousand people.Gravity-fed decentralised treatment on the DEWATS pattern: settler, anaerobic baffled reactor, anaerobic filter, planted gravel filter, polishing pond. No electricity and no chemicals.per population equivalent served

Step 2 · The milestones

7 milestones, each with the proof it needs and the check it must pass

#MilestoneEvidence the expert uploadsPass mark the verifier checks
0Scope and class
Define the river reach with an upstream and a downstream point on a map. Choose the class. Agree with the Litani River Authority or the relevant basin body that nobody else is already doing this reach.		Map with the two end points and their GPS. Photo upstream and downstream. Written note from the basin authority or the water establishment confirming the reach is not already covered.The reach has a stated length in kilometres and two GPS end points. There is a written reply, or a record of the request and the date it went unanswered.
1Upstream and downstream baseline
Before doing anything, take water samples just above and just below the reach on the same day, in dry weather, and send them to an accredited laboratory.		Chain-of-custody forms. Laboratory reports for E. coli or faecal coliforms per 100 millilitres, biochemical oxygen demand, chemical oxygen demand, suspended solids and ammonia. Photos of both sampling points with the river level visible.Both samples taken the same day, in dry weather, at least 48 hours after rain. All five parameters reported. The difference between upstream and downstream is stated. This is the number the project is judged against.
2Find and name every discharge
Walk both banks end to end. Record every pipe, channel and seep, flowing or dry. Trace each one back until you can say what it carries and who owns it.		One row per discharge with GPS, diameter, flowing or dry, photo with a scale in frame, upstream manhole reference, owner name or the sentence no owner identified. A GPS track proving both banks were walked.The GPS track covers the whole reach on both banks. Every discharge has a photo and a point. Industrial discharges are listed separately from domestic ones, with the premises named.
3Design and approvals
Design the interception or the cluster plant. Get approvals from the water establishment, the basin authority, the municipality and, for land, the owner.		Stamped drawings and calculations. Written approvals. Land agreement or lease for any plant footprint. For the cluster class, the design population, the design flow and the expected effluent quality.The stamp and Order of Engineers registration number are readable. The design effluent quality is written down as numbers with a named reference standard. Land is secured in writing, not verbally.
4Build and commission
Build the chamber, the pipe, the pumping station or the treatment units. Plant the gravel filter and let it establish before full flow.		Trench photos before backfill with a level in frame. Tightness test sheets. Photos of each treatment unit being built and filled. Delivery notes for media and plants. Commissioning sheet signed by the expert and the operator.Every buried length has a before-backfill photo and a passed tightness test. For the cluster class, the retention times built match the design; the DEWATS reference figures are settler 2 to 3 hours, anaerobic baffled reactor 8 to 12 hours, anaerobic filter 12 to 20 hours, planted gravel filter 24 to 36 hours, polishing pond 12 to 18 hours.
5Prove the river changed
After the works are live and the planted filter has had at least eight weeks to establish, repeat the milestone 1 sampling on the same points, same conditions.		New chain-of-custody forms and laboratory reports for the same five parameters. Photos from the same spots. For interception, the flow meter records showing the flow now arriving at the plant.Downstream E. coli or faecal coliform count is materially lower than the milestone 1 baseline, in dry weather. For a cluster plant, effluent meets the standard adopted at milestone 3. Regional reference values the verifier can use: Jordanian Standard JS 893/2002 for discharge to streams allows biochemical oxygen demand 60, chemical oxygen demand 150, suspended solids 60 milligrams per litre, E. coli 1000 per 100 millilitres and 1 helminth egg per litre; Tunisian Standard NT 106.03 allows biochemical oxygen demand 30, chemical oxygen demand 90 and suspended solids 30 milligrams per litre.

Hand over as-builts, the discharge register and a one-page operating routine. Name who desludges the settler and how often, and from which budget.		Signed handover note. As-built drawings. Operating routine in Arabic with a desludging date. A signed letter from the water establishment or municipality naming the budget line and the person.A named person and a named budget line, not a promise. Two operators have signed a training sheet. The desludging interval is written as a date, not as when needed.
Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Inspect within 10 working days. The bank survey and the baseline sampling within 30 days, and both must be in dry weather at least 48 hours after rain, which in the Bekaa means doing this between May and October. Design and approvals 45 to 60 days. Construction 90 to 180 days. Then at least 8 weeks for a planted filter to establish before the proving samples at milestone 5. Warranty: 24 months on civil works and pipework, 12 months on pumps and electrical, and a full growing season on the planted filter, with dead plants replaced at the expert's cost.

Money

The inventory is priced per kilometre of reach walked on both banks. Interception is priced per metre of pipe by diameter and depth plus a lump sum per pumping station. A cluster plant is priced per population equivalent served, which is the only way to compare bids fairly. Industrial visits are priced per premises including one sample. No public Lebanese unit rate exists for decentralised treatment: bracket from the first three real bids and publish the bracket. The DEWATS experience is that life-cycle costs run up to 50 per cent below conventional plants, which is a reason to ask for a life-cycle price, not only a build price. Not included: land purchase, river bank protection works, and any industrial pre-treatment, which is the factory's own duty.

Release

Nothing up front. 10 per cent at milestone 1 when the baseline samples are in. 15 per cent at milestone 2 when the discharge register is accepted. 15 per cent at milestone 3 when the design is stamped and the land is secured. 30 per cent at milestone 4 on commissioning. 30 per cent at milestone 5 when the downstream samples prove the change. For a cluster plant, hold 10 per cent for 12 months against the first summer of real operation.

Who signs off. For the Litani, the Litani River Authority is the basin body and must be told and ideally must approve. The water establishment owns the collectors and any plant. The municipality gives road-opening permission and owns the land in many villages. The Ministry of Environment sets the discharge limits and is the authority that can act on an industrial discharge. The Ministry of Agriculture matters where the water is used for irrigation. Designs must be stamped by an engineer registered with the Order of Engineers. If the works touch the river bed or banks, the Ministry of Energy and Water controls public water domain.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Sampling after rain. Rain dilutes the river and flushes the drains, so both the baseline and the proof come out wrong. In a wet week the same works can look like a miracle or like nothing. Milestones 1 and 5. The verifier checks the sample dates against rainfall.
  • Interception into a plant that is already full. Diverting a town's sewage into a plant with no spare capacity just moves the overflow, and the river gets it anyway through the plant's bypass. Milestone 0 and milestone 3. The receiving plant's inlet meter must show spare capacity before the design is approved.
  • A cluster plant with a pump in it. Add electricity and the village plant stops the first week the power fails and never restarts. The DEWATS design works because it is gravity fed, with no electricity and no chemicals. Milestone 3. The verifier checks the design for any powered item.
  • Nobody desludges the settler. An anaerobic settler that is never emptied passes solids into the filter, the filter blocks, and within two years the plant is a pond of sewage. Milestone 6. A named person, a date and a budget line.
  • Industrial discharge counted as domestic. A dairy or a tannery can carry the organic load of a small town. Treating it as household sewage sizes the works wrong and lets the polluter off. Milestone 2. Industrial discharges are listed separately and sampled.

  • Lebanese Center for Policy Studies, Lebanon's wastewater sector. 60 per cent of ten major rivers above permissible E. coli and 40 per cent above the FAO faecal coliform criterion for irrigation water, 2024 study. lcps-lebanon.org
  • CDD India, used water management. DEWATS modules and their retention times and BOD removals; over 400 systems; no electricity or chemicals; life-cycle costs up to 50 per cent lower than conventional plants. cddindia.org
  • World Health Organization Regional Office for the Eastern Mediterranean, A compendium of standards for wastewater reuse in the Eastern Mediterranean Region. Jordanian Standard JS 893/2002 and Tunisian Standard NT 106.03 limits used above as regional reference values. applications.emro.who.int
5 Village septic tanks and cesspits leaking to groundwater
Why this one

Template 5: a village inspection register for pits and septic tanks

Most Lebanese villages with no sewer use open-bottom pits, and Lebanon's karstic limestone lets whatever leaves a pit reach a spring quickly and with little filtering. Nobody has a list of which pits leak. France solved the list problem first: every non-collective system is inspected at least once every ten years by a public service, and the owner then has four years to fix a minor fault and usually under one year to fix a serious one.

Step 1 · Classify

4 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Household inspection and registerAlways first. The village has no record of what each house uses.Visit every house, open and inspect the tank or pit, record type, size, age, condition, distance to the nearest well or spring, and whether it discharges to open ground. Give the owner a written result. Build one numbered register for the village.per household
Pit to sealed tank upgradeAn open-bottom cesspit sits close to a well or a spring and the house has room.Build or install a watertight septic tank of the right size, connect it, build a soakaway or a planted filter in suitable ground, seal and fill the old pit, issue a completion certificate.per household
Cluster treatment for a group of housesTen or more houses sit together on ground too tight or too rocky for individual soakaways.A small gravity-fed system on the DEWATS pattern: settler, anaerobic baffled reactor, anaerobic filter and planted gravel filter, with no electricity and no chemicals.per population equivalent served
Scheduled desludging serviceTanks exist and are sound but are never emptied, so they pass solids straight out.A published desludging round with a fixed interval, a licensed tanker, a receipt to the householder, and a named legal disposal point that will accept the load.per household desludged
Step 2 · The milestones

7 milestones, each with the proof it needs and the check it must pass

#MilestoneEvidence the expert uploadsPass mark the verifier checks
0Scope and class
Agree the village boundary and count the houses on the map. Find and mark every spring, well and borehole used for drinking. Choose the class.		Map with the boundary, the house count, and every water point marked with GPS. Photos of the main spring or well. A copy of the council decision authorising the inspections.House count and water points are numbers on a map. There is a council decision, because inspectors will be knocking on doors and need authority to do it.
1Spring and well baseline
Before any inspection, sample the village's drinking water points and send them to an accredited laboratory.		Chain-of-custody forms. Laboratory reports for E. coli and total coliforms per 100 millilitres and for nitrate. Photos of each point on the day of sampling.Every drinking point on the milestone 0 map has a result. Results are reported per 100 millilitres. The verifier notes that any detectable E. coli in drinking water is a failure against the WHO drinking-water guideline of zero per 100 millilitres (to confirm against the current edition).
2Inspect every household
Visit each house with the owner present. Open the cover. Record the type, the size, whether it is watertight, whether there is a soakaway, where the overflow goes, and the distance to the nearest water point.		One row per house: number, GPS, occupants, system type, volume, condition, overflow destination, distance to nearest water point, photos of the open cover and of the overflow. A written result sheet handed to the owner on the day.Every house in the boundary appears, with refusals recorded by number, date and reason. Every row has at least two photos and a GPS point. Each system is graded, on the French pattern, as compliant, non-compliant without immediate risk, or non-compliant with immediate risk to health or water.
3Grade, prioritise and notify
Sort the register by risk. Write to the owners of the worst systems with a plain-language notice saying what is wrong, what has to change and by when.		The sorted register. Copies of every notice sent, with delivery proof. The municipality's published summary: how many houses, how many in each grade.Deadlines follow the French rule the municipality adopts: up to four years for a non-compliant system with no immediate risk, and under one year where there is a health risk or the property is being sold. Every notice names a person to ask questions of.
4Do the priority works
Carry out the class work on the houses at the top of the list: install the tank, build the soakaway or planted filter, seal and fill the old pit, or build the cluster system.		Per house: photos of the excavation, the tank before backfill, the soakaway media, the old pit being filled, and a water tightness test. Delivery note for the tank with its capacity marked. Owner's signature on completion.Every tank is watertight and tested before backfill, with a photo. Old pits are filled, not just capped. Any soakaway is at least the distance from a well written into the design at milestone 3; Lebanon has no published separation distance the verifier could cite, so the adopted distance must be stated and marked to confirm.
5Retest and publish
Sample the same drinking water points again, no sooner than three months after the works, and publish the register summary and both sets of results.		New laboratory reports for the same points and parameters. Photo of the published summary on the municipal board. Photos of finished works from the same spots as milestone 4.Same points, same parameters, at least three months after completion. The summary is published in Arabic. Any point still showing E. coli is named in the summary with what is being done about it.
6Hand over the register and the next round
Hand the register to the municipality as a file it can keep and update. Set the date of the next inspection round and name who pays for it.		Signed handover of the register in a form the municipality can edit. A council decision setting the next round's date and its budget line. A training sheet for the two municipal staff who will run it.The next round is within ten years at most, following the French maximum interval. A named budget line exists. The register is in the municipality's hands, not the consultant's.
Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Inspect within 15 working days of the request, because this is a survey and not an emergency. Baseline sampling within 30 days. The household inspections themselves run at roughly 6 to 10 houses per inspector per day, so a 300-house village is about six weeks with two inspectors. Notices within 14 days of the register being sorted. Priority works over the following 6 to 12 months. Retest no sooner than 3 months after the works. Warranty: 24 months on tanks and soakaways, and a full growing season on any planted filter.

Money

Inspections are priced per household visited, which keeps the incentive on coverage. Upgrades are priced per household by tank size, with rock excavation as a separate agreed rate because karst is where the money is lost. Cluster systems are priced per population equivalent. Desludging is priced per household emptied, including the disposal fee, which must be shown separately because it is the part that quietly does not happen. No public Lebanese unit rate exists for septic upgrade work: bracket from the first three real bids and publish the bracket. Not included: internal plumbing, any connection to a future sewer, and the householder's own share if the municipality decides to cost-share.

Release

Nothing up front. 20 per cent when the register at milestone 2 is accepted, paid pro rata on households actually inspected. 15 per cent at milestone 3 when notices are served. 35 per cent at milestone 4 on completed works, paid per house completed. 30 per cent at milestone 5 after the retest and publication. If the retest shows no change but the works are sound, the money is still released; the pass mark at milestone 5 is that the sampling was done properly and published honestly, not that a karst aquifer cleared in three months.

Who signs off. The municipality authorises the inspections by council decision, and that decision is what gives an inspector the right to ask to open a cover. The water establishment must be told, because it is legally responsible for wastewater in its region under Law 221/2000 and may have plans for a sewer in the same village. The Ministry of Energy and Water controls groundwater and well licensing. The Ministry of Public Health has an interest in drinking-water results. Any cluster system needs a stamped design by an engineer registered with the Order of Engineers and a land agreement. Tanker disposal must go to a point the water establishment agrees to accept in writing.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Only the easy houses inspected. If the inspector skips the locked gates and the awkward owners, the register misses exactly the systems most likely to be bad. Milestone 2. Every house numbered, refusals listed with dates and reasons.
  • A soakaway built into rock. In karst, a soakaway is a direct pipe to the aquifer. It passes an inspection and poisons a spring. Milestone 3 and 4. Ground conditions recorded at design, and the cluster class used where soakaways do not suit.
  • New tank, old pit left open. The cheapest way to fake this work is to install a tank and leave the old pit taking the overflow, which changes nothing underground. Milestone 4. A photo of the old pit being filled, not capped.
  • Tanker empties into the nearest valley. Desludging without a disposal point that will take the load just moves the pollution a kilometre and makes it someone else's spring. Milestone 0 and 4. A named legal disposal point in writing, and a receipt per load.
  • A register that lives on a consultant's laptop. An inspection scheme is only worth anything if it repeats. A file the municipality cannot open or edit dies with the contract. Milestone 6. Handed over in editable form with a date for the next round.

  • Fanack Water, water quality in Lebanon. Karstic aquifers and bacterial contamination of springs from cesspits. water.fanack.com
  • Eawag, ESRISS: Egyptian-Swiss research on innovations in sustainable sanitation. Decision tools and pilots for small-scale decentralised treatment where central connection is not possible. eawag.ch
  • CDD India, used water management. Gravity-fed DEWATS units for clusters of houses, with no electricity and no chemicals. cddindia.org

6 Combined sewers overflowing in rain
Why this one

Template 6: stopping the winter overflow in a combined sewer catchment

Beirut and many Lebanese towns run rainwater and sewage in the same pipe, so every heavy storm pushes sewage into streets and homes. Street sweepers tip swept litter into the gullies, and highway barriers were built with no openings for water to pass. People die in these floods: a seven-year-old girl in Akkar and four children in Zgharta in recent winters.

Step 1 · Classify

4 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Catchment and overflow surveyAlways first. Nobody has a map of where the combined system overflows and why.Map the catchment, walk every main line, open and inspect every overflow point and every gully, record silt depth, find the low points where flooding is reported, and rank the blockages by how much of the pipe they take.per hectare of catchment, or per kilometre of main line
Pre-season clean and screenBefore every winter, and always before spending money on anything bigger.Clean every gully and manhole in the catchment, jet the main lines, remove and weigh the silt, replace broken gully grates, fit litter screens where sweepers tip, and take everything removed to a legal disposal point.per gully or per metre of main line cleaned
Storm storageThe survey shows the pipe simply cannot carry the storm, and there is land or a street to build under.A tank or basin that fills during the storm and empties back to the sewer afterwards, with inlet and outlet controls, level monitoring, and a flushing arrangement so it does not sit full of solids.cubic metre of storage
Rainwater separation on one streetA street can realistically take a second pipe or a surface channel discharging to a watercourse or a soakaway.A separate rainwater line or channel, disconnection of roof and yard drains from the foul sewer, and reinstatement.metre of street
Step 2 · The milestones

7 milestones, each with the proof it needs and the check it must pass

#MilestoneEvidence the expert uploadsPass mark the verifier checks
0Scope and class
Draw the catchment on a map. Collect the flood reports from the last three winters, with dates, from the municipality, the civil defence and residents. Choose the class. Any existing drainage drawings.The catchment is a closed shape with an area. At least the last three winters of incidents are listed with dates. Each incident has a location the verifier can stand at.

Open every gully, manhole and overflow chamber in the catchment. Measure the silt depth against the pipe diameter. Photograph each one open.		One row per asset: reference, GPS, type, pipe diameter, silt depth in millimetres, photo of the open chamber with a measuring rod in frame, condition of the cover and grate. A map with each asset coloured by how blocked it is.Every asset in the catchment is on the list, with any that could not be opened recorded and the reason given. Silt depth is a measured number, not blocked or clear. Assets where silt fills more than half the pipe are flagged as priority.
2Plan the work and warn people
Write the cleaning or construction programme street by street with dates. Tell residents and shopkeepers in advance. Agree a traffic plan with the municipality and the Internal Security Forces.		Programme with streets and dates. Photo of the public notice in Arabic. Traffic management plan with a permit reference. For the storage and separation classes, stamped drawings and the water establishment's written approval.Every street in the programme has a date. 3Do the work

4Water test

Photos of each milestone 0 flood point during or immediately after the storm, from the same spot as the dry-weather photos. Rainfall figure for that storm from a named station. Any resident reports of flooding, with dates.No flooding at the points cleaned, for a storm at or below the design size named at milestone 2. If the storm was bigger than the design size, the result is recorded but the expert is not penalised. 6Handover and next year's round
Hand over the asset register with silt depths, the disposal tickets and a cleaning calendar. Get the municipality to fix the date of next autumn's round.		Signed handover of the register. Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Inspect within 10 working days, or within 48 hours if the request follows a flood in which someone was hurt. The survey within 30 days. All cleaning must finish before 1 November, so the contract has to start in late summer, and a contract signed in December is a contract for next year. Storage or separation works take 6 to 18 months and should be built in the dry season, roughly May to October. The first storm check happens whenever the first storm comes, so this milestone has no fixed date and the retention has to wait for it. Warranty: 12 months on cleaning, meaning any gully that silts up again within a year of the same street is recleaned free unless a new works upstream caused it, and 24 months on civil works.

Money

Cleaning is priced per gully and per metre of main line jetted, with the disposal fee as a separate visible line because that is the part that gets skipped. Storage is priced per cubic metre of storage built. Separation is priced per metre of street. No public Lebanese unit rate exists for gully cleaning or storm storage: bracket from the first three real bids and publish the bracket. For scale only, the Austerlitz basin in Paris holds roughly 50,000 cubic metres, which is far beyond anything a Lebanese municipality will build, and the right comparison for a town is tens to a few hundred cubic metres. Not included: road resurfacing, private drains inside a property, replacing undersized pipe, and any river or sea outfall works.

Release

Nothing up front. 20 per cent when the asset survey at milestone 1 is accepted. 45 per cent at milestone 3 when the work is done and the disposal tickets balance. 15 per cent at milestone 4 on the water tests. 20 per cent after the first storm check at milestone 5. If no qualifying storm has happened by 31 March, the 20 per cent is released on the strength of the milestone 4 tests, and the storm check is still carried out and published.

Who signs off. The municipality owns the storm drains and the street, and gives the road-opening and traffic permits. The water establishment owns the foul sewer and must approve anything that changes what enters it, including any new storage or separation. The Ministry of Public Works and Transport must agree if the catchment drains a classified road or a highway. The Internal Security Forces traffic branch handles lane closures on busy roads. The Ministry of Environment is the authority on where the silt and litter may be disposed of, and the disposal point must be named in writing before the first load leaves. Stamped design by an engineer registered with the Order of Engineers for storage and separation.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Cleaning done in January. A drain cleaned after the first floods is a drain that already flooded. The whole value is in finishing before the season. Milestone 2 and milestone 6. Dates in the programme, and next year's round fixed before 1 November.
  • Silt lifted out and left on the pavement. The first rain washes it straight back down the gully, so the town pays twice and the drain is blocked again. Milestone 3. Disposal tickets must match the tonnage removed.
  • Sweepers tipping litter into the gully. The reason drains refill within weeks. No amount of jetting beats a daily habit. Milestone 6. Litter screens fitted and the sweeping supervisor signs.
  • Before and after photos from different angles. A dark hole and a clean hole photographed from two positions prove nothing and are the easiest thing in this trade to fake. Milestone 3. Same spot, same angle, or the asset is not paid for.
  • Storage built with no way to flush it. A tank that holds a storm also holds the solids. Without flushing it becomes a sealed cesspit under the street and the municipality stops using it. Milestone 4. The fill and drain test must show no solids left.

Lebanon has no wastewater tariff at all and cost recovery for sewerage is zero, so every plant runs on whatever is left in a general budget after the currency collapse. That is why about half of the country's treatment capacity sat idle until recently. Before anyone asks for a sanitation charge, somebody has to be able to say what a year of running the plant actually costs.
