For the charge class: survey results by income band, the proposed charge, the lifeline band, and the forecast revenue with the collection rate assumed. For the spares class: the register with prices and lead times and the first order. For the contract class: the draft contract with its performance targets.The forecast revenue states the collection rate it assumes, and that rate is justified from the water establishment's actual water-bill collection, not invented. Performance targets in any contract are numbers with a measurement method beside each one.
4Run the pilot or the first quarter
Bill one neighbourhood, or order and receive the first stock, or operate the plant for three months under the contract.		For billing: the bills issued, the payments received, and the collection rate after 60 days. For spares: delivery notes and photos of the stock on the shelf with labels. For operation: three monthly reports with flow, power, effluent results and downtime.Collection rate is a measured number over a stated period, not a hope. Stock on the shelf matches the register. Effluent results come from an accredited laboratory with the method named, and downtime is reported in hours, with a reason per event.
5Report and decide
Publish the true cost, the gap and the pilot result. Put a decision in front of the council or the water establishment board.		A published summary in Arabic. The agenda item and the minute of the decision. The full model handed over as an editable file.The cost per cubic metre is published. A named body took a decision, recorded in minutes, even if the decision is to do nothing this year. This is the gate for the final release.
6Handover and the next twelve months
Hand over the model, the register and the reporting format. Train two staff to update it monthly. Fix the date of next year's update.		Signed handover note. Training sheet with two signatures. A written monthly reporting routine naming who sends what to whom.The model opens and recalculates on the municipality's or water establishment's own computer. Two named people have been trained. A monthly reporting routine exists on paper with names on it.
Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Inspect within 15 working days. Pulling twelve months of records usually takes 30 to 60 days because the records sit in different offices and some do not exist. The household survey for a charge study runs 3 to 6 weeks. A billing pilot needs at least two billing cycles, so 60 to 120 days, and a collection rate measured before 60 days have passed is not a collection rate. A results-based operating contract is twelve months by definition, reported monthly. Warranty does not apply to a study; instead the expert answers questions on the model for 6 months after handover at no extra cost.

Money

The cost model and the spares register are lump sums per plant. The charge study is a lump sum plus a per-household rate for the survey. The operating contract is priced per month, with a fixed part for staff and a variable part tied to cubic metres treated and to effluent results. No public Lebanese figure exists for any of this, and the country has no wastewater tariff to benchmark against: bracket from the first three real bids and publish the bracket. Not included: the cost of the repairs the model will reveal, any arrears already owed, and the billing system software if the water establishment does not have one.

Release

Nothing up front. 25 per cent when the twelve-month cost model at milestone 1 is accepted with its source documents. 15 per cent at milestone 2 when the gap is stated. 20 per cent at milestone 3 on the design. 25 per cent at milestone 4 on the pilot or the first quarter. 15 per cent after milestone 5 when the result is published and a decision is minuted. For the operating contract class, pay monthly in arrears against the performance targets, with 10 per cent of each month held and released at the end of the twelve months.

Who signs off. The water establishment is legally responsible for wastewater under Law 221/2000 and is the only body that can set or collect a charge on the water bill, so it has to be in the room from milestone 0. The municipality has to agree any charge collected through municipal fees instead. The Ministry of Energy and Water is the policy owner for tariffs. The Ministry of Finance matters if a charge needs a legal instrument. The Council for Development and Reconstruction holds the capital asset records for donor-built plants. A household survey that collects income data needs a council decision and a plain consent sheet, and personal data must not be published.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Cost built from estimates. A model made of round numbers cannot survive a challenge from a council member, and the charge it supports gets voted down. Milestone 1. One source document per cost line.
  • Dividing by design capacity. Cost per cubic metre looks respectable if you divide by what the plant could treat rather than what it did. The real figure is usually several times worse. Milestone 1. The volume must come from an inlet meter.
  • A collection rate taken on faith. Revenue forecasts in this sector routinely assume 80 or 90 per cent collection in a country where water bills often go unpaid. The plan then fails in year one. Milestone 3. The assumed rate must come from the water establishment's own water-bill record.
  • No lifeline band. A flat sanitation charge on households that cannot pay produces non-payment, not revenue, and hands opponents an easy argument. Milestone 3. The design must show what the poorest band pays.
  • A study with no decision at the end. Most of these reports stop at recommendations. Without a minuted decision by a named body, nothing changes and the next consultant starts again. Milestone 5. An agenda item and a minute, or no final payment.
Sources
  • Water supply and sanitation in Lebanon, overview article. No wastewater tariff exists and cost recovery for sewerage is zero; Law 221/2000 and the four Regional Water Establishments. en.wikipedia.org
  • Lebanese Center for Policy Studies, Lebanon's wastewater sector. About half of total treatment capacity reactivated by 2025, and the institutional reasons operation is unfunded. lcps-lebanon.org
  • SANDRP, India's non-functional sewage treatment plants, January 2025. Plants built and then left without operating budgets. sandrp.in
  • SNV, constructed wetland faecal sludge treatment in Khulna, Bangladesh. Annual operating cost of about 2,311 US dollars for salaries and electricity, used above only as an order-of-magnitude check. admin.snv.org
8 Blocked drains, open manholes and clogged canals
Why this one

Template 8: the autumn round of drains, manholes and canals

Litter, silt and encroachment block drains until sewage surfaces in the street, and in winter the same blockages turn a storm into a flood that kills people, including a seven-year-old girl in Akkar and four children in Zgharta in recent winters. An open manhole is a hole a child can fall into. This is the cheapest, most repeatable job on this list and the one a municipality can do every year without a donor.

Step 1 · Classify

4 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Gully and manhole cleaningEvery year, before the wet season, across a defined set of streets.Open, empty and wash each gully and manhole, remove silt and litter, check the trap, replace the grate if broken, take everything removed to a legal disposal point.per gully or manhole
Manhole and gully cover replacementCovers are missing, broken, rocking, or sitting proud or sunken in the carriageway.Remove the old cover and frame, rebuild the seating, set the new frame to the road level, install a cover of the right load class, and reinstate the surface around it.each
Culvert and canal desiltingAn open channel or a culvert under a road is silted or built over, and the town floods upstream of it.Clear vegetation, remove silt to the original invert, remove encroaching structures where the municipality has the legal right, repair the channel lining, and fit a trash screen at the culvert mouth with access to clean it.metre of channel, or cubic metre of silt removed
Blocked collector clearing and inspectionSewage is surfacing and the blockage is in a main line rather than a gully.Jet or rod the line, remove the blockage, and run a camera through it afterwards to see whether the pipe itself is broken or the blockage was only debris.metre of main line
Step 2 · The milestones

7 milestones, each with the proof it needs and the check it must pass

#MilestoneEvidence the expert uploadsPass mark the verifier checks
0Scope and class
List the streets or the channel covered by this round. Get last winter's flood and surcharge complaints from the municipality and residents.		A map with the streets or the channel marked and their length. A dated list of complaints with locations. Photos of each known problem point in dry weather with GPS.The round is a defined list of streets or a measured length of channel, not a district name. Complaints are dated and located. Each problem point has a dry-weather photo to compare against later.
1Count and grade the assets
Walk the round and open every gully, manhole and chamber. Measure the silt depth. Check every cover: is it there, is it broken, does it rock, is it the right load class for the road it sits in.		One row per asset: reference, GPS, type, cover condition, silt depth in millimetres, photo of the open chamber with a measuring rod in frame, photo of the cover in place. A numbered map.Every asset on the round is listed. Silt depth is a measured number. Missing and broken covers are flagged as immediate danger and made safe on the same day, with a photo of the temporary barrier. Cover load classes are stated against the European classification, with D400 for carriageways and B125 for footways used as the reference (to confirm against the municipality's own road specification).
2Programme and warn
Write the programme street by street with dates, arrange the traffic plan, and tell residents and shopkeepers before you close their street.		Programme with dates. Photo of the public notice in Arabic. Traffic permit reference. Confirmation from the disposal site that it will accept the silt, in writing.Every street has a date, and all dates fall before 1 November. The disposal point is named in writing before any work starts. Residents were told at least 3 days ahead.
3Clean, replace, clear
Do the work. Remove everything to the named disposal point the same day it is lifted. Never leave a chamber open and unattended.		Per asset: matched before and after photos from the same spot and angle. Weighbridge tickets or measured volumes per street. Disposal tickets. Delivery notes and photos of the load class marking cast into every new cover. Photo of any open chamber showing the barrier and lookout.Matched before and after photos for every asset billed. Tonnage lifted equals tonnage disposed, within the weighbridge tolerance. Every new cover shows its load class in the photo. No chamber was left open without a barrier.
4Water test and camera
Pour water into each cleaned gully and watch it drain. For the collector class, run the camera and record the whole length.		Short video per gully showing water draining. Camera footage file per length with the start and end manhole references and the distance counter visible. A defect list from the footage.Water drains away with no pooling and no backing up. Camera footage covers the full length between the named manholes. Any structural defect found is listed with its distance from the start manhole, so a future repair contract can find it. Defect coding should follow a recognised sewer condition classification (to confirm which standard the municipality adopts).
5First storm check
After the first real storm, return to the problem points from milestone 0 and photograph them during or right after the rain.		Photos from the same spots as the dry-weather photos. The rainfall figure for that storm from a named station. Any complaints received during the storm, with dates.No surcharging or flooding at the cleaned points for a storm at or below the size the round was planned for. The planned storm size is stated in millimetres per hour with its source, or marked to confirm.
6Handover and next year
Hand over the asset register with silt depths and cover conditions, all disposal tickets, and the camera footage. Fix next year's round with the council.		Signed handover of the register and footage. A council decision or signed letter setting next year's round and its budget line. A note to the street sweeping supervisor about not tipping into gullies, signed.Next year's round is dated to finish before 1 November and has a named budget line. The register is editable and in the municipality's hands. Any asset graded as needing structural repair is listed separately as the start of next year's repair contract.
Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Inspect within 10 working days, or within 24 hours where sewage is surfacing in a street or a manhole cover is missing. Survey within 21 days. The cleaning round must finish before 1 November. An emergency blockage in a collector should be cleared within 48 hours of the report and the camera run within 7 days of clearing. Cover replacement in a carriageway must be completed and the road reopened the same day, or the hole is barriered, lit overnight and finished the next day. Warranty: 12 months on cleaning, so a gully that silts again within a year is recleaned free unless upstream works caused it, and 24 months on covers and frames against rocking or settlement.

Money

Priced per gully or manhole cleaned, per cover replaced by load class and size, per metre of channel or per cubic metre of silt removed, and per metre of main line jetted and surveyed. Disposal is a separate visible line in every case. No public Lebanese unit rate exists for gully cleaning or cover replacement: bracket from the first three real bids and publish the bracket, then reuse it next year, because this is the one job a town repeats annually and can build a real local rate from. Not included: road resurfacing beyond the patch around a frame, structural repair of pipes found by the camera, and removing encroaching buildings, which is a legal matter before it is an engineering one.

Release

Nothing up front. 20 per cent when the asset register at milestone 1 is accepted. 45 per cent at milestone 3, paid per asset actually cleaned or replaced with matched photos, and reduced pro rata for any asset without them. 15 per cent at milestone 4 on the water tests and camera footage. 20 per cent after the first storm check at milestone 5. If no qualifying storm has occurred by 31 March, the last 20 per cent is released on the milestone 4 evidence and the storm check is still done and published.

Who signs off. The municipality owns the gullies, the street and usually the local sewer, and gives the road-opening and traffic permits. The water establishment owns the trunk sewers and must be told before anything is jetted into its network. The Ministry of Public Works and Transport must agree work on a classified road or a highway culvert. The Internal Security Forces traffic branch handles lane closures. The Ministry of Environment is the authority on where silt and screenings may go, and the disposal point must be agreed in writing first. Removing encroachment from a canal is a legal step that needs the municipality's own decision and, for a public watercourse, the Ministry of Energy and Water.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Assets billed but never opened. The quickest fraud in drain cleaning is to bill for gullies nobody touched. A photograph of a clean grate from the street proves nothing. Milestone 3. Matched before and after photos of the chamber open, with a rod in frame.
  • Silt dumped in the nearest valley. It ends up back in a watercourse, and the municipality has paid to move pollution rather than remove it. Milestone 2 and 3. A named disposal point in writing, and tickets that balance the tonnage.
  • Wrong load class cover. A light cover in a carriageway cracks under the first lorry and becomes an open hole, which is how people get killed. Milestone 3. The load class cast into the cover must be visible in the photo.
  • Blockage cleared, broken pipe left. If the pipe is collapsed, jetting buys a few months. Without a camera run nobody knows, and the town pays for the same clearance every year. Milestone 4. Camera footage and a defect list with distances.
  • Round done after the rain starts. The work is worth a fraction as much once the first flood has happened, and the contract becomes a clean-up rather than a prevention. Milestone 2 and 6. All dates before 1 November, and next year fixed at handover.
Sources
  • The New Arab, why Lebanon floods and what it will take to fix. Deaths of a seven-year-old in Akkar and four children in Zgharta, combined sewers, sweepers tipping litter into drains, and highway barriers with no water openings. newarab.com
  • The Daily Star, Bangladesh: why Dhaka drowns every monsoon. Blocked and encroached drains and canals as the direct cause of urban flooding. thedailystar.net
  • Water supply and sanitation in Lebanon, overview article. Municipalities operate and maintain local sewer systems while the water establishments hold legal responsibility. en.wikipedia.org
  • Litani River Authority, pollution challenges. Evidence of how little of the planned network exists, which is why surface channels still carry sewage in many towns. litani.gov.lb
9 Ageing, leaking networks
Why this one

Template 9: camera survey and a renewal rate for an old sewer network

Lebanon's older urban sewers were laid before the plants they now feed and are almost never inspected, so nobody knows how much groundwater leaks in or how much sewage leaks out. France measures this and publishes it: the national average sewer renewal rate was 0.55 per cent a year at 1 January 2025, which is roughly one pipe replaced every 180 years. A Lebanese town cannot set a renewal rate until it has a survey.

Step 1 · Classify

4 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Manhole condition surveyAlways first. It is cheap, needs no camera, and finds most of the worst defects.Open and inspect every manhole on the defined network: cover, frame, chamber walls, benching, channel, steps, connections, silt, signs of infiltration. Photograph and grade each one.per manhole
Camera survey of the mainsThe town needs to know which lengths are broken before spending anything on renewal.Clean the line, run a camera between manholes, record the full length with the distance counter visible, and produce a coded defect list with a still image and a distance for every defect.metre of main line
Infiltration measurementThe plant receives far more flow in winter than in summer, or the flow does not drop at night.Night-flow measurement in defined sub-catchments in dry weather, compared with daytime flow and with the summer baseline, to find which sub-catchment is letting groundwater in.per sub-catchment
Targeted repair or reliningThe survey has found specific broken lengths and the town has money for some of them.Patch repair, short liner or full-length liner on the lengths named in the defect list, with a post-repair camera run to prove it.metre of pipe repaired or relined
Step 2 · The milestones

7 milestones, each with the proof it needs and the check it must pass

#MilestoneEvidence the expert uploadsPass mark the verifier checks
0Scope and class
Define the network covered: which streets, how many kilometres, how many manholes. Collect any as-built drawings from the water establishment and the Council for Development and Reconstruction.		A map of the network with total length in kilometres and a manhole count. Copies of any drawings obtained, and a list of what does not exist. GPS pins for the network's two ends and its outfall or plant.Total length and manhole count are numbers. Where no drawings exist, that is written down, because it changes the price and the method.
1Open every manhole
Lift every cover on the defined network. Record what the chamber is made of, its depth, the size and direction of every pipe, silt depth, and any sign of water entering through the walls.		One row per manhole: reference, GPS, depth, pipe sizes and directions, condition grade, silt depth, photo down the chamber and photo of the benching. A drawn network schematic built from what was found.Every manhole on the map is opened or recorded as could not be opened with a reason. The schematic shows pipe sizes and flow directions, which for many Lebanese towns will be the first drawing of the network that exists.
2Clean and camera
Clean each length, then run the camera the full distance between manholes. Record the distance counter on screen throughout.		Footage file per length, named with the start and end manhole references. A defect list with a distance, a still image and a code for every defect. Cleaning disposal tickets.Footage covers the full length between the named manholes, with no gaps and the counter visible. Every defect has a distance in metres from a named manhole, so a repair crew can find it without repeating the survey. Defect coding follows a recognised sewer condition classification, which the municipality must name at milestone 0 (to confirm which standard it adopts).
3Measure the leak
Measure flow at the bottom of each sub-catchment in dry weather, over at least seven nights, and compare the 02:00 to 04:00 minimum with the daytime figure and with a summer reading.		Seven nights of logged flow per sub-catchment, dated. A note of rainfall for those nights from a named station. Photos of the meter installation.At least seven dry nights with no gaps, and at least 48 hours since rain. The expert states the night minimum as a percentage of the daily average flow for each sub-catchment, and ranks the sub-catchments. A high and steady night flow is infiltration, not use.
4Rank and cost the renewal
Turn the defect list into a ranked programme: what must be repaired this year, what can wait, and what it costs per metre. Propose an annual renewal rate for the town.		A ranked programme with lengths, defect codes, proposed method and a price per metre. A one-page renewal rate proposal with the length of network and the metres per year it implies.The programme is sorted by risk, not by convenience. The proposed renewal rate is stated as a percentage of network length per year, with the French national average of 0.55 per cent at 1 January 2025 given beside it for comparison, and the number of metres per year and cost per year that the proposed rate implies.
5Repair and prove
For the repair class, carry out the named repairs and run the camera again over each repaired length.		Before and after footage for each repaired length, with the same manhole references and the counter visible. Delivery notes for liners or repair materials. A tightness test sheet where the method allows one.Every repaired length has a matched before and after camera run. The defect that justified the repair is gone in the after footage, at the same distance. Nothing is billed as repaired without after footage.
6Handover and a standing programme
Hand over the schematic, the manhole register, all footage and the defect list in a form the municipality and the water establishment can keep. Get the renewal rate adopted in a decision.		Signed handover of the register, the schematic and the footage on physical media as well as online. The council or board minute adopting a renewal rate and a budget line. A training sheet for two staff.The footage and the register are handed over on media the municipality physically holds, not only a link. A named body has minuted a renewal rate, even a small one. Two named people have been trained to update the register.
Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Inspect within 15 working days. The manhole survey runs at roughly 15 to 25 manholes per crew per day, so a small town is 2 to 4 weeks. Camera survey is slower and depends on cleaning first; budget 300 to 600 metres per crew per day once the line is clean. Night-flow measurement needs seven dry nights, so in Lebanon it is a summer job, between June and September, and a winter measurement is a different and also useful number but must be labelled as such. Repairs 60 to 180 days. Warranty: 12 months on the survey data, meaning the expert re-runs any length the verifier finds unreadable at no cost, and 10 years on a structural liner, which is the normal manufacturer position and must be passed to the water establishment in writing.

Money

The manhole survey is priced per manhole. The camera survey is priced per metre, with cleaning as a separate visible rate because a dirty line cannot be surveyed and this is where bids differ. Night-flow measurement is priced per sub-catchment per week. Repairs are priced per metre by method and diameter. No public Lebanese unit rate exists for sewer camera survey or relining: bracket from the first three real bids and publish the bracket. Not included: excavation for open-cut replacement, road reinstatement, traffic management on a classified road, and any pumping needed to take the flow out of the line while it is being lined.

Release

Nothing up front. 20 per cent when the manhole register and schematic at milestone 1 are accepted. 30 per cent at milestone 2 on footage and defect list, paid per metre actually surveyed with readable footage. 10 per cent at milestone 3 on the night-flow data. 15 per cent at milestone 4 on the ranked programme. 25 per cent at milestone 5 on repairs proven by after footage, or, where no repair class is in scope, released at milestone 6 when the register and footage are physically handed over and a renewal rate is minuted.

Who signs off. The water establishment owns the trunk sewers under Law 221/2000 and must approve any entry, cleaning or lining. The municipality owns local sewers and the street, and gives the road-opening and traffic permits. The Ministry of Public Works and Transport must agree work in a classified road. Entry into a manhole is confined-space work: gas detection, harness and a top man are required under normal occupational safety practice, and the contractor's insurance and method statement should be checked at milestone 0. Stamped design by an engineer registered with the Order of Engineers for any structural repair.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Camera run on a dirty pipe. Silt hides the invert, which is exactly where cracks and root intrusion are. The survey looks complete and finds nothing. Milestone 2. The verifier watches the footage; if the invert is not visible the length is not accepted.
  • Defects with no distances. A defect list that says cracked pipe in Rue X sends a repair crew digging blind. The distance from a named manhole is what makes it usable. Milestone 2. Every defect needs a distance and a still image.
  • Night-flow measured after rain. Rain makes every sub-catchment look like it leaks, so the ranking is worthless and the town spends money in the wrong street. Milestone 3. The verifier checks dates against rainfall.
  • Survey done, nothing adopted. A shelf full of footage and no renewal rate means the network keeps ageing and the next survey starts again in ten years. Milestone 6. A minuted renewal rate and a budget line.
  • Data handed over as a link. Camera footage is large, consultants close, and links expire. Within two years the municipality has nothing. Milestone 6. Physical media handed over and checked open on the municipality's own computer.

  • Deltares, publication on sewer asset management and network condition. Listed in the research input as the reference on ageing networks and inspection practice. publications.deltares.nl
  • Water supply and sanitation in Lebanon, overview article. Older urban networks predate the plants they feed; the water establishments hold legal responsibility while municipalities maintain local sewers. en.wikipedia.org
  • Libnanews, Wastewater: history of an unfinished Lebanese system. Networks built in separate generations and rarely inspected. en.libnanews.com
10 Sludge with nowhere to go
Why this one

Template 10: giving a plant's sludge somewhere legal to go

Every working treatment plant makes sludge, and in Lebanon sludge handling is the operating cost nobody planned for, so it is stored on site or quietly dumped. A plant with no sludge route is a plant that will stop. Bangladesh's Khulna city built a planted drying-bed plant for trucked sludge in 2016 and runs it for about 2,311 US dollars a year, which shows the cheap end of the answer.

Step 1 · Classify

4 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Sludge audit and registerAlways first. The plant cannot say how much sludge it makes or where it goes.Measure or estimate sludge production over at least 30 days, sample it for dry solids and for the contaminants the disposal route will care about, and write down every route it currently takes with dates and destinations.per plant
Drying beds, planted or unplantedThe plant has land and a warm dry season, and needs a low-maintenance route.Lined beds with drainage layers, feed and underdrain pipework, reed planting for the planted type, a loading routine, and a return line for the drainage water back to the plant inlet.square metre of bed
Septage reception and treatmentThe town has tankers emptying village pits with nowhere legal to discharge.A tanker discharge point with a bar screen and a holding and mixing tank, a logbook of every load with truck, volume and origin, and treatment through drying beds or into the plant's own sludge line.cubic metre of septage received
Digestion and energy recovery studyA large plant with digesters wants to know whether recovery pays before spending anything.Sludge quantity and quality survey, a comparison of digestion, thermal pre-treatment and nutrient recovery options, capital and running costs, and a stamped preliminary design with a payback figure.per study
Step 2 · The milestones

7 milestones, each with the proof it needs and the check it must pass

#MilestoneEvidence the expert uploadsPass mark the verifier checks
0Scope and class
Confirm which plant, who owns it, how much sewage it treats, and where its sludge goes today. Walk the site and find every place sludge is currently stored or tipped.		GPS of the plant and of every storage or tipping point on or near it. Photos of each. Written confirmation of ownership from the water establishment. The plant's treated flow from its inlet meter.Every existing sludge location is photographed and pinned, including the ones nobody wants to show. Treated flow comes from a meter. Class chosen.
1Measure and test the sludge
Over at least 30 days, record how much sludge leaves each process. Take representative samples and test them at an accredited laboratory.		A dated table of sludge volumes over at least 30 days. Chain-of-custody forms. Laboratory reports for dry solids percentage, organic content, and the heavy metals and pathogen indicators required by the intended disposal route. Photos of sampling.At least 30 days with no gaps. Dry solids is reported as a percentage. Test parameters match the intended route: if the sludge is meant for agriculture, the sample must be tested for helminth eggs, with the WHO agricultural reuse guideline of a maximum of 1 intestinal nematode egg per litre as the reference, and for faecal coliforms, with the WHO guideline of 1,000 per 100 millilitres for crops eaten uncooked.
2Choose and secure the route
Decide where the sludge will go: drying beds then agriculture, drying beds then landfill, co-treatment elsewhere, or energy recovery. Get the receiving party to agree in writing.		A written acceptance from the landfill, the farmer group or the receiving plant, naming the volume and the quality it will accept. Land agreement or lease for any beds. Ministry of Environment correspondence.There is a signed acceptance from a named receiving party with a stated volume and quality, not an intention. Lebanon has a Ministry of Environment decision on minimum levels for treated domestic wastewater but no national wastewater reuse standard, so the quality limits used must be named and sourced, and any number without a Lebanese source is marked to confirm.
3Design and approvals
Design the beds, the reception point or the recovery works and get them approved.		Stamped drawings and calculations, including the bed area, the design loading rate, the expected drying time and the drainage water return. Written approval from the water establishment. Ministry of Environment position in writing.Bed area follows a stated loading rate with its source, or the loading rate is marked to confirm. The drainage water from the beds returns to the plant inlet, not to the ground or a watercourse. The stamp and Order of Engineers registration number are readable.
4Build and start loading
Build the beds or the reception point. Plant the reeds if planted, and let them establish before full loading. Start the logbook on day one.		Photos of the lining, the drainage layers and the pipework before they are covered. Delivery notes for liner, gravel, sand and plants. Photos of the first loads. The logbook: date, source, volume, truck.The liner and drainage layers are photographed before being covered, because after that nobody can check them. Every load into the beds or the reception point is in the logbook with a volume and an origin. For the Khulna comparison, that plant uses six vertical-flow planted wetland basins, one horizontal-flow wetland and six unplanted drying beds.
5Prove the output and the drainage water
After the first full drying cycle, test the dried sludge and the drainage water leaving the beds.		Laboratory reports for the dried sludge against the milestone 2 acceptance quality, and for the drainage water. Photos of the dried cake being lifted, with a measuring rod. Disposal or delivery tickets for the first batch that leaves site.Dried sludge meets the quality the receiving party accepted at milestone 2. Drainage water quality is reported; the Khulna planted wetland achieves treated effluent biochemical oxygen demand of 26 to 33 milligrams per litre against a local limit of 40, from incoming sludge at 400 to 500, which is the order of performance to expect from a planted bed. 6Handover, cost and the long plan
Hand over the operating routine, the logbook format and the annual cost. Say when the beds will need emptying down to the base and what that will cost.		Signed handover. Operating routine in Arabic. Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Inspect within 15 working days. The 30-day measurement at milestone 1 cannot be shortened; it is what everything else is sized on. Route agreement and approvals 45 to 90 days, because the Ministry of Environment and a receiving party both have to answer. Construction 90 to 180 days, in the dry season. Planted beds need at least one growing season before full loading, so plan the first year at reduced load. A full drying cycle in a Lebanese summer is a few weeks and in winter much longer, so the milestone 5 proof should be taken from a summer cycle and a winter cycle recorded separately. Warranty: 24 months on liners, pipework and civil works, and a full growing season on the reeds, with dead plants replaced at the expert's cost.

Money

The audit and the study are lump sums per plant. Beds are priced per square metre of bed, which is the only fair way to compare bids, with the liner as a separately stated line. Septage reception is priced per cubic metre received, with the disposal fee visible. No public Lebanese unit rate exists for drying beds or septage reception: bracket from the first three real bids and publish the bracket. For scale only, Khulna's plant was estimated at about 58,930 US dollars and finished at about 235,715 US dollars once access roads, a testing facility, landscaping and security were added, which is the honest warning that the beds are the cheap part. Not included: tankers, the cost of transporting dried sludge to its final destination, and any land purchase.

Release

Nothing up front. 15 per cent when the 30-day measurement and laboratory results at milestone 1 are accepted. 15 per cent at milestone 2 when a receiving party has signed. 15 per cent at milestone 3 on the stamped design. 30 per cent at milestone 4 on construction, with the before-covering photos as the condition. 25 per cent at milestone 5 when the first batch has left site with a ticket and the drainage water has been tested. For a study, 50 per cent on the sludge survey and 50 per cent on the stamped report with its payback figure.

Who signs off. The water establishment owns the plant and its sludge. The Ministry of Environment is the authority on sludge disposal and on any land application, and its written position should be obtained before the design, not after. The Ministry of Agriculture is involved if the sludge goes to farmland. The municipality gives planning and access permission and must be in the council minutes. The Council for Development and Reconstruction holds the asset records for donor-built plants. Tanker operators should be registered with the municipality so the logbook can name them. Stamped design by an engineer registered with the Order of Engineers.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Drainage water let go to ground. The liquid squeezed out of sludge is strong sewage. Beds that drain to the ground move the pollution from the plant to the aquifer and pass a casual inspection. Milestone 3 and 5. The design must return drainage water to the plant inlet, and the water is tested.
  • No signed receiving party. Beds get built, sludge dries, and then no landfill will take it and no farmer wants it, so it sits on site for years. Milestone 2. A signature with a volume and a quality on it, before any construction.
  • Liner and drainage layer covered before anyone looked. A bed with a punctured liner or the wrong gravel grading cannot be inspected once it is full, and it leaks for its whole life. Milestone 4. Photos before covering, or the works are not accepted.
  • Sludge to farmland with no pathogen test. Untested sludge on food crops is the fastest way to turn a sanitation project into a public health incident and to end public support for the plant. Milestone 1 and 5. Helminth egg and faecal coliform tests against the WHO agricultural reuse guideline.
  • Beds sized on nameplate capacity. Most Lebanese plants treat far less than their design flow, so beds sized on paper are several times too big and the money is wasted. Milestone 1. Thirty days of measured sludge volumes, not a calculation from capacity.
Sources
  • SNV, constructed wetland faecal sludge treatment in Khulna, Bangladesh, case study. Built 2016, operating 2017; six vertical-flow and one horizontal-flow wetland plus six unplanted drying beds; design 180 cubic metres a day against 10 to 15 actually received; effluent BOD 26 to 33 milligrams per litre against a 40 limit, from incoming sludge at 400 to 500; operating cost about 2,311 US dollars a year; construction estimated at 58,930 and finished at 235,715 US dollars; wetland emptied after seven years within a thirty-year life. admin.snv.org
  • Dutch Water Sector, sludge treatment at wastewater treatment plant Amersfoort, commissioned June 2016. Thermal hydrolysis at 150 to 170 degrees Celsius for 30 to 60 minutes, 60 per cent more biogas, 45 per cent of incoming phosphate recovered, 900 tonnes of struvite a year, sludge volume down 17 per cent, 2 million kWh a year to the grid and about a seven-year payback. dutchwatersector.com
  • World Health Organization Regional Office for the Eastern Mediterranean, A compendium of standards for wastewater reuse in the Eastern Mediterranean Region. WHO agricultural reuse guideline of at most 1 intestinal nematode egg per litre and 1,000 faecal coliforms per 100 millilitres for crops eaten uncooked; Lebanon has Ministry of Environment Decree 52/1 of 1996 and no reuse standard. applications.emro.who.int
  • Review of resource recovery from sewage sludge, on the Dutch Energy and Raw Materials Factory approach at more than 20 plants. ncbi.nlm.nih.gov
  • Libnanews, Wastewater: history of an unfinished Lebanese system. Sludge handling as a neglected operating cost at Lebanese plants. en.libnanews.com
  • Dutch Water Sector, second plant to produce Kaumera Nereda Gum from sewage sludge. Biopolymer extraction cutting sludge for disposal by 20 to 35 per cent. dutchwatersector.com

Electricity: 10 templates. Open one to read it.

1 Grid supplies only a few hours a day
Why this one

Template 1: keeping critical municipal loads on through the cuts

EDL was down to about four hours a day in July 2026, after seven to nine hours in February 2026, with roughly 1,000 MW missing from the grid. A municipality cannot fix that, but it can keep the water pump, the clinic and the street lighting circuit alive, and it can publish an honest schedule so people stop guessing.

Step 1 · Classify

4 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Load and schedule registerNo money for hardware yet, or nobody knows what the council actually runs and when the power is on.List every municipal load, measure it with a clamp meter, log grid-on hours at the main meter for 14 days, publish a feeder schedule.building
Single critical load backupOne load must not stop: a water pump, a clinic fridge, a server, a pumping station. Up to 10 kWp.Solar array, inverter or hybrid inverter, battery, changeover to the existing supply, earthing, metering.kWp
Multi-building critical backupSeveral council buildings on one site, 10 to 50 kWp, with separate essential circuits.Array, hybrid inverters, battery bank in a ventilated room, essential-circuit rewiring, monitoring with data logging.kWp
Essential-circuit separation onlyA generator or a small solar system already exists but feeds everything, so the battery empties on air conditioning.Split the board, move only essential circuits to the backed-up side, label, fit a load-limiting device.circuit
Step 2 · The milestones

7 milestones, each with the proof it needs and the check it must pass

#MilestoneEvidence the expert uploadsPass mark the verifier checks
0Scope and class
Walk the site. List every load with its nameplate rating. Clamp-meter the main for 14 days. Record how many hours a day EDL was actually present. Pick the class and write down which loads are critical and which are not.		Load list with nameplate photos. Logger file or daily readings for 14 days. Photo of the main board with the clamp meter in frame. GPS pin. Signed note from the municipality naming the critical loads.At least 14 days of readings, no gap longer than 24 hours. Critical load in kW and daily kWh stated. Class chosen. Grid-on hours recorded and compared with the national figure of about four hours a day (July 2026).
1Design and approvals
Produce a single-line diagram, array layout, cable sizes, protection ratings and battery sizing for the days of autonomy agreed. Get it stamped by an engineer registered with the Order of Engineers. Tell EDL in writing if anything touches its supply.		Stamped single-line diagram and array layout. Sizing calculation showing autonomy in hours. Order of Engineers registration number. Copy of the letter to EDL and any reply. Council decision reference.Battery sized for the agreed autonomy at the measured critical load, not at a guessed load. Stamp and registration number present. Any grid interface notified to EDL before work starts.
2Equipment on site and checked
Take delivery. Photograph every serial number. Collect the certificates before anything is installed.		Photos of module, inverter and battery serial plates. Module certificate to IEC 61215 and IEC 61730. Inverter certificate to IEC 62109. Battery datasheet with cycle life and temperature range. Delivery notes with quantities.Serial numbers on site match the certificates and the delivery notes. Modules and inverter certified, as Decree 6997 of 8 October 2020 made the LIBNOR solar standards mandatory with IRI verification. No uncertified item on site.
3Install, mount and earth
Fix the array, run DC and AC cabling in conduit, fit DC isolators, fit the battery in a ventilated place away from sleeping rooms, bond and earth everything, label every circuit in Arabic.		Photos of roof fixings before they are covered. Photo of the DC isolator within reach of the inverter. Photo of the earth electrode and the earth bar. Photo of battery ventilation. Photo of the labelled board.DC isolator present and reachable. Earth continuity proved. Earth electrode resistance measured and recorded, target below 10 ohm (to confirm against the Lebanese code). Battery not in a bedroom, kitchen or unventilated cupboard. Labels in place.
4Commissioning tests
Run the standard commissioning tests for a solar installation and write the results on one sheet.		Test sheet with open-circuit voltage and short-circuit or operating current per string, insulation resistance, polarity check, residual current device trip time, and the irradiance and temperature at the time. Photos of the meter readings. Tester make, model and calibration date.Measured open-circuit voltage within 10% of the value expected from the datasheet at that temperature (to confirm). Insulation resistance at least 1 megohm (to confirm). Polarity correct on every string. Residual current device trips at 30 mA within 300 ms (to confirm). Any failed test repeated and passed, not waived.
5Seven-day autonomy proof
Leave the system running for seven days with the monitoring on. Do not touch it. Record when EDL was on and whether the critical load ever dropped.		Seven days of logged data or daily photos of the inverter screen at the same hour. Log of any outage of the critical load, with time and cause. Water pump hours or clinic fridge temperature log where that is the load.Critical load supplied for at least 95% of the hours EDL was absent, over seven days (to confirm as the contract target). Every drop-out explained. Battery never taken below the depth of discharge in the datasheet.
6Handover and 90-day check
Hand over the manual, the as-built diagram and the spares. Train two named council staff. Come back after 90 days and read the data again.		Signed handover sheet with the two names. As-built single-line diagram. Operation and maintenance manual in Arabic. Photo of the spares. Ninety-day data export and a repeat photo of the array showing dust and shading.Two named people trained and signed. Ninety-day output within 10% of the seven-day figure once weather is allowed for (to confirm). No unexplained alarm in the log. Array clean or a cleaning plan in place. This is the gate for the final release.
Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Inspect and scope within 10 working days of the council request. Design and approvals within 20 days. Install within 60 days of the order for anything up to 10 kWp, within 120 days above that, because modules and batteries are imported and customs clearance is the usual delay. Then the seven-day autonomy proof, then the 90-day check. Warranty: two years on workmanship, manufacturer warranty on modules, inverter and battery passed to the municipality in writing with the serial numbers on it.

Money

Priced per kWp of array plus per kWh of usable storage, with the changeover, board work and earthing as separate lump sums. There is no public Lebanese unit rate for municipal solar: no public Lebanese rate, bracket from the first three real bids. As a sanity check only, a 5 ampere household solar system in Lebanon was reported at 2,000 to 7,000 US dollars, and solar energy was costed at about 0.06 dollars per kWh against about 0.44 dollars per kWh from a private diesel generator. Not included: roof strengthening, a new battery room, civil works, customs duty changes, or replacing the battery at end of life.

Release

Nothing up front. 20% on milestone 2 when the serial numbers and certificates are verified on site. 50% on milestone 4 when the commissioning tests pass. 20% on milestone 5 when the seven-day autonomy proof passes. 10% held until the 90-day check. The final 10% mirrors the defects-liability retention the ILO uses on its Lebanese contracts.

Who signs off. Municipal council decision for the spend and for roof access. Design stamped by an engineer registered with the Order of Engineers. EDL must be told in writing about anything that touches its supply, and must approve any grid connection or net metering. Ministry of Energy and Water and LCEC for any programme support. Civil defence for a lithium battery room. Written consent from the building owner where the roof is not the council's.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Sizing from nameplates, not measurements. Nameplate ratings are worst case. A system sized on them costs twice what it should, or the battery is sized for a load that never runs. Milestone 0 needs 14 days of real readings before any class is chosen.
  • Everything on the backed-up side. If air conditioning and water heaters sit on the essential circuits the battery is flat by mid-afternoon and the pump stops anyway. Milestone 0 names the critical loads and milestone 3 shows the labelled board.
  • No DC isolator, or one nobody can reach. A solar array is live whenever the sun is up. Without a reachable isolator, nobody can make it safe, and fire crews will not go near it. Milestone 3 photo, and the test sheet at milestone 4.
  • Battery in the wrong room. Lead-acid gives off hydrogen and lithium packs burn hard. Reports of fires and battery explosions from faulty installations in Lebanon are the reason this is on the list. Milestone 3 ventilation photo.
  • Commissioning sheet filled in from the datasheet. If the numbers are copied rather than measured, faults such as a reversed string or wet insulation stay hidden until something burns. Milestone 4 requires the tester make, model, calibration date, and the irradiance and temperature at the time.

  • LCEC, Lebanon, Decree 6997 of 8 October 2020 making the LIBNOR solar standards mandatory with IRI verification. lcec.org.lb
  • The Badil, Solar safety and environmental concerns in Lebanon, 2022. Solar at about 0.06 dollars per kWh against 0.44 from a generator, 2,000 to 7,000 dollars for a 5 ampere system, fires and battery explosions. thebadil.com
  • The National, Lebanon cracks down on generator operators, 14 August 2025. State power at four to six hours a day. thenationalnews.com
  • Petra news agency, Jordan, municipal solar project phase two, April 2026. 20 kW systems on 188 public buildings in 104 municipalities, 3.4 MW, 1,400 MWh and 550,000 dollars saved a year. petra.gov.jo
2 Unregulated private generator market
Why this one

Template 2: generator register, meter check and bill audit

Diesel generators made about 44% of Lebanon's carbon dioxide equivalent in 2022, and operators drew thousands of complaints in the summer of 2025. The ministry already sets a monthly price per kWh and already requires meters. What is missing at town level is a register that says which generator is where, who it serves, and whether it is billing the legal rate.

Step 1 · Classify

4 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Register onlyThe council does not know how many generators there are or who runs them.Field survey of every generator: location, owner, nameplate kVA, subscriber count, photographs, map.generator
Register plus meter and bill auditThe register exists, or is being built, and residents are complaining about flat fees.Everything above, plus a check that a meter is fitted and read, and a comparison of real invoices against the ministry tariff for that month.subscriber
Register plus safety and environment checkGenerators sit next to homes, schools or clinics, or fuel is stored badly.Everything above, plus fuel tank bunding, exhaust height, noise at the nearest window, and distance to sensitive buildings.generator
Full compliance campaignThe council has decided to enforce, with the ministry and the municipal police behind it.Register, audit, written notices, a compliance window, re-inspection, and a public list of compliant operators.generator
Step 2 · The milestones

7 milestones, each with the proof it needs and the check it must pass

#MilestoneEvidence the expert uploadsPass mark the verifier checks
0Scope and class
Draw the survey boundary on a map. Estimate the number of generators from the council's own knowledge and from subscriber complaints. Agree the class and the sample or the full census.		Map with the boundary drawn. Estimated count with how it was reached. Council decision authorising the survey. Named municipal police contact.Boundary and count agreed in writing. Class chosen. A named municipal officer accompanies the surveyors, because doors do not open otherwise.
1Field survey
Visit every generator in the boundary. Photograph the machine, the nameplate and the surroundings. Record the owner's name, the kVA rating, the fuel store and roughly how many subscribers it feeds.		One record per generator: GPS pin, photo of the machine, close photo of the nameplate showing kVA, photo of the fuel tank, owner name and phone, subscriber count. Surveyor name and date on every record.Every record has a GPS pin and a readable nameplate photo. At least 90% of the estimated count found, or the gap explained street by street (to confirm as the contract target). No record without a date and a surveyor name.
2Meter check
For each generator, check whether meters are fitted on subscriber lines, whether they are read, and whether the readings are used for billing.		Photo of a fitted meter with a readable display, for each generator. Photo of the reading sheet or the operator's book. Note of how many subscribers have meters and how many are on a flat fee.Meter fitted and read, or recorded as not fitted. The Ministry of Economy and Trade directive makes meters mandatory, so a missing meter is a finding, not a note. A meter that exists but is never read counts as no meter.
3Bill audit against the ministry tariff
Collect at least five real invoices per generator for the month being audited. Work out the price the subscriber actually paid per kWh and compare it with the ministry tariff for that same month.		Photographs of at least five invoices per generator, with the subscriber's consent and the name covered. A one-page calculation per generator: kWh billed, amount paid, effective price per kWh, ministry rate for that month, difference.For July 2026 the ministry set 40,746 Lebanese pounds per kWh on low ground and 44,821 on high ground, with a fixed monthly charge of 385,000 pounds at 5 amperes and 685,000 at 10 amperes, and 300,000 for each further 5 amperes. The rate used must be the one published for the month on the invoice, not another month. Any charge added for VAT, maintenance or solar equipment is an overcharge, because the ministry announcement forbids them.
4Safety and environment check
Look at the fuel store, the exhaust and the noise. Measure the distance to the nearest home, school or clinic window.		Photo of the fuel tank showing whether it stands in a bund. Photo of the exhaust showing its height against the nearest building. Distance in metres, measured with a tape or a laser, with the photo showing the line. Noise reading at the nearest window with the make and model of the meter.Fuel tank bunded to hold its contents. Exhaust discharging above the roof line of the nearest occupied building (to confirm against the Ministry of Environment rule). Distance and noise recorded as numbers, never as words like near or loud.
5Notices and re-inspection
Serve a written notice on every non-compliant operator, listing exactly what is wrong and by when it must be fixed. Go back when the window closes.		Copy of each notice with a delivery receipt or a photo of it being handed over. Re-inspection record with new photographs from the same spot as milestone 1.Compliance window of 45 days, which is the window the national crackdown of August 2025 used. Re-inspection photo taken from the same position as the first one. Each item on the notice marked fixed or not fixed, with a photo for each.
6Publish the register and hand over
Hand the council a clean register it can keep using, and publish the list of compliant operators so residents can see who is billing correctly.		Register file with one row per generator and every field filled. Map layer. Signed receipt from the council. Screenshot or photo of the published list.Register complete, with no blank kVA, no missing GPS and no missing owner. Published list dated and naming the tariff month it was checked against. Council names one officer to keep it updated. This is the gate for the final release.
Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Scope within 5 working days of the council request. Survey within 30 days for a town of up to about 100 generators, and pro rata above that. Bill audit within 10 days of the survey, and it must use the tariff month of the invoices collected. Notices served within 5 days of the audit. Compliance window of 45 days. Re-inspection within 10 days of the window closing. The register is a living document, so the contract should include one refresh at 12 months.

Money

Priced per generator surveyed for the register classes, and per subscriber for the bill audit, because collecting invoices is the slow part. No public Lebanese rate for this kind of survey: bracket from the first three real bids. Not included: legal costs if an operator contests a notice, enforcement itself, seizure and storage of equipment, or any compensation to subscribers. The tariff figures used in the audit come free from the ministry each month, so no data cost should appear in the bid.

Release

Nothing up front. 30% on milestone 1 when the field survey is complete and the count is reconciled. 30% on milestone 3 when the bill audit is delivered with its calculations. 25% on milestone 5 after re-inspection. 15% held until the register is published and a named council officer has signed for it.

Who signs off. Municipal council decision authorising the survey. Municipal police escort for field work. Ministry of Energy and Water sets the monthly tariff used in the audit. Ministry of Economy and Trade owns the mandatory meter directive and the consumer protection side. Ministry of Environment for exhaust and noise. Internal Security Forces where enforcement or seizure is involved. Subscriber consent before any invoice is photographed, with the name covered.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Wrong tariff month. The ministry price changes every month with the diesel price and the exchange rate. Auditing a July invoice against the June rate produces a finding that collapses the first time it is challenged. Milestone 3 requires the published rate for the month printed on the invoice.
  • Meter fitted but never read. Operators fit a meter to pass inspection and keep billing a flat fee. The meter is decoration. Milestone 2 asks for the reading sheet, not just a photo of the meter.
  • Generators inside buildings missed. Many generators sit in basements and courtyards, so a survey done from the street undercounts and the register is wrong from day one. Milestone 1 reconciles the found count against the estimate, street by street.
  • Surveyor pressure and made-up records. Operators can be hostile. A surveyor who fills in records from a distance produces a register nobody can rely on. Every record needs a GPS pin, a readable nameplate photo, a date and a surveyor name, and milestone 5 re-photographs from the same spot.
  • Publishing subscriber names. Naming individual subscribers exposes them to their operator and kills the next survey. The register is about generators, not about residents. Milestone 3 requires names covered on invoices, and milestone 6 publishes operators only.

  • The National, Lebanon cracks down on generator operators, 14 August 2025. Thousands of complaints, mandatory meters, a 45-day window, seizure for non-compliance. thenationalnews.com
  • L'Orient Today, Lebanon's generator sector: the known workings of a once illegal, largely unregulated industry. today.lorientlejour.com

3 Theft and non-payment
Why this one

Template 3: feeder loss audit and municipal meter register

Lebanon's network runs at about 16% technical losses and about 21% non-technical losses, so roughly a fifth of the electricity that leaves the plant is taken without being billed. A municipality cannot police EDL's network, but it can measure one feeder honestly, and it can put its own meters in order first.

Step 1 · Classify

4 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Municipal accounts onlyThe council does not know how many EDL meters are in its own name or what they cost.Find every council-owned meter, photograph it, read it, match it to a bill, close dead accounts.meter
One feeder loss auditEDL and the council want a number for one feeder before arguing about it.Check meter at the head of the feeder, 30 days of logging, customer census, energy in against energy billed.feeder
Feeder audit plus connection censusIllegal hooks are visible and the council wants them mapped rather than argued about.Everything above, plus a pole-by-pole count of connections and a map of hooks that match no account.km of line
Audit plus prepaid meter pilotOne block or one building agrees to a pilot and EDL will supply the meters.Everything above, plus prepaid or smart meters on an agreed block, with before and after readings.meter
Step 2 · The milestones

7 milestones, each with the proof it needs and the check it must pass

#MilestoneEvidence the expert uploadsPass mark the verifier checks
0Scope and class
Agree with EDL which feeder or which meters are in scope. Draw it on a map. Confirm in writing that only EDL staff will touch EDL equipment.		Map of the feeder or the list of council meters. Written agreement from EDL naming its contact and confirming who does what. Council decision. Named police contact if a joint inspection is planned.Scope agreed in writing by EDL and the council. Class chosen. A signed line saying no contractor will open, bridge or reconnect anything on the EDL network.
1Measure what comes in
EDL fits or reads a check meter at the head of the feeder. Log it for 30 days. For the municipal accounts class, read and photograph every council meter instead.		Photo of the check meter with its serial number and the current transformer ratio visible. Thirty days of readings or the logger export. For council meters, one photo per meter showing the serial and the reading, with a GPS pin.Thirty full days with no gap longer than 24 hours. Current transformer ratio recorded and used in the arithmetic. Every council meter photographed with a readable serial and reading.
2Count who is on the other end
Walk the feeder and count every connection. Match each one to an EDL account number. Mark the ones with no account.		One row per connection: GPS, pole or building reference, photo of the service drop, account number or blank. Survey date and surveyor name on every row.Every connection either matched to an account number or recorded as unmatched, with a photo. Counts reconciled with EDL's customer list for that feeder, and any difference explained.
3Work out the loss
Compare the energy that entered the feeder over the 30 days with the energy billed to accounts on that feeder over the same 30 days. Split technical from non-technical as far as the data allows.		One-page calculation: kWh in, kWh billed, difference, loss as a percentage. The billing extract from EDL with the same start and end dates. Estimate of technical loss with the method written out.Billing period and metering period cover the same dates, or the figures are adjusted and the adjustment is shown. Loss stated as a percentage with the arithmetic visible. Compared against the national figures of about 16% technical and 21% non-technical.
4Findings pack with EDL
Give EDL a pack it can act on: the unmatched connections, the poles, the photographs, the loss number. Agree which items EDL will act on and when.		Findings pack with a map layer. Minute of the meeting with EDL, signed, listing the agreed actions and dates. No household names published.Pack delivered and receipted by a named EDL officer. Agreed actions written down with dates. No individual named in any public document.
5Remediation on the agreed items
EDL regularises or removes the agreed connections. For the pilot class, the prepaid meters go in. The expert records what happened, and does not touch the network.		Before and after photos from the same spot for each item. EDL work order references. For the pilot, meter serial numbers, install date and the opening reading.Every agreed item photographed before and after from the same position. Work done by EDL or under its written authority, with the order reference recorded. No item closed on a verbal assurance.
6Re-measure after 30 days
Repeat the 30-day measurement on the same feeder, with the same meter and the same method, and compare.		Second 30-day logger export. Second billing extract for the same dates. One page comparing the two loss figures, with the weather and any load change noted.Same meter, same ratio, same method as milestone 1. New loss percentage stated. Any reduction attributed only to items in the milestone 5 list, not to unexplained change. This is the gate for the final release.
Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Scope within 10 working days, because EDL agreement is the slow part. Thirty days of measurement, then the census in parallel. Findings pack within 10 days of the measurement closing. Remediation window agreed with EDL, 60 days is a reasonable default. Then the second 30-day measurement. The whole job is about five months, and most of that is waiting for meters to log.

Money

Priced per feeder for the audit classes and per meter for the register and pilot classes. The check meter and any prepaid meters are EDL's cost, not the expert's, and should be shown separately. No public Lebanese rate: bracket from the first three real bids. Not included: EDL labour, disconnection, any legal action, arrears recovery, or the cost of the meters themselves.

Release

Nothing up front. 25% on milestone 1 when 30 days of clean data exist. 25% on milestone 3 when the loss calculation is delivered. 30% on milestone 4 when EDL receipts the findings pack. 20% held until the second 30-day measurement at milestone 6.

Who signs off. EDL is the only body allowed to touch its own network, and nothing in this template changes that. Written EDL agreement before scoping. Municipal council decision. Internal Security Forces or municipal police for any joint inspection. Order of Engineers registration for whoever signs the loss calculation. Personal data handled under the council's own rules, with no household named in public.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Contractor touching the EDL network. Working on a live distribution network without authority is how people die, and it voids everything that follows. Milestone 0 has a signed line, and milestone 5 needs an EDL work order reference for every item.
  • Mismatched periods. Comparing 30 days of metering with a two-month billing cycle produces a loss figure that is pure arithmetic error, usually a very large one. Milestone 3 requires the same start and end dates, or a shown adjustment.
  • Wrong current transformer ratio. Getting the ratio wrong multiplies or divides the whole result. It is the single most common metering mistake. Milestone 1 requires a photo of the ratio on the meter, and milestone 6 requires the same ratio.
  • Naming households. A public list of suspected thieves is unsafe, unfair and unenforceable. It also ends the council's ability to survey anything again. Milestone 4 forbids individual names in any public document.
  • Hooks removed without a supply offered. Removing a connection from a household with no legal option puts it back within a week. The number looks good for a month and then returns. Milestone 6 re-measures after 30 days, which is long enough for that to show.
