4 Unsafe cable webs and electrocution
Why this one

Template 4: pole safety audit and cable clean-up

Lebanese poles carry EDL cables, generator cables and telecom cables in the same tangle, and rain turns that into a killer. Kenya, which counts properly, recorded 122 electrocution deaths in the year to June 2025, with 21.7% from faulty wiring and 11.2% from illegal connections. The cheapest safety work a municipality can buy is to find out what is actually on its poles.

Step 1 · Classify

4 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Audit onlyNobody knows what is on the poles and there is no budget to change anything yet.Pole-by-pole survey: numbering, photographs, cable count, lowest clearance, condition, owner of each attachment.pole
Audit plus dead cable removalThe audit shows abandoned cables that no operator claims.Everything above, plus removal of cables confirmed dead and unclaimed, under EDL supervision.pole
Audit plus re-dressingLive attachments are tangled but legitimate, on a street the council wants to fix properly.Everything above, plus tying live attachments back to a proper arrangement, with insulated bundled cable where the owner pays for it.km of line
Hazard hot-spot fixA specific danger: a low-hanging span over a road, a leaning or broken pole, an exposed joint at head height.One-off fix of a named hazard, with EDL doing anything on its own network.each
Step 2 · The milestones

7 milestones, each with the proof it needs and the check it must pass

#MilestoneEvidence the expert uploadsPass mark the verifier checks
0Scope and class
Pick the streets. Agree with EDL and the telecom operators that a survey is happening. Set the pole numbering scheme, because most poles have no usable number.		Map of the streets in scope with an estimated pole count. Letters to EDL and to each telecom operator, with any replies. Numbering scheme written down. Council decision.Scope and numbering agreed in writing. EDL informed before anyone climbs or photographs at height. Class chosen. A signed line saying no surveyor will touch any cable.
1Pole survey
Visit every pole. Fix a durable number to it. Photograph the whole pole and then the top. Count the cables. Measure the lowest clearance over the road or footway. Note the pole condition.		One record per pole: number, GPS pin, wide photo, top photo, cable count, lowest clearance in metres measured with a laser or a marked pole, condition notes, surveyor name and date.Every pole has a number, a GPS pin and two photographs. Clearance recorded as a number in metres, never as an impression. At least 98% of the poles in the boundary surveyed, or the gap listed pole by pole (to confirm as the contract target).
2Risk scoring and priority list
Score each pole for danger: low clearance, exposed conductor at reachable height, broken or leaning pole, joints in reach of a balcony, a pole next to a school. Rank them.		Scoring sheet with the rule written out, so a second person applying it would get the same answer. Ranked list with the top hazards and their photographs. Map layer coloured by score.Scoring rule written down before the scores are given. Any pole where a live conductor is reachable from a balcony, a roof or the ground goes to the top of the list, whatever else it scores. Lowest cable over a carriageway below 5.5 metres, or over a footway below 4.5 metres, flagged as a hazard (to confirm against the Lebanese code).
3Ownership notices
Send every pole record with a foreign attachment to the owner it seems to belong to. Ask them to claim it or disown it. Anything nobody claims after the window is treated as abandoned.		Copy of each notice and its delivery receipt. Register showing, per pole, which attachments were claimed, by whom, and which were not. Photographs attached to each notice.Fourteen days to reply, stated in the notice (to confirm as the contract window). Every attachment either claimed by a named owner or recorded as unclaimed. Nothing is cut on the basis of an assumption about who owns it.
4Permit to work and proving dead
Before anything is touched, get the isolation from EDL in writing, lock it off, and prove the cable is dead with a tester at the point of work.		EDL isolation or permit-to-work document with a reference number and a named issuer. Photo of the lock and tag. Photo of the tester on the conductor showing zero, plus a photo of the same tester proving on a known live source before and after. Names and certificates of the crew.No cutting, climbing or handling without a permit reference. Tester proved live, dead, live. Crew named and competent. Any work on an EDL conductor done by EDL or under its written authority. This milestone cannot be skipped for any class.
5Clean-up and re-photograph
Remove or re-dress what the notices allow. Leave no cut end hanging. Re-photograph every pole from the same spot as milestone 1.		Before and after photo pair per pole, from the same position, with the pole number visible. Weight or length of cable removed. Disposal note for the removed cable. New clearance measurement where a span was lifted.After photo from the same position, pole number readable. No cut end left hanging or coiled on the pole. New clearance measured and above the milestone 2 threshold. Removed cable weighed and disposed of, not left for scrap collectors.
6Pre-wet-season re-check and handover
Come back before the rains, or at 90 days if that is sooner, and check nothing has grown back. Hand the pole register to the council.		Re-check photographs of a sample of at least 20% of the poles, or all hot-spot poles, whichever is more. Register file handed over with a signed receipt. List of any new attachments found.Re-check done before the first week of November, so the work stands before the wet season. New attachments counted; more than 10% of cleared poles re-cluttered means the notice process failed and is reported as such (to confirm as the contract target). This is the gate for the final release.
Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Scope within 10 working days. Survey at a realistic rate of about 60 to 80 poles a day for a two-person team on foot (to confirm from the first job). Notices served within 10 days of the survey, then a 14-day reply window. Clean-up within 30 days of the window closing. Pre-wet-season re-check before the first week of November. Hazard hot-spot class runs on its own clock: a reachable live conductor is made safe within 24 hours of being found, by EDL, and the paperwork catches up afterwards.

Money

Priced per pole for the audit and removal classes, per km for re-dressing, and each for hot-spot fixes. No public Lebanese rate: bracket from the first three real bids. Not included: new poles, EDL's own labour, insulated bundled cable where a telecom operator should pay for its own re-dressing, and any compensation for a service interrupted during isolation. Scrap value of removed cable belongs to the council and must be declared, not netted off quietly.

Release

Nothing up front. 25% on milestone 1 when the pole register is complete. 20% on milestone 3 when the notices are served and receipted. 35% on milestone 5 when the before and after pairs pass. 20% held until the pre-wet-season re-check at milestone 6.

Who signs off. EDL for every isolation and for any work on its conductors, in writing, with a permit reference. Municipal council decision and street closure where a lift is used. Ministry of Telecommunications and the individual operators for telecom attachments. Order of Engineers registration for whoever signs the risk scoring. Internal Security Forces where illegal connections are being removed. Civil defence informed where work is near a school or a hospital.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Live work by an untrained crew. This is the failure that kills the worker instead of the resident. Faulty wiring and illegal connections were behind a third of Kenya's 122 electrocution deaths in the year to June 2025. Milestone 4 needs a permit reference, a lock and tag photo, and a proved-dead test with the tester proved before and after.
  • Cutting the wrong cable. A telecom cable that looks abandoned may be feeding a clinic, and a generator cable that looks dead may be live at night when the generator runs. Milestone 3 notices and milestone 4 proving dead, in that order. Nothing is cut on a guess.
  • Hooks removed, demand left. Cutting an illegal connection from a household with no legal supply puts the hook back within days, and the second one is usually worse. Milestone 6 re-check counts re-cluttered poles and reports the figure rather than hiding it.
  • Photo without a pole number. A photo of an untidy pole proves nothing if nobody can say which pole it is, so the before and after pair cannot be made. Milestone 1 fixes a durable number first and milestone 5 needs it readable in the after photo.
  • Cut ends left coiled on the pole. A coil of cut cable is still a hazard, still a snag for a ladder, and still looks like the clutter the job was meant to remove. Milestone 5 pass mark says no cut end hanging or coiled, and the removed cable must be weighed.
Sources
  • Business Daily Africa, Kenya electrocutions hit a record 122, 2025. 122 deaths in the year to June 2025, 21.7% faulty wiring, 12.2% encroachment, 11.2% illegal connections. businessdailyafrica.com
  • The Nation, Pakistan, on electrocution deaths occurring inside homes and private premises, 24 August 2023. nation.com.pk
  • WION, India electrocution fatalities, on national crime records data. wionews.com
  • Libnanews, Electricity in Lebanon: promises against cuts, 2026. Non-technical losses of 21%, which is what the illegal attachments on these poles represent. en.libnanews.com
5 Household solar boom without standards
Why this one

Template 5: solar installation inspection and certificate

Decree 6997 of 8 October 2020 made the LIBNOR solar standards mandatory, with the Industrial Research Institute verifying, but there is still no licence to be a solar installer in Lebanon. In August 2022 only three companies sat on LCEC's qualified list in Beirut, and rooftop fires and battery explosions have followed. An inspection is the cheapest thing a municipality can buy that stops a fire.

Step 1 · Classify

4 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Desk check of paperworkA quick screen before money is released, or before a council grant is paid.Check the installer against the LCEC qualified list, check module, inverter and battery certificates, check the design has an engineer's stamp.system
Household system inspection, up to 10 kWpA house or a small shop, the normal case after the 2021 boom.Paperwork, mounting, electrical inspection, battery location, full commissioning tests and a performance check.system
Building or municipal system, 10 to 100 kWpA block of flats, a school, a clinic or a council building, usually with a battery room.Everything above, plus battery room ventilation and fire separation, string-level testing and a roof loading check.kWp
Post-fire or post-fault investigationSomething has already burned, tripped repeatedly or shocked someone.Make safe, isolate, record the scene, find the cause, write findings the council and an insurer can use.each
Step 2 · The milestones

7 milestones, each with the proof it needs and the check it must pass

#MilestoneEvidence the expert uploadsPass mark the verifier checks
0Scope and class
Agree what is being inspected and why. Record the system size, the installer's name and the install date. Make safe first if there is any sign of burning or a repeated trip.		Photo of the array from the ground. Photo of the inverter nameplate showing rating. GPS pin. Owner's consent in writing. Installer name and install date. System size in kWp.Class chosen. Size, installer and date recorded. Anything with burn marks, melted insulation or a tripping device goes straight to the investigation class and is isolated the same day.
1Paperwork check
Collect and read the documents that should already exist: design, certificates, warranty, handover sheet.		Photos or scans of the module certificate to IEC 61215 and IEC 61730, the inverter certificate to IEC 62109, the battery datasheet, the stamped design, the warranty documents and any IRI verification. Screenshot of the LCEC qualified list on the day it was checked.Certificates match the serial numbers actually on the roof, not a different model. Decree 6997 of 8 October 2020 makes the LIBNOR standards mandatory, so an uncertified module or inverter is a fail, not a note. Whether the installer appears on the LCEC list is recorded either way, with the date checked, since the list is refreshed every two months.
2Mechanical and mounting inspection
Get on the roof. Look at how the array is fixed, what it is fixed to, and what happens to the water.		Photos of the fixings, the rail ends, the roof penetrations and their seals. Photo of any ballast. Note of roof type and age. Photo of the clearance under the array. Note of any shading from tanks, walls or trees.Every rail end fixed, no free-floating panel, no brick or block used as ballast. Penetrations sealed. The roof structure can carry the array and the wind uplift, confirmed by a stamped calculation for anything over 10 kWp (to confirm). Shading recorded with the hour it was seen.
3Electrical inspection
Open the boards. Check cable sizes, fuse and breaker ratings, isolators, earthing and bonding, and where the battery lives.		Photos of the DC board, the AC board, the DC isolator, the earth bar and bonding, the cable sizes at their terminations, and the battery in its location with any ventilation visible. Photo of the labelling.DC isolator fitted and reachable. Fuse and breaker ratings not above the cable rating. Array frame and all metalwork bonded, earth continuity proved. Residual current protection present on the AC side. Battery not in a bedroom, a kitchen, a stairwell or an unventilated cupboard, and lithium packs separated from lead-acid. Labels present, in Arabic.
4Commissioning tests
Run the standard tests for a solar installation and write them on one sheet with the conditions at the time.		Test sheet showing continuity, polarity, open-circuit voltage and operating current per string, insulation resistance, residual current device trip time, and the irradiance and cell temperature at the time. Tester make, model and calibration date. Photos of the meter readings.Polarity correct on every string. Open-circuit voltage within 10% of the datasheet value corrected for temperature, and strings of the same design within 5% of each other (to confirm). Insulation resistance at least 1 megohm (to confirm). Residual current device trips at 30 mA within 300 ms (to confirm). A test that fails is repeated after a fix, never waived.
5Performance check
Measure what the system actually makes at a known irradiance and compare it with what it should make.		Irradiance reading with the meter model. Inverter output reading at the same minute. Module temperature. One-page calculation of expected against measured. Photo of the inverter display and the irradiance meter together.Measured output within 10% of the expected output for that irradiance and temperature, after allowing for shading recorded at milestone 2 (to confirm). Anything further out is investigated, not averaged away. Lebanon gets about 300 days of sunshine a year, so a weak system is a fault, not a weather story.
6Certificate and 12-month check
Issue a pass, a conditional pass with a fix list, or a fail. Where there is a fix list, re-inspect. Come back at 12 months and read the generation meter.		Signed certificate with the engineer's Order of Engineers number. Fix list with a photo per item, before and after. Twelve-month generation reading with a photo of the meter. Repeat array photo showing dust and shading.Certificate signed by a registered engineer, naming the class and the system size. Every fix item closed with a photo. Twelve-month generation within 10% of the figure predicted at milestone 5, once weather is allowed for (to confirm). This is the gate for the final release.
Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Inspect within 10 working days of the request, and within 24 hours where there is burning, melted insulation or a repeated trip. Fix list to the owner within 3 days of the inspection. Re-inspection within 10 days of the fixes being reported done. Twelve-month check on the anniversary, give or take 15 days. The certificate is valid for 12 months, or until the system is altered, whichever comes first.

Money

Priced per system for household inspections and per kWp above 10 kWp. The post-fire class is priced per hour, because nobody can guess the work. No public Lebanese rate for solar inspection: bracket from the first three real bids. As a sanity check on what the systems themselves cost, a 5 ampere household solar system in Lebanon was reported at 2,000 to 7,000 US dollars. Not included: the fixes themselves, which must be bought separately so the inspector never profits from finding faults, replacement equipment, or roof repairs.

Release

Nothing up front. 40% on milestone 4 when the commissioning tests are delivered with conditions recorded. 30% on milestone 6 when the certificate is issued. 20% when the fix list is closed, or immediately with the certificate if there was no fix list. 10% held until the 12-month check.

Who signs off. Municipal building permit where the array changes the structure or the roof line. Design stamped by an engineer registered with the Order of Engineers. LIBNOR standards are mandatory under Decree 6997 and the Industrial Research Institute does the verification. LCEC holds the qualified installer list. EDL must approve any grid connection or net metering. Civil defence for lithium battery rooms and for any post-fire scene. Owner's written consent before anyone goes on the roof.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Certificates for a different model. A folder of certificates is easy to produce. Matching them to the serial numbers on the roof is what proves the modules are the certified ones. Milestone 1 matches certificates to the serial numbers photographed at milestone 0 and on the roof.
  • Undersized DC cable behind an oversized fuse. The cable becomes the fuse. This is the classic rooftop fire, and the Bchamoun rooftop fire is the kind of case that follows. Milestone 3 compares every fuse and breaker rating against the cable size at its termination.
  • Battery in a bedroom or a closed cupboard. Lead-acid gives off hydrogen and lithium burns hard and fast. Fires and battery explosions from faulty installations are already reported in Lebanon. Milestone 3 photograph of the battery in its location with the ventilation visible.
  • Array on a roof that cannot carry it. Wind uplift, not weight, is what takes arrays off Lebanese roofs, and the panel lands on a street. Milestone 2 requires a stamped loading calculation above 10 kWp and every rail end fixed.
  • Tests copied off the datasheet. If the commissioning sheet is filled in from the catalogue, a reversed string or damp insulation goes unseen until it fails. Milestone 4 requires the tester model, its calibration date, and the irradiance and temperature at the moment of the test.

  • LCEC, Lebanon, qualified solar photovoltaic company list, updated every two months, list current to July 2026. lcec.org.lb
  • The Badil, Solar safety and environmental concerns in Lebanon. No certification process for solar companies, three qualified companies in Beirut in August 2022, a Bchamoun rooftop fire, 2,000 to 7,000 dollars for a 5 ampere system, about 300 days of sunshine. thebadil.com
  • Arab Reform Initiative, Lebanon's solar energy boom. arab-reform.net
  • MERIP, Off the grid: why solar won't solve Lebanon's electricity crisis, July 2024. merip.org
6 Utility death spiral from grid defection
Why this one

Template 6: grid defection survey and shared solar pilot

Solar in Lebanon has risen roughly eight-fold since 2020 while EDL's paying base shrinks, so the fixed cost of a network that still loses about 16% technically and 21% non-technically falls on fewer and poorer customers. A municipality cannot set a tariff, but it can count honestly who has left, who cannot leave, and what a shared system would cost the ones with no roof.

Step 1 · Classify

4 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Defection survey onlyThe council has no idea who is on EDL, who is on solar, and who is paying a generator.Sample survey of households: supply sources, monthly spend, amperes subscribed, roof access.household
Survey plus bill impact analysisThe council wants to know what its own residents actually pay per kWh from each source.Everything above, plus an analysis of cost per kWh by source and by income band.household
Survey plus shared solar pilot designA sizeable group has no usable roof: tenants, ground-floor flats, shaded buildings.Everything above, plus a design for a shared array on a council roof or plot, with how the output is shared and billed.kWp
Survey plus net-billing readiness packEDL is willing to discuss net metering or a grid fee for one feeder.Everything above, plus feeder-level export and import data and a pack EDL can take to a decision.feeder
Step 2 · The milestones

7 milestones, each with the proof it needs and the check it must pass

#MilestoneEvidence the expert uploadsPass mark the verifier checks
0Scope, sample and consent
Define the population, choose the sample, and write the consent form and the questionnaire. Get both approved by the council before a single door is knocked.		Population figure and its source. Sample size with the calculation. Questionnaire. Consent form in Arabic. Council decision. Data handling note saying where the answers are stored and who can see them.Sample of at least 384 households for a town of any size, which gives about plus or minus 5% at 95% confidence (to confirm with a statistician). Sample spread across neighbourhoods and across morning, afternoon and evening, not only whoever is home at 11 in the morning. Consent form signed before every interview.
1Field survey
Run the interviews. For every household record which sources it uses, what it pays each month, how many amperes it subscribes to, whether it has a roof it may use, and whether it has already installed solar.		One record per household: neighbourhood, sources used, monthly spend by source, amperes, roof access yes or no, solar installed and when, consent reference. Surveyor name, date and time on every record. No names, no phone numbers in the analysis file.At least 384 completed records, or the shortfall explained with the refusal rate. Interviews spread across the day and the week. Refusal rate reported, because a 40% refusal rate makes the result unusable. Names held separately from the answers.
2Cross-check against meter records
Ask EDL for the count of active accounts and the total billed energy for the same area, and compare it with what the survey found.		EDL extract with account counts and billed kWh for the area and period. One page comparing the survey's implied numbers with EDL's. Written note of any difference and the likely reason.Survey estimate of EDL-connected households within 10 percentage points of EDL's own account count for the area, or the difference explained (to confirm as the contract target). Where they cannot be reconciled, the survey is reported as an estimate and says so plainly.
3Cost per kWh by source
Turn spend into a price per kWh for each source, so households can be compared honestly rather than by monthly bill.		Calculation sheet with the assumptions written out: hours of grid supply, generator amperes to kWh, solar generation estimate, capital cost spread over life. Table of cost per kWh by source and by income band.Uses the published ministry generator tariff for the month surveyed, which in July 2026 was 40,746 pounds per kWh on low ground and 44,821 on high ground, with 385,000 pounds fixed at 5 amperes. Compared against the reported figures of about 0.44 dollars per kWh from a generator and about 0.06 from solar. Every assumption listed on the same page as the result.
4Pilot design or policy pack
For the pilot classes, design the shared array and how its output is divided. For the policy classes, write the pack EDL and the council need to decide on net billing or a grid fee.		For a pilot: site, kWp, single-line diagram, metering arrangement, the sharing rule in one paragraph, cost per participating household, stamped by a registered engineer. For a policy pack: the feeder numbers, the options, and what each does to the households in each income band.The sharing rule can be explained to a participant in one paragraph and produces the same answer whoever applies it. Costs per household stated as a number. Design stamped. No option presented without saying who pays more under it.
5Council and EDL decision record
Present the findings in public session. Record what the council decided and what EDL said, including if the answer was no.		Presentation deck. Minute of the session with the decision, the date and who was present. Written EDL response. Published summary of the findings with no household identifiable.Decision recorded with a date, even if the decision is to do nothing. EDL response in writing. Published summary contains no household-level data and no names. Refusal rate and sample size printed on the summary, so readers can judge it.
6Twelve-month repeat
Repeat the same survey, same questions, same neighbourhoods, one year on, and report the movement.		Second survey dataset. Side-by-side comparison of the two years. Note of any question that changed wording, because that breaks comparison.Same questionnaire, same sample size, same neighbourhoods. Movement reported with the margin of error shown, so a 2-point change is not reported as a trend. This is the gate for the final release.
Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Scope and questionnaire within 15 working days, because consent and data handling need the council's approval. Field survey within 30 days. EDL cross-check within 30 days of asking, and it is the item most likely to slip. Analysis within 15 days of the last interview. Council session within 30 days of the analysis. Twelve-month repeat on the anniversary, give or take 30 days.

Money

Priced per completed household record for the survey classes, per kWp for a pilot design, and per feeder for a policy pack. Price per completed record, not per attempted one, so nobody is paid for a refusal. No public Lebanese rate for household survey work: bracket from the first three real bids. Not included: building the pilot, any subsidy, translation into French, or paying respondents, which is not done because it biases the answers.

Release

Nothing up front. 30% on milestone 1 when the completed records and the refusal rate are delivered. 20% on milestone 3 when the cost per kWh analysis lands. 25% on milestone 4 on the design or policy pack. 15% on milestone 5 after the council session. 10% held until the twelve-month repeat.

Who signs off. Municipal council decision authorising the survey and the data handling. EDL for any account or billing data, and for anything touching net metering. Ministry of Energy and Water and LCEC for the policy side. Order of Engineers registration for whoever stamps a pilot design. Written consent from every household interviewed, held separately from the answers.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Surveying only whoever is home at midday. That is pensioners and people not in work, and their supply choices are not the town's. The result looks precise and is wrong. Milestone 0 fixes the time spread and milestone 1 requires the time of day on every record.
  • Comparing monthly bills instead of price per kWh. A household that uses very little from a generator pays a small bill at a terrible price. Bills hide that entirely. Milestone 3 converts everything to a price per kWh with the assumptions on the page.
  • Personal data in the analysis file. Names and phone numbers next to what a household pays and whether it has an illegal connection is a file that must never exist. Milestone 1 holds names separately, and milestone 5 publishes nothing household-level.
  • Treating solar owners as the problem. People bought solar because there was no power. A project framed as punishing them gets no interviews and no council support. Milestone 4 forces every option to state who pays more under it, which keeps the argument honest.
  • A pilot with no agreed sharing rule. Shared arrays fail on the split, not on the engineering. If two participants can read the rule differently, the pilot ends in a dispute. Milestone 4 pass mark: one paragraph, same answer whoever applies it.

Why this one

Template 7: street light inventory and LED retrofit

Lebanese streets go dark because EDL cannot power the lights and because nobody holds a list of what is installed, so nothing gets maintained. Jordan showed what the other path looks like: 410,000 lamps changed to LED for JD65 million, saving JD15 million of electricity and JD7 million of maintenance a year, repaid over seven years.

4 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit

Street-by-street table of lighting class, luminaire model, wattage, lumen output, colour temperature, optic and mounting height. Lighting calculation output for at least one street per class. Go back after dark with a lux meter and measure the road, on a grid, not at one spot under a lamp.		Lux readings at a grid of points on at least one span per street, with the grid sketched and the points numbered. Meter make, model and calibration date. Photo of the meter on the road surface. Photos of the street lit, from the same position as the milestone 1 photo.Average and minimum lux meet the class assigned at milestone 2, measured with a calibrated lux meter at road level, not a phone app. Measured at least one hour after switch-on. Uniformity reported, because a street of bright pools and dark gaps fails even when the average passes. Any span that fails is re-aimed or re-lamped and re-measured.
5Energy check
Prove the saving. Read the circuit before and after, or calculate it from the verified lamp counts and wattages and the burn hours.		Before and after readings at the feeder pillar meter, or a clamp meter reading on the circuit at night with a photo. Table of lamp counts by wattage, before and after. Burn hours assumed, with how they were reached.Saving stated in kW and in kWh a year, with the burn hours written down. Before figure measured or taken from the milestone 1 inventory, never assumed. Compared for sanity against Jordan's programme, which saved JD15 million of electricity and JD7 million of maintenance a year on 410,000 lamps.
6Twelve-month check and maintenance handover
Hand over the inventory as the council's asset register, with spares and a named keeper. Come back at 12 months and count what is still lit.		Asset register file with one row per lamp. Signed handover to a named council officer. Photo of the spares held. Night re-survey at 12 months with the percentage lit. Fault log for the year.At least 97% of the retrofitted lamps still lit at 12 months (to confirm as the contract target, since no Lebanese benchmark is published). Asset register complete with no blank pole references. A named officer and a budget line for maintenance, because Jordan's saving came half from maintenance. This is the gate for the final release.
Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Scope within 10 working days. Night survey within 20 days for a town of up to 1,000 lamps. Design within 15 days of the survey. Install within 60 days of delivery, and delivery is the long pole because luminaires are imported. Night measurement within 14 days of energising. Twelve-month check on the anniversary. Warranty: two years on workmanship, and the manufacturer's luminaire warranty, which for LED street lighting is commonly five years, passed to the council in writing (to confirm per supplier).

Money

Priced per lamp for survey and retrofit, per lamp plus per metre of cable for the circuit class, and per lamp for solar. No public Lebanese rate: bracket from the first three real bids. Jordan's figures give the shape of the deal rather than a price: 410,000 lamps for JD65 million, against JD15 million of electricity and JD7 million of maintenance saved each year, funded half by a rural fund grant and half by a development bank loan over seven years. Not included: new poles, road opening, EDL supply work, or the electricity itself.

Release

Nothing up front. 20% on milestone 1 when the inventory is delivered and reconciled. 15% on milestone 2 when the stamped design lands. 35% on milestone 4 when the night measurement passes. 20% on milestone 5 when the saving is proved. 10% held until the twelve-month check.

Who signs off. Municipal council decision. Written confirmation of who owns the lighting supply, and EDL approval where the supply or the pole is EDL's. Road closure or lane closure permit from the municipality, and from the Ministry of Public Works on a classified road. Order of Engineers registration for the lighting design. Internal Security Forces notified for night working. Ministry of Environment for disposal of mercury or sodium lamps, which are hazardous waste.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Retrofit onto a dead circuit. New lamps on a circuit with no supply stay dark, and the council has bought nothing. This is the single most common way the money is wasted. Milestone 1 records the circuit per lamp, and milestone 0 confirms who owns the supply.
  • Matching the old wattage. Replacing a 250 W sodium with a 250 W LED throws away most of the saving and usually produces glare instead of light on the road. Milestone 2 designs to a lighting class and records the old wattage only as background.
  • Lux measured with a phone. Phone light meters are not calibrated and read differently on every handset, so the pass mark means nothing. Milestone 4 requires a calibrated meter with make, model and calibration date.
  • Bright pools and dark gaps. An average that passes can hide a street where the dark stretch between lamps is exactly where people are afraid to walk. Milestone 4 requires a grid of points and a uniformity figure, not one reading under a lamp.
  • No inventory, so no maintenance. Without an asset register the council cannot buy the right spare or tell a contractor which lamp is out, and half of Jordan's saving was maintenance. Milestone 6 hands over a complete register with a named keeper and a budget line.

8 Solar street lights and off-grid assets that fail or get stolen
Why this one

Template 8: solar street lights that survive year two

Solar street lights are easy to buy and easy to lose. In Kenya a solar lighting project faced vandalism within its first year, and India's national audit found solar assets installed and then left without maintenance. The engineering is not the hard part: the battery, the theft and the maintenance budget are.

Step 1 · Classify

4 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Audit and repair of existing lightsSolar lights were installed before and many are now dark.Night and day survey, battery and controller test, replace what has failed, tag every asset.lamp
All-in-one lights on existing polesPoles exist and are sound, and the street needs modest light.All-in-one luminaire with integrated panel and battery, anti-theft bracket, tagging, commissioning.lamp
New pole with split-panel lightNo pole, or shading means the panel must be aimed separately from the lamp.Foundation, pole, separate panel on an adjustable mount, lamp, battery in a lockable compartment, tagging.lamp
Battery replacement and anti-theft retrofitThe lamps and panels are fine but the batteries are dead and the fixings are ordinary bolts.New batteries of the right chemistry, security fixings, panel cages, tagging, disposal of the old batteries under template 10.lamp

6Maintenance line and handover
Hand over the asset register, the spares and the settings. Make sure the council has actually voted a maintenance budget, not just promised one.		Asset register with tag, serial, site, install date, battery type and warranty end. Council minute showing a maintenance budget line with a figure. Photo of the spares held. Signed handover to the named officer. Training note for two council staff.A maintenance budget line exists in the council's own minute with a number on it, sized at least for battery replacement at the end of the datasheet life. Register complete with no blank tags. Two named people trained. This is the gate for the final release.
Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Scope within 10 working days, with the site survey done in daylight and after dark. Specification and order within 20 days. Install within 45 days of delivery. First night test on the night of commissioning. Autonomy test within 60 days, or sooner if the weather allows. Twelve-month survival check on the anniversary. Warranty: two years on workmanship, battery warranty per the datasheet and passed to the council in writing with the tag numbers on it.

Money

Priced per lamp, with the pole and foundation separate for the new-pole class, and battery replacement priced per unit so it can be budgeted. No public Lebanese rate: bracket from the first three real bids. As a sanity check on battery cost, refurbished second-life lithium packs in Kenya were costed at 45 US dollars per kWh with a seven-year field life, against lead-acid at roughly 12 dollars per kWh per year over three years. Not included: pole relocation, tree cutting for shade, electricity, or replacing units that are stolen after handover, which is what the maintenance line is for.

Release

Nothing up front. 15% on milestone 1 when the specification and the tagged asset list are approved. 35% on milestone 3 when the first night test passes. 25% on milestone 4 when the autonomy test passes. 15% on milestone 6 at handover with the budget line in the minute. 10% held until the twelve-month survival check.

Who signs off. Municipal council decision, including the maintenance budget line. Road or footway occupation permit for new poles, and the Ministry of Public Works on a classified road. Order of Engineers registration for the pole foundation design. EDL only where an existing pole or supply is theirs. Ministry of Environment for the disposal of the old batteries, which goes through template 10. Internal Security Forces notified where theft has already happened at the site.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Lead-acid battery in a hot housing. A lead-acid battery in a sealed box on a Lebanese street in August lasts a season. The light then dies and everyone blames solar. Milestone 1 requires the chemistry and the rated temperature range on the datasheet.
  • Ordinary bolts on the panel. A panel on standard fasteners is a ten-minute theft, and the Ngong case in Kenya shows vandalism starting almost immediately. Milestone 2 photographs the security fixings before the cover goes on.
  • No maintenance budget. India's national audit found solar assets installed and then left. Without a budget line the first dead battery is permanent. Milestone 6 needs a figure in the council's own minute, not a promise.
  • Shading nobody checked. A panel under a water tank or a tree charges for two hours a day and the light dies every winter, which looks like a battery fault and is not. Milestone 0 requires the two photographs looking up from the panel position, morning and afternoon.
  • No asset register. Without tags the council cannot say what it bought, cannot report a theft, and cannot claim on a warranty. Milestone 1 tags before install and milestone 5 reports missing units by tag number.

9 Public building energy bills
Why this one

Template 9: municipal building energy audit and rooftop solar

Lebanese councils pay generator fees for offices, schools, clinics and pumping stations at roughly 0.44 dollars a kWh, against about 0.06 from solar. Jordan put 20 kW systems on 188 public buildings across 104 municipalities for JD3.4 million and now saves about 550,000 dollars and 1,400 megawatt-hours a year. The audit has to come first, because a system sized to the roof instead of the load is money burned.

Step 1 · Classify

4 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Walk-through auditThe council has bills but no idea where the energy goes. The cheapest first step.Twelve months of bills and generator invoices, a walk-through of the building, a load list, a ranked list of no-cost and low-cost measures.building
Detailed audit with measurementThe building is large or the bills are large enough to justify metering.Everything above, plus a week of logging on the main and on the big loads, and a measure list with payback for each.building, reported per square metre
Rooftop solar up to 20 kWpThe audit is done, the easy measures are taken, and a daytime load remains.Array, inverter, metering, earthing, and a battery only if the audit shows it pays.kWp
Solar plus efficiency paid from savingsAn energy services contract is possible and the council wants no capital outlay.Everything above, plus lighting, controls and pump measures, with payment tied to verified savings.building
Step 2 · The milestones

0Scope, class and 12 months of bills

Working shown.Generator kWh derived from invoices using the published ministry tariff for each month, which in July 2026 was 40,746 pounds per kWh on low ground and 44,821 on high ground with a 385,000 pound fixed charge at 5 amperes. Exchange rate and date stated. Baseline signed by the council as agreed, before any measure is designed.
2Measurement
For the detailed classes, put a logger on the main for at least seven days and clamp the biggest loads. Walk the building at night to find what is still running.		Seven-day logger export from the main, with the logger make and model. Clamp readings on each major load. Night walk-through photos of anything still running. Load list with nameplate and measured figures side by side.Seven full days including a weekend, so the base load at night and at the weekend is visible. Base load stated in kW. List the measures in order of payback, cheapest and quickest first. Only then size any solar, and size it to the daytime load, not to the roof. Do the work. Commission the solar with the same tests as template 5 and record the results.		Photos of each measure installed. Commissioning test sheet with insulation resistance, polarity, open-circuit voltage and residual current device trip time, with irradiance and temperature at the time. Generation meter serial and opening reading.Every measure in the milestone 3 table either installed or formally dropped with a reason. Commissioning tests pass as in template 5. 5Verify the saving

Generation meter closing reading with a photo. Adjustment sheet listing any change in occupancy, floor area or equipment, with the correction applied. One page comparing baseline and actual.Full 12 months after the work, compared to the agreed 12-month baseline, whole building, with adjustments listed openly. Saving stated in kWh and in money. Jordan's programme gives the sanity check: 1,400 megawatt-hours and about 550,000 dollars a year across 3.4 megawatts on 188 buildings. A saving that cannot be seen in the bills is not a saving.

Hand over the manual, the as-built drawings and the settings. Train two named staff. Put a cleaning and maintenance plan in the council's budget.		Signed handover with two names. Photo of the array after the first cleaning.Two named people trained and signed. Maintenance budget line with a figure in the council minute. Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Scope within 10 working days, but collecting 12 months of bills often takes longer and should be started on day one. Walk-through audit within 20 days of the bills arriving. Measurement week within 30 days. Measure list within 15 days of the measurement week. Install within 90 days of the order, since modules and inverters are imported. Then a full 12 months before the saving is verified. The whole cycle is about 18 months, and any contract that promises verified savings sooner is promising something it cannot show.

Money

The audit classes are priced per building, or per square metre for large buildings. Solar is priced per kWp installed. Savings-based contracts are priced as a share of verified savings, which makes milestone 5 the whole contract. No public Lebanese rate: bracket from the first three real bids. Jordan's municipal programme cost JD3.4 million for about 3.4 megawatts across 188 buildings, roughly JD1,000 per kW, 90% funded by Italy and 10% by the national efficiency fund, which is a shape for a funder rather than a Lebanese price. Not included: roof repairs, structural strengthening, asbestos removal, electrical board replacement found during the audit, or the electricity itself.

Release

Nothing up front. 20% on milestone 1 when the baseline is signed by the council. 15% on milestone 3 when the stamped measure list lands. 35% on milestone 4 when installation and commissioning pass. 20% on milestone 5 when the 12-month saving is verified. 10% held until handover with the maintenance line in the minute.

Who signs off. Municipal council decision and a signed baseline. Building permit where the array changes the structure or the roof line. Order of Engineers registration for the design and the audit report. EDL approval for any grid connection or net metering, and for any change at the supply point. LIBNOR standards mandatory under Decree 6997 with IRI verification. LCEC for programme support and for the qualified installer list. Civil defence for any battery room.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Generator cost left out of the baseline. Most of what a Lebanese council actually pays for electricity is on generator invoices, not EDL bills. A baseline built on EDL alone makes the saving look impossible. Milestone 0 requires both, and milestone 1 converts invoices to kWh at the published monthly tariff.
  • Solar sized to the roof. A roof-filling array on a building that is empty at the weekend exports power nobody pays for, and the payback never arrives. Milestone 3 sizes against the measured daytime profile from milestone 2.
  • No generation meter. Without a meter on the solar output, every later argument about savings is opinion. Inverter displays are not evidence and reset. Milestone 4 requires a separate generation meter with its serial and opening reading photographed.
  • Baseline moved after the fact. Adjusting the baseline once the numbers are in is how energy contracts produce savings that no accountant can find. Milestone 1 has the council sign the baseline before any measure is designed.
  • Efficiency measures skipped for the shiny one. Solar is visible and lighting controls are not, so the cheap measures with one-year paybacks get dropped and the expensive one is oversized to compensate. Milestone 3 lists no-cost and low-cost measures first, and milestone 4 needs a written reason for anything dropped.

10 Battery and solar e-waste
Why this one

Template 10: battery take-back and safe storage

Every battery installed in Lebanon's solar boom since 2021 is coming to the end of its life, and there is no recycling programme and no safe landfill waiting for it. Lead-acid batteries last a few months to a few years, lithium up to ten, and about 29% of Lebanon's waste is already disposed of informally. A municipal collection point is the smallest thing that keeps them out of a valley.

4 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit

Collection, storage and licensed handoverVolumes are large enough that the council must hand on to a licensed recycler or an approved exporter.Everything above, plus consignment notes, weight reconciliation and the paperwork for transboundary movement.tonne
Take-back campaign with installersThe council wants the batteries to come in rather than waiting for them.An agreement with local solar installers to return old batteries when they fit new ones, plus household drop-off days and a public message.campaign

Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Legal check within 20 working days, and it is the item that decides whether the job can happen at all. Store ready within 45 days of the legal position. Collection runs continuously once open. Handover loads at least every 90 days, so nothing sits for a year. Reconciliation every quarter and again at 12 months. The store must never hold more than the volume agreed with civil defence, so the handover interval shortens if volumes rise.

Money

Priced per tonne handled for the collection and handover classes, per battery for triage, and as a lump sum for the campaign class. The store fit-out is a one-off lump sum. No public Lebanese rate for battery collection: bracket from the first three real bids. Scrap value of lead-acid should be shown as income to the council, not used to reduce the bid quietly. As a benchmark on what reuse is worth, second-life lithium packs in Kenya were costed at 45 dollars per kWh against lead-acid at roughly 12 dollars per kWh per year, and a peer-reviewed study found second-life batteries cut the cost of electricity for school systems by between 5.6% and 35.3%. Not included: the recycler's own gate fee, export costs, cleaning up a spill caused before collection, or solar panels, which are a separate waste stream with a thirty-year life.

Release

Nothing up front. 25% on milestone 1 when the store passes inspection with civil defence's written note. 25% on milestone 2 after the first quarter of receipted, weighed collection. 30% on milestone 4 on the first licensed handover with matching weights. 10% on milestone 5 at the first clean reconciliation. 10% held until the twelve-month report.

Who signs off. Ministry of Environment for storage, handling and any licensed recycler, and for export, which falls under the Basel Convention on transboundary movement of hazardous waste. Municipal council decision and a site the council controls. Civil defence for fire safety, especially for lithium. Ministry of Industry where a recycler or smelter is involved. Order of Engineers registration for whoever designs the bund and the ventilation. Transport of hazardous goods by road needs the correct carrier, not a council pickup truck.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • A store with no route out. Batteries arrive, nothing leaves, and within a year the council owns a hazardous waste site it cannot clear. Milestone 0 requires a named licensed destination in writing before the first battery is accepted.
  • Lithium and lead-acid stored together. Acid fumes, hydrogen and lithium fires need different handling and different extinguishers. Mixed storage turns one fault into a fire nobody can put out. Milestone 1 photographs the physical separation and the quarantine area.
  • Counting units instead of weighing. Battery weights vary enormously, so a unit count cannot be reconciled and material can leave without showing. Milestone 2 requires a calibrated scale with a certificate, and milestone 5 reconciles by weight.
  • Handing over to an informal buyer. Informal smelters strip lead in the open, poisoning the people who do it and the ground around them. About 29% of Lebanon's waste already goes this way. Milestone 4 requires a licence number and a signed receipt for every single load.
  • Reusing a pack that should be recycled. A tired or damaged lithium pack sold on as second life becomes somebody else's fire, and it destroys trust in reuse altogether. Milestone 3 sets a measured capacity floor and sends anything swollen, leaking or hot to quarantine.
Sources
  • The Badil, Solar safety and environmental concerns in Lebanon. No recycling route for solar batteries, 29% of Lebanon's waste disposed of informally, lead-acid lasting months to years, lithium up to ten years, panels about thirty. thebadil.com
  • myclimate and Solibrium, Kenya, take-back, reuse and recycling business models for off-grid solar batteries. myclimate.org
  • Energy-Storage.news, second-life lithium battery storage in Kenya at half the cost of lead-acid, 6 November 2019. 45 dollars per kWh, about 4,500 of 5,000 assessed packs suitable for reuse. energy-storage.news
  • Scientific Reports, second-life batteries for primary school solar systems, 2023. Levelised cost of electricity cut by between 5.6% and 35.3%. nature.com
  • M-KOPA, Kenya, impact page. Nearly 90% of returned solar products refurbished for resale, the model behind a working take-back scheme. m-kopa.com

Environment: 10 templates. Open one to read it.

1 Summer forest fires with weak local capacity
Why this one

Template 1: brush clearing and a village fire watch around one at-risk settlement

Fires in Akkar, Dinniyeh and the south burn for days while Civil Defence and municipalities lack equipment and fall back on loudspeaker appeals for volunteers. Tunisia shows where that ends: the area burnt each year went from about 2,400 hectares in 2012 to 25,808 hectares in 2021, and a burnt hillside takes about twenty years to come back.

Step 1 · Classify

4 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Class A: house and hamlet clearingFewer than 30 buildings sit inside or within 200 m of forest or dense scrub, and the ground is walkable.Clear scrub and dead fuel in a belt around each building, cut the lower branches of trees, thin crowded trees, remove the cuttings from the site, photograph before and after.building treated
Class B: access road and escape route clearingThe settlement has one way in or out, or the fire engine cannot turn round at the end of it.Clear a strip either side of the road, cut back branches over the road, build or clear a turning place, mark the route with signs that survive heat.km of road treated
Class C: village fire watch and early warningClearing is done or under way and the village wants trained eyes through the summer, on the French communal fire committee model.Recruit and train volunteers, agree patrol routes and hours, fit a lookout point, set up one phone tree to Civil Defence, log every patrol and every call.volunteer trained, then patrol-day
Class D: fuel break on the settlement edgeA continuous block of pine or scrub runs straight up to the houses and clearing single buildings is not enough.Cut a shaded fuel break along the settlement boundary, remove the cut material, agree with landowners, plan how it will be maintained each spring.m of break, by width band
Step 2 · The milestones

7 milestones, each with the proof it needs and the check it must pass

#MilestoneEvidence the expert uploadsPass mark the verifier checks
0Scope and class
Walk the settlement edge. Count the buildings inside or within 200 m of forest or scrub. Note which are lived in. Measure the width of the fuel between the forest and the nearest wall. Find the one way in and out. Ask the municipality and Civil Defence where the last three fires started. Choose the class.		GPS pin at every building in scope and at each fire start point the municipality names. Photo from the forest edge towards each building and back again. A sketch map, drawn by hand is fine, showing the settlement, the forest, the road in and the water points. Tape measure photo of the fuel width. Building count.Every building inside or within 200 m of forest or scrub is on the list with a GPS pin (to confirm: the 200 m figure is the French legal brush-clearing trigger). Distance from forest to the nearest wall is written down for each one. The one way in and out is identified. A class is chosen and a named owner is recorded for every plot to be cleared.
1Permission, owners and the fire service
Get the council decision. Write to the Ministry of Agriculture, which owns forest policy, and to the local Civil Defence centre. Get written consent from every landowner whose plot will be cut. Agree with Civil Defence where the work will happen and when.		Council decision number and date. Copy of the letter to the Ministry of Agriculture and its reply or the receipt stamp. Signed consent sheet, one line per plot, with the owner's name and phone number. Name and phone of the Civil Defence officer who agreed the plan.There is a named authority for the work. Every plot to be cut has a signed consent or a written council order. Civil Defence knows the dates. Nothing is cut before all three are on file.
2Clear the belt around the buildings
Cut and pull out scrub, dead branches, dry grass and anything stacked against the walls. Prune the lower branches of trees that stay. Thin the trees so the crowns do not touch. Clear gutters and roofs of pine needles. Do not burn anything.		Photo pairs before and after from the same marked spot for every building, with the GPS pin. Photo with a measuring pole showing the pruning height. Photo of the gap between crowns. Photo of the roof and gutter after clearing.A cleared belt of at least 50 m radius around each building, or to the plot boundary where the plot is smaller (to confirm: 50 m is the standard French clearance radius, set locally by the mayor). Lower branches removed to at least 2 m above the ground (to confirm). Crowns of remaining trees not touching. Nothing flammable stacked within 3 m of a wall (to confirm). No burn scar anywhere on the site.
3Remove the cuttings and clear the escape route
Take every cut branch and every heap of scrub off the site to a chipping point or a licensed site. For class B, clear the road strip, cut back the overhanging branches and finish the turning place.		Weighbridge tickets or load counts with the destination named. Photos of the cleared road from both ends. Photo of a vehicle standing in the finished turning place. Photo of the cleared strip with a tape measure across it. Photo of the site after removal, taken from the same spot as the after photo at milestone 2.No cut material left on any treated plot. Nothing burnt on site. Road strip cleared at least 2 m either side of the carriageway and branches cut back to at least 4 m above it (to confirm). A fire engine can turn round without reversing onto a slope.
4Water, access and the fire plan on one page
Find every usable water point inside and around the settlement: tanks, wells, reservoirs, pools. Check each one can be reached by a fire engine and check the fitting. Write the settlement fire plan on one page in Arabic: water points, access routes, assembly point, who calls whom.		GPS pin, photo and a capacity note in cubic metres for each water point. Photo of the access to each from the road. Photo of the coupling or fill point. The one-page plan, signed by the municipality and by the named Civil Defence officer. Photo of the plan posted where people can see it.At least one usable water point within 500 m of the settlement, reachable by a fire engine and with a fitting Civil Defence can use (to confirm). Every water point has its capacity written down. The one-page plan carries two signatures and names one assembly point.
5Train the watch and run one drill
For class C, train the volunteers: what smoke looks like early, what to report, what never to do, and how to reach Civil Defence. Agree patrol hours for the dry months. Run one drill with Civil Defence present.		Attendance sheet with names, ages and phone numbers, signed. Photos of the training and the drill. The patrol rota. A copy of the call log book with the first entries. Written note from the Civil Defence officer who attended the drill.At least eight trained volunteers for a settlement of up to 500 people (to confirm). A written rota covering the dry months. One drill completed with Civil Defence present and signed off. The call log exists and names one number to ring.
6End of season check
Come back at the end of the fire season and look at the same things again. Count how many plots have grown back. Read the patrol log.		Photos from the same marked spots as milestone 2, dated at the end of the dry season. Photo with a tape measure of any regrowth. The completed patrol log and call log. A short note from the municipality on any fire that started or was reported in the season.At least 90 per cent of treated buildings still have a clear belt, judged from the photo pairs (to confirm). Regrowth under 50 cm tall in the cleared belt (to confirm). The patrol log shows patrols on at least three quarters of the rota days for class C. No burning used as a clearing method anywhere on the site. This is the gate for the final release.
Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Inspect within 10 working days of the request. All cutting must finish before the dry season starts, so the work window is the wet half of the year: scoping from October, cutting between November and April, and nothing cut with a machine on a hot dry windy day. Class A and class B within 60 days of the council decision. Class C training before the first of June. Class D within 120 days because it needs more landowners to agree. Then the end of season check, after the last hot month.

Money

Priced per building treated for class A, per kilometre of road for class B, per volunteer trained and then per patrol-day for class C, and per metre of break by width band for class D. Removal of cut material is a separate line priced per load with the distance and destination named, because hauling brush is what makes the price move. No public Lebanese rate; bracket from first real bids. As a sanity check only, Tunisia costs replanting a burnt hectare at about 9,000 dinars and puts the loss per burnt hectare at 20,000 to 50,000 dinars. Not included: fire engines, hoses, personal protective equipment for Civil Defence, building a new water tank, and any clearing on land whose owner refuses.

Release

Nothing up front. 20 per cent at milestone 1, when the consents and the Civil Defence agreement are on file. 50 per cent at milestone 3, when the cuttings are off the site and the escape route is open. 20 per cent at milestone 5, after the drill. 10 per cent held until the end of season check at milestone 6 passes.

Who signs off. The municipal council decides first and the mayor is the person who can order clearing on private land. The Ministry of Agriculture governs forests and must be informed, and must approve any cutting of standing forest trees. Civil Defence, under the Ministry of Interior and Municipalities, must agree the plan and should attend the drill. Inside a nature reserve the Ministry of Environment and the reserve committee approve instead. Every private landowner signs. On state forest land or in a border area the army must be informed. Open burning as a clearing method is not permitted at all.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Burning the cuttings on site. The most common cause of a summer fire in a cleared village is the clearing itself. A heap of dry brush lit in April can smoulder for days. The load tickets at milestone 3 and the burn scar check in the photographs.
  • Cutting in the dry season. A strimmer blade on a stone in August starts fires. So does a hot exhaust in dry grass. The dated photographs at milestones 2 and 3, checked against the work window in the time clause.
  • Clearing only the public land. Fire does not stop at a plot boundary. One uncleared garden in the middle of a cleared hamlet carries the fire to the next roof. The building-by-building list and consents at milestones 0 and 1.
  • Cuttings left in heaps. A pile of cut brush is more dangerous than the standing scrub it came from, because it is dry and it is next to the house. The after photographs and the load count at milestone 3.
  • A volunteer watch with no drill and no number to ring. Volunteers who have never practised will fight the fire themselves instead of reporting it early, which is the one thing they are there to do. The drill sign-off and the call log at milestone 5.
Sources
  • L'Orient Today, From Akkar to south Lebanon, hectares of forest go up in smoke as anger grows, 2024. Fires in Akkar, Dinniyeh and the south, weak local equipment, loudspeaker appeals for volunteers. today.lorientlejour.com
  • Observatoire des forets francaises, Les obligations legales de debroussaillement. The French legal duty to clear vegetation for owners within 200 m of at-risk forest, enforced by mayors and prefects across about 7,400 communes. observatoire.foret.gouv.fr
  • Nawaat, Tunisian forests going up in flames, August 2024. 693 fires in 2023, area burnt up from about 2,400 ha in 2012 to 25,808 ha in 2021, 7,500 rangers against 13,300 needed, one ranger per 2,000 ha, replanting about 9,000 dinars per hectare, about twenty years to recover. nawaat.org
  • France 3 Occitanie, On est les yeux des pompiers: the communal forest fire committees. Trained village volunteers patrolling in summer as the eyes of the fire service. france3-regions.franceinfo.fr
  • UNDP Lebanon, Lebanon's Civil Defense: prepared today to save lives every day. Civil Defence centres rehabilitated with KfW funding in priority areas including Minnieh and the Beqaa since 2024. undp.org
2 Untreated sewage into rivers, lakes and sea
Why this one

Template 2: outfall survey and river water quality monitoring for one town

About 69 towns in the upper Litani basin send roughly 46 million cubic metres of untreated sewage into the river every year, and after thirty years of plans only 4 per cent of the planned sewer network, 18 km out of 441 km, has been built and only 168 houses out of 9,150 are connected. Before anyone builds another pipe, a town needs to know exactly where its own sewage leaves the ground and what the river looks like above and below that point.

Step 1 · Classify

4 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Class A: outfall survey onlyThe town has never had its discharges mapped and nobody can say how many pipes reach the water.Walk the whole watercourse inside the municipal boundary, find and pin every pipe, ditch and seep, photograph each one, estimate the flow, describe what it drains.km of bank walked, then outfall recorded
Class B: survey plus twelve months of samplingThe town wants evidence that stands up: numbers above and below the discharges through a full year of wet and dry weather.Everything in class A plus fixed sampling points, monthly samples taken to an accredited laboratory, and a public results sheet.sample analysed
Class C: survey, sampling and quick fixesThe survey finds discharges that can be stopped cheaply: a broken manhole, a pipe cut by a road job, a septic tank overflowing straight to the ditch.Everything in class B plus a costed list of quick fixes and the delivery of the ones under an agreed cost ceiling.outfall closed or diverted
Class D: community monitoring handoverSampling has run for a year and the municipality wants it to continue without paying a consultant every month.Train a village group on the Costa Rican community monitoring model, hand over field kits, agree a reporting route to the municipality and the river authority, and keep one laboratory check each quarter.monitor trained, then monitoring month
Step 2 · The milestones

7 milestones, each with the proof it needs and the check it must pass

#MilestoneEvidence the expert uploadsPass mark the verifier checks
0Scope and class
Define the stretch: every watercourse inside the municipal boundary plus 500 m upstream and 500 m downstream of it. Measure the length. Find out who else discharges upstream. Get the municipality's own list of known pipes. Choose the class.		A map of the stretch with the start and end GPS pins and the length in kilometres. Photo of the upstream and downstream boundary points. The municipality's existing list, photographed or scanned. Note of how many households the town has and whether they are on a sewer, a septic tank or neither.The stretch has a measured length and two fixed end points with GPS pins. The household count and the connection status are written down. A class is chosen. Where the town sits in the Litani basin, the Litani River Authority is named in the scope.
1Permission, laboratory and safety
Get the council decision. Write to the regional water establishment and, inside the Litani basin, to the Litani River Authority. Choose an accredited laboratory and agree what will be tested. Brief the team on sewage safety and vaccination.		Council decision number and date. Copies of the letters and any replies. The laboratory's accreditation certificate and its price list. The agreed test list. Signed safety briefing sheet with the names of everyone who will touch the water, and their vaccination record.There is a named authority. The laboratory is accredited, not a school lab. The test list includes at least biochemical oxygen demand, chemical oxygen demand, total suspended solids, ammonia, nitrate, phosphate and faecal coliforms, because Lebanese environmental standards under Ministry of Environment decision 8/1 of 30 January 2001 are written in those terms. Nobody enters the water without gloves and boots.
2Walk the bank and pin every outfall
Walk both banks of the whole stretch, in dry weather, on foot. Pin and photograph every pipe, ditch, culvert and wet seep that reaches the water, whether or not it is flowing. Give each one a number painted or tagged on the spot.		GPS pin, a photo showing the pipe mouth with a scale object, and a photo showing the pipe in its setting, for every outfall. The painted or tagged number visible in the photo. A flow estimate for each, using a bucket and a stopwatch where it can be done safely. A note on what it looks like it drains: houses, a factory, a farm, road runoff.Both banks walked end to end, proven by a continuous GPS track. Every outfall has a number, a pin, two photographs and a flow estimate or the word dry. The count of outfalls found is compared with the municipality's existing list from milestone 0 and the difference is explained.
3Sample above, below and at the worst pipes
Set fixed sampling points: one upstream of the town, one downstream of the last outfall, and one at each of the three largest discharges. Sample monthly for twelve months, at the same time of day, in a clean bottle, chilled, and at the laboratory within the holding time.		Photo of each sampling point with its marker and GPS pin. For every round: photo of the bottles labelled and in the cool box, the chain of custody form signed by the sampler and the laboratory, and the laboratory report. Rainfall note for the previous 24 hours.Twelve rounds for class B, C and D, no gaps longer than 45 days. Same points every time. Chain of custody signed at both ends. At least three rounds taken in the wet season and three in the dry. The upstream and downstream pair are taken on the same day, upstream first.
4Work out what each outfall is and rank them
Put the sampling results next to the outfall list. Work out which pipes carry household sewage, which carry industry, which carry farm runoff and which carry only rain. Rank the outfalls by the load they add. For class C, cost the fixes.		One table, one row per outfall, with its number, GPS, flow, what it carries, the evidence for that judgement and its rank. For class C, a costed fix per outfall with a photo of what needs doing. Dye test photos where a pipe's source was not obvious.Every outfall has a judgement with a reason attached, not a guess. The ranking is arithmetic, flow multiplied by strength, and the arithmetic is shown. The top three outfalls together account for a stated share of the total load. Any industrial discharge is named with the establishment behind it, as the Litani River Authority does with its own surveyed list of 209 establishments.
5Fix what can be fixed and publish
For class C, close or divert the outfalls on the agreed list. For every class, publish the map, the table and the twelve months of results on the municipality noticeboard and in a form the sponsor can post online.		Before and after photos at each closed outfall, from the same spot, plus a photo of the dry pipe mouth. Photo of the published results on the noticeboard. The data as a plain table file. Delivery note or receipt for any materials used.Every outfall on the agreed fix list is dry in the after photograph, taken at least seven days after the work. The published table carries every result, including the bad ones. No result is left out.
6Handover and the repeat round
Hand the map, the table and the routine to the municipality and, inside the basin, to the Litani River Authority. For class D, train the community monitors and watch them take one full round unaided. Then come back and repeat the upstream and downstream pair.		Signed handover note naming the municipal officer who now holds the file. For class D, attendance sheet, photos of the training, the kit inventory, and the monitors' own first results sheet next to the laboratory result for the same day and the same point. The repeat laboratory report, dated at least 90 days after milestone 5.The handover note is signed. For class D, the monitors' own reading and the laboratory reading for the same sample agree within 20 per cent for the field parameters (to confirm). The repeat round shows the closed outfalls are still dry. This is the gate for the final release.
Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Inspect within 10 working days of the request. Class A within 45 days: it is a walk, not a study. Class B, C and D run at least twelve months because the point is to cover wet weather and dry weather, and a survey that only sees August is worthless. The quick fixes in class C are due within 60 days of the ranking at milestone 4, not at the end of the year, because a broken manhole should not wait for a report. Then the repeat round at least 90 days after the fixes.

Money

Priced per kilometre of bank walked and per outfall recorded for class A, per sample analysed for class B, per outfall closed or diverted for class C, and per monitor trained plus per monitoring month for class D. Laboratory fees are a separate line, quoted per parameter per sample, because the test list is what moves the price. No public Lebanese rate; bracket from first real bids. As a sanity check only, the World Bank loan for the Lake Qaraoun pollution project was 55 million US dollars and delivered 18 km of the 441 km of sewer planned, which is what this template is meant to avoid repeating. Not included: building sewers, building or repairing a treatment plant, household connections, land acquisition, and prosecuting any polluter the survey names.

Release

Nothing up front. 20 per cent at milestone 2, when both banks are walked and every outfall is pinned. 30 per cent at milestone 4, when the ranking is delivered with its arithmetic shown. 30 per cent at milestone 5, published and fixed. 20 per cent held until the repeat round at milestone 6 passes.

Who signs off. The municipal council decides first. The regional water establishment, which is the Bekaa, North, South or Beirut and Mount Lebanon establishment, must be informed. Inside the Litani basin the Litani River Authority must be informed and should receive the data. The Ministry of Energy and Water covers watercourses. The Ministry of Environment sets the standards through decision 8/1 of 2001 and must be told if an industrial discharge is found. The Ministry of Public Health is informed where drinking water or irrigation is affected. The laboratory must be accredited. Access to private land to reach a bank needs the owner's consent, and on the coast or near a dam the army must be informed.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Sampling only in dry weather. The worst discharge in a Lebanese town is often the first hour of winter rain, when everything in the street and every overflowing tank reaches the river at once. A dry-season-only survey misses it and makes the town look clean. The rainfall note and the wet-season round count at milestone 3.
  • Outfalls missed because the bank was not walked. Counting pipes from a bridge, a car or a satellite image misses the small ones, and the small ones are most of them. The Litani lower basin count of 111 random dumps came from walking, not from a desk. The continuous GPS track at milestone 2.
  • A school laboratory instead of an accredited one. Results that no court and no ministry will accept are results that change nothing, and the whole point of the survey is to be usable as evidence. The accreditation certificate at milestone 1.
  • Bad results quietly dropped. A monitoring programme that publishes only the good months is worse than no programme, because it buys the town a clean reputation it has not earned. The published full table at milestone 5, checked against the numbered laboratory reports.
  • A report with no named polluter. An outfall described as unknown source cannot be acted on by anyone. Every pipe has an owner, and finding them is part of the work. The judgement with a reason for every row at milestone 4, and the dye tests.
Sources
