  • Council for Development and Reconstruction, Lake Qaraoun pollution prevention project. The 55 million US dollar World Bank funded sewerage and treatment programme in the upper basin. cdr.gov.lb
  • Central Pollution Control Board of India, study group report on the river Yamuna. Outfall inventory, drain-by-drain load accounting and upstream and downstream sampling as the basis of a river clean-up. cpcb.nic.in
  • Journal of Environmental Studies and Sciences, community water quality monitoring in Costa Rica, 2018. Volunteers monitoring river quality to drive municipal action where treatment lags. link.springer.com
3 Illegal quarries and sand mining
Why this one

Template 3: quarry register and rehabilitation of one abandoned face

An army survey in 2023 counted 1,607 quarry and crusher sites in Lebanon, with damage put at 2.4 billion US dollars, and reportedly only one valid licence among them. A municipality cannot close a national industry, but it can put every site inside its own boundary on a register with a photograph and a measurement, and it can make one abandoned face safe.

Step 1 · Classify

4 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Class A: register onlyThe municipality does not know how many sites it has, how big they are or whether any of them is licensed.Find every quarry, crusher and sand pit inside the boundary, measure it, photograph it, check the licence status, record the operator, record the hazards.site registered
Class B: register plus change monitoringSites are still being worked and the municipality needs to show whether they are growing.Everything in class A plus a repeat measurement every three months from fixed photo points and free satellite imagery, and a written change note each round.site monitored per quarter
Class C: make one abandoned face safeA disused face is loose, overhanging or above a road, a house or a school, and somebody could be killed by it.Scale off loose rock, cut the face back to a stable angle, build a catch ditch or bund at the toe, fence it, sign it. No replanting yet.m2 of face treated
Class D: rehabilitate one abandoned quarryThe face is already stable or has been made stable, and the site can be given back to the hillside.Reshape the benches, bring back soil, drain the site, plant native species, fence, sign, and two years of watering and replacement.m2 of restored surface

7 milestones, each with the proof it needs and the check it must pass

#MilestoneEvidence the expert uploadsPass mark the verifier checks
0Scope and class

Measure the worked area and the height of the highest face. Note what is below it and how far away.		GPS pin at the entrance and at the corners of the worked area. Copies of the letters to the Ministry of Environment, the governor and, where relevant, the army, with the stamps or replies.Every registered site has a named landowner and a named operator, or the word unknown with a note of who was asked and when. For class D only. Reshape the benches so water does not pond. Spread stored or imported soil. Plant native species grown from local seed. Fence the site and put up the permanent sign.		Delivery notes for soil and for plants, with the nursery named. Photo of a ruler standing in a test hole in the spread soil. Species list with counts. Photos of the planting and of the whole fence line. Photo of the sign.At least 30 cm of soil over the planted area (to confirm). Benches graded so water runs off and does not pond, proven by a bucket of water in the photograph. Plants are native species, no ornamental exotics, and the nursery is named. The fence has no gap a pickup can use.
6Rain season check and two year check
Come back after the first full winter and look for movement, rockfall and gullies. For class D come back again after two growing seasons and count what survived.		Photos from the same marked spots, dated after the first winter. Photo with a tape measure of any crack, slip or gully. Photo of the catch ditch showing what has fallen into it. For class D, a survival count with photographs of sample plots. For class B, the quarter-by-quarter change notes and the paired satellite screenshots.No new overhang. No slip larger than 1 m3 outside the catch ditch (to confirm). No gully deeper than 15 cm on a reshaped bench (to confirm). For class D, at least 70 per cent of planted stock alive after two growing seasons (to confirm). For class B, no registered site has grown beyond its milestone 0 outline without a licence. This is the gate for the final release.
Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Inspect within 10 working days of the request. Class A within 60 days. Class B runs at least four quarters. Class C within 90 days of the council decision, and within 30 days where the hazard list flags a face above a house, a school or a used road. Class D within 150 days, planted in the wet season and never in high summer. Then the rain season check, and for class D the two year check.

Money

Priced per site registered for class A, per site per quarter for class B, per m2 of face treated for class C, and per m2 of restored surface for class D. Soil and plants are separate lines with the source named, because imported soil and a distant nursery move the price more than the earthworks do. No public Lebanese rate; bracket from first real bids. As a sanity check only, the national damage from quarrying has been put at about 2.4 billion US dollars across 1,607 sites, which is roughly 1.5 million dollars a site, but that is a damage figure and not a repair rate. Not included: buying the land, compensating the operator, court costs, blasting, and any work on a site that is still being quarried.

Release

Nothing up front. 30 per cent at milestone 3, when the register is delivered to three named bodies with receipts. For class C and class D, 40 per cent at milestone 4 or 5, on the safe face or the planted site. 30 per cent held until the rain season check at milestone 6, and for class D half of that last share is held further to the two year survival count.

Who signs off. The municipal council decides first. The Ministry of Environment approves quarry rehabilitation and holds the national quarry policy. The governor of the muhafaza and the Ministry of Interior and Municipalities sit in the licensing chain, through the national quarries and crushers body. The Order of Engineers and Architects must stamp the face design for class C and class D, and the engineer must have stood on the site. The army must be informed where explosives, military land, a border area or a coastal site is involved, and the army's own survey is the source of the national site count. The regional water establishment is informed where the site drains to a spring, well or watercourse. The Ministry of Agriculture approves the species list for class D. Nothing here licenses extraction: this template only registers and repairs.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Politically awkward sites left off the register. A register with holes in it is a defence for the sites in the holes. The value of the document is that it is complete. The published full list at milestone 3, checked against satellite imagery of the whole boundary.
  • Rehabilitation used as cover for more extraction. Reshaping a face is a convenient reason to take more rock off the hill and sell it. It happens, and it is the single most common abuse of a rehabilitation contract. The before and after volume check at milestone 4 against the milestone 0 outline, and the quarterly satellite pairs in class B.
  • Planting on bare rock. Plants put straight onto a quarry bench with no soil die in the first summer and the site is declared restored on a photograph taken in April. The ruler in the test hole at milestone 5 and the two year survival count at milestone 6.
  • No catch ditch at the toe. A face can be perfectly angled and still drop a block onto the road below. The ditch is what stops the block, and it is the cheapest part of the job. The tape measure photograph along the ditch at milestone 4.
  • Clean water left running over the face. Rain from the hillside above pouring over a cut face will undo the work in one winter and cut gullies through the new soil. The diversion drain photograph at milestone 4 and the gully check at milestone 6.

  • The Legal Agenda, Environmental crimes in Lebanon: unlawful enrichment that kills. The licensing chain, the weakness of enforcement and the role of the courts. english.legal-agenda.com
  • Centre for Science and Environment, Grains of despair: sand mining in India. Depth limits such as no extraction below three metres in Andhra Pradesh, machinery bans in Karnataka and Maharashtra, and village-level consent through the Gramsabha and the Kerala Kadavu committees. cseindia.org
4 Open dumps and waste burning smoke
Why this one

Template 4: stopping open burning in one village

Human Rights Watch documented 941 open dumps in Lebanon, 617 of them municipal, with more than 150 burned at least weekly, and the burning follows poverty: about 192 burns a week in the Bekaa and 159 in the south against 2 a week in Jbeil and Kesrwane. Burning is already illegal under article 24 of law 444 of 2002. What is missing is a record that says who burnt what, where and when.

Step 1 · Classify

4 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Class A: burn watch and evidence logResidents report smoke but nobody has ever written down the dates, the places or the wind direction.Fixed watch points, a trained resident log, GPS and time-stamped photographs of each event, a monthly summary to the municipality and the ministry.watch-month
Class B: watch plus smoke exposure measurementA school, a clinic or a dense housing area is downwind and the health case needs numbers rather than complaints.Everything in class A plus low-cost particle monitors at the school or clinic and at a clean reference point, running for at least six months.monitor-month
Class C: remove the reason to burnThe log shows burning is being done by or for the municipality because collection has stopped or there is nowhere to put the waste.Everything in class A plus a costed collection gap analysis, an interim haulage arrangement to a licensed site, and a burning ban notice with a named enforcement route.tonne diverted from burning
Class D: agricultural and green waste alternativeMost of the burning is pruning, olive residue or crop waste rather than household rubbish.A chipping or composting point, a collection day calendar, farmer briefings, and a ban notice on field burning during the dry months.m3 of green waste diverted

The complaint route names a person at the municipality, a person at the Ministry of Environment and the 1214 hotline, and says how many hours each step takes. No watch starts without the route agreed, because a log with nowhere to go is not evidence, it is a diary.
2Set the watch up
Pick fixed watch points that see every burn site. Recruit and brief residents. Give each one the same simple form: date, time, place, what is burning, wind direction, photo. Mark the photo points so every photo is from the same spot.		GPS pin and photo of each watch point, with a reference photo of the view it covers. Attendance sheet for the briefing, signed, with names and phone numbers. Blank form and the first filled examples. Every form has the same six fields. Photos are time-stamped and GPS-tagged by the phone, and a verifier can read both on the image.
3Run the watch and log the events
Log every burning event for at least six months. Photograph each one from the marked point, with the time and GPS on the image. Send the monthly summary to the municipality and the ministry. The event log as a plain table: date, time, GPS, what burnt, estimated volume, wind direction, photo file name, who reported it, what the municipality did. Monthly summaries with the sending receipt. For class B, the monitor data files, a photo of each monitor in place, and the calibration note.At least six months of continuous logging with no gap longer than 14 days. Every logged event has a time-stamped, GPS-tagged photograph from a marked point. Every monthly summary has a delivery receipt. For class B, the monitors return data on at least 80 per cent of hours (to confirm), and one monitor sits downwind at the receptor and one at a clean reference point.
4Remove the reason or offer the alternative
For class C, work out the collection gap in tonnes a week and arrange interim haulage to a licensed site with a written acceptance. For class D, build the chipping or composting point, publish the collection calendar and brief the farmers.		For class C, the gap arithmetic, the written acceptance from the receiving licensed site, and weighbridge tickets or load counts per week. For class D, photos of the finished point, the delivery notes for the chipper or the bays, the published calendar, and the farmer briefing attendance sheet.For class C, there is a named legal destination for every tonne and a signed acceptance before any load moves. Weekly tonnage hauled is at least the gap calculated, for at least eight consecutive weeks (to confirm). For class D, the point is fenced, signed and reachable by a tractor, and the calendar is posted where farmers will see it.
5Ban notice, signs and enforcement
The municipality posts the burning ban, in Arabic, at every burn site and at the village entrances, quoting article 24 of law 444 of 2002 and the hotline number. Agree who inspects and how often.		Photo of every posted notice with its GPS pin. The council decision that authorises it. A signed note naming the municipal inspector and the inspection frequency. Copies of any notice served on an individual, with the reference number.A notice at every burn site from milestone 0 and at every village entrance, readable from three metres. 6Six-month comparison

A short written note from the school or clinic if there is one.Logged burning events down by at least 70 per cent against the watch period (to confirm). No burning at all within 100 m of a school or clinic (to confirm). For class B, the receptor's daily average particle concentration moves towards the reference point, and both are reported against the World Health Organization annual PM2.5 guideline of 5 micrograms per cubic metre. This is the gate for the final release.
Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Inspect within 10 working days of the request. The watch is set up within 30 days and runs for at least six months, because a single month tells you nothing about a seasonal habit. For class C, the interim haulage starts within 30 days of the gap arithmetic at milestone 4: waste that keeps piling up will be burnt while the report is written. The ban notice goes up within 14 days of the haulage or the alternative being available, and not before, because banning burning with nowhere for the waste to go simply moves it. Then the six-month comparison.

Money

Priced per watch-month for class A, per monitor-month for class B, per tonne diverted for class C, and per cubic metre of green waste diverted for class D. Haulage is a separate line per tonne-kilometre with the destination named. Monitors are a separate capital line and they stay with the municipality. No public Lebanese rate; bracket from first real bids. As a sanity check only, rehabilitating Lebanon's mapped open dumps has been costed at about 74 million US dollars nationally, and the Ministry of Environment put the annual cost of degradation from dumping and burning at about 10 million US dollars a year in 2010. Not included: closing or capping the dump itself, which is a different template, buying collection trucks, prosecuting anybody, and health care for anyone already ill.

Release

Nothing up front. 20 per cent at milestone 2, when the watch points and the trained watchers are in place. 30 per cent at milestone 3, after six months of unbroken logging with delivered summaries. 25 per cent at milestone 4 or 5, on the alternative being real and the notices posted. 25 per cent held until the six-month comparison at milestone 6 passes.

Who signs off. The municipal council decides first, and solid waste has been a municipal responsibility since decree 8735 of 1974. The Ministry of Environment enforces article 24 of law 444 of 2002 against open burning and must receive the log. The Ministry of Public Health runs the 1214 health complaint hotline and is informed where a school or clinic is affected. The Ministry of Interior and Municipalities covers the council decision and the Independent Municipal Fund that usually explains why collection stopped. The receiving licensed site must accept the waste in writing before any load moves. Law 64 of 1988 covers toxic waste and brings the public prosecutor in where medical or hazardous waste is found in the burn. Air monitors on a school need the school's written permission.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Banning the burning with nowhere for the waste to go. The waste does not stop arriving. It moves to the next valley, or it is burnt at three in the morning instead of at noon, and the log goes quiet while the problem grows. The sequencing rule in the time clause: the notice at milestone 5 cannot go up before the alternative at milestone 4 is working.
  • Photos with no time and no place. A photograph of smoke that cannot be tied to a date and a point proves nothing to a ministry and nothing to a court. The time-stamp and GPS check on every image at milestone 3.
  • The log stops when it gets uncomfortable. Most burning in a small village is being done by somebody everybody knows. Logs tend to stop exactly when they become useful. The no-gap-longer-than-14-days rule and the delivery receipts at milestone 3.
  • One monitor and no reference point. A single particle reading with nothing to compare it to cannot separate the burning from dust, traffic or a sandstorm. The two-monitor requirement at milestone 3, receptor and reference.
  • Medical or hazardous waste in the burn, unreported. Burning drums, batteries or health-care waste is a different offence with different consequences, and treating it as ordinary rubbish hides the worst of the harm. The what is burning field on every form at milestone 3, and the law 64 of 1988 route in the permits clause.

5 Forest dieback from pests and drought
Why this one

Template 5: forest health survey and sanitary treatment of one stand

The cedar web-spinning sawfly, Cephalcia tannourinensis, has killed more than 7 per cent of the trees at Tannourine over two decades and more than 70 per cent of the stand is now affected. Only about 17 square kilometres of cedar are left in Lebanon, roughly 0.4 per cent of the ancient cover, and the Shouf has warmed about 0.7 degrees with snow cover down from three or four months to one.

Step 1 · Classify

4 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Class A: health survey onlyTrees are dying and nobody knows how many, how fast, or what is killing them.Fixed survey plots, tree-by-tree crown scoring, pest and disease identification with samples sent to a laboratory, a map of the affected area.hectare surveyed
Class B: survey plus soil and larval monitoringA soil-dwelling pest such as the cedar sawfly is suspected, whose numbers are in the ground and not on the branches.Everything in class A plus soil sampling on a grid to count larvae or cocoons, repeated at the same points across a season.soil sample point
Class C: sanitary felling and removalDead and dying trees are holding the pest or the fungus and are seeding the next outbreak, or they are a fire and falling hazard.Mark, fell and remove only the trees on the survey list, destroy or treat the material, leave standing deadwood where it is safe and useful, record every stump.tree felled
Class D: assisted replanting with a drought-tolerant mixCanopy gaps are open, the soil is still there and natural regeneration is not coming.Local-provenance seedlings of several species, planting in the wet season, protection from browsing, three years of watering in the first summers, and a survival count.seedling planted

Copies of the letters with stamps or replies. The laboratory or institute identification letter naming the organism. Turn the plot sheets into numbers: what share of trees are healthy, thinning, severely thinning or dead, by species and by plot. Map the affected area. For class B, take the soil samples on the grid and count larvae or cocoons.		The plot data as a plain table, one row per tree. Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Inspect within 15 working days of the request, but the survey timing is set by the organism and not by the contract: a sawfly is counted in the soil in autumn and seen on the tree in spring, and a survey in the wrong month finds nothing. Class A within 60 days of the right season starting. Class B runs a full year so it catches the life cycle. Class C felling within 90 days of the treatment list being approved, and outside the bird nesting season where that applies. Class D planted only in the wet season, between November and March. Then the repeat survey a year later and, for class D, the survival count after two growing seasons.

Money

Priced per hectare surveyed for class A, per soil sample point for class B, per tree felled with the girth band stated for class C, and per seedling planted for class D, with three years of watering as a separate yearly line. Laboratory identification is a separate line. No public Lebanese rate; bracket from first real bids. As a sanity check only, Tunisia costs replanting a burnt forest hectare at about 9,000 dinars, and the Lebanese state has planted fewer than 3 million of a planned 40 million trees while non-governmental organisations have planted over 600,000 since 2010, so a rate that assumes cheap planting at scale has not been achieved here. Not included: buying the land, aerial spraying, biological control agents that are not commercially available, fencing a whole reserve, and any work inside a declared nature reserve without the reserve committee's own programme.

Release

Nothing up front. 25 per cent at milestone 2, when the damage is measured and mapped. 25 per cent at milestone 3, when the treatment list is approved with a written reason per tree. 25 per cent at milestone 4 or 5, on the clean stump count or the finished planting. 25 per cent held until the repeat survey at milestone 6, and for class D half of that last share is held to the two-season survival count.

Who signs off. The Ministry of Agriculture governs forests and must approve any felling of forest trees, including dead ones. The municipal council decides and the mayor signs. Inside a declared nature reserve the Ministry of Environment and the reserve committee approve instead, and chemical pesticides are not permitted there, which is why Tannourine moved to native microorganisms. Private landowners consent for their own plots. The Lebanese Agricultural Research Institute or an accredited laboratory makes the identification. The Ministry of Environment is informed where a protected species is affected. The army must be informed on state forest land or in a border area. Moving infested timber may need a plant health movement note from the Ministry of Agriculture.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Treating the symptom without naming the cause. Thin crowns can be drought, a soil pest, a root fungus or a fungus carried by a beetle, and the treatments are different. Felling the wrong trees costs a stand. The laboratory identification letter at milestone 1, which gates the felling list.
  • Healthy trees felled with the sick ones. A felling list padded with good timber is the classic abuse of a sanitary felling contract, and it is invisible once the trees are gone. The reason written on every row at milestone 3, and the numbered stump count at milestone 4.
  • Infested material left on site. Logs and brash with larvae in them are a nursery. Felling them and leaving them in the stand makes the outbreak worse, not better. The load tickets and the 30 day removal rule at milestone 4.
  • A single-species replanting. Replanting one species into a gap made by a pest of that species is planting the next outbreak, and drought-stressed monocultures fail together. The species mix rule and the provenance note at milestone 5.
  • Planting counted, survival not. Trees in the ground in March are a photograph. Trees alive in September are a forest. Seedlings planted with no watering agreement die in the first summer. The signed watering agreement at milestone 5 and the two-season survival count at milestone 6.

2Dig, test the drainage, prepare the soil

3Plant

Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Inspect within 15 working days of the request. Planting happens only in the wet season, between November and March, so a request arriving in May is scoped and prepared in summer and planted in the following winter. Digging and soil preparation within 45 days of the service clearances. Planting inside the wet season window. The first summer check at the end of the first dry season. The three year handover after three growing seasons. Watering runs through three summers whatever the contract length, and that obligation is written into the release schedule.

Money

Priced per tree planted with the size band stated for class A and class D, and per square metre planted or reopened for class B and class C. Three years of watering is a separate yearly line, and it is usually a third of the whole cost. Soil improvement and structural soil are separate lines with volumes. No public Lebanese rate; bracket from first real bids. Not included: buying the land, moving buried services, building a car park elsewhere to free the plot, irrigation mains, and any tree that dies because the municipality broke the watering agreement.

Release

Nothing up front. 20 per cent at milestone 2, when the pits drain and the soil is prepared. 30 per cent at milestone 3, planted correctly with the root collars visible. 20 per cent at milestone 4, watered in, protected and signed. 15 per cent at the first summer check at milestone 5. 15 per cent held until the three year handover at milestone 6 passes.

Who signs off. The municipal council decides and must own or control the land. The Ministry of Environment is informed. The Ministry of Public Works and Transport approves work in the verge of a classified road. Electricite du Liban clears overhead and buried cables, the regional water establishment clears water and sewer lines, and Ogero clears telephone lines: all three before any pit is dug. The Ministry of Agriculture agrees the species list and licenses the nursery. The Directorate General of Antiquities must be consulted where the site is historic or within a protected perimeter. Inside a protected area the reserve committee approves. Removing any existing tree, even a poor one, needs the council's written permission and a replacement.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Planting too deep. A trunk buried above the root collar rots at the base and the tree dies slowly over three or four years, long after everyone has been paid. The straight edge photograph across every pit at milestone 3.
  • No watering agreement, or one nobody signed. A young tree in a Lebanese summer needs water for three years. Without a named person and a real water source the planting is a photograph, not a forest. The signed agreement and the water source photograph at milestone 4, and the watering log at milestone 5.
  • The wrong species under a power line. A tree that will reach 15 m under an 8 m cable will be butchered by a line crew within five years, and the money is wasted twice. The looking-up photograph at milestone 0 and the mature height column on the species list at milestone 1.
  • A pit that does not drain. A planting pit dug into compacted rubble is a bucket. The roots sit in water all winter and the tree drowns. The timed fill-and-drain test at milestone 2.
  • One species everywhere. A single-species street loses every tree at once to one pest, and the ficus and eucalyptus planted this way in Lebanese towns are also the ones that lift pavements and drink most. The 30 per cent species cap on the list at milestone 1 and the species count at milestone 3.
Sources
  • Jadaliyya, on Beirut's public space, 2020. About 0.8 square metres of green space per person against the World Health Organization minimum of 9, about 17 designated public gardens of which about 8 are small memorial gardens, most accessible parks between 4,000 and 20,000 square metres, Horsh Beirut at about 300,000 square metres. jadaliyya.com
  • Horsh Beirut, encyclopaedia entry. Over 1,250,000 square metres in 1696, about 800,000 in 1967, 0.3 square kilometres today, closed for about 25 years and reopened on 3 September 2015. en.wikipedia.org
  • Harmony Urban Forest, urban heat and Miyawaki forests in India. Dense mixed native mini-forests on small municipal plots as a heat measure; practitioner evidence rather than a controlled trial. harmonyurbanforest.com
  • Citizen Matters, how Bengaluru is losing its green cover to infrastructure projects. Tree registers, felling permissions and replacement ratios as the tool for protecting existing trees. citizenmatters.in
7 Unregulated pesticide use and farm runoff
Why this one

Template 7: stream buffer strips and farmer training in one agricultural village

The Litani River Authority lists non-degradable pesticides and fertilisers among the four main sources polluting the river and Lake Qaraoun, alongside sewage, industry and solid waste. About 8,396 hectares along the river are irrigable from it and over 1,000 hectares are irrigated with sewage-contaminated water in summer, so what is sprayed on a Bekaa field comes back in the water and in the crop.

Step 1 · Classify

4 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Class A: use survey and empty container collectionNobody knows what is being sprayed, at what rate, or where the empty containers go.A confidential farmer survey, a count of products in use against the registered list, a container collection round, and safe storage of what is collected.farm surveyed, then container collected
Class B: buffer strips along the watercourseFields run to the edge of a stream, canal or river with nothing between the crop and the water.Agree a no-spray, no-fertiliser strip with each landowner, mark it on the ground, plant it with grass and shrubs, and maintain it for two seasons.m of bank, by strip width
Class C: integrated pest management training and demonstration plotsFarmers spray on a calendar rather than on a count and want a way to spray less without losing the crop.Season-long training, pest scouting and trapping, treatment thresholds, side-by-side demonstration plots, and a yield and cost comparison.farmer trained, then demonstration plot
Class D: residue and water monitoringThe village needs numbers for the water, the soil or the crop rather than a practice change alone.Fixed sampling points upstream and downstream, seasonal sampling to an accredited laboratory for the products the survey found, and a published results sheet.sample analysed

#MilestoneEvidence the expert uploadsPass mark the verifier checks
0Scope and class

Get the council decision. Write to the Ministry of Agriculture, which registers pesticides, and inside the basin to the Litani River Authority. Agree with the farmers in writing how their answers will be used, because a survey that can be used to fine them will get lies.		Council decision number and date. No individual farmer is named in any output. Every metre of buffer strip has a signed landowner consent before it is marked.

Visit each farm. Photograph the labels on the containers in the store. Record the product, the active ingredient, the rate used, how often, on what crop, and the protective equipment worn. Agree in writing that nothing is sprayed or fertilised inside it.		GPS pin at each marker. Tape measure photo of the strip width at each marker. Photo along the bank before and after. Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Inspect within 15 working days of the request. The survey at milestone 2 runs in the spraying season, because an empty store in January tells you nothing. Buffer strips are marked before the growing season starts and planted in the wet season. Training runs across a full growing season and cannot be compressed into a week. Container collection happens at least twice: once at the start and once at season end. Class D sampling covers at least one spraying period and one wet period. Then the season-end comparison.

Money

Priced per farm surveyed and per container collected for class A, per metre of bank by strip width for class B, per farmer trained and per demonstration plot for class C, and per sample analysed for class D. Laboratory residue analysis is a separate line quoted per active ingredient per sample, and it is the most expensive part: testing for everything is not affordable, so the survey at milestone 2 decides the list. Compensation for the cropped area lost to a buffer strip is a separate line agreed per landowner. No public Lebanese rate; bracket from first real bids. Not included: buying land for the strips, replacing a farmer's stock of unregistered product, treating anyone already exposed, and enforcement action against any farmer.

Release

Nothing up front. 20 per cent at milestone 2, when the use survey is delivered with label photographs. 25 per cent at milestone 3 or 4, on the marked and planted strips or the collected and punctured containers with a legal destination. 30 per cent at milestone 5, after a full season of training and paired plots. 25 per cent held until the season-end comparison at milestone 6 passes.

Who signs off. The municipal council decides first. The Ministry of Agriculture registers pesticides, holds the registered product list, licenses sellers and must receive any report of an unregistered or banned product. The Lebanese Agricultural Research Institute advises and can do the identification and the residue work. Inside the Litani basin the Litani River Authority must be informed and should receive the water data. The regional water establishment is informed where a well or spring is inside the scope. The Ministry of Environment covers the watercourse and the disposal route. The Ministry of Public Health is involved where drinking water or a food crop is affected. Empty containers are hazardous waste and need a licensed handler with a written acceptance. Every landowner consents to a strip on their own land.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • A survey that becomes an enforcement list. Farmers answer honestly once. If the first survey gets somebody fined, no survey in that village will ever be honest again, and the data is lost for a decade. The signed confidentiality sheet at milestone 1 and the no-names rule on every published output.
  • Buffer strips ploughed back in. A strip that costs a farmer cropped area and earns nothing will be under the plough by the second season unless it is marked, agreed and compensated. The permanent markers at milestone 3 and the season-end strip photographs at milestone 6.
  • Empty containers reused for water or fuel. An unpunctured pesticide drum becomes a household water container. This is how the worst poisonings happen, and it is prevented by a hole and a hammer. The puncturing photograph and the container count at milestone 4.
  • One workshop instead of a season. Integrated pest management is a habit of counting before spraying. A single day of slides changes nothing, and it is the cheapest way to look like training happened. The six sessions and the attendance-per-farmer rule at milestone 5.
  • Testing for the wrong chemicals. A laboratory panel chosen off the shelf will miss the products actually in the village stores and will come back clean, which is worse than no test. The rule at milestone 5 that the test list comes from the label photographs at milestone 2.

  • PubMed, study on pesticide exposure and agricultural runoff in Costa Rica, 2025. Intensive agrochemical use and its measurement; abstract not retrievable in this pass, so no number is taken from it. pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov
  • Journal of Environmental Studies and Sciences, community water quality monitoring in Costa Rica, 2018. Volunteer monitoring of river quality as the route to municipal action. link.springer.com
8 Coastal and marine pollution
Why this one

Template 8: beach litter survey, clean-up and a clean-beach certificate for one public beach

Lebanon's coast takes the same mix of sewage outfalls, industrial discharge and plastic as the rest of the region, and no Lebanon-specific coastal source turned up in this pass, so the first job on any beach is to produce the missing numbers. Costa Rica's Ecological Blue Flag has done this cheaply since 1996, scoring beaches on nine parameters with seawater microbiology weighted at 35 per cent, and it reached 119 awarded beaches by 2018.

Step 1 · Classify

4 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Class A: litter survey onlyThe municipality wants to know what is on the beach, how much and where it comes from, before spending anything.A fixed 100 m survey transect, item-by-item counting by category, four seasonal rounds, and a source judgement for each category.survey round per 100 m transect
Class B: survey plus bathing water samplingPeople swim there and nobody has tested the water, or a sewer outfall discharges within sight of the beach.Everything in class A plus fixed sampling points sampled through the bathing season for faecal indicator bacteria at an accredited laboratory, with the results posted at the beach.sample analysed
Class C: clean-up and source controlThe survey shows where the litter comes in: a wadi mouth, a drain, a roadside, a dump upstream.Everything in class A plus organised clean-up days, bins and a servicing round, a litter trap or screen at the named entry point, and a repeat survey.clean-up day, then m of shoreline cleared
Class D: clean-beach certificateSurvey, sampling and clean-up are all running and the municipality wants a public standard to hold itself to.A written local standard on the Blue Flag model, a scoring sheet, an inspection round, signage, a named committee, and annual renewal.beach certified per year
Step 2 · The milestones

7 milestones, each with the proof it needs and the check it must pass

#MilestoneEvidence the expert uploadsPass mark the verifier checks
0Scope and class
Walk the beach end to end. Measure its length and width. Mark a 100 m survey transect on a representative stretch, away from the single dirtiest corner and away from the single cleanest. Find every drain, wadi and pipe that reaches the shore. Choose the class.		GPS pin at both ends of the transect and at the beach ends. A photo along the transect from each end with the marker in frame. Beach length and mean width in metres. GPS pin and photo of every drain, wadi and pipe reaching the shore. A note of who owns the beach and whether entry is free.The transect is 100 m, marked with something that will still be there next season, and pinned at both ends. Every drain, wadi and pipe has a pin and a photograph. Beach length and width are recorded. A class is chosen. Whether the beach is public or private and whether entry is free is written down.
1Permission, laboratory and safety
Get the council decision. The shoreline is maritime public domain, so write to the Ministry of Public Works and Transport. Write to the Ministry of Environment. For class B, appoint an accredited laboratory. Brief the team on sharps, needles and broken glass.		Council decision number and date. Copies of the letters to the ministries with stamps or replies. The laboratory accreditation certificate and its price list. Signed safety briefing sheet with a sharps procedure and a named first aider. This is the gate for the final release.
Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Inspect within 15 working days of the request. The first survey round happens in the season the request arrives and the remaining three follow at least 60 days apart, so class A takes a full year by design. Class B sampling runs through the bathing season. Clean-up days in class C run within 45 days of the source table at milestone 4, and the trap is fitted before the first winter, because winter storms are when the wadi delivers most of the year's plastic. The repeat survey is a year after the first round, in the same season.

Money

Priced per survey round on a 100 m transect for class A, per sample analysed for class B, per clean-up day and per metre of shoreline cleared for class C, and per beach certified per year for class D. Laboratory fees, haulage of collected waste per tonne-kilometre, and the trap or screen are separate lines. No public Lebanese rate; bracket from first real bids. Volunteer labour on clean-up days is not billed as labour, and any bid that bills it should be rejected. Not included: building or diverting a sewer outfall, dredging, sand replacement, lifeguards, and enforcement against any upstream municipality.

Release

Nothing up front. 25 per cent after the second survey round at milestone 2, which proves the method is repeatable rather than a one-off. 25 per cent at milestone 4, when the sources are named with the arithmetic shown. 25 per cent at milestone 5, on the fitted trap, the serviced bins and the posted board. 25 per cent held until the repeat survey and, for class D, the scored certificate at milestone 6.

Who signs off. The municipal council decides first. The shoreline is maritime public domain, so the Ministry of Public Works and Transport, through its land and maritime transport directorate, must approve anything fixed on the beach, including bins, signs and traps. The Ministry of Environment is informed and covers the discharge side. The Ministry of Public Health covers bathing water and must be told of any failing result. The regional water establishment is informed where a sewer outfall is involved. The army must be informed where coastal access is controlled or the beach is near a military area. The receiving licensed site must accept the collected waste in writing. Where the beach is privately operated, the operator's written agreement is needed as well as the council's.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Surveying the dirtiest patch. A transect chosen for effect gives a number that cannot be compared with next year or with anywhere else, and the improvement is then manufactured by moving the transect. The permanent transect markers pinned at both ends at milestone 0, and the same-transect rule at milestone 6.
  • Clean-up without source control. A beach cleaned by volunteers in May is covered again after the first winter storm if the wadi that delivers the plastic is untouched. It is the most photographed and least useful form of this work. The source table at milestone 4, which gates the clean-up money at milestone 5.
  • One averaged bathing water number. Averaging a clean end of the beach with the water next to an outfall produces a pass, and people swim next to the outfall. The per-point, per-date reporting rule at milestone 3.
  • Sampling only in settled weather. The day after heavy rain is when a coastal town's sewage reaches the sea. A season of calm-day samples is a season of good news that does not describe the risk. The rainfall note and the after-rain sampling requirement at milestone 3.
  • A certificate awarded to a beach that failed. A clean-beach label that is given out anyway is worth less than nothing, because it tells swimmers the water is safe when it is not. The 90 per cent scoring threshold and the publish-the-failures rule at milestone 6.
Sources
  • Costa Rica Tourism Board, Ecological Blue Flag programme, from 1996.   • PLOS ONE, coastal pollution in the Gulf of Gabes, Tunisia, 2018. Transect design with stations from 400 m offshore, seafloor measurement of dissolved oxygen, pH and temperature; dissolved oxygen 6.0 to 7.8 mg per litre and pH down to 5.7 at the polluted transect against 8.0 to 9.1 mg per litre and pH 7.7 to 7.9 at the reference; loss of Posidonia oceanica as the indicator. journals.plos.org
  • World Bank, ex-post review of Rwanda's 2008 single-use plastic bag ban. Near eradication of polythene bags and better urban waste collection after a ban backed by fines. documents1.worldbank.org
  • UNDP, Umuganda: Rwanda's audacity of hope to end plastic pollution. The monthly community work day with projects chosen locally, valued at an estimated 200 million US dollars. undp.org
9 Air pollution from traffic and biomass burning
Why this one

Template 9: one year of air monitoring and a car-free street pilot

Waste-burning smoke and an old vehicle fleet make this a health problem in Lebanese towns, and no Lebanese air quality source turned up in this pass, which is the point: a town cannot argue about air it has never measured. Kigali's measured particle levels ran about ten times the World Health Organization annual guideline of 5 micrograms per cubic metre, and its monthly car-free days cut pollution by about 15 per cent and saved an estimated 200 disability-adjusted life years a year.

Step 1 · Classify

4 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Class A: fixed monitoringThe town has no air data at all and needs a baseline before it argues with anyone.Low-cost particle monitors at a roadside point, a receptor such as a school or clinic, and a background point, running a full year with a reference check.monitor-month
Class B: monitoring plus a source apportionment walkThe baseline is running and the town needs to know how much comes from traffic, from generators, from burning and from dust.Everything in class A plus a generator and chimney census, a traffic count, a burning log, and a written share estimate with its method.source point surveyed
Class C: car-free street or car-free day pilotThere is a street where the measurement says the exposure is worst and walking is possible.A closure plan agreed with traffic police, diversions, signage, marshals, monitors inside and outside the closure, and a before-and-after comparison.closure-day
Class D: school exposure and the school runA school sits on a busy road or downwind of burning and parents want it dealt with first.Monitors in the playground and at the gate, a survey of how children arrive, a drop-off relocation or a timed street closure at the gate, and a repeat measurement.school treated
Step 2 · The milestones

7 milestones, each with the proof it needs and the check it must pass

#MilestoneEvidence the expert uploadsPass mark the verifier checks
0Scope and class
Choose the monitoring points: one at the worst roadside, one at a receptor such as a school or clinic, and one background point away from roads and burning. Note what is around each: traffic, generators, chimneys, dumps, bakeries, quarries. Choose the class.		GPS pin, a photo in four directions, and a written description of what is within 100 m of each point. Photo of the power supply and the mounting position for each monitor. A note of the prevailing wind. Photo of each proposed monitor height against a measuring pole.Three points at least: roadside, receptor and background. Each has power that will not be switched off, and a mounting height between 2 and 4 m above the ground, clear of walls and of direct exhaust (to confirm). What is within 100 m of each point is written down. A class is chosen.
1Permission, siting and the reference check
Get the council decision. Write to the Ministry of Environment, which holds the national air monitoring network. Get written permission from every building owner hosting a monitor. Co-locate the monitors side by side for at least a week before deployment and record how they compare.		Council decision number and date. Copy of the letter to the Ministry of Environment with the stamp or reply. Written permission per host building, and for a school the school's own written permission. Photo of all monitors co-located on one mount. The co-location data as a plain table.There is a named authority. Every host has signed. Co-location ran at least seven days and the monitors agree within 20 per cent of each other, or the offsets are written down and applied to the data (to confirm). No monitor is deployed before the co-location is on file, because without it the differences between points are meaningless.
2Run the year
Deploy and run for twelve months. Check each monitor monthly: clean the inlet, photograph it, confirm it is still reporting. Publish a monthly one-page summary at the municipality and at the school.		The raw data files, hourly, per monitor. Monthly maintenance photos of each monitor with the date visible. A data completeness table per monitor per month. The monthly one-page summaries with the posting photograph.At least 80 per cent of hours captured per monitor per month (to confirm). No gap longer than 14 days. Data reported as 24-hour averages and as an annual average against the World Health Organization 2021 annual PM2.5 guideline of 5 micrograms per cubic metre. Summaries posted every month, including the bad months.
3Count the sources
For class B. Walk the catchment and count what is burning: diesel generators, bakery and restaurant chimneys, open burning sites, dusty roads and yards. Count traffic on the worst street across a weekday and a weekend. Log every burning event.		GPS pin and photo of every generator, chimney and burning site, with its size or capacity where it can be read. Traffic count sheets by hour and by vehicle type, with a photo of the counting position. The burning log with time-stamped photographs. A dust note for unpaved surfaces.Traffic counted for at least 12 hours on a weekday and 12 on a weekend day, by vehicle type, including motorcycles counted separately (to confirm). Every generator within the catchment has a pin and a photograph. The burning log uses the same form as the burning template. The share estimate shows its method and says plainly how uncertain it is.
4Plan the pilot with the people who live there
For class C and class D. Design the closure: which street, which hours, which days, where the diversion goes, where deliveries and emergency vehicles go. Meet the shopkeepers and residents before anything is announced. Agree with the traffic police.		A plan drawing showing the closure, the diversions, the signs and the marshal positions. Attendance sheets from the meetings with shopkeepers and residents, signed. The written agreement from the traffic police naming the officer. The announcement as it was posted, in Arabic.Every shop and every residence on the closed street has been met or has a written note of the attempt. Emergency access is kept open and is drawn on the plan. The traffic police officer is named. The announcement went up at least 14 days before the first closure (to confirm).
5Run the pilot and measure it
Run the closure days with marshals and signs. Keep one monitor inside the closure and one outside it as a control. Count how many people walk through and count what happens to the diverted traffic.		Photos of the signs, the marshals and the closed street on each day. The monitor data for the closure hours from inside and outside. Pedestrian counts by hour. A traffic count on the diversion route. Written notes from shopkeepers on takings, collected the same way each time. Incident log.At least four closure days, so one good day does not carry the result (to confirm). The control monitor runs the whole time, because without it the weather explains the result. The diversion route is counted, so the pollution is shown to have gone down and not just moved. No emergency vehicle was blocked, and the incident log is complete.
6Compare, publish and hand over
Compare the closure hours with the same hours on matched non-closure days at the same monitor, and against the control. Publish the year of data and the pilot result. Hand the monitors and the routine to the municipality.		The comparison table: closure hours against matched control hours, with the weather noted for each. The full year of data as a plain file. The published summary. Signed handover note naming the municipal officer who now holds the monitors, with the maintenance routine and the calibration schedule.The comparison uses matched hours and matched weather, not a raw before and after. A measured fall inside the closure that is larger than the change at the control point on the same day, reported with its size (to confirm; Kigali's monthly car-free days measured about 15 per cent). The full year of data is published, including any month that failed the 80 per cent capture rule, marked as such. The handover note is signed. This is the gate for the final release.
Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Inspect within 15 working days of the request. Co-location for at least seven days before deployment. Monitoring runs twelve months, because a Lebanese town's air in February and in August are two different places and a three-month study will be argued away. The source count in class B happens in both a hot month and a cold month. The pilot in class C runs after at least six months of baseline, never before, and the announcement goes up at least 14 days ahead. Then the comparison and the handover.

Money

Priced per monitor-month for class A, per source point surveyed for class B, per closure-day for class C, and per school treated for class D. The monitors themselves are a separate capital line and they stay with the municipality at handover. Reference co-location, if it is done against a ministry or university reference instrument, is a separate line. No public Lebanese rate; bracket from first real bids. Not included: vehicle emissions testing, scrapping old vehicles, repaving dusty roads, buying electric motorcycles, and any permanent street closure, which needs its own design and its own consent.

Release

Nothing up front. 15 per cent at milestone 1, when co-location is done and the hosts have signed. 35 per cent at milestone 2, after twelve months at the capture rate with every monthly summary posted. 20 per cent at milestone 4, on the agreed pilot plan with the shopkeepers met and the police named. 15 per cent at milestone 5, after the closure days with a working control. 15 per cent held until the comparison, the publication and the handover at milestone 6.

Who signs off. The municipal council decides first. The Ministry of Environment holds the national air quality network and must be informed, and should receive the data. Every building hosting a monitor gives written permission, and a school gives its own. Closing a street needs the Internal Security Forces traffic police and, on a classified road, the Ministry of Public Works and Transport. The Ministry of Interior and Municipalities covers the council decision. The Ministry of Public Health is informed where a school or clinic exceeds guideline levels. Electricite du Liban is informed where a monitor takes power from a public supply. Counting or photographing generators on private property needs the owner's consent.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • No background monitor. A single roadside number cannot tell a busy street from a dusty week or a regional sandstorm, so every result can be argued away. The three-point requirement at milestone 0 and the control monitor at milestone 5.
  • Monitors deployed without co-location. Cheap sensors differ from each other by more than the difference between a clean street and a dirty one. Without the side-by-side week, the map of the town is noise. The seven-day co-location and the 20 per cent agreement check at milestone 1.
  • A short study over one season. Three summer months in a Lebanese town will miss generator smoke in the dark months and burning in the dry ones, and the town gets a reassuring number it did not earn. The twelve-month rule and the monthly capture table at milestone 2.
  • Traffic pushed onto a poorer street. A closure that simply moves the exhaust to the next street has improved nothing and has moved the harm to people with less say. The diversion route count at milestone 5.
  • A pilot announced without the shopkeepers. Closures that surprise the traders on the street are reversed within a month and poison the next attempt, whatever the air data says. The signed attendance sheets and the 14 day notice at milestone 4.
Sources
  • International Growth Centre, The case for clean air in Kigali, Kalisa and others, August 2022. World Health Organization 2021 annual PM2.5 guideline of 5 micrograms per cubic metre, Kigali ambient PM2.5 about ten times that in 2017 to 2018, car-free days cutting pollution about 15 per cent and saving about 200 disability-adjusted life years a year, vehicle numbers up fourfold from 1999 to 2019 with over 70 per cent second-hand and older than ten years. theigc.org
  • UNDP Rwanda, government and UNDP launch retrofit electric motorcycles project. Car-free days and retrofitting petrol motorcycles as a municipal-scale measure. undp.org
  • Connexion France, France's low emission zones: the rules and whether they have made a difference. Low emission zones as the stricter version of a car-free street, and the evidence on whether they work. connexionfrance.com
  • Human Rights Watch, the health risks of burning waste in Lebanon, December 2017. More than 150 dumps burnt at least weekly, PM10, PM2.5 and dioxins as the pollutants, and the regional burn counts that make biomass smoke a Lebanese air quality issue. hrw.org
10 Soil erosion, drought and land degradation
Why this one

Template 10: erosion control on one degraded or burnt slope

Lebanon's terraced hills and post-fire slopes lose soil the way Rwanda's highlands do, and Rwanda has measured it: about 25 tonnes of topsoil per hectare per year on average, 27 million tonnes a year nationally, with only 26 per cent of the land at risk protected. A burnt or abandoned Lebanese slope loses its soil in the first winter after the fire, and once it is gone nothing that is planted there will hold.

Step 1 · Classify

4 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Class A: emergency post-fire slope treatmentA slope has burnt in the last few months and the first heavy rain has not yet fallen.Contour log or brush barriers from the burnt material, mulch on the bare ground, a cut-off drain above the slope, and nothing that needs machinery.m2 treated
Class B: repair existing terracesStone terraces exist but the walls are breached, the beds are tipping outward and gullies are cutting through them.Rebuild the breached walls with the stone that is there, re-level the beds to fall inward, cut grassed waterways where the water crosses, replant the risers.m of wall rebuilt
Class C: new contour measures on a cultivated slopeThe slope is farmed, has no terraces, and is losing soil down the rows.Survey the contours, build contour bunds or progressive terraces, plant grass strips and hedgerows on the banks, add trees on the Rwandan agroforestry model.m of contour bank
Class D: close one gullyA single gully is cutting back into the slope and taking land, a road or a house with it.Divert the water that feeds it, build check structures along it, shape and revegetate the head, plant the bed with bamboo or deep-rooted species, and monitor it for two winters.m of gully treated
Step 2 · The milestones

7 milestones, each with the proof it needs and the check it must pass

#MilestoneEvidence the expert uploadsPass mark the verifier checks
0Scope and class
Walk the slope from bottom to top. Measure the slope angle at several points. Measure the length of the slope and the area. Find where the water comes from above and where it goes below. Dig a pit and measure how much soil is left over the rock. Choose the class.		GPS pin at the top, bottom and both sides. Photos from the bottom looking up, from the top looking down, and from across the valley. Clinometer or angle app reading photographed at no fewer than five points. Photo of a ruler in the soil pit showing depth to rock. Photos and pins of every gully, rill and slip, with a tape measure in each.Slope angle measured at five or more points with the readings visible in photographs. Soil depth to rock recorded. Every gully and slip has a pin, a photograph and a measured width and depth. What is below the slope, a road, a house, a field or a watercourse, is recorded with its distance. A class is chosen. Class D needs an engineer who has stood in the gully.
1Permission, owners and the catchment above
Get the council decision. Write to the Ministry of Agriculture, which runs terracing support through the Green Plan, and to the Ministry of Environment. Get written consent from every landowner on the slope and, crucially, from whoever controls the land above it that sends the water down.		Council decision number and date. Copies of the letters with stamps or replies. Signed consent per plot with the owner's name and phone number, including the plots above the treated area. Cadastral extract or map showing the catchment above.There is a named authority. Every plot on the slope has consent. The catchment above the slope is mapped and its owners are identified, because treating a slope while the water above it is untouched is money thrown away. No earthworks start before all consents are on file.
2Cut off the water above
Build the cut-off drain or diversion along the top of the treated area so clean water from above is taken to a safe outlet, not over the work. Line or grass the outlet so it does not become the next gully.		GPS track along the finished drain. Photo with a tape measure across the drain showing width and depth. Photo of the outlet and of where the water goes after it. Photo of water actually running in the drain, from a hose if there is no rain.The drain runs the full width of the treated area with no gap. It falls continuously to the outlet with no flat or reversed section, proven by water running in the photograph. The outlet discharges onto stable ground, rock, grass or an existing watercourse, never onto bare soil or onto somebody else's field.
3Build the measure
For class A, lay contour log or brush barriers and spread mulch. For class B, rebuild the breached walls with the stone that is there. For class C, set out the contours and build the banks. For class D, build the check structures from the bottom of the gully upwards.		Photos along the whole treated area before and after, from fixed marked spots. Photo of a spirit level or a water level on the contour line. Tape measure photo of bank height and spacing, or wall height, or check structure height and spacing. Delivery notes for any imported material. A count of structures built.Structures follow the contour, proven by a level in the photograph, not the line of the old rows. Spacing set by slope: closer on steeper ground, and the spacing rule used is written down with the engineer's name (to confirm). For class B the rebuilt bed falls inward, towards the hill, so water is held and not shed. For class D the checks are built from the bottom up, keyed into both sides of the gully, with the crest lower in the middle so water crosses at the centre and not at the edges (to confirm).
4Cover the bare ground
Get something growing or lying on every square metre of bare soil. Mulch, grass seed, grass strips on the banks, hedgerows, and trees where the class calls for them. For class D, plant the gully bed with bamboo or deep-rooted species.		Delivery notes for seed, mulch and plants with the species named and the provenance where it matters. Photos of the covered ground from the fixed spots. A marked and pinned sample square metre photographed for the cover estimate. Species list with counts.No bare soil larger than one square metre anywhere on the treated area at the end of the work (to confirm). Mulch at least 5 cm deep where it is used (to confirm). Grass strips continuous along every bank. Species are native or long-established local varieties, and the mix follows the Rwandan pattern of grass on the bank, hedgerows along the contour and agroforestry through the field.
5Grassed waterway and handover
Build the grassed waterway where water has to cross the treated slope, so there is one designed place for it to go. Hand the slope and a one-page maintenance routine to the landowners and the municipality.		Photo along the finished waterway with a tape measure across it. Photo of the grass established in it, or of the matting where grass has not grown yet. Photo of where it joins the drain below. The signed handover note naming the person who clears the drains before each winter. The one-page routine, in Arabic, photographed where it is posted.There is at least one designed waterway wherever the survey at milestone 0 showed water crossing the slope. It is grassed or matted, not bare. The handover note names a person and the date they must clear the drains by, which is before the first rains and not after them. Terraces built without a waterway are the commonest cause of the terraces failing, which is why this is its own milestone.
6First winter check and second winter check
Come back after the first full winter and look at the same things. Measure any new gully. Check every structure. Count what is growing. Come back again after the second winter.		Photos from the same marked spots, dated after the first rains. Tape measure photo of any new rill, gully or breach. Photo of each check structure and of the cut-off drain. A cover count in the marked sample squares. Photo of sediment caught behind the structures, with a depth measurement. The second winter set, a year later.No breach in any rebuilt wall or contour bank. No new gully deeper than 15 cm on the treated area (to confirm). Ground cover on at least 70 per cent of the treated area after the first winter and at least 80 per cent after the second (to confirm). Sediment held behind the check structures, measured and photographed, which is the positive proof the work is doing its job. The cut-off drain is clear. This is the gate for the final release.
Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Inspect within 10 working days of the request, and within 5 for a burnt slope, because class A only works before the first heavy rain. Class A finished within 30 days of the fire being out, whatever else is in the queue. Class B and class C built in the dry months and planted at the start of the wet season, finished before the first rains. Class D within 120 days, and the checks built from the bottom up in one continuous run rather than left half finished over a winter. Then the first winter check and the second winter check.

Money

Priced per square metre treated for class A, per metre of wall rebuilt for class B, per metre of contour bank for class C, and per metre of gully treated for class D. Seed, mulch and plants are a separate line with volumes and species. Stone brought in from off site is a separate line, and a bid that imports stone for a terrace repair on a stony hillside should be questioned. No public Lebanese rate; bracket from first real bids. As a sanity check only, Rwanda costs protecting about 60 per cent of its land at risk with bench terraces, contour bank terraces and agroforestry at about 323 billion Rwandan francs over eight years, against topsoil losses of about 25 tonnes per hectare per year. Not included: buying land, compensating a landowner for the strip lost to a bank, road drainage above the slope, retaining walls designed to hold a building, and any structural work that needs a stamped engineering design beyond the erosion measures themselves.

Release

Nothing up front. 20 per cent at milestone 2, when the cut-off drain is built and water runs in it. 30 per cent at milestone 3, when the structures are built on the contour. 20 per cent at milestone 4 and 5, on the ground cover and the grassed waterway. 20 per cent at the first winter check. 10 per cent held until the second winter check at milestone 6 passes.

Who signs off. The municipal council decides first. The Ministry of Agriculture supports terracing and agroforestry through the Green Plan and approves the species list; its consent matters where a subsidy is involved. The Ministry of Energy and Water is informed where the outlet reaches a watercourse, and the regional water establishment where a spring or well is below the slope. The Ministry of Environment is informed, and inside a reserve the reserve committee approves. The Order of Engineers and Architects stamps the design for class D and for any structure retaining a road or a building. The Ministry of Public Works and Transport is involved where a classified road sits above or below the slope. Every landowner on the slope consents, and so does whoever controls the catchment above it. On state forest land or in a border area the army must be informed.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Treating the slope and ignoring the water above it. Every measure on the slope is sized for the rain that falls on the slope. Water arriving from a road, a roof or a field above will overtop all of it in the first storm. The catchment mapping at milestone 1 and the cut-off drain with water running in it at milestone 2.
  • Banks built off the contour. A bank that drifts a few degrees off the contour concentrates the water at its low end and cuts a gully exactly where the structure was supposed to stop one. The level in the photograph along every line at milestone 3.
  • Terraces with no waterway. Water has to cross the slope somewhere. If nobody designs the place, it chooses one, and it takes a terrace wall with it. Rwanda names this as the failure that destroys bench terraces. Milestone 5, which is a milestone of its own for exactly this reason.
  • Bare soil left over winter. Structures slow water down; plants and mulch are what stop the soil moving in the first place. A beautifully built terrace with bare beds still loses its topsoil. The no-bare-patch rule and the sample square counts at milestone 4 and milestone 6.
  • Gully checks built from the top down. Checks built downwards are undercut one by one as the water drops off the end of each, and the whole run fails in sequence in one storm. The dated construction photographs at milestone 3 and the keyed-in check at milestone 6.

  • World Bank, Tunisia: major push to strengthen water security and resilience, April 2026. Catchment restoration and drought resilience as a regional programme. worldbank.org
  • VigiEau, France. One national site showing each commune's current water-use restrictions, as the model for publishing drought limits in a way people can check. vigieau.gouv.fr
  • Nawaat, Tunisian forests going up in flames, August 2024. Burnt area rising from about 2,400 hectares in 2012 to 25,808 hectares in 2021, and about twenty years to recover, which is the supply of bare slopes this template treats. nawaat.org

Public Land & Pavements: 10 templates. Open one to read it.

1 Blocked sidewalks
Why this one

Template 1: clear a walking route

Beirut pavements are taken by parked cars, generators, cafe seating, rubbish and concrete blocks, so people walk in the traffic lane and a wheelchair often cannot pass at all. This is the cheapest public land job a municipality can commission, and it is measurable: the width left for walking, in metres, before and after.

Step 1 · Classify

4 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Soft clearingThe obstacles can be picked up and moved: chairs, tables, shop displays, bins, sandbags.Written notice to each occupier, removal, storage of what is taken, before and after photographs from fixed spots, a painted or studded line showing where goods may not go.linear metre of route
Bollard lineCars and motorcycles mount the kerb and park on the pavement.Steel or concrete bollards set in a concrete foundation, kerb repair where it is broken, gaps left at crossings and doorways.linear metre of route
Fixed obstacle relocationA generator, a cabinet, a pole or a transformer stands in the middle of the walking route.Survey of the obstacle and its services, agreement with the owner, new base, relocation, making good the pavement.each obstacle
Route rebuildThere is no usable pavement left, or it is narrower than 1.2 m for most of its length.New kerb line, new surface, falls set to drain, dropped kerbs at crossings, tactile paving at crossings.m2
Step 2 · The milestones

6 milestones, each with the proof it needs and the check it must pass

#MilestoneEvidence the expert uploadsPass mark the verifier checks
0Scope and class
Walk the route from end to end. Measure the clear width at every point where something narrows it. Count and photograph every obstacle. Pin both ends on GPS. Choose the class.		Photos with a tape measure in frame at the narrowest point. A numbered obstacle list with a photo and GPS pin for each. Route length in metres. Class chosen.The narrowest clear width is recorded and is under 1.2 m at one or more points, or the route does not qualify. Route length, obstacle count and class are all written down.
1Notice and permission
Get the municipal decision naming the street. Serve a dated written notice on every occupier whose goods or vehicle must move, and give them at least 14 days. Tell the traffic police branch the date.		Signed municipal decision. Photo of each notice posted or a signed receipt. The occupier list from milestone 0 ticked off. The date the traffic branch was told.A named authority signed the decision. Every occupier on the milestone 0 list has a dated notice. At least 14 days between notice and clearing.
2Clearing
Remove what is in the walking route. Store anything taken and label it with the pitch it came from. Photograph from the same spots as milestone 0.		Before and after photo pairs from the same fixed spots. Storage list with labels. Photo of the stored items.Every before photo has an after photo from the same spot. Nothing from the obstacle list is left inside the walking route. Items taken are stored and listed, not thrown away.
3Protection installed
Set bollards or repair the kerb so vehicles cannot come back. Leave gaps at crossings, doorways and bus stops.		Photo of each bollard hole before concrete, with a rod showing depth. Photo of the finished line with a tape measure between two bollards. Delivery note for the bollards.Spacing between bollards 1.2 to 1.5 m, so a car cannot get through and a wheelchair can. Bollard height 0.9 to 1.0 m so a driver sees it. Foundation at least 0.4 m deep (to confirm against Lebanese practice). A bollard cannot be rocked by hand.
4Clear width test
Walk the whole route pushing a frame or a wheelchair 1.2 m wide. Film it in one take. Measure the cross-fall at three points.		One unbroken video from one end to the other. Three cross-fall readings with a digital level, photographed. Tape measure photos at the three narrowest points.1.2 m clear for the whole length, 0.9 m absolute minimum at any single pinch point. Cross-fall no more than 2.5 per cent. The video has no cuts and nobody lifts the chair.
5Ninety-day check and handover
Come back after three months of normal trading and normal parking. Repeat the walk and the photos from the same spots.		Photo set from the same fixed spots, dated 90 days or more after milestone 4. A repeat of the 1.2 m walk video. A count of anything that has come back.1.2 m clear on at least 90 per cent of the route length. No bollard missing or loose. This is the gate for the final release.
Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Inspect within 10 working days of the report. Serve notices and allow at least 14 days. Do the clearing and the protection within 30 days of the notice period ending. Then the 90-day check. Warranty 12 months on bollards and kerb repairs: a bollard knocked out by a vehicle inside that year is replaced free once, after that the municipality pays.

Money

Priced per linear metre of route for clearing and bollards, per obstacle for a relocation, and per m2 for a rebuild. No public Lebanese rate exists for this work; bracket it from the first three real bids, as the pothole template does. Not included: fines, towing, compensation to traders, electrical work to move a generator, and any enforcement after handover.

Release

Nothing up front. 20 per cent at milestone 2 when the route is cleared and the before and after pairs match. 50 per cent at milestone 4 when the 1.2 m walk passes. 30 per cent held until the 90-day check at milestone 5.

Who signs off. The municipality decides and signs; municipal powers over pavements and public roads sit under the Municipal Act, Decree-Law 118/1977 (article number to confirm). The Ministry of Public Works and Transport must agree if the street is a classified road. The Internal Security Forces traffic branch should be told before any clearing. Electricite du Liban or the private generator owner must agree before anything touching a pole, cabinet or generator is moved. Where vendors are affected, pair this with Template 9 before clearing, not after.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Everything comes back. A clearing with no bollards, no painted line and no permit scheme lasts a few weeks. The pavement is back to how it was before the invoice is paid. Milestone 5, the 90-day check, and the 30 per cent held against it.
  • Bollards too far apart. At more than about 1.5 m a small car or a pick-up drives between two bollards and parks as before. Milestone 3, the tape measure photo between two bollards.
  • The bollard line blocks the crossing. A continuous line with no gap at the dropped kerb traps a wheelchair on the pavement, which is worse than the parked car. Milestone 4, the 1.2 m walk has to reach the crossing and get off the kerb.
  • Measured at the widest point. Quoting the width of the pavement instead of the width left clear makes a blocked route look fine on paper. Milestone 0 asks for the narrowest clear width, with a tape in the photo.
  • Vendors cleared with nowhere to go. Taking away someone's living without a replacement pitch turns the job into a fight and the stalls return. Milestone 1, the occupier list, and the requirement to run Template 9 first where vendors are on the list.
