2 Green-space deficit
Why this one

Template 2: pocket park on a public plot

Beirut has about 0.8 m2 of green space per person against a World Health Organization minimum of 9 m2. Amman, with the same problem, has about 2.5 m2 per person across 142 parks. A plot of 200 m2 that is already municipal is the fastest way to move that number, and it is small enough that one expert firm can finish it in a season.

Step 1 · Classify

4 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Micro-forestA bare plot of 100 m2 or more, dense planting wanted, low upkeep after the first two years.Deep soil preparation, dense native planting in the Miyawaki style, mulch, drip irrigation, two years of watering and weeding, then it is left alone.m2
Pocket parkA residual plot under 1,000 m2 in a dense area where people need somewhere to sit.Paths, benches, shade trees, lighting, a tap, a bin, a sign with hours and a maintenance phone number.m2
Greened stripA traffic island, a roadside strip or a wide verge that is paved or bare.Breaking the hardstanding, soil, drought-tolerant planting, drip line, kerb protection so cars stay off.m2
Shared municipal plotA fenced working site, such as a water tank, a reservoir yard or a school yard, that could open to the public outside working hours.Agreement with the operator, a separated public area, safe fencing, paths, planting, published hours, a keyholder. Modelled on Medellin's water-tank parks.m2
Step 2 · The milestones

7 milestones, each with the proof it needs and the check it must pass

#MilestoneEvidence the expert uploadsPass mark the verifier checks
0Scope, title check and class
Confirm the plot really is public. Pull the cadastral number and the area. Measure the plot on the ground. Dig two small test pits and look at the soil. Choose the class.		Cadastral extract with the plot number and area. GPS polygon of the corners. Photos of the two test pits with a rod showing depth. Photos of every boundary. Class chosen.The plot is municipal land or public domain, shown on paper, not assumed. Area recorded and at least 100 m2. Soil depth and what is under it written down. If the pits are full of builder's rubble, that is stated and the ground works price changes.
1Residents' design session
Hold at least two open sessions with the people who live within a few minutes' walk. Show them a blank plan. Let them choose what goes in it and where the entrance is.		Attendance sheets with names, signatures and phone numbers. Photos of both sessions. The marked-up plan people worked on. The final plan, signed by the municipality and by two residents.Two sessions on different days, at least one outside working hours. At least 20 residents signed in across the two sessions (to confirm against a local rule). The final plan shows at least one thing residents asked for that was not in the first draft.
2Ground works and soil
Clear rubble and rubbish. Break up any hardstanding. Bring in and spread prepared soil and compost. Set the levels so water runs into the planting, not into the street.		Photos of the rubble going out, with a weighbridge or truck count. Photos with a graduated rod pushed into the finished soil. Delivery notes for soil, compost and mulch. A soakage test video: fill a pit with water and time the drop.No builder's rubble left in the planting area. Prepared soil depth at least 0.6 m for a micro-forest, at least 0.4 m for shrubs and grass (to confirm against Lebanese nursery practice). Water in the test pit drops, so the ground drains. Delivery notes match the volume needed for the area.
3Planting
Plant only species on the agreed native and drought-tolerant list. Plant at the agreed spacing. Mulch everything. Take one photo per planting block with a marker showing the block number.		Nursery invoice listing species and counts. Photo grid, one per block, with block numbers. GPS pin for each block. Photo of the mulch depth with a ruler.Every species on the invoice is on the agreed list; anything else is removed. Plant count matches the invoice within 5 per cent. Mulch 7 to 10 cm deep (to confirm). For a micro-forest, planting density as designed, typically 3 plants per m2 (to confirm against the species list used).
4Water, furniture and opening
Lay drip irrigation to every plant. Fit the benches, bins, shade and lighting. Put up a sign with the opening hours and a phone number for maintenance. Open the gate.		Photo of the drip line running, taken while the water is on. Photo of the sign, readable. Night photo showing the lights on. Photo of the water source: tap, tank or meter number.Every planted block has a drip line reaching it, seen running in the photo. The sign shows the hours and a working phone number, tested by the verifier on the day. Paths at least 1.2 m clear so a wheelchair can use them. The gate is open at the published hours.
5Twelve-month survival check
Come back after a full year, including one summer. Count what is alive. Replace the gaps.		Photo grid from the same block positions as milestone 3, dated 12 months or more later. A count of live plants per block. Receipts for any replacements.At least 80 per cent of the planted stock alive at 12 months (to confirm). Gaps replaced at the expert's cost. Drip line still working, shown running.
6Maintenance contract handover
Hand the park over to a named maintainer with a signed contract, a monthly checklist and a budget line in the municipal accounts.		Signed contract with a start date, a duration and a monthly figure. The municipal budget line reference. The monthly checklist. The maintainer's name and phone number on the park sign.The contract runs at least three years and has money behind it in a named budget line. Bogota has 1,601 pocket parks and the lesson from them is that a park without a funded contract goes back to waste ground. The verifier calls the number on the sign and it answers.
Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Survey and title check within 15 working days of the municipality naming the plot. Design sessions within 45 days. Ground works within 90 days. Plant only in the wet season, November to March, so nothing is planted into a Lebanese summer. Twelve-month survival check after one full summer. Maintenance contract for at least three years; Amman's micro-forest programme allows two years of consolidation before a forest is left to itself.

Money

Priced per m2 of plot for ground works and surfacing, plus a per-plant rate from the nursery invoice, plus a fixed price for furniture and the sign, plus a monthly figure for maintenance. No public Lebanese rate exists; bracket it from the first three real bids. For scale only, Amman's Urban Micro-lungs added about 95,000 euro to a 5 million euro programme for three pilot sites. Not included: buying land, a new water connection, night lighting beyond what is on the plan, and any security guard.

Release

Nothing up front. 30 per cent at milestone 3 when planting is done and the invoice matches the count. 40 per cent at milestone 4 when the park is open, watered and lit. 30 per cent held until the 12-month survival check at milestone 5 passes. The maintenance contract at milestone 6 is paid monthly and separately, not from the build money.

Who signs off. The municipality owns the decision and must show the plot is public land. The Directorate General of Urban Planning must be asked if the plot is zoned for something else. The Ministry of Agriculture should agree the species list and any tree planting. The regional water establishment, for example the Beirut and Mount Lebanon Water Establishment, for a water connection or a tank. The Ministry of Environment if the plot is inside or next to a protected area. For a shared municipal plot, the operator of the site signs too.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Thirsty exotic planting. Lawn and imported ornamentals need water all summer. When the water bill arrives the park is abandoned. Native and drought-tolerant stock survives on drip and rain. Milestone 3, every species checked against the agreed list.
  • Planting into rubble. Soil spread 15 cm deep over builder's waste looks fine on handover day and kills the planting in the second year. Milestone 2, the graduated rod photo and the soakage test.
  • No maintenance contract. A park with no funded contract is a building job, not a park. This is the single most common way a pocket park is lost. Milestone 6, the signed contract with a named budget line.
  • Built then locked. A fence and a padlock turn a new park into another closed park, which is the problem in Template 7. Milestone 4, the published hours on the sign and the gate open when the verifier arrives.
  • Participation as a photograph. One session where a finished plan is shown and applauded is not participation, and the park ends up with nothing residents wanted. Milestone 1, two sessions and at least one resident change visible in the final plan.

3 Privatised coast
Why this one

Template 3: coastal violation survey and file

Lebanon's coast is 220 km long and about 170 km of it is privatised, with roughly 80 per cent of the public shoreline out of reach. The ministry counted 1,068 illegal coastal occupations by 2017 and the last full survey before that was in 1996. Nobody can enforce a law against a violation that has never been measured, so the measuring is the job.

Step 1 · Classify

4 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Desk fileA first pass on several properties, before anyone goes on site.Cadastral extract, search for an occupancy decree or licence, historic and current aerial imagery compared, a one-page summary per property.each property
Measured surveyA property is likely to be built over the maritime public domain and a number is needed that will stand up.A licensed surveyor fixes the legal boundary of the maritime public domain and the built footprint, and calculates the overlap in m2.each property
Shoreline sweepA municipality wants its whole coast recorded at once.A continuous walk and boat pass of the shoreline, GPS track, photo every 100 m, every blocked or charged access point pinned, a property list produced.km of shoreline
Removal witnessA demolition or restoration has been ordered and someone independent must record it.Before, during and after record, measurement of what was removed, confirmation that the sand or rock line is restored and open.each property
Step 2 · The milestones

6 milestones, each with the proof it needs and the check it must pass

#MilestoneEvidence the expert uploadsPass mark the verifier checks
0Scope and class
Agree with the municipality which stretch of coast is covered and which properties are in the file. Walk the ends and pin them. Choose the class.		GPS pins for the start and end of the stretch, with the length in km. A numbered property list with cadastral numbers where they are known. A signed scope note from the municipality. Class chosen.The stretch has a length in km and two GPS ends. Every property on the list has a number or is marked as unidentified. The municipality has signed the scope, so the work cannot be argued away later.
1Legal baseline
For each property, ask in writing for the occupancy decree or licence under the maritime public domain law. Record what comes back, including nothing.		Copy of each written request with its date and the office it went to. Copy of any decree or licence found, with its number and year. For each property with nothing, a written note naming the office asked, the person spoken to and the date.Every property has either a decree or licence reference, or a dated no-record note that names the office. No property is left blank. The framework is Law 144/S of 1925 on the maritime public domain and Law 64/2017 on occupation fees.
2Measured survey
A surveyor registered with the Order of Engineers and Architects fixes the legal boundary and the built footprint on the ground, and works out the overlap.		Survey drawing signed and stamped by the surveyor, with the survey method and the stated error. GPS points as a file. Dated photographs of each property from the land and from the sea.Encroachment area in m2 stated for each property, with the method and the error margin. The boundary is taken from the legal line, not from a fence or a wall. Photos from both land and sea for each property.
3Public access test
Try to walk the shoreline as an ordinary member of the public. Record every place you are stopped, charged, or turned away.		Continuous video or a dated photo series along the walk. Photo of any price list or entry sign. A receipt if a fee was paid. GPS pin, date and time at each blocked point.Every blocked point has a GPS pin, a photo and a time. Any entry fee is recorded in the currency charged. The gaps between accessible points are stated in metres, so the file shows how far a family must walk to reach free sand.
4Dossier filed
Put one complete file per property together and lodge it with the municipality and with the Ministry of Public Works and Transport. Get a stamp.		Stamped and dated receipt of filing from each body. A file index listing what is in each dossier. A copy of each dossier held by the municipality.One dossier per property, each containing the legal baseline, the survey, the photos and the access test. A stamped receipt with a date from each body. Nothing filed that is not backed by milestone 1 to 3 evidence.
5Publication and six-month follow-up
Publish the map and the register so residents can see it. Come back at six months and record what has happened to each file.		Screenshot or photo of the published register, online and on the municipal notice board. A status line per file at six months, with the reference of any order, fine or court step. Any fee applied under Law 64/2017 recorded.The register is public and a resident can find one property in under two minutes. Every file has a status at six months, even if the status is no action. This is the gate for the final release.
Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Scope within 10 working days. A desk file takes about 5 working days per property. A measured survey takes about 60 days per km of shoreline (to confirm against a Lebanese surveyor's programme). File within 120 days of the scope note. Follow-up at 6 and 12 months. The register is republished once a year, because the Lebanese Army began its own coastal survey on 19 September 2023 and the picture moves.

Money

Priced per property for the desk file, the measured survey and the removal witness, and per km for the shoreline sweep. Surveyor fees follow the Order of Engineers and Architects fee scale (to confirm). No public Lebanese rate exists for the file work itself; bracket it from the first three real bids. Not included: court fees, lawyers, demolition, restoration of the beach, and the army's own survey.

Release

Nothing up front. 40 per cent at milestone 2 when the signed survey with an m2 figure is delivered. 40 per cent at milestone 4 against the stamped filing receipts. 20 per cent held until the register is published and the six-month status review is done at milestone 5.

Who signs off. The municipality commissions and signs. The Ministry of Public Works and Transport holds the maritime public domain and must receive the files. The governor of the province has a role in occupation decisions. The Lebanese Army is running its own coastal survey and should be told, not surprised. The surveyor must be registered with the Order of Engineers and Architects or the drawing is worthless in court. Nahnoo mapped violations north to south in 2022 and a municipality should ask for that work before repeating it.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Measured from the fence. Taking the wall or fence as the boundary gives a number the owner can destroy in one hearing. The legal line is the only line that counts. Milestone 2, the signed drawing must state the method and the legal line used.
  • No record means no violation. A blank against a property lets the owner claim a licence exists somewhere. A dated note naming the office asked closes that door. Milestone 1, no property may be left blank.
  • Names published before the survey. Publishing a list without measurements invites a defamation case and loses the file. Measure first, publish second. Milestone 5 comes after milestone 2 and 4, and the release schedule enforces the order.
  • Using the 2017 count as current. The 1,068 figure is nine years old and the coast has changed. It is context, not evidence about any one property. Milestone 0, the property list has to be built from this survey, not copied from the old count.
  • A conflicted expert. A firm that has worked for a resort on the same stretch cannot produce a file a court will trust. Milestone 0, the scope note requires a written declaration of past work on the stretch.
Sources

  • Al Jazeera, Beirut's last public beach faces creeping privatisation, 2019 aljazeera.com
  • Bianet, Activists step up legal battle against privatisation of beaches on the Turkish riviera bianet.org
4 Collapsing heritage buildings
Why this one

Template 4: emergency stabilisation and record

At least 150 heritage buildings have been lost since the 1997 survey that listed 572, and the port blast damaged 640 historic buildings with about 60 at risk of collapse. A building that is propped and dry can wait for money. A building that is wet for one more winter cannot.

Step 1 · Classify

4 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Record onlyThe building is not moving and nothing needs to be touched yet, but it may be demolished or may fall.Measured survey, a full photographic record of every elevation and room, a crack map, a written condition note.each building
Emergency proppingA wall, a floor or a balcony is moving and could fall on the street or on people inside.A structural engineer's scheme, timber or steel props, raking shores, netting, footway protection and signs.each building
Weathering-inThe roof is open or windows are gone, so rain is getting in and doing the real damage.Temporary roof cover, gutters and downpipes reinstated, openings boarded with ventilation, water led away from the walls.m2 of roof and openings
Permit reviewA demolition permit has been applied for or granted on a building that may be listed.Check the listing status, check the permit against the file, write an objection with evidence, file it. Save Beirut Heritage reviewed 250 permits with the Ministry of Culture in one year and 150 demolitions were halted.each permit
Step 2 · The milestones

6 milestones, each with the proof it needs and the check it must pass

#MilestoneEvidence the expert uploadsPass mark the verifier checks
0Scope, class and safety
A structural engineer registered with the Order of Engineers and Architects walks the building and the street around it. Rate the risk. Choose the class. Fence off anything that could fall on a pedestrian the same day.		Photographs of every elevation and of every visible crack, with a scale in frame. A crack map on a sketch plan. GPS pin. The engineer's name and Order of Engineers registration number. Photos of the footway fencing.A written risk rating signed by the engineer. Class chosen. Emergency propping and weathering-in classes may only be scoped by a registered structural engineer, not by a contractor. Anything that could fall on the pavement is fenced on day one.
1Listing and ownership check
Write to the Directorate General of Antiquities at the Ministry of Culture and ask whether the building is listed, under review, or not listed. Ask the municipality for the file and the owner.		Copy of the letter with its date. The written answer, or a dated note if none came. The municipal file reference. The owner or heirs named, with how they were identified.A dated written answer from the Directorate General of Antiquities, or a dated record of asking and waiting. The owner is named or the building is recorded as owner unknown. No work beyond making safe starts before this is on file.
2Record before anything moves
Photograph and measure the building as it is now, well enough that it could be rebuilt from the record. Do this before a single prop goes up.		A photo set covering every elevation, every room, every ceiling, every decorative element, each with a scale bar or measuring rod in frame. Measured drawings: plans, two sections and every elevation. A file index.Every elevation and every accessible room is covered. Drawings at 1:50 (to confirm against the Directorate General of Antiquities requirement). The record is dated earlier than any propping photo. If a prop appears in a record photo, the record is rejected.
3Make safe
Put up the props, shores and netting to the engineer's scheme. Protect the pavement. Sign the works.		A photo of the base of every prop, showing what it stands on. A photo of the full scheme from the street. The engineer's signed sign-off against the scheme drawing. Delivery notes for the timber or steel.Every prop stands on a solid base, never on rubble, loose earth or a floor of unknown strength. The load path is drawn on the scheme and the props follow it. The footway is protected and signed. The engineer has signed after the props are up, not before.
4Water out
Cover the roof, board the openings so air still moves, and reinstate gutters and downpipes so water leaves the building and the wall bases.		Photo of the cover fixed down, from above if possible. Photo of each downpipe discharging away from the wall. A hose test video showing water running off and away. A dated photo of the inside taken after the first real rain.The hose test shows no water entering and no water pooling against a wall. The after-rain photo shows dry floors. Boarding leaves ventilation gaps; a sealed building grows damp and rot, which is a slower version of the same failure.
5Six-month check and file
Come back after six months. Read the crack monitors. Check every prop is still tight. Lodge the whole file with the municipality and the Directorate General of Antiquities.		Photos of each crack monitor with its reading, dated. Photos of each prop from the same angle as milestone 3. A stamped receipt for the file from both bodies.Crack monitors have not moved more than 1 mm since milestone 3 (to confirm against the engineer's own trigger value). No prop loose, no prop base settled. The file is lodged and stamped. This is the gate for the final release.
Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Inspect within 3 working days of a collapse or movement report, same day if the street is at risk. Record before any propping, always. Make safe within 14 days of the inspection. Weathering-in before the first rain of the season, which in Lebanon means before the end of October. Six-month re-check, then a re-check every six months until a permanent repair starts. Props are a holding measure, not a repair; the scheme should state how long it is designed to stand.

Money

Priced per building for the record and for the propping scheme, per m2 for the temporary roof and the boarding, and per permit for a permit review. No public Lebanese rate exists; bracket it from the first three real bids. Not included: permanent repair, scaffolding hire beyond the propping period, the owner's share, and any legal costs in a demolition case.

Release

Nothing up front. 30 per cent at milestone 2 when the record is complete and dated before any prop. 40 per cent at milestone 3 when the engineer signs off the props in place. 20 per cent at milestone 4 when the building is dry after real rain. 10 per cent held until the six-month check at milestone 5.

Who signs off. The Ministry of Culture, through the Directorate General of Antiquities, under the 1933 Antiquities Law (decree number to confirm), decides listing and must be told before anything is touched on a listed or possibly listed building. The municipality issues the works permit and the street closure. A structural engineer registered with the Order of Engineers and Architects must sign the propping scheme. Civil Defence must be told where there is a risk of collapse into the street. The Directorate General of Urban Planning for scaffolding or props standing on a public road. The owner must be notified, and a dated notice is part of the file even when the owner cannot be found.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Propping before recording. Once props and netting are up, the record can never be made, and if the building falls there is nothing to rebuild from. Milestone 2 must be dated earlier than milestone 3, and a prop in a record photo fails it.
  • Demolition dressed as an emergency. Calling a building dangerous is the standard route to a demolition permit. An independent engineer's risk rating and a listing check are the counterweight. Milestone 0 risk rating and milestone 1 written answer from the Directorate General of Antiquities.
  • Props standing on rubble. A prop on loose material settles, the load goes back into the cracked wall, and the propping did nothing but reassure people. Milestone 3, a photo of the base of every prop.
  • A tarpaulin that holds water. A flat sheet over an open roof fills with rain, gets heavy and collapses the roof structure it was meant to save. Milestone 4, the hose test video has to show water running off and away.
  • Listing status assumed. Plenty of buildings people call heritage are not listed, and plenty that are listed are treated as though they are not. Either mistake ends the project. Milestone 1, a dated written answer, not a phone call.

5 No wheelchair access
Why this one

Template 5: accessible route retrofit

Beirut's pavements and gardens are largely impossible to use in a wheelchair, and in the 1990s disability activists in Ain al-Mreisseh cut a kerb ramp themselves because nobody else would. Amman shows what a badly done retrofit looks like: ramps too steep to push up alone, and tactile tiles that come loose after one winter.

Step 1 · Classify

4 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Dropped kerb crossingA crossing where the kerb is a step on one or both sides.Both kerbs dropped flush, tactile warning surface, the carriageway edge made good, road markings refreshed. Counted as one crossing, not two kerbs.each crossing
Ramp at a stepA single step or a short flight blocks a doorway, a park entrance or a path.Concrete ramp with landings top and bottom, edge protection, handrails where the rise is more than 0.5 m, slip-resistant finish.each ramp
Tactile paving retrofitWarning or guidance surfaces are missing, broken, or glued on and lifting.Lifting the failed units, a proper bed, mechanically fixed or mortar-bedded tactile units, making good around them.m2
Accessible route upgradeA whole street, a park path or a route between two places needs to work end to end.All of the above along one named route, plus removal of obstacles, plus a continuous surface with no lips.linear metre of route

6 milestones, each with the proof it needs and the check it must pass

#MilestoneEvidence the expert uploadsPass mark the verifier checks

Come back after a year, including one winter, and repeat the measurements and the user test.		Repeat gradient and lip readings, photographed. A tap test on every tactile unit, filmed; a loose unit sounds hollow. A repeat of the unaided video.No tactile unit loose or missing. Gradients unchanged. Route still clear and still completed unaided. Loose tiles after one winter are the Amman failure and are the reason for the retention.
Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Audit within 15 working days of the request. Design within 30 days. Build within 60 days of the design being agreed. Measured check on the day the work is finished. Real-user test within 5 working days of the measured check. Twelve-month check after one winter. Warranty 24 months on tactile paving fixings and 12 months on concrete.

Money

Priced per crossing, per ramp, per m2 of tactile paving and per linear metre for a route upgrade. No public Lebanese rate exists; bracket it from the first three real bids. For scale only, Greater Amman Municipality put 1 million Jordanian dinars, about 1.41 million US dollars, into accessibility works in 2019, and one neighbourhood project cost about 1.41 million dollars. Not included: traffic signals and audio signals, enforcement against parking on the ramp, and works inside private buildings.

Release

Nothing up front. 60 per cent after milestone 4, when the real-user test is passed, not when the concrete is poured. 40 per cent held until the twelve-month check at milestone 5. Paying on the user test rather than the build is the whole point: a ramp that measures right and cannot be used is not a ramp.

Who signs off. The municipality decides and signs. The Ministry of Public Works and Transport must agree anything on a classified road. The Internal Security Forces traffic branch for crossings and markings. A designer registered with the Order of Engineers and Architects for any ramp with a rise over about 0.5 m. Law 220/2000 on the rights of disabled persons is the legal duty behind the work; which body signs off the technical standard is (to confirm).

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Ramp too steep. Anything steeper than 1 in 12 cannot be pushed alone, and a steep short ramp is the most common thing built because it fits the space available. Milestone 3, three level readings, and milestone 4, the unaided video.
  • Glued tactile tiles. Surface-glued units lift in the first wet winter and become a trip hazard, which is exactly what happened in Amman. Milestone 2, the photo of the fixings before covering, and milestone 5, the tap test.
  • The ramp ends in a parked car. A perfect dropped kerb with a car across it is useless. Access is a route, not a component. Milestone 4, the unaided run of the whole route, done at a normal time of day.
  • No landing at the top. Without a level landing a wheelchair user cannot stop, open a door or turn, and rolls backwards down the ramp. Milestone 1 design check and milestone 3 landing reading.
  • An audit with no disabled person in it. An engineer alone always misses something: a door that opens outwards, a gully in the wrong place, a gradient that is legal and still impossible. Milestone 0, the signed note from the named wheelchair user.

6 Public land grabs
Why this one

Template 6: municipal land register and occupation file

The Eden Bay resort was built on the Ramlet al-Bayda public domain with eight documented violations, and Dalieh is under a hotel project. Most municipalities cannot say how many plots they own or where they are. A published register is the cheapest defence public land has, because you cannot quietly take a plot that is on a list everyone can read.

Step 1 · Classify

4 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Register buildThe municipality has no usable list of what it owns.Pulling every municipal plot from the cadastre and the municipal books, one record per plot with number, area, location and stated use.each plot
Occupation checkA list exists on paper but nobody has looked at the plots.A site visit per plot, photographs, GPS of the corners, and a status: free, occupied, built on, leased, unknown.each plot
Priority violation fileOne plot is clearly occupied and the municipality wants to act on it.Full evidence file: cadastral extract, measured overlap, dated photographs, witness statements, a timeline of how the occupation happened.each plot
Recovery and reopeningA plot has been recovered and must be visibly public again before someone else takes it.Removing fencing and structures, clearing, a public sign naming the plot and the municipality, a basic surface so people can use it.m2
Step 2 · The milestones

6 milestones, each with the proof it needs and the check it must pass

#MilestoneEvidence the expert uploadsPass mark the verifier checks
0Scope and class
Agree in writing with the municipal council how many plots are covered and where the list comes from. Choose the class.		A signed council decision or scope note stating the number of plots and the source of the list. The source named: cadastre, municipal property book, or an old survey with its date.A number of plots is agreed and written down, so the work cannot be quietly shrunk. The source of the list is named with a date. Class chosen.
1Paper record
For every plot, record the cadastral number, the area on paper, the location, the registered owner, and any lease, licence or concession with its dates.		One record per plot with the cadastral extract attached. A single spreadsheet or table listing all plots. A list of the plots where something could not be found, naming the office asked and the date.Every plot has a cadastral number and a paper area, or is on the blanks list. Nothing is estimated. A guessed area is worse than a blank, because it will be quoted back in court.
2Ground check
Visit every plot. Photograph it from at least two sides. Walk the corners with GPS. Write down what is actually there.		Dated photos per plot, at least two angles. A GPS polygon per plot. A one-line status per plot: free, fenced, built on, farmed, parked on, rubbish tipped, unknown.Every plot on the list has a dated photo and a GPS polygon, or a written reason why it could not be reached. Status recorded for each. Visits spread across the working week, not all on one quiet Sunday.
3Overlay and flag
Put the paper boundary and the GPS polygon on the same map. Measure where private building sits inside the public plot. Rank the flags by area taken.		An overlay map per flagged plot. The overlap area in m2 with the method stated. A ranked flag list, biggest area first. Photos tied to the overlay.Every flagged plot has an overlap figure in m2 and a stated method and error. Flags are ranked by area, so the list cannot be arranged to protect anyone. Where a legal boundary survey is needed, the plot is marked for the measured survey in Template 3.
4Register published
Publish the register where residents can actually see it: the municipal notice board and a web page or a shared file.		Photo of the printed register on the notice board, dated. A link or screenshot of the online version. A short guide in Arabic explaining how to look up a plot.A resident who has never seen it can find one named plot in under two minutes, tested by the verifier with a real person. Every plot shows number, area, location, status and the date it was checked.
5Files lodged and six-month status
Lodge a file on each flagged plot with the municipality and, where the occupation looks criminal, with the public prosecutor. Return at six months and record what happened.		Stamped and dated filing receipts. A status line per file at six months with any order, fine or case reference. A note of any plot where the occupation has grown since milestone 2.One stamped receipt per flagged plot. A status at six months for every file, even if the status is no action taken. Any plot where the occupation has grown is re-photographed and re-measured. This is the gate for the final release.
Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Scope within 10 working days. Paper record and ground check within 90 days for up to 200 plots (to confirm against a real municipal list size). Overlay and flags within 110 days. Register published within 120 days. Status review at 6 and 12 months. The register is re-checked and republished once a year; a register that is not updated is dead within two years and worse than none, because people trust it.

Money

Priced per plot for the register, the ground check and the flagging, per file for a priority violation file, and per m2 for recovery and reopening. No public Lebanese rate exists; bracket it from the first three real bids. Not included: a licensed boundary survey, which is Template 3 class 2, court fees, lawyers, demolition, and compensation.

Release

Nothing up front. 30 per cent at milestone 2 when every plot has a dated photo and a GPS polygon. 40 per cent at milestone 4 when the register is published and a resident can use it. 30 per cent held until the six-month status review at milestone 5.

Who signs off. The municipal council decides and signs the scope. The Directorate of Land Registry and Cadastre provides the extracts. The governor of the province and the Ministry of Interior and Municipalities oversee municipal property matters. The public prosecutor receives criminal files. Municipal powers over public property sit under the Municipal Act, Decree-Law 118/1977 (article number to confirm). Where the plot touches the shore, the Ministry of Public Works and Transport is involved as well, under the maritime public domain law.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • A register that is never published. A list in a drawer protects nobody. Publication is the protection, not the list. Milestone 4, the notice board photo and the two-minute lookup test with a real resident.
  • Guessed areas. An area written down without a cadastral extract behind it will be produced by the occupier to show the register is unreliable, and then the whole register is unreliable. Milestone 1, blanks are allowed and guesses are not.
  • Only the weak occupiers get flagged. Flagging a farmer and skipping a resort is how these exercises end up making things worse. Ranking by area takes the choice away. Milestone 3, the ranked flag list, biggest area first.
  • Measuring from the fence. The occupier's own fence is not the boundary. A file built on it collapses at the first hearing. Milestone 3, the stated method, and referral to a licensed boundary survey where it matters.
  • No annual update. Occupations creep. A plot that was free in year one is fenced in year two and built on in year three, and the register still says free. The time rule: re-check and republish yearly, and the six and twelve month status reviews.

Why this one

Template 7: reopen a park and keep it open

Horsh Beirut, the city's biggest green space, was closed to most residents for decades, opened in 2016 and shut again in 2017. Opening a park that already exists is far cheaper than building one, and the risk is not the opening, it is staying open. That is what this template pays for.

Step 1 · Classify

4 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Open the gateThe park is physically fine but closed, or open only to some people.A council decision setting public hours, removal of entry conditions, a keyholder, a sign, and unannounced checks.each park

Community management agreementThe municipality cannot staff the park but a named local group can.A written agreement with a named group, defined duties, a keyholder, insurance, a budget line, and a review date.each park
Funded maintenance contractUpkeep is the problem and there is money for a contractor.A monthly contract with a written checklist: litter, planting, irrigation, lights, toilets, seats, gate opening.month

6 milestones, each with the proof it needs and the check it must pass

#MilestoneEvidence the expert uploadsPass mark the verifier checks
0Scope, class and baseline

A baseline list with counts and a photo for each item type. A plan with fixed photo spots marked. Area in m2. The current hours, and who is allowed in, written down as they really are.Counts recorded for every item type. 2Make it usable
Repair what the baseline says is broken. Get the lights working, the taps running, at least one toilet working, and the paths passable.		Repeat photos from the six fixed spots. A night photo showing the lights on. A video of a tap running. A photo inside the working toilet with soap and water present. A tape measure photo across the narrowest path.Every light on the baseline list works, shown in one night photo. At least one working toilet per park, to the standard in Template 8. Paths at least 1.2 m clear so a wheelchair can use them. Water runs.
3Opening and first month
Open on the published hours and keep opening. The verifier turns up unannounced three times in the first month, at different times and on different days.		A daily opening log signed by the keyholder. The verifier's three visit notes with photos of the gate and the time.Open at the published hours on at least 28 of the first 30 days. Open on all three unannounced visits. 4Management agreement signed

5Six-month check

Six completed monthly checklists, signed. Repeat photos from the six fixed spots.Open at the published hours on all three unannounced visits. A checklist completed for each of the six months. No more than 10 per cent of the baseline items broken again (to confirm). This is the gate for the final release.
Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Baseline within 15 working days. Council decision within 45 days. Repairs within 60 days of the decision. Open within 90 days of the start. Unannounced checks in month 1 and month 6, then twice a year. The management agreement or maintenance contract runs at least three years, because a one-year contract simply moves the closure a year down the road.

Money

Priced per m2 for the refresh, a fixed fee for the rules and agreement work, and a monthly figure for maintenance. The monthly figure is the important one and should be in the budget before the refresh starts. No public Lebanese rate exists; bracket it from the first three real bids. Not included: new build, land, fencing works, and security guards beyond what the contract names.

Release

Nothing up front. 50 per cent at milestone 3, when the park has been open on the published hours for a month and passed three unannounced visits. 25 per cent at milestone 4 against the signed agreement with a funded budget line. 25 per cent held until the six-month check at milestone 5. Nothing is released for a park that opens and then closes.

Who signs off. The municipal council decides the hours. Where a park sits with the governorate rather than the municipality, as with Horsh Beirut in Beirut, the governor must sign (to confirm which parks sit where). The Ministry of Agriculture for tree surgery and felling. Civil Defence for gates, fire access and any lock arrangement. The regional water establishment for taps and the toilet. Electricite du Liban or the local generator supplier for the lighting supply.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Opened, then closed again. This is exactly what happened at Horsh Beirut between 2016 and 2017. The opening day is easy and the second winter is not. Milestone 3 and 5, six unannounced visits across seven months, and the 25 per cent held to the end.
  • An entry rule that keeps most people out. Requiring an identity card, a booking, or a certain age turns a public park into a private club with a public budget. Milestone 1, the decision must carry no condition beyond safety.
  • A maintenance contract with no money. A signed contract without a budget line is a piece of paper. Bogota's 1,601 pocket parks are the standing example of this failure at scale. Milestone 4, the named municipal budget line.
  • Lights installed and never energised. New lamp posts with no supply agreement look like progress and leave the park unusable after sunset, which is when people in a hot city want it. Milestone 2, the night photo with the lights on.
  • Volunteers assumed, not organised. Danish research found only about 4 per cent of volunteering touches nature even where volunteer policies exist. Assuming residents will maintain a park for free is not a plan. Milestone 4, a named person with duties and a review date, not a general offer of help.

8 No public toilets
Why this one

Template 8: a public toilet on a busy route

One public toilet has been reported for the whole Beirut Corniche, with queues at weekends. Copenhagen, a much smaller city, runs about 170 public toilets, 92 of them usable by a disabled person, and has kept them free since January 2013 for about 400,000 kroner a year. ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Reopen an existing toiletA toilet block already exists and is locked, broken or filthy.Repair, new fittings, water and waste checked, a cleaning contract, published hours, a sign.each toilet

Standalone unit with a kioskThere is no building and no obvious host, but there is footfall.A prefabricated or container unit, connections, an attached kiosk whose takings pay for the cleaning, as in the LooCafe model. Free to use.each toilet
Cleaning and opening contractThe building is fine and the failure is that nobody opens or cleans it.A monthly contract with named cleaning times, a signed log inside the door, stock of soap and paper, and a phone number on the door.month

Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Survey within 15 working days. Agreement and design within 45 days. Build within 90 days of the agreement. Open within 120 days. Unannounced checks at 30 and 90 days, then twice a year. The cleaning contract runs at least three years and is budgeted before the build starts.

Money

Priced per unit for the build and per month for cleaning and opening. The monthly cleaning figure is the one that decides whether the toilet survives. For scale only, Copenhagen's decision to make its toilets free was costed at about 400,000 kroner a year, roughly 40,000 US dollars, across about 170 toilets, and its supervised toilets take about 2.5 million visits a year. No public Lebanese rate exists; bracket it from the first three real bids. Not included: extending a sewer, buying land, and staff wages beyond the cleaning contract.

Release

Nothing up front. 50 per cent at milestone 4 when it opens with water, soap, light and a sign. 25 per cent at the 30-day unannounced check. 25 per cent held until the 90-day check at milestone 5. Build money and cleaning money are separate: the cleaning contract is paid monthly against the signed log.

Who signs off. The municipality decides the site and signs. The regional water establishment, for example the Beirut and Mount Lebanon Water Establishment, for the water connection and the waste discharge. The Ministry of Public Health for a public sanitary facility (to confirm which licence applies). Electricite du Liban or the local generator supplier for the light. The Ministry of Public Works and Transport if the unit stands within a road reserve. Where the host is a mosque, a church or a private building, the holder signs the site agreement.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Built then locked. A new toilet that is never opened is the most common outcome, because opening it costs money every month and building it only costs money once. Milestone 5, three unannounced visits, and the 50 per cent released only across the checks.
  • No soap, no water. A toilet without hand-washing spreads disease and teaches people not to use public toilets at all. Milestone 5, soap and running water photographed at all three visits.
  • No accessible cubicle. Retrofitting one later means rebuilding. Copenhagen has 92 accessible toilets out of about 170, so it can be done at scale from the start. Milestone 1 design check and milestone 3 turning-space measurement.
  • Build money without cleaning money. Cleaning is the whole cost over ten years. A build budget with no monthly line is a plan for a locked door. Milestone 1, the contract and its budget line must exist before the build starts.
  • Not on any map. People will not search for a toilet they cannot see. A toilet nobody can find has zero users and gets closed as unused. Milestone 4, findable on a phone map by someone who does not know it is there.
