What the numbers look like

Time

Census within 20 working days. Meetings with the traders within 45 days. Council decision within 60 days, and never before the meetings have happened. Zones marked within 90 days. Permits issued within 120 days. Compliance checks at 30 and 90 days, then twice a year. Permits renewed yearly. Bogota gave six months for a reorganisation with no prior agreement and was criticised for exactly that; the meetings come first here for that reason.

Money

Priced per pitch for the census and the marking, per permit for the administration, and per vendor for a relocation. The permit fee should be set to cover cleaning and administration of the zone, not to price vendors off the street; a fee nobody can pay produces an unpermitted street. No public Lebanese rate exists; bracket it from the first three real bids. Not included: compensation, building stalls, enforcement staff, and the cost of Template 1 clearing works.

Release

Nothing up front. 30 per cent at milestone 3 when the zones are marked and the clear route measures up. 40 per cent at milestone 4 when the permits are issued and the refusals are in writing. 30 per cent held until the 90-day compliance check at milestone 5.

Who signs off. The municipal council decides the zones, the fees and the hours; municipal powers over public space sit under the Municipal Act, Decree-Law 118/1977 (article number to confirm). The Internal Security Forces enforce. The Ministry of Public Health licenses food stalls. Civil Defence must confirm the fire hydrant and fire route clearances. The Ministry of Public Works and Transport if the street is a classified road. Where the vendors are refugees or non-nationals, the General Directorate of General Security has a say on work rights (to confirm how this is handled locally).

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Blanket eviction. Removing everyone with nowhere to go removes the livelihood, not the problem. The stalls come back within weeks and the municipality has spent its credibility. Milestone 4, the 80 per cent permit or written refusal rule, and the relocation class.
  • Zones that leave no room to walk. Marking generous pitches and squeezing the pedestrian route recreates the original problem with official paint on it. Milestone 3 and 5, the 1.5 m tape measure at fixed sample points.
  • A fee nobody can pay. Set the fee like commercial rent and every vendor trades without a permit, so the register is fiction from day one. Milestone 1, the fee is drafted with the traders, and milestone 4, the 80 per cent coverage test.
  • Rules before agreement. A decree with a six-month deadline and no prior agreement produces a fight, a court case and a reversal, as in Bogota in 2026. Milestone 2 cannot be passed until milestone 1 attendance sheets exist.
  • A census at the wrong hour. Counting at 10am on a Tuesday misses the evening and weekend pitches, so half the street has no permit and no standing. Milestone 0, three counts at different times across two days, one of them in the evening.
Sources
  • Infobae, 95,000 informal vendors in Bogota at economic risk after the new public space decree, April 2026: Decree 117 of 2026, 17,000 by the district's count, 1.5 m clear around hydrants, six-month deadline infobae.com
  • Daily Sabah, Sidewalk hazards frustrate and endanger pedestrians in Istanbul dailysabah.com
  • Mashallah News, Beware of sidewalks (Beirut) mashallahnews.com
  • L'Orient Today, Sidewalk struggles: Beirut streets pose a challenge to pedestrians today.lorientlejour.com
  • Jordan Times, Amman municipality cracking down on illegal use of sidewalks jordantimes.com
10 Flood and heat exposure of public space
Why this one

Template 10: cool and porous street or square

Beirut has almost no tree cover, so its streets have neither shade in August nor anywhere for a storm to go in January. Izmir rebuilt 1.6 km of stream as a permeable green corridor with about 1,200 trees and about 30,000 plants, and the area stayed free of standing water in the 2020 floods that hit nearby.

Step 1 · Classify

4 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Street treesA paved street with shade nowhere and a footway wide enough to take a tree pit.Tree pits with structural soil, root barriers where services are close, irrigation for the first two years, guards, and a species list suited to heat and low water.each tree
Porous surface retrofitA square, a car park or a wide footway where rain runs straight off and floods the low point.Lifting the sealed surface, an open-graded stone base, permeable paving or gravel, edge restraint, and an overflow route.m2
Rain garden or holding squareThere is a low point that already floods and space to hold water there on purpose.A shallow basin, planting that tolerates being wet and dry, an inlet from the kerb, a measured storage volume, and a piped or surface overflow.m3 of storage
Channel or stream restorationA culverted or concreted watercourse runs through the area and could be reopened as public space.Opening the channel, permeable banks, native planting, a path alongside, and co-design workshops, as in Izmir.metre of channel
Step 2 · The milestones

7 milestones, each with the proof it needs and the check it must pass

#MilestoneEvidence the expert uploadsPass mark the verifier checks
0Scope, class and baseline
Measure the paved area. Count the trees. Go out after rain and pin every place where water stands. On a hot day, take the surface temperature at 2pm in the same spots.		Paved area in m2 and a tree count. Dated photos of standing water with GPS pins, or written accounts from residents with names. Surface temperature readings with the instrument, the time and the date in the photo. Fixed photo spots marked on a plan.Paved area and tree count recorded. At least one flood point pinned with a photo or two named resident accounts. Baseline temperatures taken at a stated time, at stated spots, with the date, so the later comparison is honest.
1Design and capacity
Work out how much rain the design holds and where the water goes when it is full. Size the tree pits by soil volume, not by the hole the paving slab leaves.		A drawing showing storage volume in m3 against a stated rainfall depth and return period. A soil volume per tree. An overflow route drawn from the site to a safe outfall. A services search showing what is buried.Storage volume stated in m3 against a named rainfall depth and return period, not just a description. Soil volume per mature tree stated; 10 to 15 m3 is the usual international rule (to confirm against Lebanese practice). An overflow route is drawn all the way to somewhere it is safe to send water.
2Soakage and soil test
Dig a test pit, fill it with water, and time how fast the level drops. Do it at least twice, in different parts of the site.		Video of each test with a ruler in the pit and a clock or timestamp visible. A note of the pit depth, the water depth and the times. Photos of what the pit shows: soil, rock, rubble, made ground.A measured soakage rate for each pit, written down with units. If the ground does not drain, the design changes to storage plus a piped overflow before any building starts. Building a soakaway into ground that does not soak is the single most expensive way to fail this template.
3Build
Lift the old surface, lay the open-graded base, build the tree pits and the basin, then lay the new surface. Photograph the base before it is covered.		Photos of the excavation with a rod showing depth. Photos of the base stone before it is covered, close enough to see the stone size. Delivery notes naming the aggregate grading. Photos of each tree pit with a rod and a tape.Base depth matches the drawing. The base stone is open-graded with no fine material mixed in; a photo showing sand or crusher dust in the base fails the milestone. Tree pit soil volume matches milestone 1, measured from the pit dimensions.
4Water test
Pour or hose a measured volume of water onto the finished surface and time where it goes.		Video with a meter reading or a counted number of measured containers, a clock, and the surface in shot. A second video following the overflow route while the site is full.The design volume soaks away with no water running off the site. The overflow, when the site is deliberately overfilled, runs where the drawing says it runs. No standing water after the stated time in the design.
5First storm and first summer
Come back after the first heavy storm of the winter, and again once in August at the same time of day as the baseline.		Dated photos from the fixed spots after the storm, within 24 hours. Rainfall figure for that storm from a named station. August surface temperature readings at 2pm at the same spots as milestone 0, photographed with the instrument.No standing water at the milestone 0 flood pins after the storm. Surface temperature measurably lower than the baseline at the same spots and the same time of day; the size of the drop to expect is (to confirm) against local measurements. Trees alive and watered.
6Two-year handover
Repeat the water test two years on, count the surviving trees, and hand over to a funded maintenance contract that includes keeping the surface clean.		Repeat water test video. Tree count with photos from the fixed spots. The signed maintenance contract with a named budget line and a sweeping schedule.At least 80 per cent of trees alive at two years (to confirm). The repeat water test passes at the design volume, which proves the surface has not clogged. A maintenance contract that names sweeping, because silt swept into a porous surface is what kills it.
Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Baseline within 20 working days, and the flood photographs must be taken after real rain, so scoping may need to wait for winter. Design within 45 days of the baseline. Build within 120 days of the design. Plant only in the wet season, November to March. First storm check within 24 hours of the first heavy rain after completion. Summer check in August. Two-year handover. Warranty 24 months on the porous surface and on tree survival.

Money

Priced per tree, per m2 of porous surface, per m3 of storage and per metre of channel. No public Lebanese rate exists; bracket it from the first three real bids. For scale only, Izmir's 1.6 km corridor carried about 1,200 trees and about 30,000 plants, and Copenhagen is planting 100,000 trees across the city towards 20 per cent canopy. Not included: main drainage works, land purchase, utility diversions, and any road reconstruction beyond the treated area.

Release

Nothing up front. 20 per cent at milestone 3 when the base is built and photographed before covering. 40 per cent at milestone 4 when the water test passes. 20 per cent after the first storm check at milestone 5. 20 per cent held until the two-year handover at milestone 6. The long retention is deliberate: porous surfaces and young trees fail in year two, not year one.

Who signs off. The municipality decides and signs. The Ministry of Public Works and Transport for road drainage and any classified road. The Ministry of Energy and Water and the regional water establishment for anything touching a watercourse or a public drain. The Ministry of Agriculture for the species list and for tree planting. The Ministry of Environment where a stream, a shoreline or a protected area is involved. Electricite du Liban and the water establishment must mark their buried services before any digging, and Ogero for telecoms ducts.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Porous paving on a fine base. Sand or crusher dust in the base blocks the pores from below. The surface drains for one winter and then behaves like concrete, and nobody can see why. Milestone 3, the close photo of the base stone before covering, and the delivery note grading.
  • Tree pits too small. A tree in a 1 m3 pit either dies in its third summer or lifts the pavement looking for room. Either way the money is gone. Milestone 1 soil volume and milestone 3 measured pit.
  • No overflow route. Every storage design fills up eventually. A design with no planned overflow sends the surplus into the nearest doorway. Milestone 1 drawing and milestone 4, the deliberate overfill video.
  • Temperature readings that prove nothing. Comparing a morning baseline with an afternoon result, or a cloudy day with a clear one, produces a number that means nothing and cannot be defended. Milestone 0 and 5, same spots, same time of day, instrument and date visible in the photo.
  • Silt swept into the surface. Street sweepings pushed onto permeable paving clog it within months. It is a maintenance instruction, not a design problem, and it is almost always missed. Milestone 6, the repeat water test and the sweeping schedule in the maintenance contract.
Sources
  • City of Copenhagen, Copenhagen Climate Adaptation Plan, 2011 international.kk.dk
  • AIPH Green City Case Study, Izmir, Turkiye: 1.6 km Peynircioglu stream corridor, about 1,200 trees, about 30,000 plants, no standing water in the 2020 floods, two-year monitoring aiph.org
  • AIPH Green City Case Study, Amman, Jordan: micro-lungs with sustainable drainage in East Amman, about 2.5 per cent urban green cover aiph.org
  • European Garden Heritage Network, Copenhagen climate adaptation plan: squares and streets that hold storm water and double as parks eghn.org
  • INTERLACE Hub, Copenhagen urban nature strategy: 100,000 additional trees, 20 per cent canopy target interlace-hub.com

NGOs & Initiatives: 10 templates. Open one to read it.

1 Primary healthcare and medicines
Why this one

Template 1: clinic session series and medicine desk

By March 2021, 78 per cent of people in Lebanon lived in poverty and 36 per cent in extreme poverty, while medicines ran short and hospitals warned they would close. A municipality cannot rebuild a health system, but it can buy a fixed number of clinic days and a stocked medicine desk.

Step 1 · Classify

4 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Mobile clinic roundThere is no working dispensary in the village or the shelter, but there is a hall.A doctor, a nurse and a dispenser for a full day in a borrowed hall, with a basic medicine box, point-of-care tests, a cool box for anything that needs a fridge, and a written referral slip for anyone who needs a hospital.clinic day
Fixed clinic session blockA dispensary or primary healthcare centre exists but cannot pay staff or buy stock.Blocks of four-hour sessions in the existing building, with staff paid, consumables bought, and the centre's own register used so the patients stay the centre's patients after the project ends.session of four hours
Chronic medicine deskThe complaint is people with blood pressure, diabetes or heart disease going without refills.A named list of chronic patients, a monthly refill of their medicines from a medicine bank, a blood pressure and blood sugar reading at each refill, and a card the patient keeps.patient-month
Community health worker roundPeople do not come to the clinic, so the clinic has to go to them.Trained residents visiting households on a fixed round, checking on pregnant women, babies and chronic patients, selling basic health goods at a small markup, and referring anything serious. BRAC runs about 100,000 such workers, each covering 250 to 300 households.household visit
Step 2 · The milestones

7 milestones, each with the proof it needs and the check it must pass

#MilestoneEvidence the expert uploadsPass mark the verifier checks
0Scope and class
Count the catchment. Walk the premises. Ask the municipality and the nearest primary healthcare centre what they already cover, so the project fills a gap instead of doubling one. Choose the class and write down the target number of patients.		GPS pin of the premises. Photos of the room to be used. A one-page gap note naming the nearest working clinic and its distance. The catchment population with where the figure came from. Class chosen and target patient count.Catchment population stated with a named source. Nearest working clinic named with a distance in kilometres. Class chosen. Target patient count written down before any work starts, because everything later is measured against it.
1Licences, staff and premises
Confirm the NGO is registered, the premises are approved by the municipality, and every clinician holds a current licence. Set up the waste bin for sharps and the referral route to a hospital.		NGO registration reference. Municipality letter or permit reference. Licence numbers for each doctor and nurse, with the issuing order named. Photo of the sharps box and the hand-washing point. A signed referral agreement with one named hospital or ambulance service.Every clinician on the rota has a licence number on file. A named municipal officer has approved the premises. A sharps box and a hand-washing point are visible in the photo. A referral route exists in writing, not as a promise.
2Stock in and medicine bank rules
Receive the medicines. Log every line with batch number and expiry. Reject anything short-dated. Lock the cupboard and put a thermometer in the fridge.		Photos of the stock on the shelf, close enough to read the boxes. Purchase invoices or a signed donation note for every line. A stock sheet with item, quantity, batch, expiry. Photo of the fridge thermometer reading. Photo of the locked cupboard.Nothing on the shelf has less than six months of shelf life left, which is the World Health Organization's rule for donated medicines. Every line on the stock sheet has an invoice or a signed donation note. If anything needs a fridge, the thermometer photo shows 2 to 8 degrees Celsius. Quantities on the shelf match the paperwork within 5 per cent.
3Sessions delivered
Run the clinic days or sessions. Record each consultation on a numbered tally sheet: code, age band, sex, reason in one word, medicine given, referred yes or no.		Signed tally sheets, one per session, with the clinician's signature and the date. A daily total. Photos of the waiting area taken at a fixed time each day. Dispensing log showing what left the cupboard.Number of sessions delivered matches the number commissioned. Each tally sheet is signed and dated by the named clinician. The dispensing log and the stock sheet agree within 5 per cent. No sheet carries a patient's name, only a code.
4De-duplication and spot-check
Check the coded list against itself for repeats and against any other NGO working the same street. Hand the verifier the coded list and the totals.		Coded beneficiary list with no names. Total unique patients. A written de-duplication note saying which fields were compared. Consent record showing who agreed to be rung.Duplicates are under 5 per cent of the list (to confirm). The verifier rings a random 10 per cent of coded entries; at least 8 in 10 of those reached confirm they were seen, on roughly the right date, and were not charged. The expert keeps the named list. It is never uploaded. Each person gets a code like KIT-014 and the upload is the coded list plus totals. The verifier rings a random sample on numbers people agreed to be rung on, and asks only what they got and when. If the verifier needs the named list, a Lebanese auditor reads it at the NGO's office under a signed confidentiality undertaking and reports only two things: the count and the number of duplicates.
5Referral and follow-up
Go back to the people who were referred or who are on chronic medicines and see what happened. Fill the refill for a second month.		Follow-up tally with coded entries: seen again, not found, referred and went, referred and did not go. Second-month dispensing log. Photos of the patient cards, names covered.At least 70 per cent of chronic patients on the list got a second refill (to confirm). Every referral has an outcome recorded, even if the outcome is 'did not go'. Blood pressure or blood sugar recorded at both visits for the chronic class.
6Close-out and stock reconciliation
Count what is left. Hand the remaining stock and the equipment to the municipality or the primary healthcare centre against a signature. Write the one-page close-out.		Closing stock count with photos. Signed handover note naming who now owns the fridge, the cupboard and the leftover medicines. Waste disposal note for expired stock. Close-out page: patients seen, unique patients, referrals, cost per patient.Stock in, minus stock dispensed, minus stock wasted, equals stock handed over, within 5 per cent. The handover note carries a name, a title and a date. Nothing expired was dispensed. This is the gate for the final release.
Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Scope within 10 working days of the municipality certifying the request. Licences, premises and first stock within 30 days. Then run the commissioned sessions over a block of 12 weeks so chronic patients get at least two refills inside the project. The follow-up round happens in the last two weeks. Close-out within 10 days of the last session. One unannounced spot-check by the verifier at any point during the 12 weeks.

Money

Priced per clinic day, per four-hour session, per patient-month or per household visit, depending on class. Medicines are priced as a separate line at invoice cost with no markup, so nobody profits from a shortage. There is no published Lebanese rate for an NGO clinic day; bracket it from the first three real bids. Not included: hospital admission, surgery, imaging, laboratory work beyond point-of-care tests, or anything needing a specialist. Those get a referral, not a budget line.

Release

Nothing up front. 20 per cent at milestone 2, when the stock is on the shelf and photographed. 50 per cent at milestone 4, when the sessions are delivered and the spot-check calls come back clean. 30 per cent at milestone 6, after the stock reconciles and the handover is signed.

Who signs off. Ministry of Public Health registers the facility and controls imported and donated medicines; no medicine moves without it. The Lebanese Order of Physicians and the Order of Nurses licence every clinician on the rota. The Ministry of Social Affairs holds the NGO's own registration. The municipality approves the premises and should be told the clinic days in advance. Medical waste needs a contracted collector. Tell the nearest public primary healthcare centre, so the same street is not covered twice.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Ghost patients. A tally sheet is easy to fill in at the end of the day. Paying per consultation makes that tempting. Milestone 4. The sampled call-backs and the dispensing log, which has to move in step with the tally.
  • Short-dated donated medicine. Donors clear their shelves. Medicine with two months left is a disposal cost dressed up as a gift. Milestone 2. The expiry column and the six-month rule.
  • Two NGOs, one street. The same families get counted twice and the next village gets nothing. This happened all over Beirut after the port blast. Milestone 0 gap note and milestone 4 de-duplication.
  • One-off consultation with no refill. A blood pressure reading with no second month of tablets changes nothing and looks good on a report. Milestone 5. The second refill is a counted pass mark, not a nice-to-have.
  • Names in the evidence pack. A photographed register or an uploaded list of patients is a permanent harm to people who are already exposed. Milestone 3 and 4. Any upload carrying a name or an identity document fails the milestone outright and must be deleted.
Sources
  • Human Rights Watch, World Report 2022, Lebanon chapter hrw.org
  • CHW Central, The BRAC shasthya shebika community health worker in Bangladesh chwcentral.org
  • Solidarity clinics and social pharmacies in Greece, study abstract, 2018 pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov
  • Direct Relief, solar power for health facilities in Lebanon, 2022 directrelief.org
  • Sphere Handbook 2018, Health chapter and Core Humanitarian Standard handbook.spherestandards.org
2 Community kitchens and food distribution
Why this one

Template 2: community kitchen run

When over a million people were displaced in Lebanon, volunteer kitchens fed them before any agency arrived. Nation Station alone counted 28,761 meals in the first weeks of the 2026 war, and 136,148 people were registered in shelters by the end of March. A kitchen run is the smallest thing a municipality can buy that people eat the same day.

Step 1 · Classify

4 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Hot meal runThere are shelters or families with no cooker and no gas.Cooking and delivering a hot meal to a named list of shelters or households on a fixed daily round, with a menu cycle, containers, and a signature from whoever receives each delivery.meal
Food parcel roundPeople can cook but cannot buy. Usually families in rented rooms rather than shelters.A standard parcel of dry goods and oil, sized for a household for a month, packed to a fixed content list, delivered against a coded list.parcel
Kitchen equipping and food safety upgradeA kitchen exists and volunteers exist, but the kitchen cannot safely cook at scale.Cookers, gas, pots, fridge or freezer, sinks, a fly screen, a thermometer, a fire extinguisher, and one day of food hygiene training for the cooks.kitchen
Shelter-linked delivery contractThe municipality runs collective shelters and wants one kitchen responsible for feeding them.A block contract to feed a named shelter for a number of days, with a head-count taken at the shelter each day by the shelter manager rather than by the kitchen.shelter-day
Step 2 · The milestones

7 milestones, each with the proof it needs and the check it must pass

#MilestoneEvidence the expert uploadsPass mark the verifier checks
0Scope, class and list
Get the list of shelters or households from the municipality and the Ministry of Social Affairs. Count heads. Choose the class. Fix the menu cycle and the per-meal energy target.		Coded list of shelters or households with head counts, no names. GPS pins of each delivery point. Menu cycle for one week. Class chosen. Target meals per day.Head counts come from the shelter manager or the municipality, not from the kitchen's own guess. The menu cycle reaches 2,100 kilocalories per person per day, which is the Sphere planning figure, or says plainly which other meals make up the rest. Class and daily target written down before cooking starts.
1Kitchen fit and food safety
Fit out the kitchen. Train the cooks for a day on hand-washing, separating raw and cooked, and holding temperatures. Put up the fire extinguisher and check the gas line.		Photos of the kitchen: sinks, fridge with a thermometer in it, covered bins, fly screens, fire extinguisher with a service date, gas bottles stored outside the cooking room. Signed training attendance sheet. Water source named and a water test result if the source is not the network.Fridge thermometer photo shows 5 degrees Celsius or below. Gas bottles are not inside the cooking room in the photo. A fire extinguisher is present with a legible service date. Every cook on the rota is on the training sheet. Hand-washing point has soap and running water in the photo.
2Supply chain and purchase record
Buy the food. Keep every receipt. Where food is donated, log it as a donation with a value and a source. Store dry goods off the floor.		Receipts or invoices for every purchase, and a signed donation note for every in-kind delivery. Photos of the store room showing goods on pallets or shelves, not on the floor. A stock card per main item.Every kilogram that goes into the pot traces to a receipt or a donation note. Stock cards balance against receipts within 5 per cent. No sacks on the floor and no open bags in the photos. Prices paid are within the local market range; three price quotes on file for any purchase above a threshold the municipality sets.
3Cook and deliver
Run the daily round. Count portions out of the kitchen. Get a signature from the shelter manager or the household representative at each drop, on a coded sheet.		Daily portion count signed by the head cook. Delivery sheets signed at each point, showing code, portions and time. One photo per day of the loaded van or the full pots, with the date visible. Core temperature reading of one dish per day.Portions out of the kitchen equal portions signed for at the delivery points, within 3 per cent. Hot food leaves the kitchen at 63 degrees Celsius or above and reaches the shelter within two hours, which is standard food safety practice. Delivery sheets are signed by someone other than the kitchen's own staff.
4De-duplication and call-back sample
Compare the coded list against itself and against other kitchens working the same area. Hand the verifier the coded list, the totals and the consent record.		Coded list, unique household or shelter count, duplication note naming the other kitchens checked against. Consent record for call-backs.Duplicates under 5 per cent of the list (to confirm). The verifier rings a random 10 per cent of coded entries; at least 8 in 10 of those reached confirm they received food, roughly on the days claimed, and paid nothing. The expert keeps the named list. It is never uploaded. Each person gets a code like KIT-014 and the upload is the coded list plus totals. The verifier rings a random sample on numbers people agreed to be rung on, and asks only what they got and when. If the verifier needs the named list, a Lebanese auditor reads it at the NGO's office under a signed confidentiality undertaking and reports only two things: the count and the number of duplicates.
5Nutrition and complaints check
Review what was actually cooked against the menu cycle. Read the complaints book. Check that families with babies, diabetics and anyone who cannot chew got something they can eat.		Menu actually served, day by day. Complaints book photographed, names covered. A short note on special diets and how many people needed one. Photos of the portion size next to a standard container.Served menu matches the planned cycle on at least 80 per cent of days, or the substitutions are explained. Every complaint has a dated response. Portion size in the photo matches the size priced. Special diets are counted, not ignored.
6Close-out and handover
Reconcile food in against meals out. Hand the equipment to the municipality or the kitchen committee against a signature. Write the close-out page.		Final stock count with photos. Signed equipment handover note. Close-out page: total meals, unique households, cost per meal, days missed and why.Food purchased, minus food in store, matches meals served at the planned portion size within 10 per cent. Equipment handover note carries a name, a title and a date. Cost per meal is stated. This is the gate for the final release.
Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Scope within 5 working days, because people are hungry now. Kitchen fit and food safety training within 10 days. Cooking starts no later than 14 days after the municipality certifies the request. A run is commissioned in blocks of 30 days so it can be stopped or extended cleanly. De-duplication in the first 10 days of each block. Close-out within 7 days of the last delivery. No warranty applies to food; the equipment carries the supplier's own warranty, normally one year.

Money

Priced per meal, per parcel, per kitchen or per shelter-day. Food is a pass-through line at receipt cost. Labour, gas, containers and transport are separate lines so a rise in gas does not quietly shrink the meal. No public Lebanese cost per meal exists; bracket from the first three real bids and publish the figure afterwards, because it is the number every later kitchen will be judged against (to confirm). Not included: fresh meat every day, bottled water, or feeding people outside the agreed list.

Release

Nothing up front except a food float, capped at 15 per cent, released at milestone 2 against receipts, because a kitchen cannot buy a month of rice on credit. 55 per cent at milestone 4, when deliveries are signed for and the call-backs come back clean. 30 per cent at milestone 6, after food in reconciles against meals out.

Who signs off. The municipality approves the premises and the delivery round. The Ministry of Public Health covers food safety and can inspect any kitchen serving the public. The Ministry of Social Affairs holds the shelter lists and the NGO's registration. Civil Defence should see the gas storage. If the kitchen sits in a public school or hall, the Ministry of Education or the owning ministry has to agree in writing. Tell the World Food Programme or whichever agency is already feeding the same shelters, so the same people are not fed twice while the next street is missed.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Meals counted, not delivered. Portions leaving the kitchen are easy to count and easy to inflate. The gap shows up at the far end. Milestone 3. Signed delivery sheets from someone outside the kitchen, reconciled against portions out.
  • The shrinking portion. Prices rise, the price per meal is fixed, so the ladle gets smaller. Nobody reports it. Milestone 5. The portion photo against a standard container, and the menu-served check.
  • Cold chain and the long round. Hot food held for hours in a van is how a kitchen poisons a shelter. One outbreak ends the project. Milestone 3. Core temperature reading and the two-hour rule.
  • The same families, three kitchens. Well-connected families are on every list. Isolated households are on none. Milestone 4. De-duplication against the other kitchens, plus the milestone 0 list coming from the municipality.
  • Donated food logged as bought. Charging the sponsor for food a supermarket gave away. It is theft, and it is common. Milestone 2 and milestone 6. Donation notes are compulsory and the final reconciliation exposes the gap.
Sources
