  • Al Jazeera, Lebanese come together to feed those forced to flee, October 2024 aljazeera.com
  • The Other Human, open-air solidarity kitchen, Greece en.wikipedia.org
  • Akshaya Patra Foundation, school meals at scale, ISO certified kitchens akshayapatra.org
  • Sphere Handbook 2018, Food Security and Nutrition, 2,100 kcal planning figure handbook.spherestandards.org
3 Emergency shelter and displacement support
Why this one

Template 3: shelter equipping round and cash grants

In October 2024 Lebanese schools became shelters overnight with no showers, no cookers and no gas. One school in Aley held 260 people, another 330, and five Aley schools together held at least 1,300. Each needed four water trucks a day just for washing. Equipping a shelter is a one-week job a municipality can commission and a verifier can count.

Step 1 · Classify

4 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Shelter equipping kit roundA building is already full of people and is missing the basics.Mattresses, blankets, pillows, a cooker and gas, pots, buckets, cleaning materials, lighting, and partitions for privacy. Counted against the head count in the building, not against a guess.shelter
Collective shelter washing and toilet upgradeThe building has toilets built for a school day, not for people living there.Extra toilets or cubicles, showers with hot water where possible, lockable doors, separate blocks for women and men, a hand-washing point at each block, and a cleaning rota with materials for 30 days.shelter
Household cash grant roundFamilies are displaced but outside official shelters, in rented rooms or with relatives.A one-off grant sized by household, paid through a traceable channel, against a coded list agreed with the municipality. Lebanese mutual aid groups paid 50, 100 or 150 US dollars depending on household size.family
Rent top-upThe family has a room but will lose it within weeks.A monthly top-up paid for a fixed number of months, against a signed tenancy note or a landlord receipt, with the family's name held by the NGO and never published.family-month
Step 2 · The milestones

7 milestones, each with the proof it needs and the check it must pass

#MilestoneEvidence the expert uploadsPass mark the verifier checks
0Scope, class and head count
Visit the building or the street with the municipality. Count heads, not families, and count by age band and sex. Measure the sleeping area and count the working toilets. Choose the class.		GPS pin. Photos of each sleeping room and each toilet block. Measured floor area of sleeping space in square metres. Head count by age band and sex, signed by the shelter manager. Working toilet count. Class chosen.Covered sleeping space is measured, not estimated, and compared against the Sphere figure of 3.5 square metres per person. Working toilets are counted and compared against the Sphere figure of one toilet per 20 people, separated by sex. Head count is signed by the shelter manager or a municipal officer. If the building is already over these figures, the gap is written down as the thing being bought.
1Agreement and de-duplication before buying
Agree the list with the municipality and the Ministry of Social Affairs. Check it against the other groups working the same shelters. Only then buy.		Coded list with head counts, no names. Written note naming which other organisations were checked against and what overlap was found. Municipality sign-off reference. Consent record for call-backs.A named municipal officer has signed the list. At least two other organisations working the same area are named in the overlap note. Overlap removed before purchase, not after. The expert keeps the named list. It is never uploaded. Each person gets a code like KIT-014 and the upload is the coded list plus totals. The verifier rings a random sample on numbers people agreed to be rung on, and asks only what they got and when. If the verifier needs the named list, a Lebanese auditor reads it at the NGO's office under a signed confidentiality undertaking and reports only two things: the count and the number of duplicates.
2Procure and show the stock
Buy the kit. Take three quotes for anything substantial. Photograph the stock before it is broken up, with the quantity visible.		Three quotes per major line. Invoices. Photos of the stock stacked in the store with a counting board showing the quantity. Delivery notes from the supplier. Specification sheet for mattresses and blankets.Quantity in the stock photo matches the invoice and matches the head count from milestone 0. Three quotes on file for every line above the municipality's threshold. Mattresses and blankets meet a written specification rather than 'as available'. Unit prices are inside the local market range.
3Install or distribute
Fit the toilets and showers, or hand out the kits. Every handover is signed on a coded sheet. Put up the privacy partitions the same day.		Signed coded handover sheets, one line per household or room. Before and after photos from the same spot for installation work. Photos of partitions and of lockable doors. Plumber's or electrician's note for any connection work.Items handed over equal items purchased, minus a stated and photographed remainder. For the washing class, every new cubicle has a door that locks from the inside and a light. Women's and men's blocks are separate and signed in Arabic. Before and after photos are from the same spot.
4Spot-check call-backs
Give the verifier the coded list, the totals and the consented numbers. Stand back.		Coded list, unique household count, consent record, and for the cash classes the payment channel's own transfer record with names removed.The verifier rings a random 10 per cent of coded entries. At least 8 in 10 of those reached confirm they got the item or the money, roughly on the date claimed, in the amount claimed, and that they paid nobody anything for it. Any report of a payment demanded stops the release at once and goes to the municipality in writing.
5Thirty-day use check
Go back after a month. Are the showers still working? Are the mattresses still in the shelter? Is the cooker being used or was it sold?		Photos from the same spots as milestone 3, dated 30 days or more later. Water meter or truck delivery count for the month. A short note from the shelter manager. Maintenance log for the new fittings.Every fitting installed is still working, or a repair is logged with a date. Water available works out at 15 litres per person per day or more, the Sphere minimum, counting trucked water. Items are still in the shelter. Losses above 10 per cent have a written explanation. This is the gate for the final release.
6Handover and close-out
Hand the fittings and the cleaning rota to the municipality or the shelter committee. Write the close-out page.		Signed handover note naming who maintains what. Cleaning rota with named roles. Close-out page: people served, items delivered, cost per person, what broke.Handover note carries a name, a title and a date. A named person is responsible for cleaning and for repairs after the project ends. Cost per person served is stated.
Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Inspect within 3 working days of the request, because displacement moves faster than anything else in this list. List agreed and de-duplicated within 7 days. Kit delivered or fittings installed within 21 days. Cash paid within 14 days of the list being signed. Then the 30-day use check. Warranty on plumbing and electrical work is 12 months; on supplied goods it is whatever the supplier gives, written into the invoice.

Money

Equipping is priced per shelter against a written kit list, with the kit list itself priced per item. Washing upgrades are priced per cubicle. Cash is priced at face value with the transfer fee shown as a separate line, and the NGO's handling cost capped as a stated percentage. The only Lebanese figure on record is the mutual aid grant of 50, 100 or 150 US dollars by household size; there is no published Lebanese unit rate for a shelter kit, so bracket it from the first three real bids. Not included: structural repair to the building, rent for the building itself, or anything for a household not on the signed list.

Release

Nothing up front for equipping. 20 per cent at milestone 2, when the stock is bought and photographed. 50 per cent at milestone 4, when handovers are signed and the call-backs come back clean. 30 per cent at milestone 5, after the 30-day use check. Cash classes are different: the cash itself moves in full at milestone 3 because a half-paid grant helps nobody, and only the NGO's fee is held back to milestone 5.

Who signs off. The Ministry of Education owns most of the buildings used as shelters and must agree in writing before anything is fixed to a wall. The Ministry of Social Affairs holds the shelter registration and the displaced lists. The municipality approves the work and should hold a copy of the kit list. The regional Water Establishment must approve any new connection to the network, and the Order of Engineers stamp is needed if the washing block changes the drainage. Electrical work connects through Electricité du Liban or the licensed local generator operator. Civil Defence sees the gas storage for cookers.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Kit sized by budget, not by head count. Two hundred mattresses arrive for 330 people because that is what the money bought. The shortfall becomes a fight inside the shelter. Milestone 0 against milestone 2. The head count is signed before the purchase, so the gap cannot be hidden.
  • Toilets without locks or lighting. An unlit, unlockable cubicle is not usable by women or girls after dark, so the count of toilets is a fiction. Milestone 3. Lock and light are explicit pass marks, photographed.
  • Cash without a traceable channel. Cash in envelopes cannot be checked and invites a cut being taken at the door. Milestone 4. The transfer record and the call-back question about paying anyone.
  • Installed and abandoned. A shower with no cleaning rota and no spare washer is broken within a month, and the money is gone. Milestone 5 and 6. The 30-day check and the named maintainer.
  • The list that leaked. A shelter list with names, nationalities and addresses is dangerous for displaced people and for refugees in particular. Milestone 1 and 4. Only coded lists are ever uploaded; an auditor under a confidentiality undertaking checks the named list on site.
Sources
  • Al Jazeera, No cookers, showers or gas: displaced people shelter in Lebanese schools, October 2024 aljazeera.com
  • Waging Nonviolence, mutual aid in Lebanon, cash grants of 50, 100 and 150 dollars, April 2026 wagingnonviolence.org
  • Sphere Handbook 2018, Shelter and WASH minimum standards: 3.5 m2 per person, 1 toilet per 20 people, 15 litres per person per day handbook.spherestandards.org
  • Norwegian Refugee Council, Jordan country programme, shelter and cash for displaced families nrc.no
  • NEAR Change Fund, locally-led pooled funding and mobile money payouts, Bangladesh near.ngo
4 Disaster clean-up and home repair
Why this one

Template 4: zone clean-up and home repair round

After the 2020 port blast at least 384 organisations registered with the Lebanese army to work in Beirut, and many more did not. The result was repeated, contradictory damage surveys and families who could not find out who was fixing their flat. The fix is not more volunteers. It is one mapped zone, one register, one organisation answerable for it.

Step 1 · Classify

4 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Zone assessment and registerBefore any repair money moves, and always first after a blast, a flood or bombardment.Walking every building in a mapped zone, recording damage on one agreed form, pinning each building, and publishing a register of building codes and damage grades that every other organisation can read.zone, priced per building surveyed
Debris and glass clearanceBuildings are standing but streets and flats are full of rubble and broken glass.Clearing debris from flats and the street, separating glass, metal, rubble and hazardous material, and hauling to a site the Ministry of Environment accepts. Workers in gloves, boots, goggles and masks.cubic metre of debris
Weatherproofing repairThe building is safe but open to the weather. This is the largest class and the fastest.Glass, window frames, doors, door locks, and a watertight roof patch, so a family can sleep in their own home before winter.housing unit
Minor structural repairA column, a beam, a slab or a staircase is damaged, but the building is repairable.A structural assessment by a licensed engineer, then the repair the engineer specifies, with the engineer signing off before and after. No structural work starts without that signature.housing unit, engineer-signed
Step 2 · The milestones

7 milestones, each with the proof it needs and the check it must pass

#MilestoneEvidence the expert uploadsPass mark the verifier checks
0Zone, class and claim
Take one mapped zone from the municipality. Claim it in writing on the shared register before starting, so no one else surveys it.		Zone boundary as a map or a list of streets. Written claim posted to the shared register with a date and time. Municipality letter assigning the zone. Class chosen. Count of buildings in the zone.The zone has a boundary a stranger could walk. The claim is dated and visible to other organisations before the first survey. A named municipal officer assigned it. No other organisation holds an overlapping claim, or the overlap is written down and settled.
1Survey every building on one form
Walk every building. Record damage on the same form everyone else uses. Grade each unit. Pin it. Never survey a building twice.		One completed form per building with a building code, GPS pin and damage grade. Two photos per building, one of the front and one of the worst damage. A zone summary: buildings surveyed, units, grades, households present.Every building in the zone boundary has a form, or an explicit note saying why it has none. Grades use one written scale for the whole zone. The zone summary totals match the forms. Photos carry the building code, never a family name or a door number tied to a person.
2Safety, permits and hazardous material
Confirm the army registration and the municipal permit. Check for asbestos, fuel tanks and unexploded material. Brief every worker and hand out the gear.		Army registration reference. Municipal permit reference. Signed toolbox-talk sheet with every worker's name on the day. Photos of workers wearing gloves, boots, goggles and masks. Note on hazardous material found and who was told. Insurance certificate for the crew.Every worker in the working photos is wearing gloves, boots and eye protection; a photo showing bare hands on broken glass fails the milestone. Insurance covers the crew for the whole period. Anything suspected to be asbestos is left alone and reported, not bagged by volunteers. Army and municipal references both present.
3Do the work
Clear, glaze or repair. Photograph each unit from the same spot before and after. Weigh or measure what is hauled away.		Before and after photo pair per unit from the same spot. Tip tickets or weighbridge notes for debris. Delivery notes for glass, frames and doors, with thickness and type written on them. Signed completion note per unit, on a coded sheet.Every unit billed has a matching before and after pair from the same spot. Debris hauled matches tip tickets within 10 per cent. Glass is the specified thickness and type; 4 millimetre glass billed as laminated fails. Each completion note is signed by the resident or the building committee, by code, not by name in the upload.
4Engineer sign-off for structural work
For the structural class only, have the licensed engineer inspect before and after and sign. Nothing structural is billed without both signatures.		Pre-repair assessment signed and stamped by an engineer registered with the Order of Engineers, with the registration number. Method statement. Post-repair sign-off with the same stamp. Photos of reinforcement and formwork before concrete is poured. Concrete delivery notes with the grade.Order of Engineers registration number is present and current on both documents. The repair done matches the method statement. Reinforcement is photographed before it is covered; there is no way to check it afterwards. Concrete grade on the delivery note matches the specification.
5De-duplication and resident call-backs
Publish the zone result to the shared register. Hand the verifier the coded list of units repaired and the consented numbers.		Coded unit list with grades and work done. Duplication note: which other organisations' registers were compared and what was found. Consent record.No unit appears in another organisation's completed register for the same work. The verifier rings a random 10 per cent of coded units; at least 8 in 10 of those reached confirm the work was done, roughly when claimed, and that they paid nothing. The expert keeps the named list. It is never uploaded. Each person gets a code like KIT-014 and the upload is the coded list plus totals. The verifier rings a random sample on numbers people agreed to be rung on, and asks only what they got and when. If the verifier needs the named list, a Lebanese auditor reads it at the NGO's office under a signed confidentiality undertaking and reports only two things: the count and the number of duplicates.
6Sixty-day check and handover
Come back after two months of weather and use. Look at the glazing, the doors and the roof patches. Hand the zone register to the municipality.		Photos from the same spots as milestone 3, dated 60 days or more later. Defect list with dates fixed. Signed handover of the zone register to the municipality. Close-out page: buildings surveyed, units repaired, cubic metres cleared, cost per unit.No leaks, no failed frames, no glass fitted without beading. Any defect found has a repair date inside 14 days. The municipality holds the register in a form it can still read in a year. This is the gate for the final release.
Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Claim the zone within 2 working days of assignment, because the value of a register falls the moment someone else surveys the same street. Survey the whole zone within 14 days. Debris clearance within 30 days. Weatherproofing within 45 days, and before the first week of November if winter is the reason. Structural repair follows the engineer's programme. Then the 60-day check. Warranty: 12 months on glazing, frames, doors and roof patches; 24 months on structural repair, which is the usual defects liability period on Lebanese works contracts (to confirm).

Money

Assessment is priced per building surveyed. Clearance is priced per cubic metre with the tip fee shown separately. Weatherproofing is priced per housing unit against a written schedule of glass area, frames and doors, so a flat with six windows does not cost the same as one with two. Structural repair is priced from the engineer's bill of quantities, never as a lump sum. No public Lebanese unit rate exists for post-blast repair; bracket from the first three real bids. Not included: furniture, appliances, redecoration, or repair to a building the municipality cannot confirm the ownership of.

Release

Nothing up front. 15 per cent at milestone 1, when the zone is surveyed and the register is published, because the register has value even if no repair follows. 55 per cent at milestone 3, when the before and after pairs and the tip tickets check out. 30 per cent at milestone 6, after the 60-day check. For the structural class, milestone 4 is a hard gate: no release at all on a structural unit without both engineer signatures.

Who signs off. The Lebanese army ran the registration and the coordination headquarters after the port blast and is the first stop in any similar response. The municipality assigns the zone and issues the work permit. The Order of Engineers licences the engineer for the structural class and its stamp is compulsory. The Ministry of Environment governs where debris goes and how asbestos is handled. The Directorate General of Antiquities must be told before any work on a heritage building, which in parts of Beirut means most of the street. Electricité du Liban and the Water Establishment must be told before cutting into services.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • The fourth survey of the same flat. Families were surveyed again and again after the blast, with contradictory findings, and stopped answering the door. Milestone 0 and 5. The dated zone claim and the shared register.
  • After photo from a different angle. A flattering angle hides the corner that was not touched. It is the single most common fake in repair work. Milestone 3. Same-spot pairs, or the unit is not billed.
  • Structural work by a contractor with no engineer. A patched column that looks fine can fail later and kill people. The repair is invisible once rendered. Milestone 4. Reinforcement photographed before concrete, and two stamped signatures.
  • Asbestos bagged by volunteers. Old Lebanese roofs and panels contain it, and untrained people in cloth masks breathe it in during clearance. Milestone 2. Suspected material is reported and left; the safety photos show the actual gear worn.
  • Cheap glass billed as safety glass. Thin glass in a blast zone recreates the injury that filled the hospitals in 2020. Milestone 3. Thickness and type on the delivery note, checked against the schedule.
Sources
  • Beirut Urban Lab, on the port blast response: 384 organisations registered with the army, repeated contradictory surveys, October 2020 beiruturbanlab.com
  • ReliefWeb, participation of local and international civil society in the Beirut port blast response, shared zone assignment reliefweb.int
  • NEAR, locally-led recovery after Cyclone Remal and floods in Bangladesh near.ngo
  • Sphere Handbook 2018, Shelter and Settlement, and the Core Humanitarian Standard on avoiding duplication handbook.spherestandards.org
5 Schooling, tutoring and school meals
Why this one

Template 5: tutoring term and school meal round

Lebanese public schools struggle to open through strikes and power cuts, and displaced children lose whole years. BRAC's answer in Bangladesh was about 23,000 one-room schools in rented premises with almost no capital cost, and Greek municipalities ran free exam tutoring with volunteer teachers. A municipality can buy one term at a time.

Step 1 · Classify

4 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Remedial and exam tutoring termChildren are enrolled somewhere but are behind, or are facing the brevet or the baccalaureate.After-school sessions in a municipal hall or a school building, a fixed subject list, a baseline test at the start and the same test at the end, and a register taken at every session.learner-term
One-room classChildren are out of school entirely, usually displaced or working.A rented or lent room, one teacher, a small group, a compressed curriculum aimed at getting the child back into the public system, and a named route back in.class-term
School meal roundChildren come to school hungry, or come only because there is food.One meal or snack per school day, cooked to a written menu, delivered to a named school, counted by the school rather than by the cook.meal
Back-to-school kit roundThe barrier is a bag, books, shoes or the registration fee.A standard kit against a written content list, or the fee paid directly to the school rather than to the family, with the school's receipt as the proof.learner
Step 2 · The milestones

7 milestones, each with the proof it needs and the check it must pass

#MilestoneEvidence the expert uploadsPass mark the verifier checks
0Scope, class and baseline
Agree with the school director and the municipality who the children are and what they are missing. Run the baseline test. Choose the class and fix the target.		Coded learner list with age and year group, no names. Written agreement from the school director. Baseline test papers scored, held by code. Room photos and seating count. Class chosen and target number of learners.Every learner on the list is agreed with a named school director or the municipality. The baseline test is the same paper that will be used at the end. Seats in the room match the learner count. Group size is at or below 25 learners per teacher (to confirm); anything larger is a hall, not a class.
1Teachers, safeguarding and premises
Hire or recruit the teachers. Run the child protection briefing. Check the room is safe: two exits, light, a toilet, a fire extinguisher.		Teacher list with qualifications and the signed code of conduct for each. Child protection briefing attendance sheet. Photos of the room, exits, lighting, toilet, fire extinguisher with a service date. Named safeguarding focal point with a contact route for children.Every adult who will be alone with children has signed the code of conduct and been briefed, with no exceptions for volunteers. A named safeguarding focal point exists and children are told who it is. The room has two ways out and a working toilet. No session runs in a room that fails this.
2Materials and meals in
Buy the books, the stationery and, for the meal class, the food. Photograph the stock. Keep the receipts.		Invoices and three quotes per major line. Photos of stock with a counting board. Menu cycle for the meal class with the energy per portion. Kit content list for the kit class.Stock photographed matches the invoice and the learner count. For meals, the menu is written down and each portion is costed; the cook does not decide the size on the day. For kits, the content list is fixed before purchase so kits cannot quietly shrink.
3Run the term
Teach the sessions. Take the register at every single one, signed by the teacher. Serve the meals, counted by the school.		Signed attendance register per session, by learner code. Weekly attendance summary. Photos of the class in session, taken from the back so faces are not the subject, one per week. For meals, the school's own daily count signed by a school staff member.Sessions delivered match sessions commissioned. Average attendance is 80 per cent or more of the enrolled learners across the term (to confirm); below that, the term is under-delivered even if every session ran. Meal counts are signed by the school, not the supplier. No photograph identifies a child by name.
4De-duplication and call-backs
Check the coded list against the school's own rolls and against other tutoring projects in the town. Hand the verifier the coded list and consented parent numbers.		Coded list, unique learner count, duplication note naming which rolls and which other projects were compared. Consent record from parents or guardians.Duplicates under 5 per cent of the list (to confirm). The verifier rings a random 10 per cent of coded entries and speaks to the parent or guardian, never the child; at least 8 in 10 of those reached confirm the child attended, roughly as often as claimed, and that nothing was paid. The expert keeps the named list. It is never uploaded. Each person gets a code like KIT-014 and the upload is the coded list plus totals. The verifier rings a random sample on numbers people agreed to be rung on, and asks only what they got and when. If the verifier needs the named list, a Lebanese auditor reads it at the NGO's office under a signed confidentiality undertaking and reports only two things: the count and the number of duplicates.
5Endline and route back into school
Run the same test again. For the one-room class, get each child a named place in a public school for the next year.		Endline test papers scored by code, with the baseline score beside it. A table of score movement. For the one-room class, a letter or registration reference per child from a named public school. Teacher's note on children who did not improve.Endline is the same paper as the baseline and marked the same way. Median score has risen; an agreed improvement threshold is set at scoping and checked here (to confirm). For the one-room class, at least 70 per cent of learners have a named school place for the next year (to confirm). Children who did not improve are named by code and have a stated next step.
6Close-out and handover
Hand the books, the furniture and the register to the school or the municipality. Write the close-out page.		Signed handover note. Photos of what was handed over. Close-out page: learners enrolled, unique learners, sessions run, average attendance, score movement, cost per learner-term, meals served.Handover note carries a name, a title and a date. Materials stay with the school, not the NGO. Cost per learner-term is stated. This is the gate for the final release.
Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Scope within 10 working days, and always align to the school calendar; a tutoring term commissioned in May is wasted. Teachers, safeguarding and premises within 21 days. A term is 12 weeks of sessions. Meals run for the school year or for a stated block of school days. Endline in the final two weeks. Close-out within 10 days of the last session. No warranty applies, but the score movement at milestone 5 is the equivalent check, and the register is kept for three years.

Money

Tutoring is priced per learner-term, which keeps the incentive on children finishing rather than starting. A one-room class is priced per class-term, covering rent, one teacher and materials, because that is how BRAC keeps the capital cost near zero. Meals are priced per meal at receipt cost plus a stated preparation fee. Kits are priced per learner against the fixed content list. No public Lebanese rate exists for NGO tutoring; bracket from the first three real bids. Not included: teacher salaries in the public system, transport for learners unless stated as a separate line, or examination fees.

Release

Nothing up front. 15 per cent at milestone 2, when materials are bought and photographed. 50 per cent at milestone 3, against the signed registers and the attendance threshold. 35 per cent at milestone 5, after the endline and the school places. If average attendance falls below 80 per cent, the milestone 3 release is cut in proportion rather than refused, so the teacher is still paid for the sessions that ran.

Who signs off. The Ministry of Education and Higher Education governs anything that looks like schooling and owns most of the buildings; non-formal education runs under its framework and a project outside it cannot lead anywhere. The school director must agree in writing to the use of the premises and the hours. The municipality approves a hall and the hours children are there. The Ministry of Social Affairs holds the NGO registration. The Ministry of Public Health inspects any kitchen making school meals. Child protection is not optional: every adult signs a code of conduct and the municipality should hold the safeguarding focal point's name.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Enrolment counted as attendance. Eighty names on a list and twelve children in the room. Paying per enrolled learner rewards exactly this. Milestone 3. The per-session signed register and the 80 per cent threshold.
  • No baseline. Without a first test there is nothing to compare, so 'the children improved' cannot be checked or disproved. Milestone 0. The baseline is a gate before teaching starts, not a report written at the end.
  • Tutoring that leads nowhere. A year of lessons outside the system, with no route into a public school, leaves the child exactly where they were. Milestone 5. The named school place is a counted pass mark.
  • Unvetted adults. Volunteer teaching projects recruit fast and check slowly. The harm is irreversible. Milestone 1. Code of conduct and briefing before any adult is alone with children, no exceptions.
  • Photographs of children. Pictures of identifiable displaced children, published for a donor, follow them for life. Milestone 3. Photos are taken from the back and carry codes; any identifying image fails the milestone.
Sources
  • Education Above All with BRAC, one-room schools in rented community premises, about 23,000 schools educationaboveall.org
  • Athens Coordination Centre for Migrant and Refugee Issues, social school tutoring by volunteer teachers accmr.gr
  • Akshaya Patra Foundation, school meals for about 2.35 million children per school day, ISO certified kitchens akshayapatra.org
  • Human Rights Watch, World Report 2022, Lebanon: poverty at 78 per cent and blackouts up to 23 hours a day hrw.org
6 Energy for critical facilities
Why this one

Template 6: rooftop solar for a critical facility

Lebanon's grid fell from about 18 hours a day to one or two, with blackouts reaching 23 hours, and hospitals came close to shutting down. Direct Relief funded solar at four health centres in Akkar and Saida with a 50,000 dollar grant and patient capacity rose 32 per cent. Lebanon gets about 300 sunny days a year, so the sun is the one input that never fails to arrive.

Step 1 · Classify

4 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Solar and battery for a clinicA primary healthcare centre or dispensary cannot keep vaccines cold or lights on.Roof survey, panels, inverter, battery sized for the critical loads only, changeover switching, earthing, a meter, and a maintenance contract. Critical loads are the fridge, the lights, the sterilizer and the pump.kWp installed
Solar pumping for waterA well, a borehole or a pumping station is idle because there is no power and no fuel.Pump survey and yield check, panels sized to the pump, a direct-drive or battery-backed controller, dry-run protection, and a flow meter so the water actually produced can be counted.kWp installed
Solar for a school or shelterA building full of people has no light after dark and no way to charge anything.Panels, inverter, a small battery, lighting circuits, and charging points, sized for lights and sockets rather than for air conditioning.kWp installed
Fuel bridge with meteringSolar cannot be installed in time and the facility will stop this month.A capped monthly fuel supply delivered against metered generator hours, with a written exit date and a solar design commissioned in parallel. Never open-ended.litre of fuel, against metered hours
Step 2 · The milestones

7 milestones, each with the proof it needs and the check it must pass

#MilestoneEvidence the expert uploadsPass mark the verifier checks
0Load survey, roof survey and class
Measure what the building actually uses, hour by hour, for a week. Look at the roof: age, slope, shading, and whether it can carry the weight. Choose the class and the size.		Week-long load log or a clamp-meter reading per circuit. List of critical loads with their watts and daily hours. Roof photos from four sides, plus a shading photo at morning, noon and afternoon. Structural note from a licensed engineer. GPS pin. Class and kWp chosen.Critical loads are listed with watts and hours, and the design is sized to them, not to the whole building. A structural note from an engineer registered with the Order of Engineers confirms the roof can carry the array. Shading is photographed at three times of day. The design yield is stated in kilowatt hours per year with the assumptions written out.
1Design, permits and the facility's agreement
Get the design stamped. Tell Electricité du Liban or the local generator operator. Get the facility to sign that it will keep the system and pay for maintenance after handover.		Stamped single-line diagram with the engineer's Order of Engineers number. Municipality permit reference. Letter to Electricité du Liban or the licensed generator operator. Signed maintenance undertaking from the facility naming who pays and who calls. Equipment specification sheets with brand, model and warranty.Single-line diagram is stamped and current. The facility has signed, by name and title, that it owns and maintains the system after handover; without that signature the system is abandoned on day 400. Panel and inverter warranties are written down: typically 10 years on the panel product, 25 years on panel performance and 5 years on the inverter (to confirm against the supplier's own sheet).
2Delivery and goods inspection
Receive the equipment. Photograph serial numbers. Check the batteries are the chemistry and capacity ordered, because this is where substitution happens.		Photos of every panel pallet, inverter and battery with serial numbers legible. Packing list against the purchase order. Battery data sheet showing chemistry, capacity in kilowatt hours and cycle life. Customs and import papers.Serial numbers photographed match the packing list one for one. Battery chemistry and capacity match the design; lead-acid delivered against a lithium design fails the milestone. Panel wattage on the label matches the design. Nothing is installed before this check.
3Install, earth and label
Mount the array, run the cables, fit the isolators, earth everything, and label every switch in Arabic so a caretaker can shut it down safely.		Photos of the mounting feet and roof penetrations sealed. Photo of the earth electrode and the earth connection. Photos of the DC and AC isolators and the labelled distribution board. Cable specification. Installer's certificate with a name and a licence number.A DC isolator is fitted next to the array and an AC isolator next to the inverter, both photographed and labelled. Earthing is installed and photographed; an unearthed array on a clinic roof fails outright. Roof penetrations are sealed and photographed before anything covers them. Labels are in Arabic.
4Commission and metered performance
Switch on. Record the meter. Leave it running for 30 days and read the meter again. Simulate a grid failure and time the changeover.		Commissioning test sheet: open-circuit voltage per string, insulation resistance, earth continuity. Meter photo at start and at 30 days. Inverter data export or daily readings. Video or timed note of the changeover test. Photo of the fridge temperature log across the 30 days for the clinic class.Measured generation over 30 days is at least 80 per cent of the modelled yield for those dates (to confirm against the design); below that, something is shaded, dirty, mis-wired or missing. The changeover keeps the critical loads alive. For the clinic class, the fridge log shows 2 to 8 degrees Celsius throughout. For the pumping class, the flow meter shows the cubic metres actually pumped.
5Training and handover
Train two named people at the facility: how to read the meter, how to clean the panels, how to isolate in an emergency, what not to touch. Hand over the manuals in Arabic.		Signed training sheet with two named staff and their roles. Photos of the training. Arabic operating instructions fixed to the wall next to the board. Maintenance schedule with dates. Signed handover note listing every item with its serial number.Two named people, not one, can show the verifier how to isolate the system. Instructions are on the wall, in Arabic, not in a folder in a drawer. The handover note lists serial numbers, so a panel that disappears can be traced.
6Twelve-month savings check
Come back after a year. Read the meter. Compare the fuel bought this year against last year and count the hours the facility stayed open.		Meter reading at 12 months with a photo. Fuel purchase records for the year before and the year after. Facility's own record of opening hours or patients seen. Maintenance log showing cleaning dates. Photos of the array showing dust and any broken panels.Generation over 12 months is within 20 per cent of the modelled annual yield (to confirm). Fuel spend has fallen and the figure is stated in both currencies used. The maintenance log shows the panels were cleaned at least four times (to confirm). Direct Relief's clinics recorded a 32 per cent rise in patient capacity, which is the kind of number this check is looking for. This is the gate for the final release.
Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Survey within 10 working days. Design stamped and permits lodged within 21 days. Equipment on site within 60 days, longer if it is imported, and the import lead time must be written into the programme rather than discovered. Installation within 14 days of delivery. Then the 30-day metered check, and the 12-month savings check. Warranty: 5 years on the inverter, 10 years on the panel product and 25 on its performance, and 2 years on the installation workmanship (to confirm against each supplier's sheet). A fuel bridge never runs longer than 6 months.

Money

Priced per kilowatt peak installed, with the battery priced separately per kilowatt hour of usable storage, because the battery is half the cost and the part most often substituted. Maintenance is a separate annual line, paid by the facility after year one, and the escrow does not cover it. No public Lebanese rate per kWp is available; bracket from the first three real bids. As a sanity check only, Direct Relief's 50,000 dollar grant covered resilient power at four health centres, about 12,500 dollars a centre. Not included: air conditioning, grid connection fees, roof replacement, or battery replacement after the warranty.

Release

Nothing up front. 30 per cent at milestone 2, when the equipment is on site with serial numbers photographed, because the expert has paid a supplier by then. 40 per cent at milestone 4, when the 30-day metered performance passes. 20 per cent at milestone 5, after training and handover. 10 per cent held for the full 12 months to milestone 6, which is what makes anyone come back and clean the panels.

Who signs off. The municipality permits the roof work. An engineer registered with the Order of Engineers stamps the structural note and the electrical design. Electricité du Liban must be informed of anything connected to its supply, and net metering runs through it and the Ministry of Energy and Water; where the building runs on a private generator, the licensed operator has to agree to the changeover arrangement. The Lebanese Centre for Energy Conservation publishes the national guidance and should be the reference for the design. For a health facility, the Ministry of Public Health must approve work that touches the cold chain. Imported panels and batteries clear customs, and that lead time belongs in the programme.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Sized for the building, not the critical loads. An array sized for air conditioning costs three times as much and still fails in December. Sizing to the fridge, the lights and the pump is what keeps a clinic open. Milestone 0. The critical load list is the basis of the design and the verifier checks the design against it.
  • Battery substitution. The design says lithium with a stated cycle life, the crate holds cheap lead-acid, and the system dies in two winters. The cost difference goes in someone's pocket. Milestone 2. Serial numbers and the battery data sheet checked before installation.
  • No earthing, no isolators. An unearthed roof array on a clinic is a fire and a shock risk, and nobody notices until it kills someone. Milestone 3. Earth electrode and both isolators photographed, or the milestone fails.
  • Nobody owns it. Systems handed to a facility with no named maintainer and no cleaning budget lose a third of their output to dust within a year. Milestone 1 signed undertaking, milestone 5 two trained people, milestone 6 cleaning log.
  • The fuel bridge that never ends. Free diesel is easier than installing solar, so the bridge becomes the project and the sponsor funds fuel for ever. Milestone 0 and 1. A fuel bridge is only commissioned with a written exit date and a solar design running in parallel.
Sources
  • Direct Relief, solar for four health centres in Akkar and Saida, 50,000 dollar grant, 32 per cent rise in patient capacity, grid at one to two hours a day, 2022 directrelief.org
  • Energy Transition, solar power in Lebanon during the crisis, 2023 energytransition.org
  • Devex, Lebanon's health sector races toward solar power amid electricity cuts devex.com
  • Human Rights Watch, World Report 2022, Lebanon: blackouts up to 23 hours a day hrw.org
7 Waste collection
Why this one

Template 7: door-to-door collection round

Municipal waste budgets collapsed with the currency, and refugee-hosting towns carry the load Jordan's towns already know. Pune's SWaCH cooperative shows the shape of the answer: over 3,500 waste pickers on a municipal contract, a collecting pair covering 150 to 400 households, and about 6.8 million dollars a year raised from household fees rather than from the town budget.

Step 1 · Classify

4 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Door-to-door collection roundA neighbourhood is not on the municipal round at all, or the round has stopped.A named crew collecting from a fixed list of households on fixed days, with bins, a cart or a small truck, protective gear, and a route sheet. Priced per household per month.household-month
Sorting at source campaignCollection exists but everything goes to one bin and there is nothing to sell.Two bins or bags per household, door-to-door explanation in Arabic, stickers, a school session, and a measured contamination rate before and after.household
Sorting point and recyclables saleMaterial is being collected but there is nowhere to sort it and nobody is buying.A covered, drained, fenced sorting area, tables, balers or bag stands, scales, protective gear, and a written buyer agreement so the material actually leaves.tonne sorted
Illegal dump clearance and closureThere is an open dump or a burning site, usually at the edge of the village.Clearing the site to a legal destination, then closing it: a barrier, signage, lighting where possible, and a replacement collection point, because a cleared dump with no alternative refills in three weeks.site
Step 2 · The milestones

7 milestones, each with the proof it needs and the check it must pass

#MilestoneEvidence the expert uploadsPass mark the verifier checks
0Scope, class and baseline weight
Walk the area with the municipality. Count households. Weigh what comes out for one week. Find out who currently collects, formally or informally, and do not put them out of work.		Coded household list with street and bin point, no names. Baseline weight for one week, measured on scales. Photos of the current situation at each collection point. A note on existing informal collectors, how many and what they earn. Class chosen. GPS pins.Household count is agreed with the municipality. Baseline weight is measured on scales, not estimated from bin volume. Existing informal collectors are counted and there is a written answer on whether they join the crew; Pune's cooperative works because it organised the pickers rather than replacing them.
1Contract, crew and safety
Get the municipal contract signed, with the route, the days and the destination site named. Equip and vaccinate the crew. Register the vehicle.		Signed municipal contract or decision reference naming route, frequency and legal destination. Crew list with roles. Photos of every worker in gloves, boots, high-visibility vest and mask. Vaccination record held by the NGO, reported as a count only. Vehicle or cart registration and insurance. Signed safety briefing.The contract names the legal destination site; a round with nowhere legal to tip becomes a new dump. Every worker in the photos has gloves, boots and a high-visibility vest. Tetanus and hepatitis B cover is recorded for every worker, reported as a count with no names (to confirm the Lebanese schedule with the Ministry of Public Health). Insurance covers the crew and the vehicle.
2Bins out and households told
Deliver the bins or bags. Knock on every door on the list and explain the days and the sorting rule in Arabic.		Signed coded delivery sheet for bins. Photos of the leaflet and the sticker in Arabic. Photos of bins in place at the collection points. Route sheet posted publicly and a phone number for complaints.Bins delivered match the household list within 5 per cent. The collection days are published where residents can see them and a working complaints number exists. Material in Arabic, not only in English or French.
3Run the round and weigh it
Collect on the published days. Weigh every load at the destination. Log misses and complaints the same day.		Weighbridge tickets or scale photos per load, with date and time. Daily route sheet signed by the crew leader. Complaints log with dates raised and dates closed. One dated photo per week of the collection point after the round, showing it empty.At least 90 per cent of scheduled collections happened on the published day (to confirm at scoping). Tonnage tipped matches the weighbridge tickets. Every complaint has a closing date within 7 days. The weekly point photos show the point empty after collection, not before.
4Sorting, sale and contamination check
Sort the recyclables. Weigh each stream. Sell them and keep the buyer's receipt. Measure the contamination rate on a sample of bags.		Weights by stream: paper, plastic, metal, glass, organic, residual. Buyer receipts showing tonnes and price. Photos of baled or bagged material before it leaves. A contamination sample: 20 bags opened, contamination recorded as a percentage.Stream weights add up to the tonnage collected within 10 per cent. Every tonne sold has a buyer receipt with a price on it, and the income is shown in the project accounts rather than disappearing. Contamination has fallen against the baseline for the sorting-at-source class. Nothing is burned; a burn mark on site fails the milestone.
5Resident call-backs and fee collection
Hand the verifier the coded household list and the consented numbers. Show what was actually collected in fees.		Coded household list with collection record. Consent record. Fee collection record by code: how many households paid, how many were exempted, total collected. Duplication note against the municipal round.The verifier rings a random 10 per cent of coded households; at least 8 in 10 of those reached confirm collection happened on roughly the published days and that no extra payment was demanded at the door. Fee collection rate is stated as a percentage and exemptions are counted, not hidden. The expert keeps the named list. It is never uploaded. Each person gets a code like KIT-014 and the upload is the coded list plus totals. The verifier rings a random sample on numbers people agreed to be rung on, and asks only what they got and when. If the verifier needs the named list, a Lebanese auditor reads it at the NGO's office under a signed confidentiality undertaking and reports only two things: the count and the number of duplicates.
6Ninety-day check and handover
Come back after three months. Is the round still running without the project? Is the old dump still closed?		Photos from the same spots as milestone 3 and, for the dump class, the same spot as clearance, dated 90 days or more later. Tonnage trend for the three months. Signed handover note naming who runs the round next and how it is paid for. Close-out page: households served, tonnes collected, tonnes diverted from landfill, recyclable income, cost per household-month.The cleared dump is still clear in the 90-day photo, and there is a working alternative collection point beside it; a refilled site is a failed project regardless of how well the clearance went. A named body runs the round after handover with a stated income source. Cost per household-month is stated. This is the gate for the final release.
Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Scope within 10 working days. Contract, crew and safety within 21 days. Bins out and the round running within 30 days. A round is commissioned in blocks of 3 months. Illegal dump clearance happens within 14 days of the contract, because a burning dump is a health emergency. Then the 90-day check. Warranty applies only to the bins and the sorting point structure, normally 12 months from the supplier.

Money

Collection is priced per household per month, which is the only unit that lets a municipality compare bids and lets a cooperative survive. Sorting is priced per tonne. Dump clearance is priced per cubic metre or per site with the tipping fee shown separately. Recyclable income is declared and deducted from the invoice, so the sponsor is not paying for material the crew has already sold. No public Lebanese household fee is available; bracket it from the first three real bids and from what households say they can pay (to confirm). Pune's cooperative raises about 6.8 million dollars a year in user fees across 2.3 million residents, which is the model rather than the rate. Not included: landfill construction, treatment plants, medical waste, or anything hazardous.

Release

Nothing up front except a bin and equipment float of up to 25 per cent released at milestone 2 against invoices and photographs, because a crew cannot start with no cart and no gloves. 45 per cent at milestone 3 and 4, against weighbridge tickets and the 90 per cent service rate. 30 per cent at milestone 6, after the 90-day check. If the service rate falls below 90 per cent, the release is cut in proportion to the collections actually made.

Who signs off. The municipality holds the legal duty for waste and must sign the contract, the route and the frequency; without a municipal decision the round is informal and nobody has to keep paying for it. The Ministry of Environment governs where waste may be tipped, sorting site approval and anything hazardous. Open burning is prohibited and must never be part of the method. The Ministry of Public Health covers the crew's vaccination and any medical waste found in the stream, which must be separated and never handled by the crew. Vehicles need registration and insurance, and the crew needs National Social Security Fund cover or an equivalent written insurance. Where the union of municipalities runs a regional facility, it has to agree to receive the tonnage.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Collected, then dumped. The load leaves the street and ends up in a valley or a burn pile. The street looks fixed and the problem moved. Milestone 3 and 4. Weighbridge tickets at a named legal destination, and stream weights that must add up.
  • The cleared dump that refills. Clearing without a replacement collection point buys three weeks. It is the most repeated waste of money in this sector. Milestone 6. The 90-day same-spot photo and the requirement for a working alternative.
  • Crew without gear or cover. People sorting mixed waste by hand catch tetanus and hepatitis, and glass and syringes are in every load. Milestone 1. Gear in the photos, vaccination counted, insurance on file.
  • Informal collectors pushed out. A funded round can destroy the livelihood of the people already doing the work, and they will not cooperate afterwards. Milestone 0. They are counted and the contract has to answer for them.
  • Recyclable income kept quiet. The crew sells the metal and the sponsor still pays the full cost. It also hides how viable the round really is. Milestone 4. Buyer receipts with prices, income declared and deducted.
Sources
  • SWaCH Pune Seva Sahakari Sanstha, waste picker cooperative: 3,500 plus members, 150 to 400 households per collecting pair, about 6.8 million dollars a year in user fees prizeforcities.org
  • Spatial Collective, rethinking waste management in Nairobi's informal settlements spatialcollective.com
  • Waste Management and Research, solid waste in refugee-hosting municipalities doi.org
  • Women's self-help groups on municipal sanitation contracts, India forum.susana.org
8 Water points and sanitation
Why this one

Template 8: water point and sanitation round

Lebanese water establishments cannot pump without power or fuel, so villages and shelters live on trucked or local water. Five schools in Aley needed four water trucks a day each just for washing. A protected spring in Kenya serving 224 people has stayed functional through checkups every three months since 2020, which is what a small, owned, maintained water point looks like.

Step 1 · Classify

4 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Spring or source protectionThe village already drinks from a spring or a shallow source that is open to contamination.A waterproof cement catchment over the eye of the spring, a discharge pipe, headwall and wing walls, a drainage channel below and diversion channels above, stone pitching, fencing, and a trained water committee.source
Water point rehabilitationA standpipe, tank, pump or short length of network exists but has failed.Finding and fixing the fault, replacing taps and valves, cleaning and disinfecting the tank, fitting a meter, and a leak survey on the pipe run so the repair is not undone next door.water point
Latrine and shower blockA collective shelter or a public building has toilets built for a school day, not for living.New or refitted cubicles with lockable doors and lighting, separated by sex, hand-washing points, a septic tank or a connection, a desludging arrangement, and cleaning materials for the first 30 days.cubicle
Household water treatment and hygiene roundWater reaches the house but is not safe, and the fix is needed this week.Jerricans, a household filter or chlorine tablets with a written dose, a door-to-door explanation in Arabic, and residual chlorine testing at a sample of houses to prove the dose is actually being used.household
Step 2 · The milestones

7 milestones, each with the proof it needs and the check it must pass

#MilestoneEvidence the expert uploadsPass mark the verifier checks
0Scope, class and water quality baseline
Count the people who will use the point. Find where they get water now and how long it takes. Take a water sample and have it tested. Choose the class.		GPS pin. Photos of the source or the block as found. User count by household and by head. Walking time and queue time measured, not asked. Laboratory test result for the source: faecal coliforms, and free residual chlorine if chlorinated. Class chosen.User count is agreed with the municipality. Walking distance and queue time are measured against the Sphere figures of 500 metres to the water point and 30 minutes queuing. A laboratory test exists before any work; no source is called safe on the strength of it being clear. Existing toilet count compared against one toilet per 20 people, separated by sex.
1Permission, ownership and the committee
Confirm who owns the water and the land. Get the Water Establishment's approval for anything touching the network or an abstraction. Form the water committee and train it before the work, not after.		Letter or reference from the regional Water Establishment. Municipality permit. Landowner's written consent for a source on private land. Committee list with roles: chair, treasurer, two maintainers, at least one third women. Signed training attendance for the one-day committee training. Bank or account arrangement for the repair fund.A named authority has approved the abstraction or the connection in writing; a spring capped without the Water Establishment's approval is a dispute waiting to happen. The committee exists on paper with named roles and a repair fund account before construction starts. Women are on the committee, because women carry the water.
2Materials and community contribution
Buy the cement, pipe, mesh and fittings. Log what the community contributes in materials and labour, because that is what makes it theirs.		Invoices and three quotes per major line. Photos of materials delivered on site with quantities visible. Cement bag count. Pipe specification with diameter and pressure rating. Log of community labour days and donated materials, valued.Materials on site match the invoice and the design quantities. Pipe pressure rating matches the design; thin pipe on a pumped line fails within a season. The community contribution is recorded in days and in materials, as the Kenyan harambee model does, so the committee has a stake it can point to.
3Build or repair
Do the work. Photograph everything that will be buried or covered before it disappears. For the block class, fit locks and lights the same day as the doors.		Progress photos from one fixed spot, at least weekly. Photos of reinforcement, the tarp and mesh foundation, and pipe bedding before backfill. Photo of the discharge pipe and the drainage channel. For blocks: photos of each cubicle door, lock, light and hand-washing point. Plumber's or mason's note with a name.Everything buried is photographed before backfill; there is no way to check it later. Surface water is diverted above the spring and drains away below it, both visible in photos. Every cubicle has a door that locks from the inside and a working light. Men's and women's blocks are separate and signed in Arabic. Hand-washing point within a few steps of each block.
4Test, disinfect and commission
Disinfect the tank or the new works. Run the water. Test it again at a laboratory. Measure the flow and the queue.		Disinfection record with the dose and the contact time. Post-works laboratory test result. Flow measurement in litres per minute, timed with a container. Photos of people using the point on the first day. Residual chlorine readings at three points for the chlorinated classes.Post-works laboratory test shows no faecal coliforms in 100 millilitres for drinking water, which is the World Health Organization guideline and the Sphere requirement. Where water is chlorinated, free residual chlorine at the tap is 0.2 to 0.5 milligrams per litre. Measured flow supports at least 15 litres per person per day for the counted users, the Sphere minimum. Queue time under 30 minutes at the busiest hour.
5Committee running and user call-backs
Hand the point to the committee with a tool kit and a spares list. Start the small monthly fee into the repair fund. Give the verifier the coded user list and the consented numbers.		Signed handover to the committee with a tool and spares list. First two months of fund records: collected, exempted, spent. Coded user list with consent record. Photo of the repair fund's written rules posted at the point.Fund rules are posted where users can read them, in Arabic. The verifier rings a random 10 per cent of coded users; at least 8 in 10 of those reached confirm the point works, that they know who to tell when it breaks, and that no one demanded a payment beyond the posted fee. Exemptions for the poorest households are written into the rules and counted. The expert keeps the named list. It is never uploaded. Each person gets a code like KIT-014 and the upload is the coded list plus totals. The verifier rings a random sample on numbers people agreed to be rung on, and asks only what they got and when. If the verifier needs the named list, a Lebanese auditor reads it at the NGO's office under a signed confidentiality undertaking and reports only two things: the count and the number of duplicates.
6Ninety-day functionality check
Come back after three months. Turn the tap. Read the fund book. Take one more water test.		Photos from the same spots as milestone 3, dated 90 days or more later. Water test result at 90 days. Fund book photographed showing balance and any repair paid for. Maintenance log. Desludging record for the block class.The point is functional on the day of the visit, which is the single check the Kenyan project has repeated every three months since 2020. The 90-day water test still meets the milestone 4 limits. The repair fund has a balance and any breakdown was fixed within 7 days. Septic tanks have a named desludger and a first date. This is the gate for the final release.
Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Inspect within 5 working days, or within 48 hours if people are drinking from an unprotected source or a shelter has no working toilet. Permissions and committee within 21 days. Construction within 45 days for a source or a block, within 14 days for a repair, and shelter blocks before the first week of November if winter is the reason. Then the 90-day functionality check. Warranty: 12 months on plumbing, fittings and pumps; 24 months on the masonry of a protected source (to confirm).

Money

Priced per source, per water point, per cubicle or per household depending on class. The community contribution in labour and local materials is shown as a line at a valued rate, not hidden, so the real cost is visible. Water testing is a separate line and is never optional. No public Lebanese unit rate exists for spring protection or a shelter latrine block; bracket from the first three real bids. Not included: network extension beyond the agreed run, drilling a new borehole, pumping station rebuilds, or the electricity to run a pump, which belongs in the solar template.

Release

Nothing up front. 20 per cent at milestone 2, when materials are on site and photographed. 45 per cent at milestone 4, when the post-works water test and the flow measurement pass; a failed bacteriological test blocks this release entirely, however good the concrete looks. 20 per cent at milestone 5, after handover to a working committee. 15 per cent at milestone 6, after the 90-day check.

Who signs off. The regional Water Establishment, meaning Beirut and Mount Lebanon, North Lebanon, South Lebanon or Bekaa, owns the network and must approve any connection, any abstraction and any new source. The Ministry of Energy and Water governs wells and groundwater. The municipality permits the works and the land use. The Ministry of Public Health sets the drinking water standard and runs the laboratories that test it; LIBNOR publishes the Lebanese standard for drinking water. An engineer registered with the Order of Engineers signs anything structural or any tank above ground. For a source on private land, the owner's written consent is needed before a single bag of cement is bought. Septic tanks and discharge need the Ministry of Environment's rules followed.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Built but never tested. A beautiful cement structure over a contaminated spring gives people confidence in water that is still making them ill. Milestone 0 and 4. A laboratory test before and after, and the release is blocked on a fail.
  • No surface water diversion. Rain runs straight into the spring eye and the protection is undone in the first storm. It is the most common spring protection fault. Milestone 3. The diversion channel above and the drainage below, both photographed.
  • No committee, no fund. A water point with nobody named to fix it lasts until the first broken tap. The Kenyan model works because the committee and the savings account come first. Milestone 1 and 5. The committee is formed before construction and the fund book is checked at 90 days.
  • Toilets nobody will use. No lock, no light, or a shared block for men and women, and women and girls stop using it after dark and go back to open defecation. Milestone 3. Locks, lights and separation are explicit photographed pass marks.
  • The septic tank with no desludger. A new block fills up in months and overflows into the street, which is worse than the toilets it replaced. Milestone 6. A named desludger and a first date, checked at 90 days.
Sources
  • The Water Project, Kenya spring protection and WASH project 20167: 224 people served, one-day committee training, functionality checkups every three months since July 2020 thewaterproject.org
  • Sphere Handbook 2018, WASH minimum standards: 15 litres per person per day, 500 metres to the water point, 30 minutes queuing, one toilet per 20 people, 0.2 to 0.5 mg/l free residual chlorine handbook.spherestandards.org
  • Al Jazeera, Lebanese schools as shelters: four water trucks a day per school in Aley, October 2024 aljazeera.com
  • ReliefWeb, the influx of Syrian refugees into Jordan and the effects on the water sector reliefweb.int
