9 Legal aid and documentation
Why this one

Template 9: legal aid desk

A child without a birth registration cannot enrol in school, and a family without a tenancy paper can be evicted in a week. The Norwegian Refugee Council reached 48,301 people with information, counselling and legal assistance in Jordan in 2025, and displaced families in Lebanon hit the same documentation and housing walls. A desk is cheap; the consequences of not having one are not.

Step 1 · Classify

4 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Civil documentation deskBirths, marriages and deaths are unregistered, or identity papers are lost or destroyed.Screening, explaining the steps in Arabic, preparing the file, accompanying people to the registry where needed, and following each case until it closes or is formally stuck.case
Residency and legal stay counsellingPeople cannot renew or regularise their stay and so cannot move, work or report a crime.An assessment of the route available to that person, the paperwork, referral to a lawyer where a lawyer is required, and a written note of what was advised and when.case
Housing, land and property deskEvictions, rent disputes, damaged property or a landlord holding papers.Reviewing the tenancy, writing to the landlord, negotiating, and referring to a registered lawyer when a court is unavoidable. Eviction cases are treated as urgent and jump the queue.case
Labour rights and wage claims deskUnpaid wages, unsafe work or a withheld work permit, common among cash-for-work and construction crews.Recording the claim, writing to the employer, referring to the Ministry of Labour or a lawyer, and tracking recovery.case
Step 2 · The milestones

7 milestones, each with the proof it needs and the check it must pass

#MilestoneEvidence the expert uploadsPass mark the verifier checks
0Scope, class and caseload target
Agree with the municipality and a community centre where the desk sits and which days it opens. Map what people actually need by asking, not by guessing. Set the caseload target.		Written agreement with the host centre or municipality naming days and hours. A short needs note from a sample of conversations, counted by type, with no names. Class chosen. Caseload target and the expected mix of case types. Privacy and data plan, one page.Opening days and hours are published somewhere a resident can find them. The needs note is built from counted conversations, not assumption. The privacy plan says where files are stored, who can open them, how long they are kept and when they are destroyed, before a single case is opened.
1Staff, bar association and consent forms
Hire or second the caseworkers. Confirm that anyone representing a client in court is a registered lawyer. Print the consent form in Arabic and make sure every caseworker can explain it.		Caseworker list with qualifications and signed confidentiality undertakings. Bar association registration numbers for any lawyer. Sample consent form in Arabic. Signed briefing sheet on confidentiality and on referral routes. Lockable cabinet or encrypted storage, photographed.Only a lawyer registered with the Beirut or Tripoli Bar Association appears before a court; a caseworker who is not a lawyer may advise and prepare but may not represent. Every caseworker has signed a confidentiality undertaking. The consent form is in Arabic and explains that saying no does not cost the person their help. Files are locked or encrypted, photographed as proof.
2Open the desk and record intake
Open on the published days. Open a file per case with a code, the case type, the date, and the consent recorded. Screen out what the desk cannot do and refer it on the same day.		Intake register by code: case type, date opened, sex and age band, referral in or out. Daily attendance count. Photos of the desk and the waiting arrangement showing a private space to talk. Referral directory used.Every case has a code, a type, a date and a recorded consent. There is a space where a person can speak without being overheard, visible in the photo; a legal aid desk in an open hall is not a legal aid desk. Cases the desk cannot handle are referred out within one working day and the referral is recorded.
3Casework and progress
Work the cases. Record every step with a date. Chase the registry, the landlord or the employer. Keep the client told.		Case log by code showing steps taken with dates, and the date the client was last updated. Counted totals by type and by stage. Copies of letters sent, with client identifiers removed in anything uploaded. A stuck-case list with reasons.Every open case shows a step in the last 30 days or a written reason why not. Every client was updated in the last 30 days. Uploaded copies of letters carry no names, no identity numbers and no photographs of documents. The stuck-case list is honest; a desk with no stuck cases is not recording properly.
4Outcomes
Close the cases that can close. Record the outcome as it really was, including the ones that failed.		Outcome table by code: document obtained, stay regularised, eviction stopped or delayed, wages recovered with an amount, referred and closed, withdrawn, failed. Total wages or costs recovered, as a sum. Median days from opening to outcome.At least 70 per cent of cases opened in the period have a recorded outcome by the end of it (to confirm at scoping), and 'no outcome yet' is itself recorded rather than left blank. Failed cases are counted and explained. Median days from opening to outcome is stated, because a desk that takes a year is not solving an eviction.
5Independent check without seeing files
Hand the verifier the coded outcome table and the consented numbers. Arrange the auditor visit for anything that needs the named file.		Coded outcome table, totals, consent record. A signed confidentiality undertaking from the auditing lawyer. The auditor's one-page finding.The verifier rings a random 10 per cent of coded closed cases; at least 8 in 10 of those reached confirm they were seen, roughly when claimed, were told the outcome, and paid nothing. Where a file must be checked, a Lebanese lawyer bound by professional secrecy reads it at the NGO's office under a signed undertaking and reports only the count and whether the recorded outcome matches the file. The verifier never sees a client's name, nationality, address or identity document. Any upload containing one fails the milestone and is deleted.
6Close-out, referral map and handover
Write up what the caseload showed about the law and the registry, because that is the part a municipality can act on. Hand the referral map to the municipality. Archive or destroy the files as the privacy plan says.		Close-out page: cases opened, closed, by type, outcomes, median days, amounts recovered, cost per case. A pattern note: the three barriers that came up most. Updated referral map handed to the municipality. Signed record of what was archived and what was destroyed.The pattern note names specific, checkable barriers rather than general complaints; it is the thing the municipality can take to a ministry. Files are archived or destroyed exactly as the milestone 0 privacy plan said, with a signed record. Cost per case is stated. This is the gate for the final release.
Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Scope within 10 working days. Staff, consent forms and secure storage within 21 days. The desk opens within 30 days and is commissioned in blocks of 3 months. Eviction and detention cases are seen within 48 hours of walking in, whatever the queue. Every client is updated at least every 30 days. Close-out within 14 days of the block ending. There is no warranty on legal work, and nobody may promise an outcome; the honest measure is the recorded outcome rate and the median days at milestone 4.

Money

Priced per case, with a different rate per class because a birth registration and an eviction defence are not the same work. Court fees, registry fees and translation are pass-through lines at receipt cost. A registered lawyer's fee for representation is a separate line and is capped. No public Lebanese rate per legal aid case is available; bracket from the first three real bids. Not included: paying fines on a client's behalf, bribes of any kind, or any payment that is not receipted and attributable to a fee schedule. A desk that cannot explain a payment has to stop.

Release

Nothing up front. 20 per cent at milestone 2, when the desk is open with secure storage and consent forms in use. 40 per cent at milestone 3, against the case log and the 30-day activity rule. 25 per cent at milestone 4, against the outcome table. 15 per cent at milestone 6, after the close-out and the archive record. Payment is never tied to winning, only to work properly done and recorded, because paying for wins pushes a desk to take only the easy cases.

Who signs off. The Beirut Bar Association and the Tripoli Bar Association regulate who may represent a client before a Lebanese court; nobody else may, whatever the NGO's registration says. The Ministry of Social Affairs holds the NGO's own registration. Civil documentation runs through the Directorate General of Personal Status and the local registry, and the municipality issues many of the underlying certificates, so the municipality has to know the desk exists. General Security handles residency. The Ministry of Labour handles work permits and wage complaints. The host community centre or municipality must agree to the premises and to a private room. Where a case involves a child, child protection referral routes apply and the desk cannot handle it alone.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Advice given, nothing tracked. Counting conversations makes a desk look busy while nobody gets a document. Advice without follow-through is not legal aid. Milestone 3 and 4. The outcome table, and the rule that every case shows a step within 30 days.
  • Non-lawyers in court. It is unlawful, it gets the case thrown out, and it exposes the client to worse than they started with. Milestone 1. Bar association registration numbers on file for anyone who represents.
  • Client data in the evidence pack. A photographed identity document or a named case list, uploaded for a verifier, can end in detention or eviction for the person it belongs to. Milestone 5. Only coded tables are uploaded; a named file is read on site by a lawyer under a confidentiality undertaking.
  • Cherry-picking easy cases. Paying per closed case pushes a desk towards simple paperwork and away from the evictions and detentions that matter most. Milestone 4. The case mix is set at scoping and the stuck-case list is compulsory.
  • Consent taken as a formality. A person who does not understand what they signed has not consented, and the call-back then becomes an unwanted phone call about their legal status. Milestone 1 and 2. The Arabic consent form, the caseworker briefing, and the call-back script that never mentions the case type.
Sources
  • Norwegian Refugee Council, Jordan: 48,301 people reached with information, counselling and legal assistance in 2025 nrc.no
  • New Lines Institute, how Jordan's midsized NGOs can help Syrian refugees newlinesinstitute.org
  • Human Rights Watch, World Report 2022, Lebanon chapter hrw.org
  • Sphere Handbook 2018 and the Core Humanitarian Standard, on protection, consent and data minimisation handbook.spherestandards.org
10 Livelihoods and cash-for-work
Why this one

Template 10: cash-for-work round

With wages worth a fraction of what they were, paying residents to fix their own town beats a handout twice over: the work gets done and the money stays local. Jordan's programmes ran mixed Syrian and Jordanian teams with a mandated 30 to 50 per cent minimum share for the host community, and 86 per cent of participants said they had made friends across the two nationalities.

Step 1 · Classify

4 classes, chosen at scoping

ClassWhenWhat it includesUnit
Municipal task roundThere is visible unskilled work the municipality cannot pay for: clearing, sweeping, drain clearing, painting, planting.Mixed teams on a fixed roster of days, paid per day worked, with a named supervisor, gear, insurance, and a task list agreed with the municipality before the first day.worker-day
Skilled crew roundThe work needs trades: masons, plumbers, electricians, glaziers, usually alongside the repair template.Trade teams paid at a skilled day rate, with a foreman, a measured output per task, and the work signed off by whoever the output belongs to.worker-day
Savings group formationThe cash round is ending and the money will leave the town with it.Forming small savings groups from the workers, a written constitution, a lockable box with three keys, a ledger, and training, so weekly savings keep circulating after the wages stop.group
Micro-enterprise start grantA worker has a trade and a plan but no tools or stock.A small grant paid as tools and stock rather than cash, against a one-page plan, with the assets photographed and a check at 90 days to see whether the enterprise is trading.enterprise
Step 2 · The milestones

7 milestones, each with the proof it needs and the check it must pass

#MilestoneEvidence the expert uploadsPass mark the verifier checks
0Scope, class, tasks and wage
Agree the task list with the municipality and what finished looks like for each task. Find out the local unskilled daily wage by asking three employers. Set the rate at or just below it. Choose the class.		Task list with a measurable output per task, agreed and signed by the municipality. Three local wage quotes with who gave them. Proposed daily rate and the number of worker-days. Class chosen. GPS pins of the work sites.Every task has an output a verifier can measure: metres of drain, square metres painted, number of trees planted. The daily rate is at or below the local unskilled market rate and the three quotes are on file; a rate above the market pulls people out of real jobs and breaks the local labour market. No public Lebanese cash-for-work rate is available, so the three quotes are the only defensible basis (to confirm).
1Selection, mix and permits
Select workers openly against published criteria. Hold the host and displaced mix. Get work permits for anyone who needs one. Arrange insurance.		Published selection criteria and where they were posted. Coded worker list with sex, age band and host or displaced status, no names. Selection committee minutes including a municipal representative. Work permit references for non-Lebanese workers. Insurance certificate covering every worker for the period. Grievance route with a phone number.The host community share is at least 30 per cent of worker-days, following the Jordanian rule of a 30 to 50 per cent minimum host share, and the displaced share is not zero either; a single-community team turns a cohesion project into a grievance. Women are a stated share of the roster, set at scoping. Every non-Lebanese worker has a work permit reference or the class is not lawful. Insurance covers every worker. A grievance number is published where workers can see it.
2Induction, gear and safety
Brief every worker on the task, the hours, the pay, the safety rules and how to complain. Hand out gear. Name the supervisor.		Signed induction sheet, one line per worker. Photos of workers in gloves, boots, high-visibility vests and, where needed, helmets and eye protection. Photo of the first aid kit and the water supply on site. Supervisor named with a contact number. Written pay terms each worker keeps a copy of.Every worker on the roster is on the induction sheet. Everyone in the working photos has gloves, boots and a vest. Drinking water and shade are on site, visible in the photos, and a first aid kit is present. Each worker holds a written note of the daily rate and the payment date; a worker who does not know what they are owed cannot report being underpaid. No one under 18 is on the roster.
3Work the roster and measure output
Run the days. Take attendance at the start and end of each day, signed by the supervisor. Measure the output against the task list.		Daily attendance sheet by worker code, signed by the supervisor and countersigned by a municipal officer at least weekly. Output measurement per task with photos before and after from the same spot. Weekly progress summary. Complaint log.Worker-days claimed match the signed attendance sheets exactly. Output measured matches the task list; 400 metres of drain claimed and 180 measured is not a rounding error. Before and after photos are from the same spot. The municipal countersignature appears at least weekly. Complaints are logged with a closing date.
4Pay and prove it reached the worker
Pay through a traceable channel on the published date. Never in an envelope through a middleman.		Payment record from the bank, mobile money or exchange operator, matched to worker codes, with names removed in the upload. Payment date against the promised date. Written record of any deduction, with the reason. Consent record for call-backs.Worker-days paid equal worker-days on the signed attendance sheets. Payment landed within the promised number of days, normally 7 after the pay period closes. The verifier rings a random 10 per cent of coded workers; at least 9 in 10 of those reached confirm the exact amount they received and that nobody took a cut, and the threshold is higher here than elsewhere because this is wages. Any report of a deduction, a kickback or a broker fee stops the release at once and goes to the municipality in writing. The expert keeps the named list. It is never uploaded. Each person gets a code like KIT-014 and the upload is the coded list plus totals. The verifier rings a random sample on numbers people agreed to be rung on, and asks only what they got and when. If the verifier needs the named list, a Lebanese auditor reads it at the NGO's office under a signed confidentiality undertaking and reports only two things: the count and the number of duplicates.
5Handover of the work and the assets
Hand the finished work to the municipality against a signature. Hand tools to the crew or the municipality, whichever the contract says, listed and photographed.		Signed acceptance note from the municipality per task, naming what was accepted. Tool list with photos and a signed handover. For the enterprise class, photos of the tools and stock with the worker, face not required, and the one-page plan.A named municipal officer has accepted each task in writing; work nobody accepts was not worth commissioning. Every tool bought is either handed over on a signed list or accounted for as consumed. No asset is left in the NGO's own store without a written reason.
6Ninety-day check on money and cohesion
Come back after three months. Is the savings group still meeting? Is the enterprise trading? Did the work last? Ask both communities how it went.		Savings group ledger photographed: members, weekly savings, loans out, balance. Photos of the work from the same spots as milestone 3, dated 90 days or more later. For the enterprise class, photos of the business trading. A short cohesion note from a sample of workers from both communities, counted, no names.The savings group has met at least 10 times in 90 days and the ledger balances (to confirm at scoping). The work is still in the state it was accepted in, or the defect is logged. At least 70 per cent of start-grant enterprises are still trading at 90 days (to confirm). The cohesion note reports what both communities said, not only the host community; Jordan's programmes measured 86 per cent reporting cross-community friendships, which is the kind of question to ask. This is the gate for the final release.
Step 3 · Time, money, release

What the numbers look like

Time

Scope within 10 working days. Selection, permits and insurance within 21 days. Work starts within 30 days. A round runs 20 working days over one month, or 16 days a month over a longer block, which are the two shapes Jordan's programmes settled on; contracts there ran from 2 weeks to 6 months. Pay within 7 days of each pay period closing, every time, because a late wage undoes the whole point. Then the 90-day check. No warranty on labour, but the work handed over at milestone 5 carries whatever warranty the task itself would carry under its own template.

Money

Priced per worker-day at a rate set from three local quotes, with unskilled and skilled rates listed separately. Tools, gear, insurance and supervision are separate lines so they cannot be taken out of the wage. Savings groups are priced per group formed and trained. Start grants are priced per enterprise and paid as goods, not cash. No public Lebanese cash-for-work rate exists; bracket it from the first three real bids and the three local wage quotes (to confirm). Not included: materials for the task, which belong to whichever template covers the task itself, and any payment to a broker or labour agent, which is never allowed.

Release

A wage float of up to 30 per cent is released at milestone 2, before the first pay date, because workers cannot wait for an escrow cycle and a project that pays late is worse than no project. 45 per cent at milestone 4, against the attendance sheets, the payment record and the call-backs. 15 per cent at milestone 5, when the municipality has accepted the work. 10 per cent at milestone 6, after the 90-day check. Wages are never held back for a quality dispute; the dispute is settled against the expert's fee, not against the workers' pay.

Who signs off. The Ministry of Labour issues work permits, and a non-Lebanese worker without one cannot lawfully be paid, which makes this the first check, not the last. The municipality is the work-giver, agrees the task list and signs the acceptance notes. The National Social Security Fund or a written accident insurance must cover every worker for the period. Where the tasks touch roads, water, electricity or waste, the relevant authority signs off as it would for that trade: the Ministry of Public Works, the regional Water Establishment, Electricité du Liban or the Ministry of Environment. Child labour is prohibited and nobody under 18 may be on the roster. The International Labour Organization's employment-intensive programmes in Lebanon are the reference for how labour-based municipal work is contracted and certified.

Step 4 · How it usually goes wrong

5 things the verifier looks for

  • Ghost workers on the sheet. Names on an attendance sheet who never came, with the wage collected by whoever wrote them down. It is the standard fraud in cash-for-work. Milestone 3 and 4. Supervisor and municipal countersignature, traceable payment, and the 9 in 10 call-back threshold.
  • A cut taken at the pay point. A broker or a supervisor takes a share of each wage. Workers rarely report it because they want the next round. Milestone 4. The call-back asks the exact amount received, and the grievance number from milestone 1 is published independently of the supervisor.
  • Days paid, nothing finished. Paying per day with no measured output produces a month of sweeping that leaves no trace, and the municipality gets nothing it can point to. Milestone 0 and 3. Every task has a measurable output, measured and photographed.
  • One community only. A roster drawn from one community turns a project meant to reduce tension into the proof that the other side gets everything. Milestone 1. The host and displaced shares are counted pass marks.
  • Money gone the week after. A cash round with no savings group ends exactly where it started, which is why Jordan's and India's programmes attach savings or self-help groups to the wage. Milestone 6. The savings group ledger and the enterprise trading check at 90 days.
Sources
  • Cash-for-work in Jordan for Syrian refugees and hosts: 30 to 50 per cent minimum host share, contracts of 2 weeks to 6 months at 16 to 20 working days, 86 per cent reporting cross-community friendships, 1,847 participants surveyed pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov
  • Women's self-help groups on urban municipal sanitation contracts, India forum.susana.org
  • Centre for Science and Environment, India's women-led self-help groups as a microfinance model cseindia.org
  • SWaCH Pune, worker-owned cooperative on a municipal contract prizeforcities.org
  • Human Rights Watch, World Report 2022, Lebanon: 78 per cent in poverty, 36 per cent in extreme poverty hrw.org

Verifier register

Every accredited verifier on the platform, their record side by side. Sort any column — the numbers are the same ones shown on each request, gathered in one place so they can be compared.

Second-line verifiers

Appointed from the table above, not recruited: a current licence, at least thirty decisions, and an overturn rate in the bottom half. They review the first-line verifier’s sign-off on every request before it opens for pledges, and every change to cost or timeline after — pseudonymously, seeing no names. The record is published under the pseudonym.

Variances approved

Every change to a published cost or timeline, on one page, with the request, the change and both verifiers who approved it. It is the cheapest fraud signal a ledger can carry: a verifier who approves many variances for the same implementer stands out here before anyone complains.

Rejection rateShare of milestones sent back rather than passed. Neither a high nor a low number is automatically good — but a number far from everyone else’s is worth asking about.
OverturnedDecisions later found to be wrong and reversed. A zero is only meaningful if something was actually looking.
Median daysEvidence submitted to decision made. Fast is not free: somebody has to go and look.
LicenceAccreditation number and the date it lapses. Past that date a verifier cannot be assigned.
VariancesChanges to a published cost or timeline this verifier approved. Many for one implementer is the thing to ask about.
Agreement rateShare of first-line sign-offs a second-line verifier confirmed rather than sent back. Same caveat as rejection rate: only a number far from the others means anything.

What this page does not do. It publishes the record. The second-line table is where sign-offs and variances get a second opinion. Releases get one check, and one in ten gets a second afterwards. An outlier in the first table now carries a consequence in the standing column, under the rules above. The way back from a drop is the course, linked above and described on the , and the reason this register is the first of four steps rather than the whole answer.
